Wood (2025), §4.2, footnote 3 (p. 4): "Notably, such 'tools' could ultimately become so causally removed from their human-based initiation—or humans may become so causally-neutral—that there could be a point at which they rightly be considered autonomous agents. e.g. contracts may offer bounties to humans for being sent transactions to initiate their execution." ↑

  28. Buterin (2014), pp. 28–29 of the PDF: "An attacker creates a very long infinite loop with the intent of forcing the miner to keep computing for such a long time that by the time computation finishes a few more blocks will have come out and it will not be possible for the miner to include the transaction to claim the fee. However, the attacker will be required to submit a value for STARTGAS limiting the number of computational steps that execution can take, so the miner will know ahead of time that the computation will take an excessively large number of steps." ↑

Part 2 · Smart contracts and applications

Chapter 14. Token standards: what ERC-20 and 721 decide and what they leave undecided

Key takeaway

A token is one balance ledger inside a contract account from Chapter 13. "Subtract X from A and add X to B, provided that A has X and that A has approved it." That is all, and Buterin called it "a database with one operation." A token standard (ERC-20, ERC-721) is an agreement that unifies the names, inputs, and outputs of the functions that handle that ledger, so that wallets and exchanges can handle tokens they have never seen before. A standard decides what the functions do, but it does not decide what the token means in the world (a voting right, a claim to a share of revenue, a link to a picture file). That is a promise the issuer made outside the standard, and the legal nature of that promise is decided by law, not by code. After this chapter you will be able to separate what the sentence "I bought an NFT" means technically from what that sentence does not say.

Learning objectives

  1. Distinguish coins (assets built into the protocol) from tokens (ledgers inside a contract), and explain that a token is "one mapping in a contract's storage."
  2. [Intermediate] Read the six functions and two events of ERC-20 and the ownership, transfer, and approval functions of ERC-721, and separate what the standards fix as "MUST," what they leave "OPTIONAL," and what they are silent on altogether.
  3. See how the difference between fungible and non-fungible tokens shows up in the data structure.
  4. [Intermediate] Read "what a token points to" in two parts: on-chain rights (what the code enforces) and off-chain promises (what the issuer said).

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. A token standard is only an agreement on function names. What rights a token carries is decided not by the standard but by the issuer's promise outside it.

1. What failure this technology grew out of

[Basic] The "simple storage" contract in Chapter 13 stored one number. What happens if you store a number for each address? Buterin's 2014 white paper says that this is money: "The key point to understand is that all a currency, or token systen [sic], fundamentally is is a database with one operation: subtract X units from A and give X units to B, with the proviso that (i) X [sic] had at least X units before the transaction and (2) the transaction is approved by A. All that it takes to implement a token system is to implement this logic into a contract."1 The white paper writes the logic out in six lines and lists its uses as ranging from "sub-currencies representing assets such as USD or gold to company stocks, individual tokens representing smart property, secure unforgeable coupons, and even token systems with no ties to conventional value at all, used as point systems for incentivization."2 Keep this list in mind. The same six lines can be a share of stock, a coupon, or a game score. The code does not know the difference.

[Basic] The problem arose because everyone wrote those six lines differently. If one contract calls its sending function send and another calls it transfer, a wallet program has to write separate code for every token. The motivation section of ERC-20 is a single sentence: "A standard interface allows any tokens on Ethereum to be re-used by other applications: from wallets to decentralized exchanges."3 2 years later ERC-721 adapted the same frame to assets that are distinct from one another: "EIP-20 is insufficient for tracking NFTs because each asset is distinct (non-fungible) whereas each of a quantity of tokens is identical (fungible)."4 Both grew out of the inefficiency of having no agreed function names, and both answered by unifying the function names. They did nothing more.

2. Intuition: coins, tokens, and a single ledger

[Basic] First, the words. A coin is an asset the protocol itself knows about: Bitcoin's BTC, Ethereum's ETH (ether). Ether is recorded in an account's balance field (Chapter 11) and is used to pay for gas. The white paper gives ether two roles: "providing a primary liquidity layer to allow for efficient exchange between various types of digital assets and, more importantly, of providing a mechanism for paying transaction fees."5 A token is an asset the protocol does not know about. Inside the storage of some contract account there is one "address → quantity" mapping, and the functions of that contract change the mapping. To the protocol, a token transfer is just "two storage slots of some contract changed." That is why the cost of writing to storage, seen in Chapter 13, makes up a large share of the gas for a token transfer. The share depends on whether the recipient's slot was empty (20,000 from 0 to non-0), already held a value (2,900), and whether the slot is being touched for the first time in that transaction (+2,100). In an ordinary transfer where both slots already held values, it is smaller than the base transaction cost of 21,000.

[Intermediate] The second example in the Solidity documentation quoted in Chapter 13 ("Subcurrency Example") is exactly this ledger. The documentation introduces it like this: "The following contract implements the simplest form of a cryptocurrency. The contract allows only its creator to create new coins (different issuance schemes are possible). Anyone can send coins to each other without a need for registering with a username and password, all you need is an Ethereum keypair."6 The code has two essentials. One mapping that pairs each address with a quantity is the ledger, and the two lines inside the send function that subtract from the sender's balance and add to the recipient's balance are the white paper's "one operation" (this book has written new Python code that does the same thing, in Section 6 below). What the documentation adds about mappings shows the nature of a token well: "Mappings can be seen as hash tables which are virtually initialized such that every possible key exists from the start and is mapped to a value whose byte-representation is all zeros. However, it is neither possible to obtain a list of all keys of a mapping, nor a list of all values."7 So a token contract does not have a list of "who has this token." Give it an address and it tells you that address's quantity, and that is all. Every address's balance "exists" as 0 from the start. For a lawyer who pictures a "register of holders," this point is not a small one.

3. ERC-20: the six functions a fungible token promises

[Intermediate] The ERC-20 specification is short. Nine functions and two events make up the whole of it, and three of the functions are optional. The table is this book's summary of the descriptions in the original, and the original wording is in the footnote.8

Function Meaning Level required by the standard
totalSupply() Total quantity of the token Required
balanceOf(owner) Balance of owner Required
transfer(to, value) Moves value from the caller's balance to to and must emit a Transfer event. Should fail if the balance is insufficient (SHOULD) Required
transferFrom(from, to, value) Moves tokens from the balance of from to to. For the "withdraw workflow": lets a contract, on your behalf, move tokens. Should fail unless from has given the caller authority in advance (SHOULD) Required
approve(spender, value) Allows spender to withdraw from the caller's account several times, up to a total of value. Calling it again overwrites Required
allowance(owner, spender) The amount spender may still withdraw from owner Required
name() · symbol() · decimals() Name, symbol, number of decimal places Optional: "interfaces and other contracts MUST NOT expect these values to be present"
Transfer(from, to, value) event Must fire whenever tokens are moved, including transfers of 0 Required
Approval(owner, spender, value) event Fires on every successful approve Required

[Intermediate] Three points. First, why there is an approve/transferFrom pair. Chapter 13 said that contract accounts have no private key. So a contract cannot move your tokens with your signature. Instead, you first record with approve that "this contract may take up to this much of my tokens," and the contract then takes them with transferFrom. This is how the exchange contract in Chapter 15 receives tokens. Second, the standard itself attaches a warning to approve: "To prevent attack vectors like the one described here and discussed here, clients SHOULD make sure to create user interfaces in such a way that they set the allowance first to 0 before setting it to another value for the same spender. THOUGH The contract itself shouldn't enforce it, to allow backwards compatibility with contracts deployed before"9. Which attack this is, the code below reenacts. It is the first case in which the order of transactions changes the outcome, and a preview of Chapter 17. Third, the standard does not set rules for issuing (minting) or burning. There is only a recommendation (SHOULD) to emit a Transfer event with _from set to the zero address when new tokens are created. Who may create how many, and on what conditions, is entirely up to the issuer.

[Intermediate] Where the standard says "SHOULD," implementations diverge. The Uniswap v2 white paper writes that "The ERC-20 standard requires that transferand transferFromreturn a boolean indicating the success or failure of the call [4]. The implementations of one or both of these functions on some tokens—including popular ones …—instead have no return value," and says that it changed its own code to handle such tokens.10 "Follows the standard" is closer to "has the same function names," and the detailed behavior has to be read contract by contract. A token using the same names is not the same as a token being the same thing.

4. ERC-721: a ledger of things that are each different

[Intermediate] The ledger of a non-fungible token (NFT) is not "address → quantity" but "token number → owner address." ERC-721 says: "Every NFT is identified by a unique uint256 ID inside the ERC-721 smart contract. This identifying number SHALL NOT change for the life of the contract. The pair (contract address, uint256 tokenId) will then be a globally unique and fully-qualified identifier for a specific asset on an Ethereum chain."11 The key functions are ownerOf(tokenId) (who owns this number), balanceOf(owner) (how many this address has), and transfer and approval. There are two transfer functions. transferFrom warns in capital letters that "THE CALLER IS RESPONSIBLE TO CONFIRM THAT _to IS CAPABLE OF RECEIVING NFTS OR ELSE THEY MAY BE PERMANENTLY LOST," and safeTransferFrom, if the recipient is a contract, calls that contract's onERC721Received and fails unless a set magic value comes back.12 It is a device for blocking, at the token level, the problem of "coins sent to an address with no key" seen in Chapter 11. Code can ask whether a contract is ready to receive. It cannot ask a person.

[Intermediate] There are also two kinds of approval. approve(approved, tokenId) puts one agent on one token, and setApprovalForAll(operator, approved) turns on "approval for a third party ('operator') to manage all of msg.sender's assets." The standard explains this operator concept as "a powerful set of tools for wallet, broker and auction applications to quickly use a large number of NFTs."13 There is no ERC-20-style allowance because "every NFT is unique, the quantity is none or one."14 The standard also states what it does not decide: "Creation of NFTs ('minting') and destruction of NFTs ('burning') is not included in the specification. Your contract may implement these by other means."15 And while the documentation of the transfer functions, in the standard's words, "only specify conditions when the transaction MUST throw" and an implementation "MAY also throw in other situations," the standard gives as examples "Disallow transfers if the contract is paused," "Blocklist certain address from receiving NFTs," "Charge a fee to both parties of a transaction," and "Read only NFT registry — always throw from safeTransferFrom, transferFrom, approve and setApprovalForAll."16 That an NFT contract following the standard can block transfers is written in the standard itself.

Metadata: where is the "picture"?

[Basic] The pictures, music, and documents people have in mind when they say "NFT" are not on the chain. ERC-721's metadata extension is optional (OPTIONAL), and what it contains is three functions: name(), symbol(), and tokenURI(tokenId). tokenURI returns "A distinct Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) for a given asset," and "The URI may point to a JSON file that conforms to the 'ERC721 Metadata JSON Schema'" (may, in lowercase). That schema has three entries: name, description, and image, "A URI pointing to a resource with mime type image/ representing the asset to which this NFT represents [sic]."17 So what is written on the chain is one address string*, and the file that address points to holds, in turn, the address of the picture. The standard is candid about why it chose this design. It considered the alternative to "put all metadata for each asset on the blockchain" and dropped it as "too expensive."18 The storage cost of Chapter 13 made the decision here.

[Basic] The standard gives two more warnings. "The URI MAY be mutable (i.e. it changes from time to time). We considered an NFT representing ownership of a house, in this case metadata about the house (image, occupants, etc.) can naturally change." And: "We also remind everyone that any smart contract can use the same name and symbol as your contract. How a client may determine which ERC-721 smart contracts are well-known (canonical) is outside the scope of this standard."19 The chain guarantees the token number and the owner. It does not guarantee the contents of the file the token points to, whether that file will stay where it is, or whether the contract is the "real" contract of that artist. The authors of the standard wrote so themselves.

A lawyer's question

What has a person who "bought an NFT" bought? What is written on the chain is the fact that the person's address went into the owner slot of a (contract address, number) pair, and one string returned by tokenURI. The picture file sits on an outside server that the string points to, and the standard says the string can change. Copyright (저작권) is not written anywhere. Then is the object of the sale (매매의 목적물) the token, the file the token points to, some right in the file, or the fact of "pointing" itself? If the issuer shuts down the server and the picture disappears, what has perished (멸실)? If another contract is deployed with the same name and symbol, which one is the "genuine article (진품)"? And if the issuer of an ERC-20 token promised "revenue sharing" or "voting rights (의결권)," is that promise in the code or outside it? → Chapter 28 · Chapter 27

5. What a token points to: on-chain rights and off-chain promises

[Basic] Reduced to one line, this chapter's claim is this. What the code enforces and what the issuer said sit on different layers. What the code enforces are state transitions such as "move this address's quantity to that address," "the owner of this number is this address," and "block the transfer under this condition." What the issuer said are sentences such as "this token is a share of our company's earnings," "you can vote with this token," and "this token is ownership of this picture," and those sentences are in white papers, on websites, and on message boards. The standards deal only with the former.

[Basic] The event in which history showed this distinction most clearly is "The DAO" of 2016. The detailed analysis belongs to Chapter 26, and here we look only at the relation between tokens and promises. The 2017 report of investigation by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) sets out the facts this way: "In exchange for ETH, The DAO created DAO Tokens (proportional to the amount of ETH paid) that were then assigned to the Ethereum Blockchain address of the person or entity remitting the ETH. A DAO Token granted the DAO Token holder certain voting and ownership rights." Token holders cast votes on funding proposals "weighted by the number of tokens they controlled," and they were told in promotional materials that they "would receive 'rewards,' which the White Paper defined as, 'any [ETH] received by a DAO [Entity] generated from projects the DAO [Entity] funded.'"20 What the code enforced was voting in proportion to the number of tokens, and the movement of funds. "Rewards" and "ownership" were words in the white paper and on the website. And the legal nature of those words was decided not by code but by the SEC. The report concluded that "DAO Tokens are securities under the Securities Act of 1933 ('Securities Act') and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ('Exchange Act')," and at the outset (p. 2) it wrote: "The automation of certain functions through this technology, 'smart contracts,' or computer code, does not remove conduct from the purview of the U.S. federal securities laws."21 Whether this conclusion is right, and how another jurisdiction would see the matter, is outside the scope of this book, and Part 5 also treats it only as a survey. What this chapter takes away is the structure. Even when the six lines inside the token contract are identical, whether the token was a security, a coupon, or a game score was decided by facts outside the code.

6. Code: imitating the two ledgers and recomputing the numbers the standards wrote down

[Intermediate] We imitate the two ledgers with Python dictionaries. Signature verification was done in Chapter 5, so "who called" is represented by a name, and events are written to a list. All of it is for study.

# NB14-1: imitating the ERC-20 ledger — balance and allowance dictionaries, the six functions, the two events, and the approve race condition (for study)
class ERC20Toy:
    """Only the required functions of EIP-20. Failures raise exceptions (the standard's SHOULD throw). Events are written to self.events."""
    def __init__(self, name, symbol):
        self.name, self.symbol = name, symbol             # OPTIONAL items — may or may not be present
        self.balances = {}                                 # "every address is 0 from the start" — read as 0 if not in the dictionary
        self.allowances = {}                               # (owner, spender) -> remaining allowance
        self.events = []
    def totalSupply(self):          return sum(self.balances.values())
    def balanceOf(self, owner):     return self.balances.get(owner, 0)
    def allowance(self, o, s):      return self.allowances.get((o, s), 0)
    def mint(self, to, value):                            # outside the standard — issuance rules are up to the issuer. Only a Transfer event from 0x0 is recommended (SHOULD)
        self.balances[to] = self.balanceOf(to) + value
        self.events.append(("Transfer", "0x0", to, value))
    def transfer(self, caller, to, value):
        if self.balanceOf(caller) < value:
            raise ValueError(f"insufficient balance: {caller} has only {self.balanceOf(caller)}")
        self.balances[caller] -= value
        self.balances[to] = self.balanceOf(to) + value
        self.events.append(("Transfer", caller, to, value))   # emit the event even for a quantity of 0 (MUST)
        return True
    def approve(self, caller, spender, value):
        self.allowances[(caller, spender)] = value            # "calling it again overwrites"
        self.events.append(("Approval", caller, spender, value))
        return True
    def transferFrom(self, caller, frm, to, value):
        if self.allowance(frm, caller) < value:
            raise ValueError(f"insufficient allowance: the amount {frm} allowed {caller} is {self.allowance(frm, caller)}")
        if self.balanceOf(frm) < value:
            raise ValueError("insufficient balance")
        self.allowances[(frm, caller)] -= value
        self.balances[frm] -= value
        self.balances[to] = self.balanceOf(to) + value
        self.events.append(("Transfer", frm, to, value))
        return True

tok = ERC20Toy("Toy Token", "TOY")
tok.mint("Alice", 1000)
tok.transfer("Alice", "Bob", 250)
print("balances — Alice:", tok.balanceOf("Alice"), "Bob:", tok.balanceOf("Bob"), "Carol (an address never seen before):", tok.balanceOf("Carol"), "| total supply:", tok.totalSupply())
try:
    tok.transfer("Bob", "Carol", 300)
except ValueError as e:
    print("Bob → Carol 300:", e)

# approve / transferFrom — the withdraw workflow in which a contract (here 'Exchange') takes tokens on Alice's behalf
tok.approve("Alice", "Exchange", 100)
tok.transferFrom("Exchange", "Alice", "Dave", 60)
print("Exchange withdraws 60 from Alice → Dave:", tok.balanceOf("Dave"), "| remaining allowance:", tok.allowance("Alice", "Exchange"))

# the approve race condition — reenacting, as a sequence, why the standard recommends "set it to 0 first"
tok2 = ERC20Toy("Toy", "TOY"); tok2.mint("Alice", 1000)
tok2.approve("Alice", "Spender", 100)                      # ① Alice: allows Spender 100
# Alice sends approve(Spender, 50), thinking "100 is too much, cut it to 50." But the order in which transactions enter a block is not the order in which they were sent.
tok2.transferFrom("Spender", "Alice", "Spender", 100)      # ② Spender takes out all 100 before Alice's transaction
tok2.approve("Alice", "Spender", 50)                       # ③ then Alice's approve(50) is applied — because it "overwrites," a fresh 50 is opened
tok2.transferFrom("Spender", "Alice", "Spender", 50)       # ④ Spender takes out another 50
print("race condition — Alice meant to allow only 50, but the amount Spender took:", tok2.balanceOf("Spender"), "(= 100 + 50)")
print("number of events:", len(tok2.events), "| last three:", tok2.events[-3:])

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
balances — Alice: 750 Bob: 250 Carol (an address never seen before): 0 | total supply: 1000
Bob → Carol 300: insufficient balance: Bob has only 250
Exchange withdraws 60 from Alice → Dave: 60 | remaining allowance: 40
race condition — Alice meant to allow only 50, but the amount Spender took: 150 (= 100 + 50)
number of events: 5 | last three: [('Transfer', 'Alice', 'Spender', 100), ('Approval', 'Alice', 'Spender', 50), ('Transfer', 'Alice', 'Spender', 50)]

[Intermediate] The last reenactment is the first appearance of the "transaction order" problem. Alice sent a transaction to reduce the allowance from 100 to 50, and if it is processed after Spender has taken out the 100 first, a fresh 50 is opened. This is because approve "overwrites" rather than "adds," and because Alice does not decide the order in which transactions enter the chain. Who decides that order is the subject of Chapter 17.

# NB14-2: imitating the ERC-721 ledger — number → owner, approvals and operators, the recipient check in safeTransferFrom, a mutable URI (for study)
MAGIC = "onERC721Received-magic"                           # in reality bytes4(keccak256("onERC721Received(address,address,uint256,bytes)")) — computed in NB14-3 below

class Wallet:                                              # imitates a "contract recipient." A contract that is ready to receive returns the magic value
    def __init__(self, ready): self.ready = ready
    def onERC721Received(self, operator, frm, tokenId, data): return MAGIC if self.ready else "something else"

class ERC721Toy:
    def __init__(self):
        self.owner = {}            # tokenId -> owner
        self.approved = {}         # tokenId -> approved address
        self.operators = set()     # (owner, operator)
        self.uri = {}              # tokenId -> URI string (metadata extension, OPTIONAL)
        self.events = []
    def ownerOf(self, tid):
        if tid not in self.owner: raise KeyError(f"invalid NFT {tid}")   # a query about an invalid NFT (one assigned to the zero address, etc.) fails — the gist of the ownerOf comment in the original
        return self.owner[tid]
    def balanceOf(self, who):  return sum(1 for o in self.owner.values() if o == who)
    def mint(self, to, tid, uri):                           # outside the standard — creation rules are up to the issuer
        self.owner[tid] = to; self.uri[tid] = uri; self.events.append(("Transfer", "0x0", to, tid))
    def tokenURI(self, tid):   self.ownerOf(tid); return self.uri[tid]
    def _authorized(self, caller, tid):
        o = self.ownerOf(tid)
        return caller == o or self.approved.get(tid) == caller or (o, caller) in self.operators
    def approve(self, caller, approved, tid):
        o = self.ownerOf(tid)
        if not (caller == o or (o, caller) in self.operators): raise PermissionError("only the owner or an operator can approve")
        self.approved[tid] = approved; self.events.append(("Approval", o, approved, tid))
    def setApprovalForAll(self, caller, operator, ok):
        (self.operators.add if ok else self.operators.discard)((caller, operator))
        self.events.append(("ApprovalForAll", caller, operator, ok))
    def transferFrom(self, caller, frm, to, tid):
        if not self._authorized(caller, tid): raise PermissionError(f"{caller} has no authority to move {tid}")
        if self.owner[tid] != frm: raise ValueError("_from is not the current owner")
        if to == "0x0": raise ValueError("cannot send to the zero address")
        self.owner[tid] = to; self.approved.pop(tid, None)   # "the approval is reset on transfer"
        self.events.append(("Transfer", frm, to, tid))
    def safeTransferFrom(self, caller, frm, to, tid, data=b"", contracts=None):
        self.transferFrom(caller, frm, to, tid)
        if contracts and to in contracts:                      # if the recipient is a contract, ask whether it is ready to receive
            if contracts[to].onERC721Received(caller, frm, tid, data) != MAGIC:
                self.owner[tid] = frm; self.events.pop()       # roll back (in reality the whole transaction reverts)
                raise ValueError(f"recipient {to} did not return the magic value, so the transfer was rolled back")

nft = ERC721Toy()
nft.mint("Alice", 7, "https://example.invalid/meta/7.json")
print("owner of #7:", nft.ownerOf(7), "| tokenURI:", nft.tokenURI(7))
contracts = {"ReadyContract": Wallet(ready=True), "DumbContract": Wallet(ready=False)}
try:
    nft.safeTransferFrom("Alice", "Alice", "DumbContract", 7, contracts=contracts)
except ValueError as e:
    print("safeTransferFrom → contract not ready:", e, "| owner is still", nft.ownerOf(7))
nft.transferFrom("Alice", "Alice", "DumbContract", 7)       # an "unsafe" transfer sends without asking — this is where the standard's capital-letter warning applies
print("transferFrom → same contract: owner", nft.ownerOf(7), "(locked forever if the contract has no code to get it out)")

nft.mint("Bob", 8, "https://example.invalid/meta/8.json")
nft.setApprovalForAll("Bob", "Marketplace", True)           # Bob makes the marketplace contract an operator
nft.transferFrom("Marketplace", "Bob", "Carol", 8)           # the operator moves Bob's token to Carol
print("owner of #8 after the operator's transfer:", nft.ownerOf(8), "| Bob's count:", nft.balanceOf("Bob"), "| Carol:", nft.balanceOf("Carol"))

nft.uri[8] = "https://example.invalid/meta/8-v2.json"       # the issuer changes the URI — the owner slot stays as it is
print("after the URI change — owner:", nft.ownerOf(8), "| tokenURI:", nft.tokenURI(8), "(the chain guarantees the left; the right can change)")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
owner of #7: Alice | tokenURI: https://example.invalid/meta/7.json
safeTransferFrom → contract not ready: recipient DumbContract did not return the magic value, so the transfer was rolled back | owner is still Alice
transferFrom → same contract: owner DumbContract (locked forever if the contract has no code to get it out)
owner of #8 after the operator's transfer: Carol | Bob's count: 0 | Carol: 1
after the URI change — owner: Carol | tokenURI: https://example.invalid/meta/8-v2.json (the chain guarantees the left; the right can change)

[Intermediate] Two scenes carry this chapter's point. safeTransferFrom recognized a contract that was not ready to receive and rolled the transfer back, but transferFrom sent without asking, and the token was locked in a contract with no code to get it out. And when the issuer changes the URI string, the owner slot does not budge. The chain guarantees "the owner of #8 is Carol" and does not guarantee "what #8 points to."

[Advanced] Recomputing the numbers the standards wrote down: function selectors and interface identifiers

[Advanced] The text of ERC-721 says that "the ERC-165 identifier for this interface is 0x80ac58cd," that the metadata extension's is 0x5b5e139f, and that the receipt magic value is bytes4(keccak256("onERC721Received(address,address,uint256,bytes)")). Where do these numbers come from? Ethereum calls a function not by its name but by its selector, that is, the first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the function's signature string. ERC-165 says: "We define the interface identifier as the XOR of all function selectors in the interface."22 Just as Chapter 12 recomputed the hash of the genesis block and matched it to the public value, here we recompute the numbers the standards wrote down and match them.

[Advanced] There is one snag. Ethereum's Keccak-256 is not the same as sha3_256 in Python's hashlib. The two use the same sponge function but different padding bytes (0x01 in the original Keccak proposal, 0x06 in the NIST standard SHA-3). So the code below writes out the Keccak-f[1600] permutation directly, without a library, verifies the implementation against itself by checking that with padding byte 0x06 it gives the same value as hashlib.sha3_256, and then changes the padding byte to 0x01 to obtain Ethereum's Keccak-256. It is a study implementation and is not for real use.

# NB14-3: Keccak-256 by hand — a single padding byte separates SHA3-256 from Keccak-256. Then recompute the ERC-165/721 identifiers (for study, not for real use)
import hashlib
from functools import reduce

RC = [0x0000000000000001, 0x0000000000008082, 0x800000000000808A, 0x8000000080008000, 0x000000000000808B, 0x0000000080000001,
      0x8000000080008081, 0x8000000000008009, 0x000000000000008A, 0x0000000000000088, 0x0000000080008009, 0x000000008000000A,
      0x000000008000808B, 0x800000000000008B, 0x8000000000008089, 0x8000000000008003, 0x8000000000008002, 0x8000000000000080,
      0x000000000000800A, 0x800000008000000A, 0x8000000080008081, 0x8000000000008080, 0x0000000080000001, 0x8000000080008008]
ROT = [[0, 36, 3, 41, 18], [1, 44, 10, 45, 2], [62, 6, 43, 15, 61], [28, 55, 25, 21, 56], [27, 20, 39, 8, 14]]   # rotation amounts r[x][y]
M64 = (1 << 64) - 1
def rol(v, n): return ((v << n) | (v >> (64 - n))) & M64 if n else v

def keccak_f(A):                                           # A[x][y]: 5×5 lanes of 64 bits. 24 rounds of θ·ρ·π·χ·ι
    for rc in RC:
        C = [A[x][0] ^ A[x][1] ^ A[x][2] ^ A[x][3] ^ A[x][4] for x in range(5)]
        D = [C[(x - 1) % 5] ^ rol(C[(x + 1) % 5], 1) for x in range(5)]
        A = [[A[x][y] ^ D[x] for y in range(5)] for x in range(5)]                       # θ
        B = [[0] * 5 for _ in range(5)]
        for x in range(5):
            for y in range(5):
                B[y][(2 * x + 3 * y) % 5] = rol(A[x][y], ROT[x][y])                      # ρ, π
        A = [[B[x][y] ^ ((~B[(x + 1) % 5][y]) & B[(x + 2) % 5][y]) for y in range(5)] for x in range(5)]   # χ
        A[0][0] ^= rc                                                                    # ι
    return A

def sponge256(msg: bytes, pad_byte: int) -> bytes:        # capacity 512 bits → rate 1088 bits = 136 bytes, output 256 bits
    rate = 136
    padded = bytearray(msg) + bytearray([pad_byte]) + bytearray((-len(msg) - 2) % rate) + bytearray([0x80])
    if len(msg) % rate == rate - 1:                        # when only one byte is left: fill it with the single byte pad_byte | 0x80
        padded = bytearray(msg) + bytearray([pad_byte | 0x80])
    A = [[0] * 5 for _ in range(5)]
    for off in range(0, len(padded), rate):
        block = padded[off:off + rate]
        for i in range(rate // 8):                          # lane i → (x, y) = (i % 5, i // 5), little-endian
            A[i % 5][i // 5] ^= int.from_bytes(block[8 * i:8 * i + 8], "little")
        A = keccak_f(A)
    return b"".join(A[i % 5][i // 5].to_bytes(8, "little") for i in range(4))

def sha3_256_manual(m): return sponge256(m, 0x06)          # NIST SHA-3: padding suffix 0x06
def keccak256(m):       return sponge256(m, 0x01)          # Ethereum Keccak-256: padding suffix 0x01

for m in [b"", b"abc", b"a" * 200]:
    print(f"{m[:12]!r:16} by-hand SHA3-256 == hashlib.sha3_256 ? {sha3_256_manual(m) == hashlib.sha3_256(m).digest()}")
print("keccak256(b'')    =", keccak256(b"").hex())
print("sha3_256(b'')     =", hashlib.sha3_256(b"").hexdigest(), "(only one padding byte differs, yet the value is entirely different)")

def selector(sig: str) -> int: return int.from_bytes(keccak256(sig.encode())[:4], "big")
print()
print("transfer(address,uint256) selector =", f"0x{selector('transfer(address,uint256)'):08x}")
print("supportsInterface(bytes4) selector =", f"0x{selector('supportsInterface(bytes4)'):08x}", "(ERC-165 uses this value as the identifier)")

erc721 = ["balanceOf(address)", "ownerOf(uint256)", "safeTransferFrom(address,address,uint256,bytes)",
          "safeTransferFrom(address,address,uint256)", "transferFrom(address,address,uint256)", "approve(address,uint256)",
          "setApprovalForAll(address,bool)", "getApproved(uint256)", "isApprovedForAll(address,address)"]
erc721_meta = ["name()", "symbol()", "tokenURI(uint256)"]
xor = lambda sigs: reduce(lambda a, b: a ^ b, (selector(s) for s in sigs))
print(f"ERC-721 identifier (XOR of 9 functions)    = 0x{xor(erc721):08x}   standard's text: 0x80ac58cd → match {xor(erc721) == 0x80ac58cd}")
print(f"ERC-721 Metadata identifier (3 functions)  = 0x{xor(erc721_meta):08x}   standard's text: 0x5b5e139f → match {xor(erc721_meta) == 0x5b5e139f}")
print(f"onERC721Received magic value               = 0x{selector('onERC721Received(address,address,uint256,bytes)'):08x}   standard's text: 0x150b7a02 → match {selector('onERC721Received(address,address,uint256,bytes)') == 0x150b7a02}")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
b''              by-hand SHA3-256 == hashlib.sha3_256 ? True
b'abc'           by-hand SHA3-256 == hashlib.sha3_256 ? True
b'aaaaaaaaaaaa'  by-hand SHA3-256 == hashlib.sha3_256 ? True
keccak256(b'')    = c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470
sha3_256(b'')     = a7ffc6f8bf1ed76651c14756a061d662f580ff4de43b49fa82d80a4b80f8434a (only one padding byte differs, yet the value is entirely different)

transfer(address,uint256) selector = 0xa9059cbb
supportsInterface(bytes4) selector = 0x01ffc9a7 (ERC-165 uses this value as the identifier)
ERC-721 identifier (XOR of 9 functions)    = 0x80ac58cd   standard's text: 0x80ac58cd → match True
ERC-721 Metadata identifier (3 functions)  = 0x5b5e139f   standard's text: 0x5b5e139f → match True
onERC721Received magic value               = 0x150b7a02   standard's text: 0x150b7a02 → match True

[Advanced] All three numbers written in the standard documents are recomputed. The third value is the one the original gives as the ERC-165 identifier of the receiver interface ERC721TokenReceiver, while the magic value itself is written only as the expression bytes4(keccak256(…)). That interface has only one function, so the two values are the same. "Supporting an interface" comes down to knowing these 4-byte numbers: a wallet asks a contract it has never seen supportsInterface(0x80ac58cd), and if true comes back, it believes that "the ERC-721 functions are there." That means the functions exist, not that they behave as expected. As Section 4 showed, the standard also allows implementations that block transfers.

7. Summary

[Basic] A token is one mapping in a contract's storage, and a standard is an agreement on the names of the functions that handle that mapping. ERC-20 handles "address → quantity" and ERC-721 handles "number → owner," and neither decides issuance, burning, or meaning. The standard itself says that an NFT's "picture" is off the chain and that its address can change. The same six lines can be a share of stock, a coupon, or a score, and which one it is gets decided outside the code. The next chapter, Chapter 15, looks at contracts that swap these tokens without people. The way those contracts receive tokens is exactly this chapter's approve and transferFrom. What this chapter adds to misconceptions ② ("Smart contracts are contracts") and ⑫ ("If it is decentralized, no one is responsible") in Appendix B is the fact that even the authors of the standards left "who issues it and what it means" outside the standards.

Part 2 · Smart contracts and applications

Chapter 15. Decentralized exchanges and AMMs: price formation without an order book

Key takeaway

On an exchange, people call out prices. Buyers and sellers post quotes, and an operator matches them. An automated market maker (AMM) has neither quotes nor an operator. One contract keeps two tokens in a pool and accepts every trade by a single rule: "the product of the two quantities does not decrease." The price then becomes the ratio of the two quantities in the pool, and a large order pushes the price up by itself (slippage). The people who put tokens into the pool (liquidity providers) receive a fee on every trade, but when the relative price of the two tokens moves, they end up with less than if they had "simply held" the two tokens (impermanent loss). The two effects are the two pans of the same scale. After this chapter you will have checked with formulas that the operator, the counterparty, and the quotes that the word "exchange" presupposes are not present here, and you will see why the question in Part 5, "whom do we regulate?", looks empty.

Learning objectives

  1. Contrast price formation on an order-book exchange with price formation in a constant-product AMM, and say what "price" in an AMM is a ratio of.
  2. [Intermediate] From the constant product x·y=k, derive the amount received Δy and the execution price for an order of size Δx, and see where the fee is taken out.
  3. [Intermediate] Derive the liquidity provider's share calculation, the accrual of fees, and impermanent loss 2r1+r−1, and read impermanent loss symmetrically with the fee income.
  4. [Advanced] See how concentrated liquidity (supply within a price range) cuts the constant-product curve into pieces and uses one of them, and why an AMM spot price gets manipulated when it is used as an oracle.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. In an AMM the price is not called out by people. It is the ratio of the two quantities in the pool. A large order pushes the price up by itself.

1. What failure this technology grew out of

[Basic] A traditional exchange runs on an order book. The 2020 paper by Philip Daian and his coauthors describes it neatly: "Classic exchanges … generally share an accepted and common exchange design known as a continuous-limit orderbook. Such an orderbook consists of a list of all open offers from buyers and sellers in the system. Prospective buyers place a limit buy order, which specifies a maximum price at which they are willing to buy an asset; sellers correspondingly place limit sell orders. A centralized counterparty, the exchange operator, matches buyers and sellers, completing transactions automatically when there is a sell order on the books with a lower price than a buy order on the books."1 Moving this structure onto a blockchain as it is runs into two problems. First, "on-chain, smart-contract-mediated trades are slow." Every step of placing and canceling an order has to wait for a block, and in the meantime orders that have already been filled or canceled look as if they were still live.2 Second, there is the question of who holds the order book. In the decentralized exchanges the paper examined, "Order books are typically maintained off-chain," and so the paper writes that "'Decentralized' exchange is something of a misnomer, as many such systems have centralized components; … could more accurately be classified as non-custodial: users trade without surrendering control of their funds to a third party in the process."3

[Basic] The other design that followed was to do away with the order book. The same paper describes it: "A more radical DEX design, called an automated market maker [3], bypasses order books altogether. The DEX consists of a smart contract that itself holds a reserve of tokens and/or Ether. Consider two assets A and B. The contract allows a user to trade between A and B at any time using its reserves as a counterparty, at a set rate. If a user buys A using B, the price of A denominated in B offered by the smart contract for the next trade is increased. If a user instead sells A for B, the price decreases. In this way, single parties can trade without counterparty discovery or matching. Consequently, constant arbitrage between these and other exchanges is required to keep the rate offered in lockstep with the market rate for a commodity."4 Keep this last sentence in mind. An AMM does not "know" the market price. It offers a wrong price until arbitrageurs come from outside and correct it. That is the seed of Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

2. Intuition: a pool of two tokens and one product

[Basic] A pool holds x units of token X and y units of token Y. There is one rule. After a trade, x·y cannot be smaller than x·y before the trade. This is the "constant product" rule, the formula used by Uniswap v1 and v2. In the words of the v2 white paper: "Each Uniswap v1 pair stores pooled reserves of two assets, and provides liquidity for those two assets, maintaining the invariant that the product of the reserves cannot decrease. Traders pay a 30-basis-point fee on trades, which goes to liquidity providers."5

[Basic] Say you put in Δx of X and want to take Y out. The pool's X becomes x+Δx, and to keep the product, only k/(x+Δx) of Y may remain. So the Y you receive is the difference. As a numerical example, if you put 100 X into a pool containing 1,000 X and 1,000 Y (k=1,000,000), 1,000,000/1,100≈909.1 Y has to remain, so you receive about 90.9 Y. You put in 100 X and received 90.9 Y, so the execution price is 0.909 Y per X. But the "price" just before the trade was y/x=1. The execution price was more than 9% worse than the price just before the trade. This is slippage, and it grows the larger the order is relative to the pool. The ratio after the trade is 909.1/1,100≈0.826. The next person starts at 0.826 Y per X. No one "set" the price. Only the ratio changed.

[Basic] Look again at the absence of people here. Your counterparty is the pool. The people who put tokens into the pool (liquidity providers) collectively act as the counterparty, but they neither know about your trade nor consent to it. There is no operator either. The v2 white paper writes that "the contract is not generally upgradeable," yet discloses that "there is a private key that has the ability to update a variable on the factory contract to turn on an on-chain 5-basis-point fee on trades."6 There is no operator, but there is a key that controls a switch. These are the sentences to look for when reading how far the word "decentralized" reaches.

A lawyer's question

Exchange regulation usually presupposes an "operator": someone who registers (등록), conducts listing review (상장 심사), monitors for market manipulation (시세조종), and keeps customer assets segregated (고객 자산 분리 보관). Where is that someone in a constant-product AMM? Is it the person who deployed the code, the thousands of liquidity providers who put tokens into the pool, the address with the key to the fee switch, the majority of governance-token holders, or no one at all? When you traded with the pool, who was the "counterparty (상대방)," and if the price was wrong, who got it wrong? → Chapter 27 · Chapter 28

3. Formulas: constant product, fee, execution price

[Intermediate] Set out the symbols. x,y are the reserves before the trade, k=xy, Δx is the amount put in, and Δy is the amount received. Without a fee,

(x+Δx)(y−Δy)=k⟹Δy=y−kx+Δx=yΔxx+Δx.

Reading the symbols: the numerator is "Y in proportion to what was put in," and the denominator is "X after putting it in." A numerical example: with x=y=1,000 and Δx=100, Δy=1,000×100/1,100≈90.91. The execution price is Δy/Δx≈0.909, the marginal price just before the trade is y/x=1, and the marginal price after the trade is (y−Δy)/(x+Δx)≈0.826.

[Intermediate] Marginal price. The v2 white paper writes: "The marginal price offered by Uniswap (not including fees) at time t can be computed by dividing the reserves of asset a by the reserves of asset b." pt=rta/rtb.7 Mathematically, it is the slope of the curve y=k/x, |dy/dx|=y/x. It is the price of "a very small trade," and an actual trade gets a worse price than that. The difference is slippage. Written as a fraction of the marginal price, slippage is

slippage=1−Δy/Δxy/x=1−xx+Δx=Δxx+Δx.

It is set only by the ratio of the order size to the pool size. Put 100 into a pool of 1,000 and it is 100/1,100≈9.1%; put in 10 and it is 10/1,010≈1.0%; put in 1,000 and it is 50%. The larger the pool, the smaller the slippage on the same order. That is the whole of why liquidity providers are needed.

[Intermediate] Fee. v1 and v2 take 0.3% off the amount put in and keep the product with the rest. The white paper writes, "Uniswap v1's trading fee is applied by reducing the amount paid into the contract by 0.3% before enforcing the constant-product invariant. The contract implicitly enforces the following formula:" (x1−0.003·xin)·y1≥x0·y0, and since in v2 both assets can come in at once, it generalizes this to (x1−0.003·xin)(y1−0.003·yin)≥x0y0.8 Reading the symbols: subscript 0 means before the trade, 1 means after it, and xin is the X that came in. With the fee γ=0.003 taken out, the amount received is

Δy=y(1−γ)Δxx+(1−γ)Δx

A numerical example: put 100 into the same pool and (1−γ)Δx=99.7, Δy=1,000×99.7/1,099.7≈90.66. You receive 0.25 fewer than the 90.91 you would receive without a fee. Where did those 0.3 X (= 100 × 0.003) go? They stay in the pool. After the trade the pool holds 1,100 X and 909.34 Y, and their product is about 1,000,273, larger than before the trade. The fee is not sent off anywhere separately. It accumulates inside the pool in the form of a larger k, and the liquidity providers later take out the enlarged pool in proportion to their shares. This is the key to the next section.

4. Supplying liquidity: fee income and impermanent loss are the two pans of one scale

[Basic] Why does anyone put tokens into a pool? Because the fee taken on every trade accumulates in the pool. Is it free, then? No. When the relative price of the two tokens moves, the pool rebalances automatically, selling the token that rose and buying the token that fell, because arbitrageurs come and correct the ratio. As a result the provider ends up with less than if they had "simply kept the two tokens," and this difference is conventionally called impermanent loss. The v2 white paper uses the term too. In v1, ether was part of every pair, so "All liquidity providers have exposure to ETH, and suffer impermanent loss based on changes in the prices of other assets relative to ETH."9 The name "impermanent" means that the loss disappears if the price goes back to the original ratio, not that the loss is light. This book does not call supplying liquidity "profit." It puts fee income and impermanent loss in the same table, and it leaves which of the two is larger as an empirical question that depends on trading volume and price movement.

[Intermediate] Shares. A provider receives "liquidity tokens (shares)" in proportion to what it put in. The first depositor receives s=xdepositedydeposited, and later depositors receive in proportion to the existing reserves: sminted=xdepositedxstartingsstarting.10 On withdrawal, a provider receives both tokens in proportion to its share, at the ratio of that moment. So if trading fees have made k larger, the same share gets more, and if the price has moved, the mix of the two tokens is different. The white paper measures the accrued fees as "the growth in k." The fees accumulated between t1 and t2, as a fraction of the pool at t2, are f1,2=1−k1/k2.11

[Intermediate] The formula for impermanent loss. Suppose the relative price moves from p to rp (r is the price multiple). Assuming no fee and that arbitrage fully corrects the ratio, the two quantities in the pool become x′=x/r and y′=yr (the product is unchanged, and the ratio is y′/x′=ry/x). Measuring value in units of Y, the supplying side is Vpool=x′·rp+y′=2yr, and the side that simply holds the tokens is Vhold=x·rp+y=y(1+r), so

VpoolVhold=2r1+r,impermanent loss=2r1+r−1≤0.

Reading the symbols: at r=1 it is 0, and the farther r moves from 1 (in either direction), the larger the negative value. A numerical example: at r=2, 22/3−1≈−5.7%; at r=4, 4/5−1=−20%; and r=1/4 also gives −20%. This formula is this book's derivation, and the derivation is in the [Advanced] box below and in NB15-2. What matters is the shape. It is a loss whichever the direction, it is larger the larger the move, and whether the fees make up for it is a separate number. The code below puts the two numbers in one table.

[Advanced] Deriving impermanent loss, and concentrated liquidity: cutting up the curve

[Advanced] Derivation. Reserves (x,y), k=xy, and the relative price before the trade p=y/x (the price of one X in Y). The outside price has become rp. Arbitrageurs trade until the pool's marginal price y′/x′ equals rp. Solving the two conditions x′y′=k and y′/x′=rp=ry/x gives x′2=k/(rp)=x2/r, that is, x′=x/r and y′=yr. The pool's value in Y is x′·rp+y′=(x/r)(ry/x)+yr=2yr. The value of holding the tokens is x·rp+y=ry+y. The ratio is 2r/(1+r), which is at most 1 by the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, 1+r2≥r. Equality holds only at r=1. With fees, k grows a little with every trade, and the pool's value increases by that much. So the provider's final net result is set by the product of "k grown by fees" and "2r/(1+r)."

[Advanced] Concentrated liquidity. The constant-product curve spreads liquidity over the whole price range (0,∞). The v3 white paper writes that this "is simple to implement and allows liquidity to be efficiently aggregated, but means that much of the assets held in a pool are never touched."12 So v3 lets a provider choose a price range [pa,pb] and place liquidity only in that range. "A position only needs to maintain enough reserves to support trading within its range, and therefore can act like a constant product pool with larger reserves (we call these the virtual reserves) within that range." Measuring the size of liquidity as L=k, the real reserves follow the curve13

(x+Lpb)(y+Lpa)=L2

Reading the symbols: the added terms in the parentheses are the "virtual" part. When the price reaches pb, X runs out, and when it reaches pa, Y runs out. "When the price exits a position's range, the position's liquidity is no longer active, and no longer earns fees. At that point, its liquidity is composed entirely of a single asset …."14 A numerical example: with a current price of 1, the range [0.5,2], and L=1,000, the virtual reserves are xv=L/P=1,000 and yv=LP=1,000, but the amounts that actually have to be put in are x=L/P−L/pb=1,000−707.1≈292.9 and y=LP−Lpa=1,000−707.1≈292.9. Putting in only 29% of a full-range pool, the position provides the same slippage within the same range. The cost is that once the price leaves the range, the provider is left with only one asset. The statement that this realizes impermanent loss more steeply than a full-range pool is this book's explanation; the original goes only as far as "inactive, no fees, a single asset." The fee was also split into three tiers (0.05%, 0.30%, 1%), so that each pair can have several pools.15 This book does not say which design is better. One uses the whole curve, and the other cuts it up.

5. A spot price is not an oracle: the bridge to Chapters 16 and 17

[Basic] The ratio in an AMM looks like a "price" anyone can read. So other contracts are tempted to take it as price information. The v2 white paper shows why that is dangerous with a single attack: "Suppose some other contract uses the current ETH-DAI price to settle a derivative. An attacker who wishes to manipulate the measured price can buy ETH from the ETH-DAI pair, trigger settlement on the derivative contract (causing it to settle based on the inflated price), and then sell ETH back to the pair to trade it back to the true price. This might even be done as an atomic transaction, or by a miner who controls the ordering of transactions within a block."16 As Section 2 showed, a large order pushes the ratio. If some contract reads that pushed ratio as the "price," then push → be read → push back can be bundled into a single transaction. In a footnote, the white paper points to one outside article as "a real-world example of how using Uniswap v1 as an oracle can make a contract vulnerable to such an attack."17 This book has not obtained that article, so it does not describe the case.

[Basic] v2's response is a time-weighted average. It accumulates the price just before the first trade in each block, and dividing the difference between the accumulated values at two points in time by the elapsed time gives the average price over that interval. "Choosing a longer period makes it more expensive for an attacker to manipulate the TWAP, although it results in a less up-to-date price."18 It is a trade-off between the cost of manipulation and freshness. Even so, the white paper admits that a miner (or an attacker who uses enough gas to fill an entire block) can manipulate the price at the end of a block, and adds that "unless they mine the next block as well, they may not have a particular advantage in arbitraging the trade back." The larger problem of "bringing facts from off the chain onto the chain" is taken up by Chapter 16, and "the person who decides the order of transactions" by Chapter 17.

6. Code: a constant-product pool, the slippage curve, and the two pans of the scale

Constant-product pool and slippage

[Intermediate] We build one pool class. The sandwich simulation in Chapter 17 reuses this class as it is. All units are numbers of tokens in the pool, and there is no currency unit.

# NB15-1: constant-product pool — swaps (with fee), adding and removing liquidity, the slippage curve (for study)
import math

class ConstantProductPool:
    """x·y = k pool. fee is a fraction charged on the amount put in (default 0.003 = 30 bp). Shares are sqrt(x·y) at first, proportional after that."""
    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float, fee: float = 0.003):
        self.x, self.y, self.fee = float(x), float(y), fee
        self.shares = {"LP0": math.sqrt(x * y)}            # the first provider's share = geometric mean (v2 equation (13))
    @property
    def k(self): return self.x * self.y
    @property
    def price_x_in_y(self): return self.y / self.x           # marginal price: the price of one X in Y (v2 equation (1))
    def quote_x_for_y(self, dx: float) -> float:              # put in dx of X: how much Y comes back (keeps the product after taking the fee)
        eff = dx * (1 - self.fee)
        return self.y * eff / (self.x + eff)
    def swap_x_for_y(self, dx: float) -> float:
        dy = self.quote_x_for_y(dx)
        self.x += dx; self.y -= dy                             # the fee portion stays in the pool and k grows
        return dy
    def swap_y_for_x(self, dy: float) -> float:
        eff = dy * (1 - self.fee)
        dx = self.x * eff / (self.y + eff)
        self.y += dy; self.x -= dx
        return dx
    def add_liquidity(self, who: str, dx: float) -> float:     # put in X dx and Y dx·(y/x) at the current ratio (v2 equation (12))
        dy = dx * self.y / self.x
        minted = dx / self.x * sum(self.shares.values())
        self.x += dx; self.y += dy
        self.shares[who] = self.shares.get(who, 0) + minted
        return minted
    def remove_liquidity(self, who: str):                      # returns both tokens in proportion to the share, at the ratio of that moment
        s_total = sum(self.shares.values())
        frac = self.shares.pop(who) / s_total
        out_x, out_y = self.x * frac, self.y * frac
        self.x -= out_x; self.y -= out_y
        return out_x, out_y

pool = ConstantProductPool(1000, 1000)
print(f"start: x={pool.x:.1f} y={pool.y:.1f} k={pool.k:,.0f} marginal price (price of one X in Y)={pool.price_x_in_y:.4f}")
print(f"{'order Δx':>8} {'received Δy':>12} {'exec price Δy/Δx':>17} {'slippage':>9} {'marginal price after':>21}")
for dx in [1, 10, 100, 500, 1000]:
    p = ConstantProductPool(1000, 1000)
    before = p.price_x_in_y
    dy = p.swap_x_for_y(dx)
    exec_price = dy / dx
    print(f"{dx:>8} {dy:>12.3f} {exec_price:>17.4f} {1 - exec_price / before:>9.2%} {p.price_x_in_y:>21.4f}")

# where did the fee go — look at k after putting in 100
p = ConstantProductPool(1000, 1000); dy = p.swap_x_for_y(100)
print(f"\nafter putting in 100: Δy received={dy:.3f} (90.909 without a fee), pool x={p.x:.1f} y={p.y:.3f}, k={p.k:,.1f} (1,000,000 before the trade — the 0.3 X fee stayed in the pool and k grew)")

       1        0.996            0.9960     0.40%                0.9980

[Intermediate] The table confirms the arithmetic of Section 2. When the order is 1% of the pool, slippage is about 1% (1.28% including the fee); at 10% it is about 9% (9.34%); put in as much as the pool holds and you lose half. The figures in this table are set only by the structural variable "pool of 1,000:1,000," and have nothing to do with what the tokens are. This chapter's interactive figure W7 moves only these two variables (pool size and order size).

The two pans of the scale: impermanent loss and fees

# NB15-2: the two pans of the scale — impermanent loss by price multiple r, and how far sqrt(k) grown by fees makes up for it (for study)
import math

def impermanent_loss(r: float) -> float:                     # this book's derivation: V_pool / V_hold − 1 = 2√r/(1+r) − 1
    return 2 * math.sqrt(r) / (1 + r) - 1

print("price multiple r and impermanent loss (assuming fee 0 and full correction of the ratio by arbitrage):")
print(f"{'r':>6} {'value if kept (Y)':>18} {'value in pool (Y)':>18} {'impermanent loss':>17}")
x0 = y0 = 1000.0
for r in [0.25, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.25, 2.0, 4.0]:
    hold = x0 * r * (y0 / x0) + y0                              # X valued at the new price r·(y/x), plus Y
    pool_val = 2 * y0 * math.sqrt(r)
    print(f"{r:>6.2f} {hold:>18.1f} {pool_val:>18.1f} {impermanent_loss(r):>17.2%}")

# the fee pan of the scale — trades go back and forth so the ratio returns to where it was, but k grows. Count the growth of sqrt(k) by trading volume (as a multiple of the pool).
print("\nfee accrual: swaps of size 10, alternating X→Y and Y→X, N times (the ratio stays almost in place, k grows)")
print(f"{'round-trip volume/pool':>22} {'sqrt(k) growth (= fee accrual per share)':>40} {'r where V_pool = V_hold (formula under assumptions)':>51}")
for n_pairs in [10, 100, 1000]:
    p = ConstantProductPool(1000, 1000)
    k0 = p.k
    for _ in range(n_pairs):
        p.swap_x_for_y(10); p.swap_y_for_x(10)
    growth = math.sqrt(p.k / k0) - 1                           # g = √(k2/k1) − 1. Related to f = 1 − √k1/√k2 in v2 equation (4) by f = g/(1+g) (the reference points differ)
    # the r at which fee growth g exactly offsets impermanent loss: (1+g)·2√r/(1+r) = 1 → the two roots of a quadratic
    a = 1 + growth
    disc = (2 * a) ** 2 - 4
    s1, s2 = (2 * a - math.sqrt(disc)) / 2, (2 * a + math.sqrt(disc)) / 2   # the two roots for √r
    print(f"{2 * n_pairs * 10 / 1000:>21.1f}x {growth:>40.4%} {f'{s1**2:.3f} ≤ r ≤ {s2**2:.3f}':>51}")

[Intermediate] The tables above are this chapter's scale. The left table shows that if the price moves in either direction, the provider ends up worse off than by holding the tokens. The right table shows, as trading volume builds up to some multiple of the pool size, up to what range of price movement the fees make up for it. All the figures in both tables are in pool units and come with assumptions (0.3% fee, full correction by arbitrage, round-trip trades). Which side is larger in a real pool is an empirical question settled by that pool's trading volume and the price movement over that period, and this book does not give those figures. Neither "supplying liquidity makes a profit" nor "it makes a loss" is the conclusion of this chapter. The conclusion is that the two terms enter one formula as a product.

7. Summary

[Basic] An AMM does away with the order book and the operator and accepts trades by a single rule, "the product does not decrease." The price is the ratio of the two quantities, a large order pushes the ratio and produces slippage, and the fee stays in the pool and makes k larger. Providers share that growth according to their shares, but end up worse off than by holding the tokens to the extent that the price has moved. It is arbitrageurs who bring the ratio in line with the market, and that is why the spot ratio is dangerous to use as an oracle. The next chapter, Chapter 16, looks at the more fundamental problem that "the chain does not know the outside," and Chapter 17 takes this chapter's pool class as it is and looks at "who decides the order of transactions."
