  15. Same paper, §1 and §3.1 (pp. 1 and 3): "The swap fee is no longer locked at 0.30%. Rather, the fee tier for each pool (of which there can be multiple per asset pair) is set on initialization (Section 3.1). The initially supported fee tiers are 0.05%, 0.30%, and 1%." ↑

  16. Adams et al. (2020), §2.2 (p. 2): "However, Uniswap v1 is not safe to use as an on-chain price oracle, because it is very easy to manipulate. Suppose some other contract uses the current ETH-DAI price to settle a derivative. An attacker who wishes to manipulate the measured price can buy ETH from the ETH-DAI pair, trigger settlement on the derivative contract (causing it to settle based on the inflated price), and then sell ETH back to the pair to trade it back to the true price. This might even be done as an atomic transaction, or by a miner who controls the ordering of transactions within a block." Emphasis added. "ETH-DAI" is the original's example notation, and this book does not evaluate any particular token. ↑

  17. Footnote 1 on the same page: "For a real-world example of how using Uniswap v1 as an oracle can make a contract vulnerable to such an attack, see [3]." Reference [3] is samczsun, "Taking undercollateralized loans for fun and for profit," Sept. 2019 (a blog post). This book has not obtained this post as source material and does not quote its contents. ↑

  18. Same paper, §2.2 (p. 3), equations (2) and (3): "Uniswap v2 accumulates this price, by keeping track of the cumulative sum of prices at the beginning of each block in which someone interacts with the contract. Each price is weighted by the amount of time that has passed since the last block in which it was updated …"; "Users of the oracle can choose when to start and end this period. Choosing a longer period makes it more expensive for an attacker to manipulate the TWAP, although it results in a less up-to-date price."; "A miner (or an attacker who uses enough gas to fill an entire block) could manipulate the price at the end of a block, but unless they mine the next block as well, they may not have a particular advantage in arbitraging the trade back." ↑

Part 2 · Smart contracts and applications

Chapter 16. The oracle problem: bringing facts from outside the chain into it

Key takeaway

A blockchain knows only what happens inside it. How much sits at which address, and what is written in which storage slot of which contract, every node can compute identically. But "today's temperature in New York," "yesterday's exchange rate" and "whether that flight was delayed" are not in the chain. The device that brings them into the chain is called an oracle, and an oracle in the end is someone writing a value in. Whether to have one such someone or several, and whether to make them forfeit a deposit if they are wrong, are questions of design, and no design brings "the people you have to trust" down to 0. After this chapter you will understand why the slogan "code is law" holds only inside the chain, and the paradox that when an oracle puts in a wrong value, a contract can be executed exactly and be wrong at the same time.

Learning objectives

  1. Explain, through determinism (every node performs the same computation), why a blockchain cannot fetch outside facts by itself.
  2. Name the three branches of oracle design (a single provider, aggregation over multiple providers, economic collateral) and what each of them requires you to trust.
  3. [Intermediate] Starting from the definition of the "ideal oracle," sort out at which layer each of these failures lies: data-source error, oracle collusion, Sybil attacks and mirroring, and front-running of reports.
  4. Explain, connecting it to Chapter 15, why using an AMM's spot ratio as an oracle invites manipulation.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. The slogan "code is law" holds only inside the chain, and facts from outside the chain come in only if you trust someone.

1. What failure this technology grew out of

[Basic] The contracts of Chapter 13 were boxes that release value when a condition is met. But the conditions people want to write are mostly out in the world. Buterin's 2014 white paper says that "Financial derivatives are the most common application of a 'smart contract', and one of the simplest to implement in code," and goes straight on to the obstacle: "The main challenge in implementing financial contracts is that the majority of them require reference to an external price ticker; … The simplest way to do this is through a 'data feed' contract maintained by a specific party (eg. NASDAQ) designed so that that party has the ability to update the contract as needed, and providing an interface that allows other contracts to send a message to that contract and get back a response that provides the price."1 The first application of a system built to do away with the trusted third party presupposes a contract maintained by a specific party. This tension is the whole of this chapter.

[Basic] The Yellow Paper records the same pattern too, as one of "several patterns of contracts engineering," "two of these that we will briefly discuss" (data feeds and random numbers). "A data feed contract is one which provides a single service: it gives access to information from the external world within Ethereum. The accuracy and timeliness of this information is not guaranteed and it is the task of a secondary contract author—the contract that utilises the data feed—to determine how much trust can be placed in any single data feed." As for the rest, "the second part of the pattern would be for an external server to run an Ethereum node, and immediately on discovery of a new block, creates a new valid transaction, sent to the contract, updating said value in storage. The contract's code would accept such updates only from the identity contained on said server."2 In short: one server, one key, and one number that key writes. This is the point where the word "decentralized" wears thinnest.

2. Why the chain does not know the outside

[Basic] The reason lies in the chain's very strength. Chapter 13 said that every node executes the same transactions in the same order and reaches the same state. That "sameness" is the condition for consensus. If a contract could say mid-execution, "now go and read the temperature from an outside server," a node in Seoul and a node in São Paulo would read different values at different moments and reach different states, and block validation would split from node to node. So contract code can read only what is in the chain, and an outside value becomes part of the chain only after someone writes it in with a transaction. That is this book's explanation; the 2017 Chainlink white paper states the same thing as a conclusion: "[B]ecause of their underlying consensus protocols, the blockchains on which smart contracts run cannot support native communication with external systems. Today, the solution to this problem is to introduce a new functionality, called an oracle, that provides connectivity to the outside world. Existing oracles are centralized services. Any smart contract using such services has a single point of failure, making it no more secure than a traditional, centrally run digital agreement."3

[Basic] The examples the same white paper gives will be familiar to lawyers: "Securities smart contracts such as bonds, interest rate derivatives, and many others will require access to APIs reporting market prices and market reference data, e.g. interest rates. Insurance smart contracts will need data feeds about IoT data related to the insurable event in question, e.g.: was the warehouse's magnetic door locked at the time of breach, was the company's firewall online, or did the flight you had insurance for arrive on time. Trade finance smart contracts will need GPS data about shipments, data from supply chain ERP systems, and customs data about the goods being shipped …."4 Whether an insurance claim is paid, the conditions for paying the price, the moment collateral is disposed of: almost all of the conditions that contract law deals with lie outside the chain. What code enforces automatically goes as far as "if the condition is true, pay," and "is the condition true?" comes in from outside.

3. The ideal oracle, and why it cannot be had

[Intermediate] To define the "security" of an oracle, Section 3 of the Chainlink white paper sets up a thought experiment. "Imagine that a trusted third party (TTP)—an ideal entity or functionality that always carries out instructions faithfully to the letter—were tasked with running an oracle. … suppose that the TTP obtains data from a perfectly trustworthy data source Src." There are only three things to ask of that ideal oracle ORACLE: "1. Accept request: Ingest from a smart contract USER-SC a request Req = (Src, τ, q) that specifies a target data source Src, a time or range of times τ, and a query q; 2. Obtain data: Send query q to Src at time τ; 3. Return data: On receiving answer a, return a to the smart contract." This is integrity. "For example, if Src is https://www.FountOfKnowledge.com, τ is 4 p.m., and q = 'price for ticker INTC', the integrity of ORACLE guarantees that it will provide USER-SC with exactly the price of INTC as queried at 4 p.m. at https://www.FountOfKnowledge.com."5

[Intermediate] The white paper then sets out, in two layers, why this definition is out of reach in practice. The first layer is the data source. "There is, of course, no perfectly trustworthy data source Src. Data may be benignly or maliciously corrupted due to faulty web sites, cheating service providers, or honest mistakes. If Src isn't trustworthy, then even if ORACLE does operate exactly like a TTP as instructed above, it still doesn't completely meet the notion of security we want. … If the true price of Intel is $40 and https://www.FountOfKnowledge.com misreports it as $50, for example, then ORACLE will send the incorrect value a = $50 to USER-SC. This problem is unavoidable when using a single source Src." The second layer is the oracle itself. "A bigger issue, of course, is the fact that our TTP for ORACLE is just an abstraction. No service provider is unconditionally trustworthy. Even the best-intentioned may be buggy or hacked."6 That an oracle can operate exactly as instructed and still be wrong: this is where this chapter's question box stands.

4. Three branches of design: what has to be trusted

[Basic] Oracle designs differ by where they put "what has to be trusted." The table is this book's arrangement; the basis for each cell is in the text below.

Design What writes the value What has to be trusted Shape of failure
Single provider (data feed contract) One server's key That operator and that source Operator error, hacking or source error passes straight onto the chain
Aggregation over multiple providers The answers of n nodes, combined by majority vote, median and the like "There are enough honest nodes," "the sources are independent of one another" If the sources copy one another, majority voting means nothing; one party poses as several nodes (Sybil)
Economic collateral As above, but nodes post a deposit and lose it if wrong "The penalty is larger than the benefit from manipulation" In a trade where manipulation would bring in more than the deposit, collateral is no deterrent
Reading an in-chain ratio as it stands (Chapter 15) The two quantities of an AMM pool "Nobody pushed the ratio at that moment" Push, get read, and revert, all within one transaction

[Intermediate] Distributing sources. "A simple way to deal with a faulty single source Src is to obtain data from multiple sources, i.e., distribute the data source. … One, for example, is majority voting. If a majority of sources return the identical value a, the function agg returns a; otherwise it returns an error. In this case, provided that a majority (> k/2) sources are functioning correctly, ORACLE will always return a correct value A. … For example, agg might discard outliers (e.g., the largest and smallest values ai) and output the mean of the remaining ones." But the white paper adds a limit at once. "Of course, faults may be correlated across data sources in a way that weakens the assurances provided by aggregation. If site Src1 = EchoEcho.com obtains its data from Src2 = TheHorsesMouth.com, an error at Src2 will always imply an error at Src1."7 Majority voting means something only when the voters are independent of one another. It is like ten newspapers that run the same wire-service story printing the same error.

[Intermediate] Distributing oracles. Along with the sources, the oracle nodes too are multiplied, and the aggregation is done "in-contract." "CHAINLINK-SC—which, again, denotes the on-chain part of ChainLink—will itself aggregate oracle responses. … CHAINLINK-SC will compute A = Agg(A1, A2, . . . , An) for some function Agg (similar to agg, as described above), and send the result A to USER-SC." As benefits it lists "Conceptual simplicity," trustworthiness, in that "As CHAINLINK-SC's code can be publicly inspected, its correct behavior can be verified," and flexibility.8 If the aggregation code sits on the chain, you do not have to trust the way of aggregating. What has to be trusted moves to the assumption that "of the n nodes, the honest ones are a majority." The 2021 follow-up white paper restates this in the language of Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT): "Most BFT algorithms require at least n=3f+1 nodes, where f is the number of potentially faulty nodes; … We refer to the committee O as honest if it meets this requirement, i.e., has greater than a 2/3-fraction of honest nodes."9 Chapter 10's "2/3" comes back here. But the 2021 white paper adds that the security of the two kinds of system cannot be measured with the same yardstick: "Compromising a PoW or a PoS blockchain via 51% attack requires that an adversary obtain majority resources ephemerally and potentially anonymously … In contrast, compromising a committee-based system means corrupting a threshold number (typically one-third) of its nodes, where the nodes may be publicly known, well resourced, and trustworthy entities."10 Which is safer depends on who the attacker is.

[Intermediate] Economic collateral and reputation. In the order-matching design of the 2017 white paper, "When an oracle service provider bids on a contract, they commit to it, specifically by attaching the penalty amount that would be lost due to their misbehavior, as defined in the SLA."11 And a reputation system records "Total number of assigned requests," "Total number of completed requests," "Total number of accepted requests" (accepted "when compared with peer responses"), "Average time to respond" and "Amount of penalty payments."12 This is the same logic as slashing in Chapter 10. Honesty is rational only if there is something to lose by being wrong. Yet the white paper itself records what this device does not stop: Sybil attacks and mirroring. "Both our simple and in-contract aggregation protocols seek to prevent freeloading in the sense of dishonest nodes copying honest nodes' answers. But neither protects against Sybil attacks [9]. Such attacks involve an adversary that controls multiple, ostensibly independent oracles. This adversary can attempt to dominate the oracle pool, causing more than f oracles to participate in the aggregation protocol and provide false data at strategic times, e.g., in order to influence large transactions in high-value contracts." And: "Attacks or faults involving > f oracles are especially pernicious in that they are undetectable from on-chain behavior alone."13 Collateral changes the incentive of a single node. That several nodes are in fact one, collateral does not find out.

[Advanced] A fourth road: trusted hardware, and what it shifts

[Advanced] What the 2017 white paper put forward as its "long-term strategy" was not distribution but hardware. "A distributed oracle network aims to offer a high degree of protection against faulty oracles. In most deployment scenarios, it seeks to attain a correct response in the face of f Byzantine faults (for f<n/2 in our simple aggregation protocol). Trusted hardware can offer much more …." Run the oracle in a trusted execution environment (an enclave) such as Intel SGX and distribute its attestations, and you get "very strong assurance that the oracle is executing a particular application," and "an oracle running in an enclave that can connect to a data source via HTTPS can provide a strong assurance that the data it retrieves has not been tampered with."14 Then there is confidentiality. A distributed oracle writes its queries on a public chain, so it runs into the limit that "At some point a server needs to send a query to a target data source server. Thus it must see the query …"; decrypting and processing the query inside the enclave gets past that limit. In Appendix B the white paper discusses separately "the issue of Intel as a root of trust."15 Trust has not vanished; it has moved to the chip maker and its attestation system. If this chapter's table were given a fourth row, its "what has to be trusted" cell would read "the hardware maker's attestations, and an enclave implementation free of flaws." Another road is written down as well. It is an infrastructure change (TLS-N): if data sources digitally signed the data they serve, "then oracles would not need to be trusted to refrain from tampering with data." But the white paper writes that "Few data sources are likely to in the near future."16 The cleanest solution is one under which the outside world has to change.

5. At which layer does manipulation happen?

[Basic] The phrase "oracle manipulation" lumps several layers together. This book separates four.

  1. Error or manipulation at the source. The "site that reports USD 40 as USD 50" of Section 3. The oracle was faithful; the source was wrong.
  2. Collusion or Sybil attacks among oracle nodes. Section 4's "more than f nodes give false data at strategic times." The aggregation code was faithful; the inputs were wrong.
  3. Reading an in-chain ratio as an oracle. The attack in Section 5 of Chapter 15. As the Uniswap v2 white paper puts it, "An attacker who wishes to manipulate the measured price can buy ETH from the ETH-DAI pair, trigger settlement on the derivative contract (causing it to settle based on the inflated price), and then sell ETH back to the pair to trade it back to the true price. This might even be done as an atomic transaction, or by a miner who controls the ordering of transactions within a block."17 Here there is no separate oracle at all. A contract simply read two storage slots of another contract (the two reserves) as "the price," and those two slots held values that anyone could push with a transaction. The white paper's answer (a time-weighted average) was a trade-off that raises the cost of manipulation and gives up freshness.
  4. Front-running the report itself. If the transaction by which an oracle honestly posts a new value is visible in the public queue, someone slips a transaction in ahead of it. The 2021 white paper describes it: "Consider the common design pattern of using an oracle to supply various price feeds to an on-chain exchange: periodically (say every hour), the oracle collects price data for different assets and sends these to an exchange contract. These price-data transactions present obvious arbitrage opportunities: For example, if the newest oracle report lists a much higher price for some asset, an adversary could front-run the oracle report to buy up assets and immediately resell them once the oracle's report is processed."18 The oracle, the source and the aggregation were all correct. Nothing was wrong; only the order became money. That is Chapter 17.

[Basic] One often hears that the third of these four is "a common route for DeFi incidents." This book did not measure that frequency. The Uniswap v2 white paper points to a single blog post as a "real-world example" (footnote in Chapter 15), and none of the primary documents this book obtained tallies incidents by type or by size of loss. So this chapter goes only as far as "this is the structure of manipulation," and puts off the judgment "it is common" until tallied data are obtained (a task for the Trend notes in Appendix A).

A lawyer's question

An oracle put in a wrong value, and the contract executed exactly on that value. An insurance claim was not paid, or collateral was disposed of, or a derivative was settled at a wrong price. The code did not deviate by a single line. Is this performance (이행), or is it mistake (착오)? If it is mistake, whose mistake is it: the oracle operator who wrote the value in, the contract author who chose to trust that oracle, or the party who chose to use that contract? What if the wrong value came from the data source (a website), and that site had a contract with no one? If more than 1/3 of many nodes colluded, what did they do jointly? And if a contract merely read "two storage slots of another contract" as a price and nobody ran an "oracle," what did the person who pushed that value manipulate? → Chapter 28

6. Summary

[Basic] Because every node performs the same computation, the chain cannot read the outside, and an outside value comes in only when someone writes it in with a transaction. Put one such someone in charge and you must trust that person; put several in charge and you must trust that they are independent; make them post deposits and you must trust that the deposit is larger than the benefit from manipulation; read an in-chain ratio and you must trust that nobody pushed the ratio at that moment. "Code is law" holds inside the chain, and whether a condition is true comes in from outside it. The next chapter, Chapter 17, looks at the problem raised at the end of this one: "everything was correct, and the order became money." The basis for misconception ⑨ in Appendix B ("code is law") is shared between this chapter and Chapter 26.

Part 2 · Smart contracts and applications

Chapter 17. MEV and transaction ordering: the power to set the order

Key takeaway

Chapter 8 said that the rules do not dictate which transactions a miner puts into a block, or in what order. Chapter 15 said that an AMM's price changes with the order of trades. Put the two together and you get this: whoever makes the block can set the order of transactions, and can extract money just by setting the order. That money was named "miner extractable value (MEV)" by a paper that first appeared as a 2019 preprint and was published in 2020; after the move to proof of stake it is read as "maximum extractable value" (the form used on ethereum.org's PBS page). The easiest shape to grasp is the sandwich. Put my buy in front of someone else's buy order and my sell behind it, and the formula of Chapter 15 is applied to my two trades, and the difference stays with me. Where traditional markets prohibit front-running by law, here there is no "intermediary" to stop it, and code does not stop it either. The response Ethereum chose is not prohibition but a division of labor. It splits the one who assembles the block (the builder) from the one who proposes it (the proposer), so that the power to set the order does not pile up with a few validators. After this chapter you will know that the saying "decentralized markets have no operator" needs a rider: "instead, there is someone who sets the order."

Learning objectives

  1. Explain how front-running, back-running and the sandwich follow from two facts: transactions are visible in a public waiting area (the mempool) before they get into a block, and the block producer sets the order.
  2. [Intermediate] Apply Chapter 15's constant-product formula twice to compute the sandwich attacker's profit and the victim's loss in pool units, and see how the victim's slippage tolerance limits the size of the attack.
  3. [Intermediate] Read the priority gas auction (PGA) as "an auction in which the losers pay too," and see why MEV threatens the stability of the consensus layer (rewinding attacks).
  4. Know what proposer–builder separation (PBS) changes and what it does not, and whether, as of October 2026, it sits inside or outside the protocol.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. Blockchains too have "someone who sets the order," and that someone can extract money from the order. The traditional market's prohibition of front-running is not enforced by code here.

1. What failure this technology grew out of

[Basic] Transactions drift around the network before they get into a block. From the 2020 paper by Philip Daian and coauthors: "Ethereum transactions are routed in a peer-to-peer gossip multicast protocol by client node software. This means that all transaction information is available to all participants in this network, but earlier to participants with advantageous positions in the gossip topology. Additionally, nodes can simulate the outcome of every transaction given the current or expected system state."1 If you send a large buy order to an AMM, others can read that order before it gets into a block and calculate how far it will push the price. And those others can act by "observing them and placing their own orders with higher fees to ensure they are mined first."2 This is front-running.

[Basic] Traditional markets have front-running too, and the paper contrasts the two: "Traditional exchanges experience a classic form of predatory market behavior called frontrunning [4]. In regulated markets, frontrunning is often illegal, and has resulted in prosecutions [26] and tarnished the reputations of financial institutions caught practicing it. Frontrunning generally exploits information asymmetries created by power structures within a financial structure, e.g., brokers having privileged access to user information. Because there is no single party playing the role of a broker in decentralized systems, information asymmetries can arise for actors in advantageous positions in underlying infrastructure."3 The "broker" at which regulation was aimed has gone, but the asymmetry remains. The seat of the asymmetry has moved to network position and block-production authority.

[Basic] The deeper difference the paper points to is atomicity. "Because of the atomic batch-based processing of transactions, and because transactions can themselves be initiated by smart contracts, is possible [sic] to build bots that trade across exchanges through proxy contracts. These proxy contracts can execute batches of orders sequentially within a single transaction, reverting previous trades by throwing an exception if any trade in the batch fails. This means arbitrageurs have the opportunity to compose single transactions that execute multiple trades across multiple exchanges atomically, with an all-or-nothing failure model."4 Chapter 13's "running out of gas leaves no half-finished state" becomes an attack tool here. There is no risk that only one of two trades goes through, so if there is an arbitrage profit it is taken with certainty, and if there is none only the fee is lost.

2. The intuition: slip in front, slip in behind, slip in on both sides

[Basic] Let us sort out three words. The definition in the 2021 Chainlink 2.0 white paper is concise: "Front-running exemplifies a class of transaction-ordering attacks: There are a number of related attacks such as back-running and sandwiching (front-running plus back-running) …."5

  • Front-running. Knowing that the victim's order will raise the price, you put in an order in the same direction ahead of it. Once the victim raises the price, you already have what you bought.
  • Back-running. You put in an order in the opposite direction behind the victim's order. Knowing that the price the victim pushed up will come back down, you take that reversion.
  • Sandwich. Combine the two. Buy in front; the victim raises the price; sell behind. Chapter 15's formula is applied three times, and two of the three are yours.

[Basic] Drawn with Chapter 15's pool, a sandwich looks like this. The pool holds 1,000 each of X and Y, and the victim wants to buy X with 100 Y. Alone, the victim would get about 90.7 X by Chapter 15's formula. If the attacker first buys X with 100 Y, the pool becomes Y 1,100 / X 909.3, and the price of one X has already gone up. The victim now gets only about 75.6 X for the same 100 Y. Then the attacker sells its 90.7 X back and receives more than 100 Y. The attacker's profit is that difference, and the victim's loss is "90.7 − 75.6." The units are all counts of tokens in the pool. The code below runs exactly this arithmetic.

[Basic] One point matters here. The attacker did not change the victim's order. The victim's transaction was executed exactly as the victim signed it. What changed was the state of the pool at the moment that transaction was executed, and what changed it was the order. It has the same shape as the approve race condition in Chapter 14.

3. Who sets the order: auctions and producers

[Intermediate] The one who sets the order is whoever makes the block. But even if the block producer does not build sandwiches itself, bots run auctions to buy the order from the producer. The paper calls this a "priority gas auction (PGA)." "In Ethereum, the PGA game we observe consists of transactions issued with the same (account, nonce) pair, expressing a bid to a miner … To place a bid on an arbitrage opportunity, an arbitrageur simply issues a smart contract transaction with associated gas price g … If they later wish to increase this bid, … they simply reissue the transaction with the same nonce and a higher gas price g′. If two arbitrageurs are bidding against each other, what emerges is essentially an auction …."6 The nonce of Chapter 11 is used here as a device for "updating a bid in the same slot." And this auction has a peculiar property: the losers pay too. The losing transaction "is also mined and included in the final block, as each (account, nonce) pair can include one transaction in the next block to be mined as per the protocol. Miners are incentivized to include even failed transactions, as these transactions pay for attempted execution. … In game theoretic terms, each auction represents a variant of all pay auction …."7 This is where Chapter 13's "when the gas runs out the execution is reverted, but the fee remains" becomes the losers' cost.

[Intermediate] A few of the paper's observations are carried over because they show the structure (the amounts are not carried over). The bots competed to cut their latency, and the size of bid raises converged over time to the minimum raise (12.5%) allowed by the Parity client, which was widely used at the time; the paper reads this as consistent with "a convergence toward elements of cooperative equilibrium."8 Most of the auctions observed were games among two or three players, and most pure revenue opportunities drew no competition. As one reason for this, the paper offers the hypothesis (Appendix C) that bots that keep losing become discouraged and leave the market, and it adds the arithmetic that, as the number of participants grows, the reward must grow in proportion to the cost of losing for taking part to be profitable. These observations cover the period shown in the paper's figures (horizontal axis 2017-07 to 2019-03) and only the "pure revenue opportunities" on the exchanges the paper supported (which included the top five DEXes by volume at the time), so they are a lower bound, and the paper itself writes at length about the limits of its measurement.9 What this book takes away is not the numbers but the shape. The order is sold at auction, the auction is one in which the losers pay too, and the auction proceeds go to the block producer.

MEV, and why it is a problem for the consensus layer

[Intermediate] Here comes the concept the paper named. "OO fees represent one case of a more general quantifiable value we call miner-extractable value (MEV). MEV refers to the total amount of Ether miners can extract from manipulation of transactions within a given timeframe, which may include multiple blocks' worth of transactions." The money that bots pay in these auctions is the price of what the producer could have done directly. "To capture OO fees, a miner can reorder users' transactions and potentially insert their own, reaping profit in Ether directly to their account. For example, a miner could execute the pure revenue transactions described in this work themselves, while still claiming the PGA fees for all the 'losing' arbitrage bots attempting to do the same."10

[Intermediate] And the paper's conclusion ties this chapter to Part 1. "In a stable blockchain, block rewards incentivize honest miner behavior. As we show empirically in this section, though, order optimization (OO) fees … can exceed the block reward and instead incentivize forking attacks." It gives two attacks. One is "a previously shown undercutting attack [11] that forks a block with significant MEV" (first analyzed by the paper "On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward," which Chapter 20 takes up); the other is a newly named attack, the time-bandit attack. "Suppose a blockchain has a suffix (subchain) [height0, height1], with current block height height1, in which stealable value exceeds block rewards. An adversary can rewind to height0 and use the resulting MEV to subsidize a profitable 51% attack that mines a fork up to or past height1."11 Chapter 9 said that rewinding grows costlier as blocks pile up. What Chapter 17 adds is that if something to be had from rewinding lies within the order of transactions, an incentive arises to bear that cost. In the paper's words, "a key result of our work is that application-layer security poses a current and direct threat to consensus-layer security."12 The cost side of the calculation goes to Chapter 20, and the strategy side to Chapter 23.

A lawyer's question

The sandwich attacker did not change a single character of the victim's order. It only placed two orders of its own in front of and behind the victim's, and all three were executed as the code dictates. Is this market manipulation (시세조종)? Is there a "market price" (시세) that was manipulated: can the ratio of two quantities in a pool be called a market price? Who is the "actor" who manipulated it: the bot operator who placed the orders, the producer who took that order and put it in a block, or the relaying party that sold that order at auction? Where are the "market" and the "exchange" that regulation presupposes? Do the grounds for prohibiting front-running in traditional markets (fiduciary duty (신인의무), the abuse of information asymmetry) still stand where there is no intermediary? And if the producer ran the sandwich itself, what did it do in its own block? → Chapter 28

4. The response, not prohibition but a division of labor: proposer–builder separation

[Basic] A law prohibiting front-running cannot be put into code. Code does not know which transaction is the "victim" and which is the "attack," and the power to set the order is of the essence of block production. What Ethereum researchers took aim at was a different problem: concentration. Buterin's research post of June 2021: "A major risk threatening the ongoing decentralization of consensus networks is the economics around miner extractable value (MEV), sophisticated tricks to extract profit from the ability to choose the contents of the next block. … While normal PoS rewards are reasonably egalitarian, as single validators earn the same rate of return as powerful pools, there are significant economies of scale in finding sophisticated MEV extraction opportunities. A pool that is 10x bigger will have 10x more opportunities to extract MEV but it will also be able to spend much more effort on making proprietary optimizations to extract more out of each opportunity."13 Chapter 10's question, "is PoS a structure in which the rich get richer?", finds a new ground here. Rewards stay proportional, but the money extracted from the order goes more to the larger side.

[Basic] The proposal is to split the roles. "The best-known solution is proposer/block-builder separation. Instead of the block proposer trying to produce a revenue-maximizing block by themselves, they rely on a market where outside actors that we call block-builders produce bundles consisting of complete block contents and a fee for the proposer, and the proposer chooses the bundle with the highest fee. The proposer's choice is reduced to picking the highest-fee bundle, an algorithm so simple that in a decentralized pool it can even be done inside an MPC to prevent cheating."14 The key is that the proposer chooses without seeing the block contents. One of the five desirable properties the post lists is "Bundle un-stealability: proposers should not be able to take bundles proposed by block builders and extract transactions from them to make their own bundles …."15 The design does not abolish MEV; it concentrates the work of extracting MEV in specialist builders and has every proposer receive the payment for it through an auction. Ethereum's official documentation states the same point: "The block builders might have done sophisticated MEV extraction, but the reward for it goes to the block proposer. This means that even if a small pool of specialized block builders dominate MEV extraction, the reward for it could go to any validator on the network, including individual home stakers."16

[Intermediate] Before this design went inside the protocol, an implementation running outside it appeared first. A post from the Flashbots side in November 2021 sets out the design: "This document outlines the design for a marketplace for block construction (often referred to as block proposer / block builder separation or PBS) compatible with the upcoming Ethereum merge fork. This trust based solution closely resembles the current Flashbots auction design with modifications to enable solo staker participation without introducing changes to Ethereum consensus." The structure runs users and searchers → builders → relays → proposers, and "Validators receive execution payload headers from relays (execution payloads stripped of the transaction content). … The validator selects the most valuable header, signs the payload, and returns it to the relay …." "Since the execution payload header does not include the transaction content, the risk of validators frontrunning is eliminated. … However, this design also requires validators to trust the relay to filter invalid payloads, accurately report payload value, and reveal the transaction content once the header is signed."17 The software is called MEV-Boost, and the README of its repository calls it "open source middleware run by validators to access a competitive block-building market … an initial implementation of proposer-builder separation (PBS) for proof-of-stake (PoS) Ethereum," and writes that "In the future, proposer/builder separation will be enshrined in the Ethereum protocol itself …."18

[Basic] So the picture as of 2026-10 is this. Inside the protocol there are only proposers; there are no builders or relays. The division of labor is run by middleware and relay operators outside the protocol, and Ethereum's official roadmap page writes: "PBS is in an advanced stage of research, but there are still some important design questions that need to be resolved before it can be prototyped in Ethereum clients. There is no finalized specification yet."19 This sentence dates quickly, so it is entered in the Trend notes in Appendix A and checked again with each edition. The same page writes that PBS could also be used for censorship resistance (a design in which proposers use "inclusion lists" to force in transactions that builders left out), but it says that this too is "an area of active research."

[Basic] Let us also record what the division of labor does not change. Sandwiches still happen. What has changed is who shares the profit from them. The builder extracts it, the proposer receives it through the auction, and the user still gets a worse price. The other roads for protecting users (sending transactions straight to a builder instead of to the public queue, queues with encrypted transaction contents, and the "fair sequencing services" proposed in the Chainlink 2.0 white paper20) are each designs that trust someone else, and this book evaluates none of them. How the sequencer of a layer-2 rollup handles this problem differently, by keeping its own queue private, is taken up in Chapter 18.

5. Code: running the sandwich in pool units

Three transactions in turn: front, victim, back

[Intermediate] The pool class of Chapter 15 is written out again as it is (so that the notebook runs on its own), and three transactions are put in in order. Units are all counts of tokens in the pool, and "attacker profit" is used only to show the structure. These figures are not values from any real market.

# NB17-1: the sandwich — take Chapter 15's constant-product pool as it is and put in three transactions in order, "front, victim, back" (for study, in pool units)
import math

class ConstantProductPool:                                 # same class as NB15-1 in Chapter 15 (swap part only)
    def __init__(self, x, y, fee=0.003):
        self.x, self.y, self.fee = float(x), float(y), fee
    @property
    def price_x_in_y(self): return self.y / self.x
    def swap_x_for_y(self, dx):
        eff = dx * (1 - self.fee); dy = self.y * eff / (self.x + eff)
        self.x += dx; self.y -= dy; return dy
    def swap_y_for_x(self, dy):
        eff = dy * (1 - self.fee); dx = self.x * eff / (self.y + eff)
        self.y += dy; self.x -= dx; return dx

def sandwich(pool_x, pool_y, victim_y, attacker_y):
    """The victim buys X with Y victim_y. The attacker, in front of it, buys X with Y attacker_y and, behind it, sells all of that X back.
    Returns: (Y the attacker got back − Y put in, X the victim received, X the victim would have received alone)"""
    alone = ConstantProductPool(pool_x, pool_y).swap_y_for_x(victim_y)
    p = ConstantProductPool(pool_x, pool_y)
    front_x = p.swap_y_for_x(attacker_y) if attacker_y > 0 else 0.0     # ① front: the attacker buys
    victim_x = p.swap_y_for_x(victim_y)                                 # ② the victim buys, at the already raised price
    back_y = p.swap_x_for_y(front_x) if attacker_y > 0 else 0.0         # ③ back: the attacker sells
    return back_y - attacker_y, victim_x, alone

print("Pool X 1,000 / Y 1,000. The victim buys X with Y 100.")
print(f"{'attacker in Y':>14} {'attacker net profit (Y)':>24} {'victim got X':>14} {'X if alone':>12} {'victim loss X':>14} {'victim loss ratio':>18}")
for a in [0, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 2000, 5000, 20000, 100000]:
    profit, vx, alone = sandwich(1000, 1000, 100, a)
    print(f"{a:>14} {profit:>24.3f} {vx:>14.3f} {alone:>12.3f} {alone - vx:>14.3f} {1 - vx / alone:>18.2%}")

        100000                   94.020          0.010       90.661         90.651             99.99%

[Intermediate] Read the table. The more the attacker puts in, the larger the victim's loss, and the attacker's net profit approaches the 100 Y the victim put in but does not exceed it. What the attacker takes is in the end what the victim paid, and putting in capital far larger than the victim's order leaves nothing more to take (this is why the net profit stops near 94 in the lower rows of the table; the rest stays in the pool as fees). So what binds this attack is not the attacker's capital. The structural variables, the size of the victim's order and the size of the pool, set the ceiling, and what binds the attacker hardest in practice is the variable in the next cell.

The slippage tolerance binds the attack

# NB17-2: the victim's slippage tolerance caps the size of the attack — add a "minimum amount received" condition and find the attacker's best input (for study, in pool units)
def best_attack(pool_x, pool_y, victim_y, tolerance, fee=0.003, grid=2000):
    """Assume the victim attached to its transaction the condition "I must receive at least (1 − tolerance) of the X I would have received alone."
    Among the attacker inputs Y that do not break that condition (= the victim's transaction is not reverted), find by grid search the one with the largest net profit."""
    alone = ConstantProductPool(pool_x, pool_y, fee).swap_y_for_x(victim_y)
    min_out = alone * (1 - tolerance)
    best = (0.0, 0.0)                                          # (net profit, input)
    for i in range(1, grid + 1):
        a = pool_y * 2 * i / grid                              # sweep from 0 up to twice the pool's Y
        profit, vx, _ = sandwich(pool_x, pool_y, victim_y, a)
        if vx < min_out:                                       # if the victim's trade fails, the sandwich fails too (only the front trade remains, at the attacker's loss)
            break
        if profit > best[0]:
            best = (profit, a)
    return best, alone, min_out

print("Pool X 1,000 / Y 1,000. Victim order Y 100. The attacker's best input and net profit for each slippage tolerance the victim attached to the transaction:")
print(f"{'tolerance':>9} {'victim min X':>16} {'attacker best input Y':>21} {'attacker net profit (Y)':>24}")
for tol in [0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50]:
    (profit, a), alone, min_out = best_attack(1000, 1000, 100, tol)
    print(f"{tol:>9.1%} {min_out:>16.3f} {a:>21.1f} {profit:>24.3f}")
print("\nThe narrower the tolerance, the smaller the attack that can be slipped in (on this 1 Y grid it is 0 at 0.1%). Net profit is nearly proportional to the tolerance, and the best input grows faster than that.")

The narrower the tolerance, the smaller the attack that can be slipped in (on this 1 Y grid it is 0 at 0.1%). Net profit is nearly proportional to the tolerance, and the best input grows faster than that.

[Basic] If the victim attaches to its transaction a narrow condition, "cancel the trade if I would receive less than this" (a slippage tolerance), the attack the attacker can slip in shrinks accordingly (on the 1 Y grid of the table above it came out as 0 at 0.1%, but on a finer grid a small attack goes through). The narrower the condition, the greater the chance that one's own transaction fails, so the victim trades the risk of failure against the risk of a sandwich. This variable is in the victim's hands. This chapter's interactive figure W10 moves only four structural variables (pool size, victim order, attacker input, tolerance) and uses no currency units.

6. Summary

[Basic] Transactions are public before they get into a block, the one who makes the block sets the order, and the order changes an AMM's price, so the order itself becomes money. Bots buy that order at auction (an auction in which the losers pay too), the producer can also do it directly, and when that money exceeds the block reward it becomes an incentive for rewinding attacks. Ethereum's response is not prohibition but a division of labor (PBS), and as of 2026-10 that division runs on middleware and relays outside the protocol, with no finalized specification. How the fee market dealt with this problem (the design intent that burning the base fee reduces the producer's incentive to manipulate fees) continues in Chapter 21, the calculation of attack costs in Chapter 20, and the equilibrium of strategies in Chapter 23. The last chapter of Part 2, Chapter 18, looks at designs that move transactions to another layer altogether. There too is someone who sets the order (the sequencer).

Part 2 · Smart contracts and applications

Chapter 18. Scalability: layer 2 and rollups

Key takeaway

A blockchain is secure because every node recomputes every transaction in exactly the same way. For the same reason it is slow. Adding nodes does not raise throughput, because everyone is doing the same work. Making blocks bigger raises throughput, but running a node then takes a more powerful machine, and fewer people take part. This tension is often called the "scalability trilemma," and the name is a design heuristic, not a theorem. The path Ethereum took is rollups. The execution of transactions happens on an outside chain (layer 2), and only the transaction data and a summary of the results are written to the main chain (layer 1). The head office's ledger records only the totals and the branches handle the details, but when a dispute arises it is settled at the head office. There are two ways of "settling." An optimistic rollup "treats a result as correct until someone proves it wrong" and allows a challenge period, and a zero-knowledge rollup "attaches a mathematical proof of correctness every time." After this chapter you will see that layer 2 is not "a faster blockchain" but a structure that entrusts the data to the main chain and splits off execution, and that inside that structure there is again someone who "decides the order" (the sequencer).

Learning objectives

  1. Explain why throughput is bounded by "capacity per block ÷ block interval," and why making blocks bigger is not free.
  2. Distinguish the three things a rollup posts to the main chain (transaction data, a state summary, forced-inclusion messages) and what each one guarantees.
  3. [Intermediate] Compare how the challenge period and interactive fraud proof (bisection) of optimistic rollups and the validity proof of zero-knowledge rollups differ on the question "who has to be honest?"
  4. Recognize the "trilemma" as a design heuristic, and identify where rollups moved trust to rather than eliminating it (the sequencer, upgrade authority, the data availability layer).

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. Layer 2 is a structure in which "the head office's ledger records only the totals and the details are handled at the branches," and when a dispute arises it comes back to the head office.

1. What failure this technology grew out of

[Basic] Chapter 13 said that every node executes the same transactions in the same order. That "everyone does the same work" is the bottleneck. The ZKsync documentation puts it concisely: "Ethereum's decentralized network has limited transaction throughput because its capacity doesn't scale with the number of validators. In essence, each validator performs the same job of validating each processed transaction, creating a bottleneck. In contrast, in Web2 scalability improves with the addition of more servers, as the network's capacity to handle requests increases linearly with each new server."1 An ordinary server farm divides the work; a blockchain replicates it. Replication is the source of the security, and replication is the source of the slowness.

[Basic] Throughput is bounded by simple arithmetic. The upper limit is the amount that fits in one block divided by the time between blocks. Bitcoin divides a block weight of 4,000,000 units by a target interval of 600 seconds. Ethereum divides the block gas limit by a slot interval of 12 seconds.2 The gas limit is not a protocol constant but a value that validators move a little with each block, and the value observed on this book's reference date was 60,000,000 (as of 2026-10; Chapter 21 and Appendix A).3 That makes 5,000,000 gas per second the upper limit, and if we assume that only the simplest transactions of Chapter 13 (intrinsic gas 21,000) come in, about 238 transactions per second is the theoretical upper limit. This calculation is this book's own, and it is the upper limit "when blocks are filled entirely with the simplest possible transactions," not measured throughput. The easiest way to raise that limit is to enlarge the gas limit (the block size), but then every node has to compute more and store more for every block. That is the constraint the official Ethereum documentation sets out: "While speed and throughput are important, it is essential that scaling solutions enabling these goals remain decentralized and secure. Keeping the barrier to entry low for node operators is critical in preventing a progression towards centralized and insecure computing power."4

[Basic] This tension among throughput, decentralization, and security is often called the "scalability trilemma." The name needs care. It is not a proven theorem that "you can have only two of the three." It is a heuristic in which designers sum up their experience that the three goals pull against one another. The three pages of official documentation that this book checked against the source (the "Scaling" page above and the two rollup pages below) list the three goals but do not use the word "trilemma." A claim that some design has obtained all three "at once" depends on how each of the words is measured, and this chapter does no such measuring. Instead it looks only at the structure Ethereum chose. The official documentation sums up that choice as follows: "For a long time, sharding the blockchain was expected to scale Ethereum. … However, scaling by layer-2 rollups has taken over as the primary scaling technique."5

2. The structure of a rollup: execution outside, data and disputes inside

[Basic] Here is the one-line definition in the official documentation: "Rollups perform transaction execution outside layer 1 and then the data is posted to layer 1 where consensus is reached. As transaction data is included in layer 1 blocks, this allows rollups to be secured by native Ethereum security."6 There are two components: "Onchain contracts: The optimistic rollup's operation is controlled by smart contracts running on Ethereum. This includes contracts that store rollup blocks, monitor state updates on the rollup, and track user deposits. … Offchain virtual machine (VM): Although contracts managing the optimistic rollup protocol run on Ethereum, the rollup protocol performs computation and state storage on another virtual machine separate from the Ethereum Virtual Machine. The offchain VM is where applications live and state changes are executed …."7

[Basic] The most important distinction in this chapter is what a rollup posts to the main chain. A table in the OP Stack documentation, on the Optimism side, divides it into three: "Three different things go to the parent chain, and conflating them is the most common source of confusion about rollup security."8

What is posted Where What it buys
Transaction data Blobs or calldata Anyone can reconstruct the chain without the sequencer (derivable)
Deposits (forced-inclusion messages) Deposit contract The main chain can force transactions into layer 2 (censorship resistance)
Output roots (state summary) Dispute game contract The main chain can authenticate layer 2 state and process withdrawals (settleable)

[Basic] A sentence the same document adds links back to Part 1: "Transaction data is what makes the chain derivable. Output roots are what make it settleable. A chain that published data but no output roots would still be a chain anyone could verify, but no one could withdraw from it. A chain that published output roots but no data would be unverifiable, and its proposals uncheckable." (Emphasis added.) This has the same shape as the Merkle root of Chapter 6. A summary (the root) is small, and to check that the summary is true the original data has to be somewhere. That is why "data availability" becomes the central term of rollup design. The ZKsync documentation: "If the state of the rollup is unknown to observers of Ethereum, then in scenarios where the validators (centralized or decentralized) stop processing, it becomes impossible to make state transitions without relying on a trusted validator. However, if the data is always available to observers, it's feasible to restore the state and continue processing the network even if the trusted validator ceases its operation."9

[Intermediate] There are two places to post data: a transaction's calldata (the transaction data field of Chapter 13, which stays in the chain's history permanently) and blobs. A blob is a data space, added by the Dencun fork (EIP-4844) in March 2024, that is "not stored by the execution layer." Blobs are priced in a separate fee market, and "the protocol defines only a minimum window of roughly 18 days over which the network must serve blob data. That is a serving obligation rather than a deletion deadline: blob data is not permanent archival storage the way execution-layer history is, and longer-term access depends on archival services."10 That "roughly 18 days" comes from MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_BLOB_SIDECARS_REQUESTS: 4096 epochs in the consensus-layer configuration (32 slots per epoch × 12 seconds = 6.4 minutes; 4,096 epochs ≈ 18.2 days) (as of 2026-10, Appendix A).11 Chapter 13 showed why writing to storage is costly. Blobs are a design that sets aside a separate place, "one that not every node keeps permanently," so that rollup data can be posted at low cost, and the price of that design is a new question: "who is keeping it after 18 days?"

3. Optimistic rollups: correct until proven wrong

[Basic] The first approach is "optimistic." "Optimistic rollups are considered 'optimistic' because they assume offchain transactions are valid and don't publish proofs of validity for transaction batches posted onchain. … Optimistic rollups instead rely on a fraud-proving scheme to detect cases where transactions are not calculated correctly. After a rollup batch is submitted on Ethereum, there's a time window (called a challenge period) during which anyone can challenge the results of a rollup transaction by computing a fraud proof." If the challenge succeeds, "the rollup protocol re-executes the transaction(s) and updates the rollup's state accordingly. … the sequencer responsible for including the incorrectly executed transaction in a block receives a penalty." If the period elapses without a challenge, the batch "is deemed valid and accepted on Ethereum."12 The slashing of Chapter 10 and the "it hardens only as time passes" of Chapter 9 come back into use here. The difference is that in Chapter 9 the hardening was a probability, and here it is a clock called the challenge period.

[Basic] The place where users see that clock is withdrawal. "If a user initiates an L2 > L1 transaction to withdraw funds escrowed on L1, they must wait until the challenge period—lasting roughly seven days—elapses." (as of 2026-10, Appendix A)13 Inside layer 2 things are fast, but going back to the head office carries a challenge period. To avoid waiting there is a route in which "A liquidity provider assumes ownership of a pending L2 withdrawal and pays the user on L1 (in exchange for a fee)," and that means trusting yet another counterparty.

How does a fraud proof work? Bisection

[Intermediate] How do you prove that something "is wrong"? Rerunning all the transactions on the main chain would cost too much. So an interactive bisection is used. The Arbitrum documentation explains it most clearly: "The idea of interactive proving is that Alice and Bob will engage in a back-and-forth protocol, mediated by an L1 contract, to resolve their dispute with minimal work required from the L1 contract. Arbitrum's approach is to dissect the dispute. If Alice's claim covers N steps of execution, she posts two claims of size N/2, which combine to yield her initial N-step claim, then Bob picks one of Alice's N/2-step claims to challenge. Now the size of the dispute has been cut in half. This process continues, cutting the dispute in half at each stage, until they are disagreeing about a single step of execution. Note that so far, the L1 mediator hasn't had to think about execution 'on the merits.' It is only once the dispute is narrowed down to a single step that the L1 mediator needs to resolve the dispute by looking at what the instruction actually does and whether Alice's claim about it is correct."14 A dispute over N steps shrinks to a single step in log2N round trips. It is the same mathematics by which the Merkle proof of Chapter 6 proved inclusion with log2n hashes.

[Intermediate] The OP Stack specification describes the same device as three components: "A fault proof … consists of 3 components: Program: given a commitment to all rollup inputs (L1 data) and the dispute, verify the dispute statelessly. VM: given a stateless program and its inputs, trace any instruction step, and prove it on L1. Interactive Dispute Game: bisect a dispute down to a single instruction, and resolve the base-case using the VM."15 "[P]rove it on L1" means placing a contract on layer 1 that imitates one instruction of the layer 2 virtual machine (for example, a single MIPS instruction) and running just that one step on the main chain. In effect, a contract that reproduces one instruction of a different machine sits on top of the EVM of Chapter 13.

[Intermediate] The security claim of this design comes down to a single line: one honest person is enough. The Arbitrum documentation: "The key security property of the rollup protocol is that any one honest validator can force the correct execution of the chain to be confirmed. This means that executing an Arbitrum chain is as trustless as executing an Ethereum chain. You, and you alone (or someone you hire), can ensure your transactions are processed correctly. And this is true no matter how many malicious people are trying to stop you." It also says that a dispute protocol called BoLD has attached a time bound to that guarantee: "a single honest party can force confirmation of the correct outcome with a known, fixed amount of time, regardless of how many adversaries participate or how much they place as bond."16 The official documentation says the same: "the validity of the chain relies on the existence of one honest node. … If there are no honest nodes a malicious operator can steal funds by posting invalid blocks and state commitments."17 Compare this with the "2/3" of Chapter 10. An optimistic rollup runs not on a majority vote but on one person's challenge. The assumption is that this one person is actually awake and has the bond and the skill to raise a challenge.

[Intermediate] One more point. What a fraud proof overturns is a claim, not the chain. The OP Stack documentation: "The fault proof system governs only the third row: it decides whether a claim about L2 state is accepted on L1, and it does not reorder the L2 chain. A defeated proposal removes a claim about the chain; it does not roll the chain back."18 The moment the transaction data is posted to the main chain, the order has hardened ("hard finality" in the Arbitrum documentation), and a fraud proof deals only with whether the results computed from that data are correct.

4. Zero-knowledge rollups: a proof of correctness attached every time

[Basic] The second approach does not wait. "Zero-knowledge rollups (ZK-rollups) bundle (or 'roll up') transactions into batches that are executed offchain. … ZK-rollup operators submit a summary of the changes required to represent all the transactions in a batch rather than sending each transaction individually. They also produce validity proofs to prove the correctness of their changes. The ZK-rollup's state is maintained by a smart contract deployed on the Ethereum network. To update this state, ZK-rollup nodes must submit a validity proof for verification. … the validity proof is a cryptographic assurance that the state-change proposed by the rollup is really the result of executing the given batch of transactions."19 The verifier contract on the main chain checks the proof, and if the proof passes, the new state root becomes canonical. Instead of recomputing nearly everything, the main chain checks "a short proof that the computation was correct," and so "There are no delays when moving funds from a ZK-rollup to Ethereum because exit transactions are executed once the ZK-rollup contract verifies the validity proof."20

[Basic] On the name, here is a warning the official documentation sets down. Because of the word "zero-knowledge," it is easy to misunderstand that transactions become secret. "ZK-rollups use succinct validity proofs to establish that offchain state transitions were computed correctly. Succinctness keeps proofs compact and verification efficient relative to the underlying computation, allowing Ethereum to verify state transitions without re-executing every transaction. A proof system may additionally provide zero knowledge, meaning its proofs reveal no information about private inputs beyond what follows from the public statement. These are separate properties: using validity proofs for scaling does not, by itself, make a rollup's transactions confidential."21 What rollups use from this technology is the property of being "short"; the property of "hiding" is a bonus, or goes unused. As Section 2 described, the data is made public on the main chain: "the published data is public. … Publishing this data is what makes permissionless verification possible; it is not a privacy mechanism."

[Intermediate] There are two broad families of proof systems. SNARKs have "small proof sizes and constant-time verification," but they need a trusted setup: "creating a Common Reference String (CRS) is necessary," and "if information used to create public parameters fall [sic] into the possession of malicious actors they may be able to generate false validity proofs." So several participants conduct a ceremony (an MPC ceremony) in which each adds randomness and destroys their own share, and "As long as one honest participant destroys their input, the security of the ZK-SNARK system is guaranteed." STARKs do without that setup and use "publicly verifiable randomness" instead, and they are considered secure against quantum computers, but "they produce larger proof sizes, which are more expensive to verify on Ethereum."22 The mathematics of the proofs is outside the scope of this book (Appendix E does not cover it either). A lawyer needs to take away one thing: even "a proof of correctness" rests on premises that have to be trusted. In some systems, that one of the participants in the setup ceremony was honest; in every system, that the proof circuit translated the actual virtual machine exactly. The official documentation states that "Proving general-purpose EVM computation in circuits is more difficult and resource-intensive than proving simple computations …."23

[Intermediate] The ZKsync documentation counts four components: "Node Implementation: This component is responsible for receiving transactions from users and processing them. It maintains the off-chain state and handles the aggregation of transactions into batches as well as sends sealed batches onchain. ZK Circuits: These circuits are intricate mathematical constructs that represent verifiable computation logic. They are responsible for determining what can be verified as a valid proof. … Prover: The prover constructs the cryptographic proofs that attest to the correctness of the transactions processed off-chain. … Smart Contracts: These contracts are the on-chain component of the zkRollup. They are responsible for verifying the proofs submitted by the prover and updating the Ethereum blockchain's state accordingly."24 Of the four, the prover needs heavy machinery. From the table of drawbacks in the official documentation: "Producing validity proofs requires specialized hardware, which may encourage centralized control of the chain by a few parties."25 Where an optimistic rollup obtains decentralization from "anyone can challenge," a zero-knowledge rollup acquires a different concentration: "few people can produce the proofs."

5. Comparing the two approaches: who has to be honest?

[Basic] The table rearranges the tables of pros and cons on two pages of the official documentation according to this book's criterion, "what has to be trusted."26

Optimistic rollup Zero-knowledge rollup
Basis for correctness No one submitted a fraud proof within the challenge period The verifier contract accepted the validity proof
What has to be trusted One honest node is awake and able to challenge The premises of the proof system (setup ceremony, correctness of the circuit) and its mathematics
Withdrawal to the main chain Wait out the challenge period (roughly 7 days, as of 2026-10) As soon as the proof is verified
Data posted to the main chain All of the transaction data (because a challenger has to re-execute) The minimal data needed to rebuild the state (original: "the minimal data required to rebuild the latest state")
Who can advance the chain Any ordinary node (computing a fraud proof needs no special hardware) Whoever can produce proofs (special hardware)
EVM compatibility Easy (uses the EVM as it is, or something close to it) Hard (the EVM has to be translated into circuits)
Common weakness The sequencer can influence transaction ordering Same

6. Trust does not disappear; it moves

[Basic] The last row ties this chapter to Chapter 17. Both approaches have a sequencer that receives transactions, decides their order, and builds batches. The OP Stack documentation notes that "The sequencer's mempool is private, unlike L1 Ethereum's public one, which limits the MEV opportunities a public pending-transaction pool creates."27 The front-running of Chapter 17 arose from transactions being visible in a public queue. If a single operator holds the queue privately, front-running by bots goes down, but that operator decides the order. The same document draws the boundary of trust in just those terms: "The trust boundary moves as a transaction ages. Before its data is published, a user is trusting the sequencer not to reorder or drop it. After, they are trusting the DA layer."28 The Arbitrum documentation separates the same thing with two terms. The order the sequencer sends out in real time is soft finality, because "it depends on the Sequencer keeping its promises," and once that order has been posted to Ethereum in a batch and has hardened, it is hard finality.29 The "finality" of Chapter 9 turns two-layered again here.

[Basic] Against a sequencer omitting transactions there is a defense: the second row of the table in Section 2, forced inclusion. "Users can also submit their transactions on L1 instead of to the sequencer, in which case the sequencer has to include the transaction within a certain time limit to continue to produce valid blocks."30 Omission can be prevented, but the order belongs to the sequencer. And if a chain chooses to replace the data availability layer with something other than Ethereum ("Alt-DA"), the documentation says that "the chain's security becomes a function of that layer's availability guarantees rather than Ethereum's," and adds that in that case "the claim that anyone can reconstruct the chain from Ethereum no longer holds."31 A rollup has not reduced trust to 0. It is a design that divides what is entrusted to the main chain from what the operator keeps in hand, and the dividing line differs from rollup to rollup. The current state of things, such as how much a given rollup has entrusted to the main chain or who holds the upgrade keys, changes quickly, so it is not written in the text and is left to the Trend notes in Appendix A (with a reference date and sources).

7. Summary: closing Part 2

[Basic] Rollups move execution outside and post the data and a state summary to the main chain. Optimistic rollups secure correctness with "one honest person's challenge" and a challenge period; zero-knowledge rollups secure it with "a short proof of correctness" and the premises of the proof system. In both, the sequencer decides the order, and in both, security depends on where the data is. The "trilemma" is a name for that tension, not a theorem.

[Basic] Looking back over Part 2: Chapter 13 covered a ledger that executes code and the gas that stops it; Chapter 14, the ledgers (tokens) on top of it and what those ledgers do not say; Chapter 15, a pool that swaps tokens without people; Chapter 16, the fact that the chain knows nothing of the outside; Chapter 17, the power to decide order; Chapter 18, the structure that moves execution to another layer. One thing recurred across the six chapters. What code enforces and what people have promised sit on different layers, and between them remain the places that the word "decentralized" could not erase (operators, oracles, sequencers, keys). Part 3 reads that structure again through economics. Chapter 19 asks why a token that nothing backs can have a positive price, Chapter 20 asks how much it costs, per block, to keep all this secure, and Chapter 21 takes up the fee formula that Chapter 13 put off.
