Part 3 · Economics

Chapter 19. The functions of money and the "zero intrinsic value" equilibrium

Key takeaway

Neither "it has no intrinsic value, so it will end up at zero" nor "the quantity issued is fixed, so it has value" is a conclusion of economics. The functions approach (medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value) is a checklist, not a proof of value, and a positive price for an object that pays no dividend holds as one among several equilibria in which the belief that "others will accept it later" fulfills itself. The three models read in this chapter (Garratt–Wallace, Schilling–Uhlig, Biais et al.) all assume or write down an equilibrium with a price of zero (Schilling–Uhlig through the backward self-elimination in their §7), say that positive-price equilibria exist alongside it, and say that even within the positive-price equilibria the price path is not pinned down to one. Listing equilibria is not a forecast. After this chapter, when you meet the sentence "virtual assets have no intrinsic value" in a judgment or a paper, you will be able to separate what it says in economic terms from what it does not.

Learning objectives

  1. Check crypto-assets against the three functions of money (medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value), while knowing that the check is not a device for deciding whether something has value. Be able to use the distinction between inside money and outside money.
  2. [Intermediate] Know what the equation of exchange MV=PT says, and why it is hard to use as a tool for explaining prices when the velocity V cannot be observed.
  3. [Advanced] Read in equations why, in the overlapping generations model (Garratt–Wallace), the zero-price equilibrium, the constant-price equilibrium and the sunspot-collapse equilibrium exist together; why, in the infinitely lived agents model (Schilling–Uhlig), the "fundamental pricing equation" becomes a martingale condition; and why, in the transactional benefits model (Biais et al.), the "fundamental value" depends on the price itself.
  4. Distinguish what the three models say in common (multiplicity of equilibria, self-fulfilling beliefs) from what they do not say (which equilibrium is realized, the direction of the price).

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. Neither "it has no intrinsic value, so it is a fraud" nor "it is scarce, so it has value" is a conclusion of economics. What economics says is that both can be equilibria, and the model does not settle which one is realized.

1. The question this chapter tries to answer

[Basic] In Part 1 we looked at what a coin is, byte by byte. It is a chain of outputs linked by signatures (Chapter 5, Chapter 11), and rewriting that chain means redoing the proof of work (Chapter 7, Chapter 8). Nowhere in it is there any "value." Nor is there any promise from an issuer to give anything back. Yet people exchange it for goods. Why can they, and how long can that go on? The two common answers to this question run as follows. One is "there is no dividend and no redemption, so the fundamental value is zero, and the price will end up there." The other is "the cap on issuance is fixed in code, so it is scarce, and being scarce it has value."

[Basic] Economics takes neither answer as it stands. The first is half right. A price of zero is one equilibrium. But there are also positive-price equilibria, and theory does not settle which of them is realized. The second answer is missing a premise. Scarcity supports value "if others accept it," but it does not create that "if they accept it." The world is full of scarce things that nobody accepts. In place of these two answers this chapter puts what economics has actually produced, namely a listing of equilibria. That listing is not a forecast, and nowhere does this chapter state a price.

2. The functions approach: a checklist, not a proof

[Basic] When economics textbooks define money, the framework they use is three functions. A 2023 paper by Gary Gorton and Jeffery Zhang puts it this way: "money has several important properties, with the three most commonly stated ones being a unit of account, a store of value, and a medium of exchange." And they add a fourth: "The most obvious (yet not explicitly stated) property is that money must also satisfy the no-questions-asked (NQA) principle, which requires that the money be accepted in a transaction without due diligence on its value."1 Documents on the legal side use the same framework. The 2017 report of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on The DAO quotes the definition of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) in a footnote, defining "virtual currency" as "a digital representation of value that can be digitally traded and functions as: (1) a medium of exchange; and/or (2) a unit of account; and/or (3) a store of value, but does not have legal tender status … in any jurisdiction."2 The "and/or" catches the eye. The definition does not require all three functions; doing any one of them is enough.

[Basic] Run crypto-assets through this framework and the result is no surprise. They are used as a medium of exchange, but narrowly; they are hardly used as a unit of account (their prices are quoted in other currencies); and as a store of value they fluctuate widely. This is a qualitative summary, and the measurements are Makarov–Schoar and Athey et al. in section 3 below. One 2015 paper runs this check, starting from the premise that "In order to serve as money Bitcoin should fulfil the roles of unit of account (Dwyer, 2014), means of payments and store of value," and then writes that the speculative side of Bitcoin overwhelms its other functions, so that its price is at the mercy of market sentiment, and that this erodes its role as a unit of account.3 But when the check is done, the original question remains. Doing the functions poorly and having to be priced at zero are different propositions. The functions approach is a checklist for deciding what to call money; it is not a device for deciding whether an object can have a positive price. To answer the question of price, another tool is needed.

Inside money and outside money

[Basic] Before turning to that tool, we bring in one distinction. Rodney Garratt and Neil Wallace's 2018 paper opens its account of how to view bitcoin with this distinction: "Most economists distinguish between inside and outside money. Inside money is inside the economy in the sense that each unit is someone's asset and someone else's liability. … Examples of inside money are checking accounts and grocery-store coupons. Outside money, in contrast, does not disappear when balance sheets are consolidated. Examples are gold coins under a gold standard and Federal Reserve notes since August 15, 1971 when Nixon closed the gold window. In terms of that dichotomy, bitcoin is best viewed as an outside money. In particular, the issuer of bitcoin makes no promise to redeem it for any other object."4 This is exactly what we saw in Chapter 11. A UTXO is nobody's liability. So this chapter's question becomes "why does an object with no promise of redemption have a price?", and that is the same question economics has long asked about gold coins and fiat paper money.

[Basic] The same paper states the premise of its model in one sentence: "people give up other things to get bitcoin only because they think that others in the future will do the same. In other words, ownership of bitcoin does not yield utility as might ownership of a Picasso, and is not an input into the production of other things as is farmland, a factory, or a 3D printer. Nor does such ownership entitle the owner to a dividend stream of other valuable objects." And it adds: "When it comes to bitcoin, there is no commodity value to ignore. You cannot even use it as wall paper—as some stories suggest was performed with German marks during the 1922–1923 hyperinflation."5 If Hume and the founders of the quantity theory analyzed gold and silver money by ignoring its commodity value, bitcoin is the pure case in which there is nothing to ignore. On that premise, the question of the equilibrium price is asked.

3. [Intermediate] The equation of exchange and its limits

[Intermediate] The oldest framework for explaining prices by quantities is the equation of exchange. For the money stock M, the velocity V, the price level P and the volume of transactions T,

MV=PT

Reading the symbols: this is an identity saying that the number of times money changes hands in a period (V) times the money stock equals the value of what was traded in that period (PT). A numerical example: if 1,000 coins are each spent twice on average in a period and 4,000 units of goods are traded, the coin price of one unit of goods is P=MV/T=0.5. The appeal of this equation for crypto-assets is plain. M is set by the protocol (Chapter 20) and T is written on the ledger, so it looks as if putting the two in would give the price.

[Intermediate] A 2019 paper by Linda Schilling and Harald Uhlig shows what this equation looks like inside a model. In their model all money is spent once every period, so they write that "the velocity of both currencies equals one. In a world with only one currency, classical quantity theory yields yt=Dt/Pt," and that with two currencies the market-clearing condition becomes6

yt=DtPt+QtPtBt(9)

Reading the symbols: yt is the output of goods, Dt the quantity of dollars, Pt the dollar price level, Bt the quantity of bitcoins, and Qt the dollar price of bitcoin. What stands out here is that there are two unknowns (Dt and Qt). If the central bank moves Dt to target Pt, then as Bt grows on its fixed schedule, what happens to Qt is not determined by this equation alone. One theorem the paper draws from this equation is of interest: "The block rewards are not a tax on Bitcoin holders but are financed through Dollar taxes imposed by the Dollar central bank." The logic is that when block rewards make Bt larger, satisfying equation (9) at the same Pt and Qt requires Dt to shrink, and that shows up as a lump-sum tax on the dollar side.7 The intuition taken up in Chapter 20, that "issuance dilutes holders," does not carry over as such to a model of currency competition. This conclusion, though, is tied to the model's premises (the two currencies are perfect substitutes in trade, and all money is spent every period).

[Intermediate] The limit of the equation of exchange is V. Because it is an identity, defining V as PT/M makes it always true, so its explanatory power comes from the additional assumption that V is stable. To test that assumption for crypto-assets you have to measure "economically meaningful transaction volume," and the volume written on the ledger is not that. A 2021 study by Igor Makarov and Antoinette Schoar built a database that groups addresses into entities and reports that "90% of transaction volume on the Bitcoin blockchain is not tied to economically meaningful activities but is the byproduct of the Bitcoin protocol design as well as the preference of many participants for anonymity," and that "Starting from 2015, 75% of real bitcoin volume has been linked to exchanges or exchange-like entities …."8 When T wobbles that much, V is a residual, not a measurement. A 2016 model by Susan Athey and her coauthors says that "In steady state, exchange rates are determined by the ratio of transaction volume to the supply of Bitcoins," yet after checking it against price data the authors themselves write that it provides "mixed evidence about the ability of the model to explain prices." Their analysis of usage data then records the concentration, that "investors and infrequent users held the majority of Bitcoins," and the share of transaction volume taken by investors, and from this the authors draw the conclusion that "exchange rates are likely to be more sensitive to beliefs about the future of Bitcoin and less sensitive to current transaction volume for its own sake," with the parenthetical caveat "(though current volume is likely a signal of the future)".9 We went in through the framework of quantities and came out through the framework of beliefs. The next section is the model of those beliefs.

4. The "zero intrinsic value" equilibrium: three models

[Basic] We read three papers. The depth of the mathematics differs, but the shape of the conclusions is the same. Here is the gist first, without equations.

Model Agents Shape of the conclusion
Garratt–Wallace (2018) Generations that live two periods overlap A zero-price equilibrium always exists. A constant positive-price equilibrium may also exist. There is also an equilibrium that "goes to zero some day, but on a day nobody knows." The day of the collapse cannot be predicted
Schilling–Uhlig (2019) Agents live forever, alternating between consuming and producing If both currencies are used and the price is uncorrelated with the pricing kernel, the dollar price of the coin is a martingale (Proposition 1); if there is a correlation, its sign sets the direction of the expected change (Corollary 1). Price fluctuations do not invalidate the medium-of-exchange function
Biais et al. (2023) Generations that live two periods overlap, and the coin provides transactional benefits The "fundamental value" is the present value of future transactional benefits, but because those benefits depend on the price, it has no anchor. Sunspots enter the price, and there are many equilibria

4.1 Overlapping generations: four questions

[Intermediate] Garratt and Wallace put bitcoin B, as an outside money, into Samuelson's two-period overlapping generations model. Each period N people are born. They receive perishable goods wyoung when young and wold when old; when young they give up goods to acquire coins, and when old they sell the coins to the next generation. If ptB is the goods price of the coin, consumption when young is ctyoung=wyoung−ptBbt and when old ctold=wold+pt+1Bbt (equations (1) and (2)). Rather than map the whole set of equilibria, the authors ask four questions: "(i) Is there an equilibrium in which the value of bitcoin is constant and positive? (ii) Is there an equilibrium in which the value of bitcoin is always zero? (iii) Is there an equilibrium in which the value of bitcoin is zero at some known date T and is positive at some earlier dates? (iv) Is there an equilibrium in which the value of bitcoin is random in the following way: if it has been positive and constant at each date 1, 2, …, t − 1, then with probability π the value is equal to that constant at t; otherwise, it is zero at t and thereafter."10

[Intermediate] The answers are as follows. (i) is "maybe." If the utility function and the income stream give an incentive to save when young (scenario (a) of Figure 1), there is a constant positive saving sB*, and the price is set by sB*=pB(B/N). Otherwise there is none. (ii) is "yes." "Suppose at any t, the young at t believe that bitcoin will be worthless at t + 1; that pt+1B=0. Then, each young person chooses bt=0 at time t at any ptB>0. (Why give up goods which can be consumed when young in order to acquire an asset that will be worthless when it is sold?) Because this conclusion holds for each t, there is an equilibrium in which ptB=0 for all t." (iii) is "no." If the price is zero at T, nobody acquires the coin at T−1, and by backward induction nobody acquires it before that either. (iv) is a conditional "yes." If π is close enough to 1, such an equilibrium exists.11 Here (ii) and (iii) have to be read together. A price of zero is always an equilibrium, but "it goes to zero on a known date" is not an equilibrium. Of the four questions, the route by which a collapse enters an equilibrium is (iv), that is, a collapse that comes with a small probability every period, and the authors add in their conclusion that generalizing the nature of the randomness makes the set of equilibria larger.

[Basic] The example the authors attach to (iv) shows the point of this chapter in numbers: "Suppose the answer to question (iv) is positive, that π=0.99, that we are living at date 68, that heads has been experienced at all earlier dates, but that tails has occurred at date 68. Someone might be tempted to criticize economists for not having predicted the collapse in the value of money at date 67. At t=1, someone who knows the model and the equilibrium would have said that the probability of a collapse at some time in the first 68 periods is (1−.9968)=0.495, almost one-half. However, from the vantage point of date 67, a collapse at date 68 happens only with probability 0.01. In other words, … although a collapse at some time is likely, predicting when it will occur is not possible."12 NB19-1 below runs this arithmetic as it stands. Heads and tails can be read in two ways. They may be a purely extrinsic sunspot (Cass–Shell), or intrinsic events such as "the appearance of a preferred version of bitcoin, say bitcoin 2," a disruption in which "someone hacks the protocol," or "the passage of a law outlawing bitcoin." In a footnote the authors name the launch of Bitcoin Cash on August 1, 2017 as a candidate for such an event and write only "Time will tell …."13

[Intermediate] With two currencies the problem grows. If there are no storage costs and the two monies are perfect substitutes, a constant-price equilibrium requires only one condition, equation (11) s*=pBB/N+pMM/N, so "this allows a wide array of constant money price combinations." Only by assuming strong preferences, of the kind "Suppose a fraction α of each generation only wishes to hold B and a fraction 1−α of each generation only wishes to hold M," is the value pinned down, by equation (13) pB=αNs/B, and "So the price of each money is increasing in the fraction of people that prefer to use it and decreasing in the stock of each money." The authors then write that this analysis "extends easily to bitcoin 1, bitcoin 2, …, bitcoin n," and that "absent strong preferences over equivalent types of outside money there would be a high degree of price indeterminacy, even in the simplest, constant price equilibrium."14 This is where the title's "Bitcoin 1, Bitcoin 2, …" comes from. The fact from Part 1 that copying code costs almost nothing reads, in economics, as a fact that makes the belief propping up value thinner. Last comes interest. If the coin pays interest d>0 in some other valuable object, then because "the yield on bitcoin is d/p, which for a given d>0 goes to infinity as p goes to zero," the zero-price equilibrium and the type (iv) equilibrium disappear.15 Put the other way round, the multiplicity in this chapter comes from "no dividend." If that premise changes, so does the conclusion.

4.2 Infinitely lived agents: the fundamental pricing equation and the martingale

[Intermediate] In Schilling and Uhlig's model, two types of agents live forever and alternate between consuming and producing in odd and even periods. So in each period they split into sellers and buyers, and money is needed. There are two monies: dollars, which the central bank adds and withdraws to meet its price-level target, and bitcoins, whose quantity only grows on a fixed schedule. The condition that must be satisfied in the "fundamental" case, where both monies are used in trade, is the paper's Proposition 1, the fundamental pricing equation. If bitcoin trades take place in both periods,

𝔼t[u′(ct+1)PtPt+1]=𝔼t[u′(ct+1)Qt+1/Pt+1Qt/Pt](1)

and "If u′(ct+1)/Pt+1 is uncorrelated with Qt+1, conditional on time-t information, then the stochastic Bitcoin price process {Qt}t≥0 is a martingale Qt=𝔼t[Qt+1]. (2)"16 Reading the symbols: u′(c) is the marginal utility of consumption, P the dollar price level, and Q the dollar price of bitcoin. The left side is the real return from keeping dollars and spending them next period; the right side is the real return from keeping bitcoin and spending it next period; and for sellers to accept both, the two must be equal. A numerical example: if there is no correlation and today Qt=100 (a unitless model value), the conditional expectation of tomorrow's Qt+1 is 100. If an increase is likely, there must be a possibility of a correspondingly large decrease. The authors' commentary states exactly what this equation means: "The goods seller will sell against the currency which offers a higher risk-preference adjusted return. Due to the currency competition, sales against both Bitcoins and Dollars implies seller indifference. The risk-adjusted returns, therefore, have to be the same." They add that this is "a version of the celebrated result in Kareken and Wallace (1981)," and that in the case without randomness it reduces to Qt=Qt+1, that is, to "their 'exchange rate indeterminacy result' for time t = 0, that any Q0 is consistent with some equilibrium".17

[Intermediate] Next comes the part that belongs to this paper alone. Agents who live forever can keep coins without spending them. Proposition 2 states the "speculative price bound" that must be satisfied in an equilibrium where coins are kept in this way, and the gist is that for coins to be kept, the price must rise in expectation. But Proposition 1 said that when both monies are used, the price is a martingale. Put the two side by side and add "mutual impatience" (Assumption 3: today's marginal utility is greater than tomorrow's discounted expected marginal utility), and Theorem 1 follows: "all Bitcoins are spent and (1) holds in every period t." In the authors' words, "price volatility does not invalidate the medium-of-exchange function of Bitcoin."18 The circle runs like this. The side keeping the coins wants a rise; for sellers to accept coins, tomorrow's price must not be too low; for that, today's price must be high; and if today's price is that high, the reason to keep the coins disappears. In a non-stochastic economy the conditions are Qt+1≤Qt≤β2Qt+2/(πt+2πt+1), and since β<1 and π≥1, the contradiction is immediate.19

[Advanced] The martingale is the special case "if there is no correlation." The general formula, Corollary 1, is Qt=𝔼t[Qt+1]+κt·corrt(mt+1,Qt+1) (equation (5)), where mt=u′(ct)/Pt is the nominal pricing kernel and κt>0. "the Dollar denominated Bitcoin price process is a supermartingale (falls in expectation) if and only if in equilibrium the pricing kernel and the Bitcoin price are positively correlated," and "under negative correlation, the Bitcoin price process is a submartingale and increases in expectation."20 Even inside the model the direction depends on the sign of the correlation, and the model does not fix that sign. So the authors do not just say that equilibria "exist"; they give a recipe for building them. Following equation (8), Qt+1=Qt+ϵt+1−covt(ϵt+1,mt+1)/𝔼t[mt+1]: "Pick the initial Bitcoin price Q0 and pick some sequence ϵt with 𝔼t[ϵt+1]=0 … recursively construct the sequence Qt+1, going forward in time."21 Both Q0 and ϵ are picked. There is not one equilibrium but as many as there are ways to pick. NB19-2 runs this construction with a few choices of ϵ and shows the paths that branch off from the same Q0. Those paths are model variables, not prices. Separately, if there is a cap on issuance and dollar inflation is positive, there is Proposition 3 (Real Bitcoin Disappearance): "the purchasing power of the entire stock of Bitcoin shrinks to zero over time." This too is a conditional proposition, "Only a sufficiently high risk premium can avoid the Bitcoin disappearance," and the authors write that once the free entry of §7 of the paper is added, the result "may no longer obtain".22

4.3 Transactional benefits: a "fundamental value" with no anchor

[Intermediate] The 2023 paper by Bruno Biais and coauthors gives the coin transactional benefits: the benefit that "citizens of Venezuela or Zimbabwe can use Bitcoin to conduct transactions even when their national currencies and banking systems are in disarray. Cryptocurrencies can be used for cross-border transfers when high costs or government controls hinder transfers via traditional financial institutions," and the costs of "limited convertibility into traditional currencies, transaction costs on exchanges, fees that agents must pay to have their transactions mined, and the risk of a crash of the cryptocurrency."23 The coin then comes to resemble a stock. "transactional benefits are to cryptocurrencies what dividends are to stocks. There is however a major difference. In perfect markets, dividends do not depend on stock prices and provide a real anchor for valuation. In contrast, the transactional benefits provided by a cryptocurrency depend on its price: the higher the price of the cryptocurrency, the stronger is its purchasing power relative to the standard currency, and consequently the higher are the transactional benefits it delivers."24 Equation (12) of Proposition 1 writes the price as the discounted sum of future transactional benefits Tt+kpt+k, and pt+k sits inside it. The fundamental value is a function of the price. Hence, "Because cryptocurrency prices reflect beliefs about future prices rather than real variables independent of prices, equilibrium can reflect exogenous sunspots." The authors construct two kinds of equilibrium: constant-price equilibria, one for each probability of a crash, and volatile-price equilibria, in which the sunspot moves the price every period. "There are multiple equilibria, one for each possible distribution of the sample path of the sunspot. Within each equilibrium there is extrinsic volatility, since cryptocurrency prices change in response to realizations of the sunspot variable, even when fundamental variables remain constant."25

[Advanced] The paper also fits the model to data. From mining fees, events such as exchange openings and closures, events such as merchant acceptance, and data on hacks, it builds indices of transaction costs and benefits and calibrates the model under an assumption of risk neutrality. The authors write in advance that "we do not claim statistical significance or estimation of population parameters because of the relatively short size of our sample and the likely non stationarity of our variables," and summarize the result this way: "changes in fundamentals explain only a small share (around 5%) of the variance of Bitcoin returns. Under the hypothesis that our model is well-specified and our proxies accurate, this implies that most of Bitcoin return variation reflects extrinsic volatility unrelated to fundamentals."26 When you carry this figure over, you must not cut off the conditional clause. "Around 5%" is a calibrated value under the assumption that the model and the proxies are right, and the authors themselves do not call it an estimate. What this chapter takes from the figure is not its size but the admission that even the authors of this model could not explain most of the data with "fundamentals."

[Advanced] The words "bubble" and "Ponzi": where rational bubbles fit

[Advanced] The multiplicity in this chapter has the same root as the results of the rational bubbles literature of the 1980s. A 1982 paper by Olivier Blanchard and Mark Watson shows that the solution of the arbitrage condition 𝔼(pt+1|Ωt)−pt+xt=rpt (equation (1)) is not just the single pt*, "the present value of expected dividends": every pt=pt*+ct (equation (3)) obtained by adding any ct that satisfies 𝔼(ct+1|Ωt)=(1+r)ct is a solution too. "the market price can deviate from its market fundamental value without violating the arbitrage condition." They then give as an example a bubble of which "In each period, the bubble will remain, with probability π, or crash, with probability 1−π" (equation (4)), the same shape as Garratt–Wallace's (iv).27 Jean Tirole's 1985 paper, which gives necessary and sufficient conditions for an aggregate bubble to exist in an overlapping generations economy, writes: "Since Samuelson [30] developed his consumption loan model it has been well known that there exist economies in which money has a positive value in spite of the fact that it is intrinsically useless (i.e., its market fundamental is zero). In other words there can exist a bubble on money where a bubble is defined as the difference between the market price and the market fundamental."28 In the language of this literature, the value of fiat money is itself a "bubble." Here the word is not a term of abuse but a defined term. The problem of judging statistically that "it was a bubble" is taken up in Chapter 25; how Maarten van Oordt's 2024 model defines the "bubble equilibrium" and "Ponzi-scheme equivalent payoffs," and how the issuance rule (in particular fee burning) changes that distinction, come up again in Chapters 21 and 22.29

5. Code: the listing of equilibria in numbers

[Intermediate] The two cells below do not deal with prices. What they deal with are variables and probabilities inside models. The first cell runs Garratt–Wallace's "date 68" arithmetic; the second builds equilibria according to Schilling–Uhlig's equation (8).

# NB19-1: Garratt–Wallace question (iv) — a collapse that comes with probability 1−π each period. The probability of "some time" and the probability of "the very next period" differ (for study)
pi = 0.99                                            # probability of surviving one more period (the paper's example)
print(f"π = {pi}: conditional probability of a collapse in the next period = {1 - pi:.2f}")
print(f"{'n':>6} {'P(collapse within n) 1−π^n':>26} {'P(survive through n) π^n':>26}")
for n in [1, 10, 30, 68, 100, 300, 1000]:
    print(f"{n:>6} {1 - pi**n:>26.3f} {pi**n:>26.3f}")
print("\nThe probability of a collapse within 68 periods is almost one-half, but the probability of a collapse at date 68, seen from date 67, is still 0.01 (the arithmetic on pp. 1891–1892 of the paper).")
print("The date of the collapse follows a geometric distribution, and its expected value is", round(1 / (1 - pi)), "periods: there is a mean but no date.")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
π = 0.99: conditional probability of a collapse in the next period = 0.01
     n P(collapse within n) 1−π^n   P(survive through n) π^n
     1                      0.010                      0.990
    10                      0.096                      0.904
    30                      0.260                      0.740
    68                      0.495                      0.505
   100                      0.634                      0.366
   300                      0.951                      0.049
  1000                      1.000                      0.000

The probability of a collapse within 68 periods is almost one-half, but the probability of a collapse at date 68, seen from date 67, is still 0.01 (the arithmetic on pp. 1891–1892 of the paper).
The date of the collapse follows a geometric distribution, and its expected value is 100 periods: there is a mean but no date.

# NB19-2: Schilling–Uhlig equation (8) — "pick" an initial value Q0 and a mean-zero shock ε, and one equilibrium path is built. There are as many equilibria as there are ways to pick (for study)
# Note: Q is a model variable (unitless). It is not the price of any asset, and the paths below are not forecasts.
import random
random.seed(19)

def construct_path(Q0, steps, eps_draw, cov_term=0.0):
    """Eq. (8): Q_{t+1} = Q_t + ε_{t+1} − cov_t(ε_{t+1}, m_{t+1}) / E_t[m_{t+1}].
    With cov_term=0 this is a martingale (Proposition 1, eq. (2)). With a correlation, cov_term adds an expected change (Corollary 1)."""
    Q = [Q0]
    for _ in range(steps):
        Q.append(Q[-1] + eps_draw() - cov_term)
    return Q

Q0, steps = 100.0, 12
draws = {
    "ε≡0 (Kareken–Wallace constant price)": lambda: 0.0,
    "ε ~ uniform(−5, 5)":                   lambda: random.uniform(-5, 5),
    "ε ∈ {−20, +20}, each 1/2":             lambda: random.choice([-20.0, 20.0]),
}
print(f"Q0 = {Q0}, {steps} periods. Three equilibrium paths from the same Q0 (martingale, cov term 0):")
for name, d in draws.items():
    path = construct_path(Q0, steps, d)
    print(f"  {name:<36} → " + " ".join(f"{q:6.1f}" for q in path))

# Numerical check of the martingale property: the mean over many paths stays near Q0 (it neither rises nor falls in expectation)
N = 20000
end_values = [construct_path(Q0, steps, draws["ε ~ uniform(−5, 5)"])[-1] for _ in range(N)]
print(f"\nMean at the end of period {steps} over {N:,} uniform-shock paths: {sum(end_values)/N:.2f} (Q0 = {Q0}). The mean stays put; only the spread grows")
print(f"  End of period {steps}: min {min(end_values):.1f}, max {max(end_values):.1f}")

# Corollary 1: positive correlation with the pricing kernel gives a supermartingale (falls in expectation), negative a submartingale (rises). The model does not fix the sign.
for cov_term, label in [(1.0, "cov > 0 → supermartingale"), (-1.0, "cov < 0 → submartingale")]:
    mean_end = sum(construct_path(Q0, steps, draws["ε ~ uniform(−5, 5)"], cov_term)[-1] for _ in range(N)) / N
    print(f"  {label}: mean at the end of period {steps} = {mean_end:.2f}")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
Q0 = 100.0, 12 periods. Three equilibrium paths from the same Q0 (martingale, cov term 0):
  ε≡0 (Kareken–Wallace constant price) →  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0  100.0
  ε ~ uniform(−5, 5)                   →  100.0  101.8  104.6  104.8  104.9  103.9  108.8  106.7  103.2  100.8   98.4   96.7   94.4
  ε ∈ {−20, +20}, each 1/2             →  100.0   80.0  100.0  120.0  100.0   80.0   60.0   40.0   20.0   40.0   60.0   40.0   20.0

Mean at the end of period 12 over 20,000 uniform-shock paths: 99.94 (Q0 = 100.0). The mean stays put; only the spread grows
  End of period 12: min 64.7, max 138.4
  cov > 0 → supermartingale: mean at the end of period 12 = 87.89
  cov < 0 → submartingale: mean at the end of period 12 = 112.12

[Intermediate] The three paths in the second cell are all equilibria as long as they satisfy the conditions of equation (8) (a positive price, the upper bound of Corollary 2). The model does not say which one is the "right" path. The first path is Kareken–Wallace's constant price; the second and third start from the same Q0 and differ only in the size of the shock picked. That the mean of 20,000 paths stays at Q0 is what a martingale means, and the last two lines are a numerical version of Corollary 1, in which the sign of the correlation alone changes the direction of the mean. What to take from this cell is not the shape of the paths but the verb "pick."

6. What the models say and what they do not

[Basic] Laid over one another, the three models have two things in common. First, a price of zero is always an equilibrium. Garratt–Wallace and Biais et al. state that this equilibrium exists (Biais et al. write in a footnote that "There always exists an equilibrium such that pt=0 ∀t" and analyze the positive-price equilibria), and Schilling–Uhlig, following Kareken–Wallace in their §7, write down the backward self-elimination: "if tomorrow's price of a currency is zero, its price today is zero as well."30 Second, positive-price equilibria are held up by beliefs and are not pinned down to one. The more clone coins there are (Garratt–Wallace), and the more transactional benefits depend on the price itself (Biais et al.), the thinner the anchor of that belief. And there are things none of them says: which equilibrium is realized, which equilibrium today's price sits on, which direction the next period goes. In their conclusion Garratt and Wallace write: "none of the equilibria described in this paper provide a good description of its value. … That is why we said at the outset that the number of equilibria is huge."31 That is why this chapter holds on to the phrase "a listing of possibilities."

[Basic] So look again at the two clichés. "It has no intrinsic value, so it will go to zero" turns the fact that (ii) is an equilibrium into the claim that (iii) holds. The model allows "some day," but it rules out "when." "It is scarce, so it has value" looks only at the fact that B is in the denominator of equation (13) and leaves out the fact that α (the share of people who want to use it) is in the numerator. If α=0, then however small B is, pB=0. Both clichés are propositions with their conditional clauses deleted, and in a legal document a proposition whose conditions have been deleted is hard to use as material for fact-finding.

[Basic] Last, before moving on to the box below, look at the place the models give to legal tender. Biais et al. note that the price of the standard currency could also go to zero, but "As Starr (1974) shows, however, this can be prevented when the government levies taxes that must be paid in that currency: even if agents anticipate that others will not to accept [sic] the standard currency, as long as they know that the government will accept it for the payment of taxes, demand for the standard currency is strictly positive at prices bounded away from zero," and so they analyze only equilibria in which the price of the standard currency is positive.32 Garratt and Wallace too, at the opening of their paper, gave as the reason why Kareken and Wallace's conditions for indeterminacy do not fit national currencies that Kareken and Wallace "did not assume that the taxes levied by a country have to be paid in the form of that country's currency or that some prices denominated in the currency of a country are fixed or sticky."33 Nowhere in the three models is there a mechanism by which value arises because "the law calls it money." What there is, is a floor of demand called taxation. That is the line that separates bitcoin from the dollar at the opening of Garratt–Wallace and in Biais et al.; in Schilling–Uhlig the central bank's supply adjustments toward its price-level target play that part, and in §IV of Garratt–Wallace the storage cost of fiat money does. The line of taxation is drawn by law, not by technology.

A lawyer's question

Are legal tender and "money" the same thing? In this chapter's models, what separated national currency from bitcoin was not the fact that "the law calls it money" but the floor of demand created by "taxes must be paid in it." Then what changes when the law calls an object "money": the effect of discharging debts (legal tender), its status as a unit of account, its standing as the object of criminal provisions (counterfeiting and currency offenses), the framework of taxation, or something else? Conversely, in which areas of law is an object that people accept, without the law calling it anything, treated as "money," and in which as "property"? Of the three functions in the functions approach, how many does the law require? This book does not answer; in Part 5 it points to each jurisdiction's definitional provisions and the layout of scholarly views. → Chapter 27

7. Summary

[Basic] The functions approach is a checklist. Crypto-assets do not score well on it, but that does not mean a price of zero. The answer economics has given to the question of price is a listing of equilibria. An outside money with no dividend has both a zero-price equilibrium and positive-price equilibria, and the positive-price equilibria are held up by the belief that "others will accept it" and are not pinned down to one. The overlapping generations model shows that a collapse can come "some day" but that "when" cannot be predicted; the infinitely lived agents model shows that when two currencies are used together the price is a martingale (if it is uncorrelated with the pricing kernel) and that the sign of the correlation sets the direction of the expected change; and the transactional benefits model shows that the "fundamental value" depends on the price itself and so has no anchor. This chapter never once stated a price, and the chapters that follow do not either. Chapter 20 looks at how the issuance rule Bt, which this chapter treated as "given," is the source of funding for security, and Chapter 21 at how fees, the other half of that funding, are set.

Part 3 · Economics

Chapter 20. The security budget: from rewards to fees

Key takeaway

The security of a blockchain is not free. It is an upkeep cost paid every block. The reward that miners (or validators) receive every block draws out the spending of the honest participants, and the size of that spending is the height of the wall an attacker has to get over. Eric Budish writes this as three equations: the zero-profit condition N*c=pblock, the incentive-compatibility condition A*N*c·t(A*)>Vattack, and the equilibrium constraint that combines the two, pblock>Vattack/(A*t(A*)). In words, the reward per block must at all times be large relative to the value that can be obtained by attacking. Bitcoin's reward is made up of the subsidy (new coins) and fees, and the subsidy is designed to halve every 210,000 blocks and go to 0. Fees then have to fill its place, and Miles Carlsten and his coauthors show that in a world where only fees remain, the mining game itself becomes unstable. After this chapter you will know how to calculate "the cost of a 51% attack," which variables enter that calculation in place of the coin price, and why a halving is an event for the security budget, not a price event.

Learning objectives

  1. Confirm from the constants in the Core source that the block reward is made up of the subsidy and fees, and that Bitcoin's subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks so that the total converges to 21 million.
  2. [Intermediate] Read Budish's three equations (zero profit, incentive compatibility, equilibrium constraint) and say what it means that the cost of a majority attack is a flow, not a stock. Calculate the attack cost as "hash-rate share × duration × unit price," knowing that the inputs are hash rate, unit price, and time, not the coin price.
  3. [Intermediate] Calculate the expected duration t(A,e,k) of a double-spending attack with the formula of Budish's Proposition 3, and reproduce Table II. Place the time-bandit attack of Chapter 17 in the same framework (equation (3)), and know where it differs from the setting of Proposition 3.
  4. [Advanced] Read why the mining game in a world where the subsidy has reached 0 (Carlsten et al.: the mining gap, undercutting, and selfish mining with the back door open) differs from the block-reward world, and how "the stock loss of specialized capital" (Budish §V) changes the cost calculation.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. The security of a blockchain is not free. It is an upkeep cost paid every block, and the source of that upkeep is shifting from new coins to fees.

1. The question this chapter answers

[Basic] In Chapter 8, proof of work was a device under which "rewriting one block means redoing that much computation," and in Chapter 9 the probability that an attacker catches up with the honest chain shrank with the number of confirmations z as long as the share q did not exceed one half. Both chapters assumed that "the attacker does not have that much computing power." Where does that assumption come from? Computing power can be bought and rented. There is no reason an attacker cannot assemble more computing power than the honest participants are using now. What there is, is only cost. The question then becomes this. Why are the honest participants spending that much computing power, what decides the size of that computing power, and how much does it cost to exceed it?

[Basic] Nakamoto's white paper gave this question half a page, §6, "Incentive": "By convention, the first transaction in a block is a special transaction that starts a new coin owned by the creator of the block. This adds an incentive for nodes to support the network, and provides a way to initially distribute coins into circulation, since there is no central authority to issue them. … The incentive can also be funded with transaction fees. … Once a predetermined number of coins have entered circulation, the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees and be completely inflation free." And one sentence on the attacker: "If a greedy attacker is able to assemble more CPU power than all the honest nodes, he would have to choose between using it to defraud people by stealing back his payments, or using it to generate new coins. He ought to find it more profitable to play by the rules, such rules that favour him with more new coins than everyone else combined, than to undermine the system and the validity of his own wealth."1 This chapter rewrites that half page in economics. To give the conclusion first, the last sentence of the white paper holds only conditionally, and the condition is "when what an attack would obtain is small relative to the block reward."

2. The two parts of the reward: subsidy and fees

[Basic] The person who makes a block receives two things: coins the protocol newly creates (the subsidy, block subsidy) and the fees paid by the transactions in that block. As we saw in Chapter 11, a fee is the difference between the sum of the inputs and the sum of the outputs, and the subsidy is the output of the coinbase transaction (in the genesis block of Chapter 12 that value was 50 BTC). The subsidy rule is written as constants in the Bitcoin Core source: the halving interval nSubsidyHalvingInterval = 210000, the initial subsidy 50 * COIN, and the GetBlockSubsidy function, which shifts 50 BTC right by as many bits as the quotient of the height divided by 210,000 and gives back 0 if that quotient is 64 or more.2 Because the shift is applied to the integer 5 billion in satoshis, the subsidy falls below 1 satoshi and becomes 0 at the 33rd halving, and the total converges to a value short of 21 million BTC. NB20-1 below computes that sum in integer arithmetic.

[Basic] What this rule means is that the composition of the reward changes over time. At first it was almost entirely subsidy, and, as Nakamoto wrote, at the end it becomes entirely fees. The 2016 paper by Carlsten and his coauthors calls this transition a move from the block-reward regime to the transaction-fee regime, and announces that the transition breaks "an unexamined belief that in terms of the security of the block chain (including incentives of the mining game), it is immaterial whether miners receive (say) 25 bitcoins in each block as a block reward or 25 bitcoins in expectation as transaction fees."3 Section 6 looks at that argument. Before that, we need a framework that decides how large the reward has to be.

# NB20-1: Bitcoin's subsidy schedule, a port of Core's GetBlockSubsidy in the same integer arithmetic (for study)
COIN = 100_000_000                      # 1 BTC = 1e8 satoshis (consensus/amount.h)
HALVING = 210_000                       # nSubsidyHalvingInterval (chainparams.cpp)

def block_subsidy_sat(height: int) -> int:
    halvings = height // HALVING
    if halvings >= 64:                  # validation.cpp: 0 after 64 or more halvings (guards the shift width)
        return 0
    return (50 * COIN) >> halvings      # halve 50 BTC `halvings` times; an integer bit shift, so anything below 1 satoshi is discarded

print(f"{'halvings':>8} {'start height':>12} {'block subsidy (BTC)':>20} {'cumulative issued by end (BTC)':>30}")
cum = 0
for h in range(0, 36):
    start = h * HALVING
    sub = block_subsidy_sat(start)
    cum += sub * HALVING
    if h <= 6 or sub == 0 or h in (10, 20, 32, 33, 34):
        print(f"{h:>8} {start:>12,} {sub / COIN:>20.8f} {cum / COIN:>30.8f}")
    if sub == 0:
        break
total = sum(block_subsidy_sat(h * HALVING) * HALVING for h in range(0, 64))
print(f"\nSum of the subsidy in integer arithmetic: {total:,} satoshis = {total / COIN:.8f} BTC ({21_000_000 - total / COIN:.8f} BTC short of 21,000,000)")
tip = 972_958                           # chain-tip height observed 2026-10-24 UTC (data/hashrate_2026-10-25.json)
print(f"Height on the reference date {tip:,}: after {tip // HALVING} halvings, block subsidy {block_subsidy_sat(tip) / COIN} BTC, next halving at height {(tip // HALVING + 1) * HALVING:,} (about {((tip // HALVING + 1) * HALVING - tip) * 10 / 60 / 24:.0f} days away, assuming 10 minutes per block)")

Height on the reference date 972,958: after 4 halvings, block subsidy 3.125 BTC, next halving at height 1,050,000 (about 535 days away, assuming 10 minutes per block)

[Basic] On the reference date (as of 2026-10), Bitcoin is in the interval after the fourth halving, and the block subsidy is 3.125 BTC.4 This figure is listed in Appendix A. At the next halving it becomes 1.5625 BTC. This chapter treats a halving only as an event for the security budget. For the same fee revenue, one halving cuts the subsidy portion of the reward per block in half, and in an equilibrium where equation (1) of Section 3 holds, it lowers the wall of attack cost by that much. To keep the wall where it is, fees have to make up that portion.

3. Budish's three equations: security is a flow

[Intermediate] Budish's 2025 paper sums itself up: "The core argument is three equations."5 We read them in turn, using the paper's own symbols. N is the total quantity of "trust support" (hash rate under proof of work, coins locked up as collateral under proof of stake), c is the cost of supplying one unit of it for one unit of time, and pblock is the reward a participant receives for adding one block (subsidy and fees together).

First, the zero-profit condition. Anyone can enter and leave, so competition drives participants' profit to 0. The probability that participant i gets the next block is the share xi/N, and if difficulty D is the expected trust support·time per block, a block appears on average every D/N time. The profit per unit of trust support per unit of time is 1NDNpblock−c, and normalizing so that one block appears per unit of time (D*=N*) gives Proposition 1.

N*c=pblock(1)

Reading the symbols: what all the honest participants spend per unit of time equals the block reward paid in that time. A numerical example: if the reward per block is worth 3.2 BTC, the electricity and equipment cost that all honest miners spend every 10 minutes is also worth 3.2 BTC. Budish writes that this is "the standard characterization of a rent-seeking tournament: the prize in the tournament, pblock, is dissipated by expenditures aimed at winning the prize, N*c," and that "Prat and Walter (2021) provide empirical support that equation (1) describes actual equilibrium behavior in the Bitcoin mining market …."6 Look at what the difficulty adjustment of Chapter 8 does here. More hash rate does not mean more blocks (the very property Schilling and Uhlig describe when they write that "the increase in the hash rate has no impact on the total Bitcoin production"21), so added spending only splits the reward more ways, and spending therefore rises or falls until profit reaches 0.

Second, the incentive-compatibility condition. Add one attacker rather than all the honest participants. The attacker brings AN* units (A>1) to get a majority of AA+1, and spends AN*c per unit of time. If t(A) is the expected time until the attack ends, the gross cost of attack is AN*c·t(A), and the attacker picks the A* that minimizes A·t(A). With Vattack the value obtained from the attack,

A*N*c·t(A*)>Vattack(2)

is the condition under which the system is "incentive compatible (IC) against an outsider attack, on a gross-cost basis."7

Third, the equilibrium constraint. N*c appears in both equations, so substituting (1) into (2) gives Theorem 1.

pblock>VattackA*·t(A*)(3)

"In words: the equilibrium per block payment to participants for providing trust support on the blockchain must be large relative to the benefits of attacking the blockchain."8 Reading the symbols: the denominator A*t(A*) is a pure number (no unit) that measures "how many honest blocks' worth of cost one attack amounts to," and Table II in Section 4 gives its value. We will give the numerical example after looking at that table. What to take from here is the shape of the equation. Time sits on the right-hand side. The attacker pays only while the attack lasts and loses nothing afterward. In Budish's words, "Nakamoto trust is memoryless—it is as secure at a moment in time as the amount of trust support at that moment." Security is a flow, not a stock. Hence the analogies that follow: "Imagine if users of the Visa network had to pay fees to Visa, every ten minutes, that were large relative to the value of a successful attack on the Visa network. Imagine a brand was only as trustworthy as its flow investment in advertising. Imagine that a country were only as secure as its flow expenditure on soldiers at the border."9 The difference from traditional trust (law, reputation, collateral) is economies of scale. Courts deter many crimes with the mere threat of punishment, and the police protect many banks without standing in front of any one of them. Nakamoto trust has no such lever. "[I]f attacking the system grows 1,000 times more attractive, then the cost of securing the system must grow 1,000 times as well."10

[Intermediate] One caveat here connects to Chapter 10. Budish says repeatedly that the three equations are not limited to proof of work: "Trust support can take the form of providing computational work as in Bitcoin ('proof of work'), … or posting cryptocurrency coins in a proof-of-stake protocol, such as Ethereum." Under proof of stake, c is "the opportunity cost per unit time to supply one unit of stake." Stake does differ from work in one respect: "stakes are not as memoryless as computational work: stakes can be locked up on chain for a period of time, like collateral, … This opens up the possibility of punishing attackers by confiscating their locked stakes (slashing) …."11 That is the "stock loss" of Section 7.

4. How long an attack takes and what it costs: Proposition 3 and Table II

[Intermediate] To fill in the denominator A*t(A*) of equation (3), we need to know how long an attack takes. Budish sets out a double-spending attack in five steps: "(i) The attacker sends cryptocurrency in exchange for goods or assets … (ii) The attacker allows those transactions to be added to the blockchain in the usual way … (iii) The attacker works in secret to create an alternative longest chain that does not include the transactions in (i). … (iv) The attacker waits for any escrow periods to elapse … (v) The attacker releases their alternative longest chain." He then turns the probability calculation of Chapter 9 into an expected time. Let k be the number of blocks in which the attacker placed transactions and e the escrow (the number of confirmations the receiving side waits for), and suppose the honest side produces one block per unit of time and the attacker A blocks, both as Poisson processes. Proposition 3 then gives12

t(A,e,k)=(k+e)+∑i=0k+e(i+1A−1)·(2(k+e)−1−i)!(k+e−i)!(k+e−1)!(A1+A)k+e−i(11+A)k+e(6)

Reading the symbols: the first term k+e is the attacker's best case (already ahead while the honest side produces k+e blocks), and each term of the sum is "the probability that the attacker is i blocks behind at that point × the expected time (i+1)/(A−1) to make up that deficit." As A→∞, t→k+e, and as A→1+, t→∞. Budish notes that "Prior work by Grunspan and Pérez-Marco (2018, 2022) derives closely related mathematical results for the analysis of an attacker with less than 50% of the total hash power." That is the very paper we read in Chapter 9.13

# NB20-2: Budish's Proposition 3, the expected duration t(A, e, k) of a double-spending attack and the gross cost A·t in units of honest block rewards (for study)
# The only inputs are the attacker multiple A (share A/(1+A)) and the block count k+e. No coin price, no fiat unit price.
from math import lgamma, log, exp

def attack_duration(A: float, ke: int) -> float:
    """Equation (6). Factorials via log-gamma, to avoid overflow at large ke. Unit: honest block time (≈10 minutes)."""
    t = float(ke)
    for i in range(0, ke + 1):
        log_comb = lgamma(2 * ke - i) - lgamma(ke - i + 1) - lgamma(ke)   # (2ke−1−i)! / ((ke−i)! (ke−1)!)
        log_prob = (ke - i) * log(A / (1 + A)) + ke * log(1 / (1 + A))
        t += (i + 1) / (A - 1) * exp(log_comb + log_prob)
    return t

rows = [1.05, 1.10, 1.20, 1.33, 1.50, 2.00, 5.00]
cols = [1, 6, 12, 36, 144]
print("Expected duration t (unit: honest block time). Columns = k+e (double-spent blocks + escrow)")
print(f"{'A (share)':>14}" + "".join(f"{c:>10}" for c in cols))
for A in rows:
    print(f"{A:>5.2f} ({A/(1+A):4.0%})" + "".join(f"{attack_duration(A, c):>10.2f}" for c in cols))
print("\nGross cost A·t (unit: honest trust-support cost per block N*c = block reward p_block)")
print(f"{'A (share)':>14}" + "".join(f"{c:>10}" for c in cols))
for A in rows:
    print(f"{A:>5.2f} ({A/(1+A):4.0%})" + "".join(f"{A * attack_duration(A, c):>10.2f}" for c in cols))

# The attacker picks the A that minimizes A·t. Grid search at k+e = 12 (the paper's base case)
ke = 12
best = min(((A / 100) * attack_duration(A / 100, ke), A / 100) for A in range(101, 600))
print(f"\nk+e = {ke}: the A that minimizes A·t is A* ≈ {best[1]:.2f} (share {best[1]/(1+best[1]):.0%}), minimum A*·t(A*) ≈ {best[0]:.2f} block rewards")
print(f"→ equation (3): p_block > V_attack / {best[0]:.1f}, i.e., the reward per block must exceed {1/best[0]:.2%} of the attack value")

[Intermediate] This output reproduces Budish's Table II to the second decimal place (p. 36 of the paper). Here is how to read it. An attacker with a 51.2% share (A=1.05) wins in the end, statistically, but at k+e=12 the attack takes 56.6 blocks on average (about 9.5 hours) and costs 59.4 block rewards. Raise the share to 60% and these fall to 13.4 blocks and 20.1 block rewards. As Budish writes, "It is true that a 51% majority is enough to ensure statistically that the attack will eventually succeed, but a cost-minimizing attacker will choose a somewhat larger majority."14 The last line is the numerical example for equation (3). At k+e=12, A*≈1.43 and A*t(A*)≈20.0, so the reward per block must exceed 5.00% of the attack value. Budish's Table III starts from this 5.00%: "A cost of 5% per block amounts to 720% of the value secured against attack per day, and about 263,000% of the value secured against attack per year. For example, to secure the system against a $1 billion attack requires $2.63 trillion of annual security expense." Conversely, a longer escrow lowers the cost: if e+k is a week (1,008 blocks), it is 0.09% per block.15 These dollar figures are values from a thought experiment that assumes a Vattack; they are not the price of any asset. What this book takes from them is the proportion. If the value to be protected is ten times larger, the security budget must also be ten times larger, and either users pay for it as fees or holders bear it through issuance.

The net cost may be zero

[Intermediate] The calculation above is the gross cost. The attacker also makes blocks during the attack, and if the attacker's chain wins, the attacker receives the rewards for those blocks. Budish's Theorem 2 states the extreme case: "If the attacker does not face any cost frictions relative to the costs of honest participants (κ = 0), the attack concludes without any difficulty adjustment (D′=D*), and the attack does not cause the value of the cryptocurrency to fall (Δattack=0), then the net cost of attack is zero." The proof is one line. By equation (1), the attacker's cost At·N*c equals the reward the attacker receives, At·pblock. "The intuition behind this result is that the attacker is fully compensated for their trust-support costs for the same reason that honest participants are fully compensated for their trust-support costs under honest play. In effect, permissionless consensus treats the attacker as if they are an honest participant, because the majority determines the truth."16 The author himself writes that "zero attack frictions seems unrealistic," but the theorem brings out what the probability calculation of Chapter 9 missed. What costs the attacker most is not hashing but frictions (less efficient equipment, the cost of starting and stopping) and the fall in value.

The time-bandit attack of Chapter 17 is the same calculation

[Intermediate] Chapter 17 described the time-bandit attack of Daian and his coauthors and left the cost calculation to this chapter: "Suppose a blockchain has a suffix (subchain) [height0, height1], with current block height height1, in which stealable value exceeds block rewards. An adversary can rewind to height0 and use the resulting MEV to subsidize a profitable 51% attack that mines a fork up to or past height1."17 Placed in Budish's framework, Vattack is the extractable value of that suffix, and the logic of equation (3) (whether the benefit of the attack exceeds the block rewards spent over the attack period) applies as it stands. It is not, however, the same as the setting of Proposition 3. The attacker of Proposition 3 builds the secret chain side by side with the honest chain from the moment of the double spend, whereas the time bandit starts already behind by the height1−height0 blocks that have been settled, so the expected number of blocks needed to catch up is larger than the values in Table II (this book does not derive that formula). The only condition Daian et al. state is that "stealable value exceeds block rewards," and the sentence Chapter 17 quotes, that "application-layer security poses a current and direct threat to consensus-layer security," points to the shape of this comparison. And that threshold falls as the block reward gets smaller. Ethereum's burning of the base fee, which Chapter 21 covers, is one of the designs aimed at this point.

5. An attack-cost calculator: the inputs are hash rate, unit price, and time

[Intermediate] Now we build the calculator the design called for. There are three inputs: the network hash rate H on the reference date (data bundled), the multiple A of additional hash rate the attacker brings (or the share q=A/(1+A)), and the cost c per unit of hash rate per unit of time, which the user enters. The output is A·H·c·t(A,e,k). The coin price enters nowhere. The unit of the cost is decided by what the user enters as c. Enter electricity unit prices and equipment rental and it is fiat currency; if you know none of these, leave it in "block-reward units," as below. Equation (1) allows this. Since N*c=pblock, the attack cost is A·t·pblock, that is, "so many block rewards."

# NB20-3: attack-cost calculator. Inputs: hash rate (snapshot), attacker multiple, unit price, duration. The coin price is not an input (for study)
import json, os

# Hash-rate snapshot for the reference date (data bundled; if the file is missing, a constant with the same value is used, so it runs on Colab without the file)
try:
    with open(os.path.join("data", "hashrate_2026-10-25.json"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
        snap = json.load(f)
    H_network = float(snap["estimate"]["hashrate_H_per_s"])
except FileNotFoundError:
    H_network = 1.006294e21                 # H/s, estimated from difficulty 140,577,680,051,919.6 as D·2^32/600 (600 seconds assumed)
print(f"Estimated hash rate on the reference date H = {H_network:.3e} H/s = {H_network/1e18:,.0f} EH/s (2026-10-24 UTC, estimate assuming 600 seconds; about 7% below the comparison value)")

def attack_cost(A, ke, c_per_hash_second=None, p_block=None):
    """Gross cost. Given c_per_hash_second, in "unit-price units × hash-seconds"; given p_block, in "block-reward units" via equation (1)."""
    t_blocks = attack_duration(A, ke)
    seconds = t_blocks * 600
    out = {"t_blocks": t_blocks, "hours": seconds / 3600, "attacker_hashrate_hs": A * H_network}
    if c_per_hash_second is not None:
        out["cost_in_price_units"] = A * H_network * c_per_hash_second * seconds
    if p_block is not None:
        out["cost_in_block_rewards"] = A * t_blocks            # equation (1): N*c = p_block
        out["cost_in_coin_of_reward"] = A * t_blocks * p_block
    return out

p_block_subsidy_only = 3.125                 # subsidy on the reference date (BTC). The fee portion F varies from block to block, so this is a lower bound with it set to 0
print(f"\n(a) In block-reward units: a lower bound with fees set to 0, p_block = {p_block_subsidy_only} BTC (subsidy only)")
print(f"{'share':>6} {'A':>5} {'k+e':>4} {'expected blocks':>15} {'time (h)':>8} {'block rewards':>13} {'BTC equiv. (subsidy only)':>25}")
for q in [0.55, 0.60, 0.67]:
    A = q / (1 - q)
    for ke in [6, 12, 144]:
        r = attack_cost(A, ke, p_block=p_block_subsidy_only)
        print(f"{q:>6.0%} {A:>5.2f} {ke:>4} {r['t_blocks']:>15.1f} {r['hours']:>8.1f} {r['cost_in_block_rewards']:>13.1f} {r['cost_in_coin_of_reward']:>25.1f}")

print("\n(b) In the user's unit-price units: c is not the cost per 1 hash but 'the cost of running 1 H/s for 1 second'. The value below is a hypothetical unit price that only fills the slot.")
c_demo = 1e-19                                # hypothetical unit price (no unit). The user enters actual electricity and equipment unit prices
for q in [0.55, 0.60]:
    A = q / (1 - q)
    r = attack_cost(A, 12, c_per_hash_second=c_demo)
    print(f"  share {q:.0%}, k+e=12: attacker hash rate {r['attacker_hashrate_hs']:.2e} H/s × {r['hours']:.1f} hours × unit price → cost {r['cost_in_price_units']:,.0f} (unit-price units)")
print("\nAt the same share and the same duration, the cost is proportional to the unit price c. Enter half the unit price and the cost halves: what this calculator tells you is a proportion, not a level.")

[Intermediate] What to notice in the "block rewards" column of (a) is that the number of block rewards does not depend on the size of the reward. At a 60% share and k+e=12 it is 20.1 block rewards. If a halving cuts the subsidy in half, the BTC equivalent of those 20.1 block rewards is cut in half too, in this table, where fees are set to 0 (if fees are positive, it falls by that much less). That is what "a halving is an event for the security budget" means. The unit price in (b) is a hypothetical value that only fills the slot. This book does not give actual electricity unit prices or equipment rental. This chapter's interactive figure W6 moves only three variables, share, unit price, and duration; it reads the reference-date hash rate from the bundled snapshot and has no price input field.

6. [Advanced] A world where the subsidy has reached 0: Carlsten et al.

[Advanced] How the mining game changes when only fees remain

[Advanced] Carlsten and his coauthors take as their model Bitcoin after the block reward has shrunk to 0. They assume that fees accumulate at a constant rate over time (the fees of the transactions announced in an interval of length t sum to t), that difficulty is set so that one block appears per unit of time, and that there is no latency. The authors write that they chose these simplifications on purpose: "our results are only made stronger by simplifying assumptions, because we are claiming that weird and undesirable consequences arise even if one is willing to grant simplifying assumptions."18

[Advanced] First, the mining gap. "Without a block reward, immediately after a block is found there is zero expected reward for mining but nonzero electricity cost, making it unprofitable for any miner to mine." If one mining rig accounts for a fraction a of the total effective hash power and its electricity cost per unit of time is p, then "a miner must wait t = p/a time steps after a block is found before mining becomes profitable again." As a result, miners end up "mining for a smaller and smaller fraction of the time between the arrival of blocks (with the difficulty dropping to compensate)," and "the effective hash power in the network would drop, and it would become easier for a malicious miner to fork."19 When there is a block reward, there is a reward even right after a block, so this gap does not arise.

[Advanced] Second, undercutting. When the reward differs from block to block, "which block to build on" becomes a strategy. When there is a fork, the default client extends the block it heard first, but miners "can do strictly better by mining on the block that leaves the most transactions [sic] fees unclaimed" (PettyCompliant). If even some miners behave this way, a strategy opens up of deliberately forking when the head block of the chain is worth more than the unclaimed fees it leaves, and taking slightly fewer fees (undercutting). The authors show (i) that learning, non-atomic miners drift in simulation toward ever more aggressive undercutting, and (ii) that there is nonetheless an equilibrium in which every miner uses the same function-based strategy (Theorem 5.1, with f(x) written in terms of the Lambert W function), and that "in any such equilibrium, the expected number of backlogged transactions after n time steps is Θ(n)," that is, unprocessed transactions pile up without end. And (iii) they add the analytical result that "even if 66% of miners remain default compliant, undercutting is profitable." This is because the condition for the expected reward of undercutting to exceed 1, when the fraction using the default strategy is y, is y≤2/3.20

[Advanced] Third, the back door into selfish mining. Selfish mining (Eyal and Sirer), which we read in Chapter 23, has a share threshold in the block-reward world. In the fee world, blocks can be withheld selectively: "Intuitively, imagine you are mining and find yourself solving a new block immediately after a previous block was announced and before any new transactions have been announced. This block is literally worthless, so instead of publishing, why not use it to try and selfish mine? There is no cost, but a positive probability that you build a lead of two, no matter your hash power. Similarly, imagine instead that just by chance an hour goes by since the last block was found and you just solved a new block including all transactions that arrived during that period. This block is worth roughly six 'normal' blocks, so why risk losing it?" So the Selfish-Mine(β) strategy, which withholds only "small" blocks, for all α, γ<1 "strictly outperforms both default mining and 'vanilla' selfish mining in the transaction fees model"; it is profitable "for a miner with an arbitrarily low hash power share, and who is arbitrarily poorly connected within the network"; and "the attack is profitable as soon as it is deployed" (classic selfish mining becomes profitable only after the difficulty adjustment). At α=1/3, "both selfish mining and default mining achieve expected reward of ≈1/3, but selfish mining with the optimal cutoff achieves an expected reward of ≈.38, a 13.6% increase!"22

[Advanced] What the authors write at the end of their introduction is advice on design: "Nakamoto appears to have viewed the block reward as a necessary but temporary evil to achieve an initial allocation of bitcoins in the absence of a central authority, with the transaction fee regime being the ideal, inflation-free steady state of the system. But our work shows that incentivizing compliant miner behavior in the transaction fee regime is a significantly more daunting task than in the block reward regime. Perhaps instead, designers of new cryptocurrencies must resign themselves to the inevitability of monetary inflation and make the block reward permanent."23 This is one of the four problems that Ethereum's EIP-1559 lists in its motivation section: "In the long run, blockchains where there is no issuance (including Bitcoin and Zcash) at present intend to switch to rewarding miners entirely through transaction fees. However, there are known issues with this that likely leads to a lot of instability, incentivizing mining 'sister blocks' that steal transaction fees, opening up much stronger selfish mining attack vectors … There is at present no good mitigation for this."24 The rest of that design is in Chapter 21.

7. [Advanced] When a stock is at stake: specialized capital and collapse

[Advanced] If the attacker loses capital, by how many orders of magnitude does the cost grow?

[Advanced] Budish's §V adds what the cost model of Section 3 left out: "If the capital used to maintain the blockchain is specialized (as opposed to repurposable), and a majority attack causes the attacker's capital to lose its value or be confiscated, then the attacker cost model needs to be modified. In addition to charging the attacker the flow cost of the attack, we also need to charge the attacker the stock value of their loss of specialized capital." Bitcoin's ASICs (chips "useless for any other application that does not involve performing a large number of SHA-256 hashes") and the stake of proof of stake are capital of this kind. Splitting cost as c=rC+η (the rental cost of capital + variable costs), equation (1) becomes N*(rC+η)=pblock (7); the approximate condition for an outside attacker who loses all its capital is N*C>Vattack (8); and with the capital share μ=rC/(rC+η), N*C=μpblock/r (9), so that

pblock>rμVattack(10)

"This is several orders of magnitude more secure than equation (3) because r is the interest rate per unit time." Budish's illustrative calculation takes μ=0.4 and an annual discount rate for ASICs of 50%, giving r≈0.0008% per block and r/μ=0.002%; set against the 5.0% of equation (3), this is "a roughly 2,500-fold improvement in the cost of security."25

[Advanced] The question then becomes "how does the attacker lose capital?" Budish gives three ways. (1) The attack collapses the value of the currency, and the capital collapses with it: "But vulnerability to collapse is itself a serious problem … and raises the possibility of an attack motivated by this collapse per se" (sabotage). (2) Legal punishment, which "certainly would work but concedes that Nakamoto trust fails without support from rule of law." (3) The protocol algorithmically confiscates the attacker's capital alone: the companion paper (Budish, Lewis-Pye & Roughgarden 2024) shows that "this approach (i) is impossible for a broad class of permissionless consensus protocols that includes Bitcoin's; (ii) is possible for a class of permissionless consensus protocols that includes proof-of-stake Ethereum's, but only under a strong assumption about network reliability and only if the attacker is less than proportion ρ=2/3 of the total."26 This is where the slashing of Chapter 10 sits. Against an attacker below 2/3, the attack can be made to put a stock at stake rather than a flow, but against a larger attacker, outside trust (law) is needed. That is Budish's reading.

A lawyer's question

The rule that the subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks is written in code, and code can be changed by a majority (Chapter 23). This chapter has said that the subsidy is the source of the security budget and that the shift of that source to fees may be unstable. Then suppose that one day a majority of nodes and miners change the rule to "keep the subsidy permanently," in exactly the direction Carlsten et al. advised. Are the rights of existing holders infringed? Is what a holder has some right to the "21 million cap," or only the ability to satisfy the locking conditions of a UTXO? If a minority that did not agree to the rule change stays on the chain with the old rules, which of the two is "the" Bitcoin? This book does not answer, and points to Part 5 and to the discussion of the quantum transition in Part 6. At the quantum transition, "a soft fork that blocks spending of vulnerable coins" poses a question of the same structure, more sharply. → Chapter 27 · Chapter 29

8. Summary

[Basic] The block reward is made up of the subsidy and fees, and Bitcoin's subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks on its way to 0. That reward draws out the honest participants' spending (zero profit), that spending is the wall an attacker has to get over (incentive compatibility), and so the reward per block must at all times be large relative to the value that can be obtained by attacking (equilibrium constraint). Security is a flow, not a stock; the attack cost is calculated as "attacker hash rate × duration × unit price," and Proposition 3's formula gives the duration. The inputs are hash rate, unit price, and time, not the coin price. A halving is an event that lowers the pblock of this equation, and if fees do not fill its place, the wall gets lower. The mining game in a world where only fees remain differs from the block-reward world (the mining gap, undercutting, selfish mining with the back door open), and Ethereum took the path of making the reward permanent and changing the structure of fees (stating that motive is the job of the design document, and the motivation section of EIP-1559 lists this problem as one of four items). Chapter 21 looks at that second path: how fees are set and to whom they go. Chapter 23 asks whether the people this chapter has called "honest participants" really have an incentive to behave honestly.
