[Intermediate] Now read the table. With γ=0 (in a race, the honest miners always hear their own side's block first), selfish mining does worse than honest mining at α=0.30 and better from 0.34. With γ=0.5 the boundary is near 0.25, and with γ=1 even the smallest pool comes out ahead. The simulation and the closed form agree within the Monte Carlo error (about ±0.005 at 400,000 events). That closed form and the boundary are the subject of the next section.

[Advanced] The closed form, the threshold share, and why 1/3, 1/4 and 0

[Advanced] Solve for the stationary probabilities of the state machine (the CACM version says "the details are in our full report," and arXiv v5 sets them out as equation (1), the system of equations, and (2)–(5), the solution), and the probabilities of states 0, 0′, 1 and k≥2 come out as rational functions of α. Multiply them by the reward for each transition and add them up, and the result is the pool's relative revenue. It is equation (3) of the CACM version and equation (8) of arXiv v5.

Rpool=α(1−α)2(4α+γ(1−2α))−α31−α(1+(2−α)α),0≤α≤12

Reading the symbols: α is the pool's ratio of the mining power, and γ is the ratio of honest miners who, in a race, extend the pool's block. A numerical example: at α=0.4 and γ=0, Rpool≈0.484, larger than the share of 0.4. Solving for the range in which this formula exceeds α gives Observation 1: "For a given γ, a pool of size α obtains a revenue larger than its relative size for α in the range 1−γ3−2γ<α<12."11 At γ=0 the lower bound is 1/3, at γ=1/2 it is 1/4, and at γ=1 it is 0. The authors' explanation says why: "Note that the pool is only at risk when it holds exactly one block secret, and the honest miners might publish a block that would compete with it. For γ=1, the pool can quickly propagate its one-block branch if the others find their own branch, so all honest miners would still mine on the pool's block. In this case, the pool takes no risk when following the Selfish-Mine strategy and its revenue is always better than when following the honest algorithm. The threshold is therefore zero, and a pool of any size can benefit by following Selfish-Mine. In the other extreme, γ=0, the honest miners always publish and propagate their block first, and the threshold is at 1/3."12 Then Observation 2: "For a pool running the Selfish-Mine strategy, the revenue of each pool member increases with pool size for pools larger than the threshold." This is because revenue rises against share with a slope steeper than 1, and so "rational miners will preferentially join the selfish pool to increase their revenues. … The selfish pool would therefore increase in size, unopposed by any mechanism, towards a majority."13 The moment the conventional wisdom's "X% gets X%" breaks, the force that caps the size of a pool disappears.

[Advanced] That the pool can raise γ is what makes the attack realistic: "a savvy pool operator can perform a sybil attack on honest miners by adding a significant number of zero-power miners to the Bitcoin miner network. These virtual miners act as advance sensors by participating in data dissemination, but do not mine new blocks. … once they hear of block X, they ignore it and start propagating block P. … By adding enough virtual nodes, the pool operator can thus increase γ. The result (see Observation 1), is a threshold close to zero." The authors' fix therefore changes the honest side's tie-breaking rule: "when a miner learns of competing branches of the same length, it should propagate all of them, and choose which one to mine on uniformly at random. … This yields γ=1/2, which in turn yields a threshold of 1/4." Because it works "independent of the adoption of the change at other miners," "it does not require a hard fork" (backward compatibility and gradual adoption are in other sentences on the same page), and it "does not introduce new vulnerabilities to the protocol," since "Currently, when there are two branches of equal length, the choice of each miner is arbitrary, effectively determined by the network topology and latency."14 Even with that fix, though, the authors write that "the system remains vulnerable: there already exist pools whose mining power exceeds the 25% threshold, and at times, even the 33% theoretical hard limit."15 And the conclusion changes the number in the conventional wisdom: "at least 2/3 of the network needs to be honest to thwart selfish mining; a simple majority is not enough."16

[Basic] Two properties of this attack should be recorded. First, it is hard to detect: "It is easy to hide Selfish-Mine behavior, and difficult to ban it. A selfish pool may never reveal its size by using different Bitcoin addresses and IP addresses, and by faking block creation times." There are two signs, an increase in abandoned blocks and a distortion in the distribution of block intervals, but "neither are easy to measure definitively."17 Second, "collapse" does not mean a value of 0. What the authors call a "collapse" is "a state in which a single entity controls the entire currency system," and "such a collapse does not immediately imply that the value of a Bitcoin drops to 0. The controlling entity will have an incentive to accept most transactions, if only to reap their fees, … It may also choose to remain covert, and hide the fact that it can control the entire currency."18 The loss of decentralization may not be visible from outside. The proposition of Part 5, "If it is decentralized, no one is responsible" (misconception ⑫ in Appendix B), is shaken once more here. Having no one responsible is different from the one responsible being invisible.

5. Other places in the same frame: the coordination game, the cooperative equilibrium, undercutting

[Basic] Selfish mining came out of one freedom: "the miner can choose when to publish a block." That is not the miner's only freedom. The strategy language of Carlsten et al., seen in Chapter 20, names three: "Which block to extend. How much of the available transactions (and associated fees) to include in the block they are solving. For each unpublished block, whether or not to publish."19 Each of the three freedoms carries a question of equilibrium.

[Intermediate] Which block to extend: the coordination game. When two branches of the same length compete, what matters to a miner is not "which one is right" but "which one will the others extend." The side that the majority extends wins, and blocks built on the losing side are discarded. This is the textbook coordination game, a game with two equilibria (everyone on A / everyone on B). That is why the protocol supplies a focal point, "the one heard first," and Eyal and Sirer's γ and their fix (random tie-breaking) were meant to keep an attacker from manipulating that focal point. A hard fork is this coordination game played for high stakes. When the chain with changed rules and the old chain split, what decides which side is "Bitcoin" or "Ethereum" is not the code but where the participants coordinate. As the SEC's report on The DAO, seen in Chapter 14, notes, after the hard fork of July 20, 2016, "A minority group, however, elected not to adopt the new Ethereum Blockchain created by the Hard Fork because to do so would run counter to the concept that a blockchain is immutable. Instead they continued to use the former version of the blockchain, which is now known as 'Ethereum Classic.'"20 Both chains survived, and which one is "the real one" is the result of coordination, not of proof. Chapter 26 takes up this event.

[Intermediate] How much to include: the undercutting equilibrium. We read this in Section 6 of Chapter 20. When the reward is fees alone, the strategy of "extending the block that leaves the most fees unclaimed" is strictly better, on top of that, undercutting, "deliberately forking and taking less of the fees," becomes an equilibrium, and in that equilibrium unprocessed transactions pile up without end (Theorem 5.1). Translated into the language of this chapter, the conclusion of Carlsten et al. is that a strategy that was an equilibrium when the reward was constant stops being one when the reward varies. In the block reward model, "With non-atomic miners, DefaultCompliant is trivially an equilibrium, and this result is robust to general models of latency … Now, in the transaction-fee model, even when miners are non-atomic, equilibrium behavior is complex and undesirable …."21

[Intermediate] Bots competing over order: the cooperative equilibrium. This is what Chapter 17 handed on. Daian and his coauthors observed bots in priority gas auctions converging, in a race to outbid one another, to a cooperative state in which they take turns raising by the minimum increment, and they modeled it with a grim-trigger strategy of a repeated game: "Consider two players who coordinate with the following strategies: at set intervals, players alternate their bids, each time bidding the minimum increase. If any player deviates either by bidding too soon or by raising the bid higher than they are supposed to, the other player will respond by raising their bid such that the game is no longer profitable." Observation 3 says that "In a grim-trigger cooperative PGA, … the optimal choice for bids is W[0]=s and W[i]=W[i−1]×(1+ι)," that is, the minimum increment each time, and Theorem 1 says that "For parameters consistent with Ethereum PGAs, there exist a grim-trigger Nash equilibria [sic] for a 2 player PGA where both players follow a D,W cooperative strategy." The authors are careful: "We stress that we don't claim that perfect cooperation is occurring or even that our exact equilibrium is on play. We do claim, however, that players are converging to a more cooperative state, that is approximated by our model, in which they allow opportunities for other players in an effort to maximize their own expected profit over time."22 The convergence to 12.5% (the minimum increment of the Parity client) recorded in a note to Chapter 17 was the evidence. That an auction designed for "competition" can drift into tacit collusion when the participants are few is a long-standing caution of auction design, and a convergence resembling it was observed on chain, even if, as the authors caution, it is not "our exact equilibrium."

[Basic] Lay the three places over one another and the proposition of this chapter comes into view. The white paper's "honesty pays" is an equilibrium for the case in which participants are small, the reward is constant, publication is immediate, and there is nothing to extract from ordering. Each time one of the four conditions was relaxed (large pools, fee rewards, blocks that can be withheld, MEV), a different equilibrium appeared. The rules are still the same. What changed was whether following the rules pays.

# NB23-2: the 2×2 payoff table and the "threshold" — fill a publish/withhold game between two small players with the relative revenue of selfish mining and read off the equilibrium (for study)
# Two pools P (share a) and Q (share b) each choose "honest (publish at once)" or "withhold (selfish mining)". The rest (1−a−b) are honest.
# Simplification: if only one pool withholds, its revenue is R_pool(α, γ); if both withhold, neither knows the other's hidden blocks, so each uses R_pool and the effect of the other also withholding is ignored (limitation stated).
def payoff(a, b, P_selfish, Q_selfish, gamma):
    rp = R_pool_closed_form(a, gamma) if P_selfish else a
    rq = R_pool_closed_form(b, gamma) if Q_selfish else b
    return rp, rq

for gamma in [0.0, 0.5]:
    print(f"\nγ = {gamma}: threshold (1−γ)/(3−2γ) = {(1-gamma)/(3-2*gamma):.3f}")
    for a, b in [(0.20, 0.20), (0.30, 0.30), (0.40, 0.20)]:
        print(f"  P={a:.2f}, Q={b:.2f}  (rows: P's choice; columns: Q's choice; cells: P's revenue, Q's revenue)")
        print(f"  {'':>10}{'Q honest':>18}{'Q withhold':>18}")
        for ps, pl in [(False, "P honest"), (True, "P withhold")]:
            cells = []
            for qs in [False, True]:
                rp, rq = payoff(a, b, ps, qs, gamma)
                cells.append(f"({rp:.3f}, {rq:.3f})")
            print(f"  {pl:>10}{cells[0]:>18}{cells[1]:>18}")
        best_P = "withhold" if R_pool_closed_form(a, gamma) > a else "honest"
        best_Q = "withhold" if R_pool_closed_form(b, gamma) > b else "honest"
        print(f"  → P's dominant strategy {best_P}, Q's dominant strategy {best_Q}  (below the threshold share honest is dominant, above it withhold is)")
print("\nThis table rests on the simplification 'whatever the other does, my revenue is set by the threshold'. The interaction when both pools withhold at the same time is outside the model.")

[Intermediate] The second cell puts this chapter's numbers into the textbook payoff table. For a pool whose share is below the threshold, honest is dominant; for one above it, withholding is. This follows because the simplification made each pool's revenue independent of the other's choice; it is not a finding. So within this table, in a world with only small pools "everyone honest" is the equilibrium, and as soon as even one pool passes the threshold, "withhold" is the equilibrium strategy for that pool. As the cell's comments state, the case in which two pools withhold at the same time is outside this simplification. Its analysis is beyond the scope of this book.

A lawyer's question

After a hard fork both chains survived. They share the same history, the rules diverged from a certain block on, and each side says it is "the" ledger. This chapter wrote that what decides which side wins is the coordination of the participants. Then who decides which ledger is "real": a majority of the hash rate, a majority of node operators, the exchange that attaches the name to one side, the developers, or no one at all? A person who held coins before the fork holds the same balance on both chains after it. Does that person have one thing or two? If a contract said "pay 1 bitcoin," the 1 on which chain? What has a person who deviated within the rules, like a selfish miner, violated: the rules, an expectation, or nothing? This book does not answer, and points to two sections of Part 5. → Chapter 27 · Chapter 28

6. Summary

[Basic] The white paper's "more profitable to play by the rules" is one claim of equilibrium, and the equilibrium holds when the reward is large compared with the value of an attack (Chapter 20), when participants are small, when the reward is constant, when blocks are published at once, and when there is nothing to extract from ordering. Eyal and Sirer argued that the strategy of hiding blocks gives more than honesty from a share of 1/3 (0 if the pool controls propagation), and that this revenue grows with pool size and pushes the pool toward a majority. So it is not "safe if a majority is honest" but "more than 2/3 must be honest," and even that under optimistic assumptions. If only fees remain, undercutting becomes an equilibrium (Chapter 20); the bots of the ordering auction converge to tacit cooperation (Chapter 17); and the choice of fork is a coordination game, so the "real" chain is decided by coordination, not by proof. The rules stay the same while the equilibrium changes: that is what this chapter meant by "conditional." Chapter 24 looks at the same "multiple equilibria in which belief decides the outcome" in another place, the bank run on a token that carries a promise of redemption.

Part 3 · Economics

Chapter 24. Stablecoins: design types and the structure of a bank run

Key takeaway

The coin of Chapter 19 was an outside money that promises nothing. A stablecoin is the opposite: a token that carries the promise "1 token will be paid back as 1 dollar," and at that moment the problem moves from monetary economics to the economics of banking. In Gorton and Zhang's words, the technology is new but "the economics is centuries old," and issuers are "unregulated banks." Depending on what assets back the promise, stablecoins divide into fiat-backed, crypto-overcollateralized, algorithmic and synthetic types, but all four types sit on the same scale. When redemption demands bunch up, reserve assets have to be sold; if they cannot be sold, or cannot be sold at full value, the 1-dollar promise breaks (a depeg); and the belief that it might break itself brings on redemption demands. This is the structure of a bank run exactly as Diamond and Dybvig set it down in 1983: "A demand deposit contract which is not subject to runs provides no liquidity services." After this chapter you will know that the "stability" of a stablecoin is a property not of its price but of its balance sheet and its redemption procedure, and you will see how far the run of March 2023 resembled the textbook picture and where it differed (the secondary market). The chapter does not compare the safety of particular coins. It looks only at the structure of the types.

Learning objectives

  1. Define a stablecoin as "a token that carries a promise of redemption," and draw the balance sheets of the fiat-backed, crypto-overcollateralized, algorithmic and synthetic types. Know how it differs from the outside money of Chapter 19.
  2. [Intermediate] Define the collateral ratio and the redeemable ratio, and calculate what the liquidity composition of reserve assets decides when redemption demands bunch up. Know why the "no questions asked" (NQA) principle and information sensitivity are central.
  3. [Advanced] Read in equations the two equilibria of the Diamond–Dybvig model (the good one and the run), why the choice between them can turn on "almost anything," and what suspension of convertibility and deposit insurance each change. See the reflexive feedback of the algorithmic type in a simple model.
  4. Read the runs of May 2022 and March 2023 through the figures of empirical studies (sample, period, estimate), and tell apart which parts match the textbook and which differ (the existence of a secondary market).

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. A stablecoin sits somewhere between a bank deposit and an MMF, and so it is exposed to the same runs that banks are.

1. The question this chapter tries to answer

[Basic] Chapter 19, following Garratt and Wallace, placed bitcoin as an outside money: money of which it is not true that "each unit is someone's asset and someone else's liability."1 A stablecoin sits on the opposite side of that definition. Because the issuer promises "bring me one of these tokens and I will give you 1 dollar," the token is an asset of the holder and a liability of the issuer. It is inside money. And the value of inside money rests not on belief but on whether the issuer can keep its promise. That question is one banking has dealt with for hundreds of years. It is why Gary Gorton and Jeffery Zhang titled their 2023 paper "Taming Wildcat Stablecoins": "While the technology underlying cryptocurrencies is new, the economics is centuries old. … In this case, the new technology has recreated circulating private money in the form of stablecoins, which are similar to the banknotes that circulated in many countries during the nineteenth century. The implication is that stablecoin issuers are unregulated banks."2

[Basic] This chapter asks four questions in turn. What backs the promise (the types)? What conditions must the balance sheet meet for the promise to be kept (the collateral ratio and liquidity)? Why can a run happen even when those conditions are met (Diamond–Dybvig)? And how closely did actual runs match that picture (the evidence)? The names of particular coins are used only to point to settled historical events, and the chapter does not ask which coin is safer. Its unit is the type and the structure.

2. Four types: what backs the promise

[Basic] The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Annual Economic Report 2022 divides them in two: "The two main types of stablecoin are asset-backed and algorithmic. Asset-backed stablecoins … are typically managed by a centralised intermediary who invests the underlying collateral and coordinates the coins' redemption and creation. Assets can be held in government bonds, short-term corporate debt or bank deposits, or in other cryptocurrencies. In contrast, algorithmic stablecoins … rely on complex algorithms that automatically rebalance supply to maintain their value relative to the target currency or asset. To avoid reliance on fiat currency, they often do so by providing users with an arbitrage opportunity relative to another cryptocurrency."3 Dividing the asset-backed type again by the kind of collateral, and adding a fourth type taken up by a 2026 Federal Reserve Bank of New York blog post, gives the table below. The balance sheet in each row is this book's account of the structure of a type, not the actual books of any coin.

Type Assets (reserves) Liabilities How "1 dollar" breaks
Fiat-backed Cash and bank deposits, short-term government securities, repurchase agreements, (sometimes) commercial paper, etc. Issued tokens = claims to redemption at par Reserve assets cannot be sold in time at full value (frozen deposits, discounted commercial paper); doubts about the solvency of the issuer itself
Crypto-overcollateralized Other crypto-assets (locked in excess of face value because they are volatile), or other stablecoins Issued tokens A sharp fall in collateral value uses up the excess; cascading liquidations; contagion from the depeg of another stablecoin held as collateral
Algorithmic The issuer's promise to exchange into its own second token (no real reserves) Issued tokens If demand for the second token disappears, there is nothing to exchange for "1 dollar's worth": a reflexive spiral
Synthetic Long staked crypto-assets + short perpetual futures (delta hedge) Issued tokens If the funding rate turns negative or margin costs rise, keeping the hedge in place runs at a loss: feedback between redemptions and liquidations

[Basic] Box A of the BIS report sets out the mechanism of the third type through the events of May 2022: "An algorithmic stablecoin, it maintained value by adjusting supply in an automated arbitrage trading strategy with another cryptocurrency, Luna, on the Terra blockchain. UST aimed to keep a one-for-one peg to the US dollar by being convertible into one dollar's worth of Luna, and vice versa. For example, should Terra fall to 99 cents, a user could purchase UST on an exchange for 99 cents and then exchange their UST for $1 worth of new units of Luna on the Terra platform. A crucial aspect of this arrangement was that users would only be willing to exchange UST into Luna if Luna's market capitalisation exceeded that of UST."4 The fourth type is explained in a June 2026 post from the New York Fed: "synthetic stablecoins … target their dollar peg through financial engineering: they combine a long position in cryptocurrency (typically ether staked in a staking pool …) with an offsetting short position in perpetual futures contracts. … This structure creates a 'synthetic' dollar position without requiring actual dollar reserves." And: "The key fragility, however, is that the hedge depends on continuous liquidity in derivatives markets and a consistently positive funding rate. If funding turns negative or margin costs rise, the synthetic dollar becomes expensive to maintain and redemptions begin."5 The collapse of Terra itself is taken up in Chapter 26. This chapter takes only the mechanism.

Collateral ratio and redeemable ratio

[Intermediate] Whatever the type, the conditions under which the promise is kept can be written with the same two numbers. If S is the number of tokens issued and A the current value of the reserve assets, the collateral ratio is

CR=AS

and when redemption demands bunch up to a fraction q of issuance, the redeemable ratio is the disposal value of the assets that can be sold right now to meet those demands, divided by the amount demanded:

RR(q)=∑iℓiAi(1−hi)qS

Reading the symbols: Ai is the value of asset class i, ℓi∈[0,1] is the share of it that can be disposed of immediately (1 for cash, 0 for a frozen deposit), and hi is the discount when it is sold in a hurry. A numerical example: with issuance 100 and reserves 100 (cash 10, government bonds 60 (discount 0.5%), bank deposits 25, commercial paper 5 (discount 5%)) and no frozen deposits, at q=0.3 the disposable value is 10+59.7+25+4.75=99.45, comfortably above the demand of 30. But if the deposits of 25 are frozen and q=0.8, the disposable value is 74.45 against a demand of 80, so RR=0.93 and redemption at par is impossible. And this with the collateral ratio still at 1.0. The collateral ratio is a number about solvency and the redeemable ratio a number about liquidity, and a run starts with the second number. NB24-2 below runs this arithmetic dynamically.

3. Why runs happen: the economics of "no questions asked"

[Basic] Gorton and Zhang say that stablecoins are not yet money, and give as the reason the NQA principle we saw in Chapter 19: "it cannot just be assumed that an object will be used as a medium of exchange. For that to happen, the object must satisfy the NQA principle. Imagine attempting to purchase goods and services, or enter into contractual arrangements, when the value of the medium of exchange fluctuates because parties are differentially informed about its value. Engaging in such transactions would be incredibly difficult. Private producers of money therefore try to design an instrument that is information insensitive: no party to a transaction would engage in due diligence on its value because doing so would be too expensive. And because all parties to the transaction know this, they accept the instrument at par." Gorton and Zhang write that the best way to get that insensitivity is "backing the debt with debt," "by backing private banknotes with state bonds, by backing demand deposits with portfolios of loans, or by backing sale and repurchase agreements (repos) with specific bonds" (restating the argument of Dang, Gorton, Holmström and Ordoñez).6 What, then, is a run? "if the price is to stay fixed and not vary (as other prices usually do in response to changes in demand), then it is the quantity that must sometimes adjust. During times of heightened economic uncertainty, the quantity can adjust very quickly to zero in a bank run, a situation in which the backing of the money becomes suspect."7 Because the price is nailed down, a shock escapes through the quantity, and the adjustment of quantity becomes a queue in which those who come first are paid first.

[Basic] Here stablecoin issuers stand in a different place from banks. "Stablecoin issuers therefore face a trade-off with respect to opacity and transparency. On one hand, it would be best if the backing for their stablecoins were so opaque that nobody would find it profitable to produce information about the backing assets. On the other hand, if the backing were not credible, then the market would want to produce information about the backing. Stablecoin issuers may take the view that transparency is best, because they are not regulated and cannot rely on bank examiners (and, thus, cannot be opaque)."8 Banks used deposit insurance and examination to make it "unnecessary to ask"; stablecoins, with monthly attestation reports, say "ask and we will answer." The two solutions are not the same. Being able to ask also means that, once there is a reason to ask, everyone asks at once. A 2023 New York Fed report reports what that "asking" finds: "stablecoins exhibit an even wider range of risk profiles than MMFs. Some stablecoins report that they are backed by safe assets, such as cash and US Treasuries, … Others, instead, are reportedly backed by riskier collateral, such as corporate debt or even other crypto assets." And: "Reporting quality, however, varies across stablecoin issuers, because there is no standardized or regulatory reporting requirement."9 Section 6 looks at this report's figures.

4. [Advanced] Diamond–Dybvig: a run is an equilibrium

[Basic] The 1983 paper answers with one model why banks exist and why they are vulnerable to runs. The authors' summary: "Our model demonstrates three important points. First, banks issuing demand deposits can improve on a competitive market by providing better risk-sharing among people who need to consume at different random times. Second, the demand deposit contract providing this improvement has an undesirable equilibrium (a bank run) in which all depositors panic and withdraw immediately, including even those who would prefer to leave their deposits in if they were not concerned about the bank failing. Third, bank runs cause real economic problems because even healthy banks can fail, causing the recall of loans and the termination of productive investment."10 Put another way, liquidity services and vulnerability to runs are two sides of the same thing. "It is precisely the transformation of illiquid claims into liquid claims that is responsible both for the liquidity service provided by banks and for their susceptibility to runs."11

[Advanced] The skeleton of the model, two equilibria, and two remedies

[Advanced] There are three periods (T=0,1,2) and one good. The production technology turns 1 unit put in at period 0 into R>1 at period 2, but if it is interrupted at period 1 it gives back only the original 1. That is, "long-term capital investments are somewhat irreversible." Everyone is alike at period 0 and learns their own type privately at period 1. Type 1 wants to consume only at period 1 (a fraction t), and type 2 consumes at period 2.12 If types were public information, the optimal insurance contract would give type 1 c1*>1 and type 2 c2*<R, sharing risk between the two. But types are private information, so a market cannot use that contract, and the bank imitates it with demand deposits. "the demand deposit contract gives each agent withdrawing in period 1 a fixed claim of r1 per unit deposited in period 0. Withdrawal tenders are served sequentially in random order until the bank runs out of assets."13 The amount V1 received by someone who takes r1 at period 1, and the amount V2 received by someone who waits and withdraws at period 2, are

V1(fj,r1)={r1fj<r1−10fj≥r1−1,V2(f,r1)=max{(1−r1f)R1−f, 0}

(equations (6) and (7)). Reading the symbols: fj is the fraction of withdrawals served before me, and f is the total fraction withdrawn at period 1. If r1f exceeds 1, the bank's assets run out and those further back in line get 0, and those who waited share the remaining (1−r1f) grown by a factor of R.14

[Advanced] Two equilibria. Set r1=c1*: "If this contract is in place, it is an equilibrium for type 1 agents to withdraw at T = 1 and for type 2 agents to wait, provided this is what is anticipated. This good equilibrium achieves optimal risk-sharing. Another equilibrium (a bank run) has all agents panicking and trying to withdraw their deposits at T = 1: if this is anticipated, all agents will prefer to withdraw at T = 1. This is because the face value of deposits is larger than the liquidation value of the bank's assets." And: "For all r1>1, runs are an equilibrium. … if r1=1, the bank simply mimics direct holding of the assets, … A demand deposit contract which is not subject to runs provides no liquidity services."15 Which equilibrium is realized lies outside the model. "This could happen if the selection between the bank run equilibrium and the good equilibrium depended on some commonly observed random variable in the economy. This could be a bad earnings report, a commonly observed run at some other bank, a negative government forecast, or even sunspots. … The observed variable need not convey anything fundamental about the bank's condition. The problem is that once agents have deposited, anything that causes them to anticipate a run will lead to a run."16 The sunspots of Chapter 19 come back here. There they were a device for selecting a collapse to a value of 0; here, for selecting a run.

[Advanced] Two remedies. The first is suspension of convertibility. "If banks can suspend convertibility when withdrawals are too numerous at T = 1, anticipation of this policy prevents runs by removing the incentive of type 2 agents to withdraw early." With a suspension point f^, "no type 2 agent will withdraw at T = 1 because no matter what the agent anticipates about others' withdrawals, the agent receives higher proceeds by waiting until T = 2 to withdraw … Therefore, there is a unique Nash equilibrium which has f=t. In fact, this is a dominant strategy equilibrium …." But "This contract works perfectly only in the case where the normal volume of withdrawals, t, is known and not stochastic."17 If t is random, Proposition 1 holds, "Bank contracts (which must obey the sequential service constraint) cannot achieve optimal risk-sharing when t is stochastic …," and suspension of convertibility prevents runs but leaves behind the inefficiency of locking in, after the fact, some type 1 agents. The second is deposit insurance. "Demand deposit contracts with government deposit insurance achieve the unconstrained optimum as a unique Nash equilibrium (in fact, a dominant strategies equilibrium) if the government imposes an optimal tax to finance the deposit insurance." The key is that the government can tax after the withdrawals are over. "As the government can impose a tax on an agent who has withdrawn, the government can base its tax on f, the realized total value of T = 1 withdrawals. This is in marked contrast to a bank, which must provide sequential service and cannot reduce the amount of a withdrawal after it has been made." And: "for all possible anticipated withdrawal policies of other agents, participating in a bank run never pays. As a result, no strategic issues of confidence arise."18 The authors add that the lender of last resort (the discount window) can do the same work as deposit insurance when the technology is riskless.19

# NB24-1: Diamond–Dybvig's two equilibria — with a demand deposit r1 > 1, for each total period-1 withdrawal fraction f, is the share from "waiting," V2, larger than "withdrawing," r1? (for study)
R, r1, t = 1.5, 1.2, 0.25          # period-2 output R, promised period-1 payment r1 (> 1), fraction t of type 1 (those who must consume at period 1)

def V2(f):                          # equation (7): the share of those who wait
    return max((1 - r1 * f) * R / (1 - f), 0.0) if f < 1 else 0.0

print(f"R = {R}, r1 = {r1}, type-1 fraction t = {t}. Withdrawal fraction at which the bank runs out, 1/r1 = {1 / r1:.3f}")
print(f"{'Period-1 f':>12} {'Waiting V2(f)':>16} {'Payout r1':>10} {'Type 2 best':>14}")
for f in [t, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70, 0.80, 0.83, 0.90, 1.00]:
    v = V2(f)
    print(f"{f:>12.2f} {v:>16.3f} {r1:>10.2f} {'wait' if v > r1 else 'withdraw (run)':>14}")
# The threshold where waiting becomes worse than withdrawing: (1 − r1 f)R/(1 − f) = r1  →  f* = (R − r1)/(r1 (R − 1))
f_star = (R - r1) / (r1 * (R - 1))
print(f"\nThreshold f* = (R − r1)/(r1(R − 1)) = {f_star:.3f}. If you believe others will withdraw more than this, withdrawing is your best response too: belief decides the outcome.")
print(f"At f = t = {t} (normal), type 2 waits and receives {V2(t):.3f} (> r1). At f = 1 (run), everyone shares an average of 1 and the back of the line gets 0: everyone is worse off than with no bank.")
print("\nAdd suspension of convertibility (period-1 payments stop when f reaches the suspension point) and the share of those who wait cannot fall below r1, so waiting becomes a dominant strategy for type 2 — when t is known.")

5. Carrying it over to stablecoins: what is the same and what is different

[Basic] Put the stablecoin counterpart in each place in the model. Bank = issuer. Illiquid assets = the reserve assets that cannot be sold right now, or cannot be sold without a discount (ℓi and hi in Section 2). Demand deposit = claim to redemption at par. Sequential service = the redemption queue in the primary market (the issuer's window). The two equilibria and the sunspot selection carry over unchanged. Two things are different.

[Basic] First, there is no deposit insurance. Table 1 of Gorton and Zhang lays out the options. The status quo and "Implement bank-like regulations on stablecoin issuers, but no insurance" solve neither runs nor NQA, and only three, "Issue stablecoins from within the insured-bank regulatory perimeter," "Require stablecoins to be backed one-for-one by Treasuries or central bank reserves," and "Replace stablecoins with a central bank digital currency," solve both, the authors write.20 Why one-for-one backing removes runs can be seen directly from Diamond–Dybvig. If r1=1 and all the assets can be disposed of immediately, a run is not an equilibrium, and at that price the core of banking, liquidity transformation, disappears as well. This book does not say which option is right. Which one each jurisdiction chose is for the survey in Chapter 27.

[Basic] Second, there is a secondary market. Bank deposits are not transferable, but stablecoins trade on exchanges. A December 2025 note from the Federal Reserve Board points to this difference in the events of March 2023: "Unlike bank deposits, stablecoins are actively traded on exchanges in the secondary markets. This means that the suspension of redemption on the primary market cannot arrest a run, as temporarily closing a bank would."21 The first remedy of Diamond–Dybvig, suspension of convertibility, works differently here. Close the window in the primary market and the redemption pressure escapes into the price on the secondary market (the Fed note writes of "[p]ent up redemption pressure" while the window was closed). The feedback by which a falling price brings on more redemption demands is not something the note reports; it is an assumption of this book's model, and NB24-2 below puts it in as a simple rule.

Reserve composition and redemption demand

# NB24-2: reserve composition × redemption demand → depeg feedback — types A, B and C are illustrations of structure, not the books of any coin (for study)
# Feedback rule (this book's simplification): if the redeemable ratio RR < 1, or the issuer closes the window, the secondary-market price moves down toward RR,
# and if the price is below 1, more holders come forward to redeem (by the 'sensitivity' below). Prices and quantities are all model variables.
def run_dynamics(reserves, q0, sensitivity=1.5, rounds=6, window_open=True):
    """reserves: [(name, weight, disposable share ℓ, fire-sale discount h)], weights sum to 1 (collateral ratio 1.0). q0: initial redemption demand fraction."""
    S = 1.0                                   # issuance normalized to 1
    q, price, history = q0, 1.0, []
    redeemed = 0.0
    for r in range(1, rounds + 1):
        liquid = sum(w * l * (1 - h) for _, w, l, h in reserves)        # value that can be disposed of right now (per issuance of 1)
        demand = min(q, 1.0) - redeemed
        rr = liquid / demand if demand > 0 else float("inf")
        if window_open and rr >= 1:
            redeemed += demand; price = 1.0
            history.append((r, q, round(rr, 2), price, "redeemed at par"))
            break
        price = max(min(rr, 1.0), 0.0) if window_open else max(price - 0.05, 0.0)   # if the window closes, the price slides (rule)
        history.append((r, round(q, 3), round(rr, 2), round(price, 3), "window open" if window_open else "window closed"))
        q = min(1.0, q + sensitivity * (1 - price) * (1 - q))          # if the price is below 1, more holders come forward to redeem
    return history

types = {
    "A Mostly cash and T-bills":            [("cash", 0.20, 1.0, 0.0), ("T-bills", 0.75, 1.0, 0.005), ("bank deposits", 0.05, 1.0, 0.0)],
    "B Deposits and CP mixed in":           [("cash", 0.05, 1.0, 0.0), ("T-bills", 0.40, 1.0, 0.005), ("bank deposits", 0.30, 1.0, 0.0), ("commercial paper", 0.25, 1.0, 0.05)],
    "B′ B with all bank deposits frozen":   [("cash", 0.05, 1.0, 0.0), ("T-bills", 0.40, 1.0, 0.005), ("bank deposits (frozen)", 0.30, 0.0, 0.0), ("commercial paper", 0.25, 1.0, 0.05)],
    "C Crypto-overcollateralized (initial collateral ratio 1.5 → 0.83 after a 45% sharp fall in collateral)": [("collateral crypto-asset — value left after a 45% sharp fall, fire-sale discount 15%", 1.5 * 0.55, 1.0, 0.15)],
}
for name, res in types.items():
    cr = sum(w for _, w, _, _ in res)
    print(f"\n[{name}] collateral ratio {cr:.2f}")
    for q0 in [0.10, 0.40, 0.80]:
        hist = run_dynamics(res, q0)
        last = hist[-1]
        print(f"  initial demand {q0:.0%}: {len(hist)} round(s) → demand {last[1]:.0%}, redeemable ratio {last[2]}, price {last[3]} ({last[4]})")

print("\n[B′ with the issuer closing the window] — with a secondary market, closing the window still carries the run into the price")
for row in run_dynamics(types["B′ B with all bank deposits frozen"], 0.40, window_open=False):
    print("  round {} demand {} RR {} price {} {}".format(*row))

[Intermediate] When reading the table, do not get caught on the type names. A, B and C differ only in the composition of their reserve assets, and this book does not say which type is in fact which coin. Three things show. Even with the same collateral ratio of 1.0, the disposable share ℓ and the fire-sale discount h decide the outcome (B and B′), and this is a problem of liquidity. Even with an initial collateral ratio of 1.5, a 45% sharp fall in the collateral takes the collateral ratio itself below 1 (0.83) (C), so the break from par in that case is a problem not of liquidity but of solvency; in the overcollateralized type the two problems are tied together through a single collateral price. And if the rule that the price slides when the window closes is put into the cell, closing the window, unlike at a bank, does not stop the run. This third point is not a result the cell showed but a consequence of the assumption that a secondary market exists, and the basis for that assumption is the Fed note below. The interactive figure W8 for this chapter moves only the three variables of this cell (the redemption demand fraction, the liquidity composition of reserve assets, and the collateral ratio) and uses no coin names.

Algorithmic type: a promise of exchange in place of reserves

[Advanced] Reflexive feedback in the algorithmic type: a simple model

[Advanced] The algorithmic type backs its 1 dollar not with reserve assets but with a promise of exchange into a second token. Translated into model variables, the mechanism the BIS describes runs like this. There is a stable token S and a volatile token L, and one S can always be exchanged for "1 dollar's worth of L." If the price of L is pL, one S is burned and 1/pL new units of L are minted. For this arrangement to work, there must be demand to take up L, and in the BIS's terms users would only be willing to exchange "if [L's] market capitalisation exceeded that of [S]." When demand wavers and pL falls, more L has to be minted to hand over the same 1 dollar's worth, the added supply pushes pL down further, and that brings on more redemptions. This is the mechanism of what the BIS calls "a classic run dynamic,"22 and what actually happened in May 2022, and in what order, is read in Chapter 26. The cell below imitates this feedback with a single demand function. Every number is a model value and is fitted to no data.

# NB24-3: reflexive feedback in the algorithmic type — does a spiral arise from just three things: the exchange promise "one S = 1 dollar's worth of L," the demand curve for L, and redemptions that grow once the backing breaks? (for study, model variables)
def algorithmic_spiral(S0, L0, p0, eps=1.0, rounds=10, base_redeem=0.05, panic=0.6, shock_round=3, shock=0.3):
    """Demand curve for L: p_L = D / L**(1+eps). With eps > 0, the price falls more than proportionally as supply rises (demand is inelastic; with eps=1, L market cap = D/L).
    Each round some S holders burn S and receive 1/p_L units of L. If the backing (L market cap / S) is below 1, the redemption fraction grows by panic.
    At shock_round the demand level D shrinks by a factor of shock. All numbers are model values."""
    S, L = float(S0), float(L0)
    D = p0 * L ** (1 + eps)
    print(f"{'Round':>5} {'S supply':>9} {'L supply':>11} {'p_L':>8} {'L mcap / S':>12} {'Redeem share':>12}")
    for r in range(1, rounds + 1):
        if r == shock_round:
            D *= shock                                        # demand shock (model variable)
        p_L = D / L ** (1 + eps)
        backing = L * p_L / S                                 # dollars' worth that all of L can pay back per S
        share = base_redeem + (panic * (1 - backing) if backing < 1 else 0.0)
        share = min(share, 0.9)
        print(f"{r:>5} {S:>9,.0f} {L:>11,.0f} {p_L:>8.4f} {backing:>12.2f} {share:>12.2f}")
        burn = S * share
        S -= burn
        L += burn / p_L                                       # mint new L worth "1 dollar" for each S burned
    return S, L, D / L ** (1 + eps)

S_end, L_end, p_end = algorithmic_spiral(S0=1_000, L0=2_000, p0=1.0)
print(f"\nEnd: S {S_end:,.0f}, L {L_end:,.0f}, p_L {p_end:.4f}.")
print("After the demand shock, once the market cap of L falls below S (once the BIS condition breaks), redemptions mint more L, the added supply pushes p_L down further, and that brings on more redemptions — a spiral.")
print("The numbers in this table are model values fitted to no data. What shows is only the shape: when the backing is \"demand for another token,\" the backing disappears when that demand disappears.")

The numbers in this table are model values fitted to no data. What shows is only the shape: when the backing is "demand for another token," the backing disappears when that demand disappears.

6. Evidence: two runs

[Intermediate] Three empirical studies have set down the runs of May 2022 and March 2023 in data. This book takes from them only the figures about structure, and attaches a sample and period to each figure.

Study Data and period Findings Limitations
Anadu et al., NY Fed Staff Report 1073 (2023/2024) Daily stablecoin flows and prices; stress events in crypto markets (identified by days of large declines in the price of Bitcoin) Flight to safety: on stress days, net outflows from coins whose reserve assets are "risky" by the issuer's report into "safe" coins. Depeg threshold: at a price of 1 dollar or above, flows are unrelated to price, but once the price drops below 1 dollar the daily outflow rate jumps by 34 bp (compare the "95-cent" threshold for MMFs). The May 2022 run started in algorithmic and risky-collateral coins; the March 2023 run started in a coin previously regarded as "safe" and spread to other coins that held that coin as collateral. Flight tends to happen within the same blockchain The "safe/risky" classification depends on the issuers' self-reports (footnote 6). The threshold estimate is identified from the discontinuity around a price of 1 dollar: an observed response, not a causal one
Du, Sonawane and Watsky, FEDS Note (2025-12-17) Hourly primary-market net issuance, secondary-market prices and trading volume for 2023-03-09 to 14 (data providers Allium and CryptoCompare) The issuer disclosed that it held USD 3.3 billion, about 8% of total reserves, on deposit at the failed bank → redemption demands spiked → the primary market was effectively halted over the weekend → secondary-market low of 86 cents → recovery after the authorities announced full protection of deposits, and back to the peg after redemptions resumed on Monday. Once the primary market closed, secondary-market trading jumped (about USD 2 billion per hour), and decentralized exchanges accounted for most of the trading. Contagion, because another coin held this coin as collateral through a 1:1 exchange facility A description of a single event, with no counterfactual (stated by the authors). Policy discussion is outside its scope
Anadu et al., Liberty Street Economics (2026-07-31) The same issuer's reserve composition (weighted average maturity of the reserve MMF, repo share, bank-deposit share), monthly and quarterly, 2023–2026 After the event, the weighted average maturity of the reserve MMF fell below the 5th percentile of the distribution for Treasury-only MMFs and stayed there; the repo share jumped from 0 to over 90% and then came back to 69%; bank deposits fell below their pre-event level and became concentrated in large (GSIB) banks → the type of risk changed, "away from interest-rate risk and toward counterparty risk" Voluntary disclosures of a single issuer

23 24 25

[Intermediate] Put the three studies on top of each other and what resembles the textbook separates from what does not. What resembles it is the redemption queue in which those who come first are paid first, and contagion (to other coins that held one coin as collateral). Two things differ. First, the trigger was not a sunspot but fundamental information: the disclosure that about 8% of reserves were tied up, and the Fed note too writes that "Solvency concerns around [the issuer] are likely to have played a part."27 Second, the secondary market. Over the weekend when the window was closed, trading crowded into the secondary market and the price hit its low. The recovery came in two stages: the price "recovered sharply" after the authorities' announcement on protecting deposits, and "fully recovered" on the Monday the issuer resumed redemptions. Because the note does not deal with counterfactuals, these data cannot say which of the two stopped the run. What can be said is only the order, and the structure in which the second remedy of Diamond–Dybvig (deposit insurance) was applied not to the stablecoin itself but to the bank where its reserve assets sat.

[Advanced] Go one step further and there is feedback on the reserve-asset side as well. BIS Working Paper 1270 "examines the impact of dollar-backed stablecoin flows on short-term US Treasury yields using daily data from January 2021 to March 2026," and reports that "Using local projections and a granular instrumental variable exploiting idiosyncratic variation in stablecoin growth at the token-blockchain pair level, we find a $3.5 billion (2-standard deviation) inflow lowers 3-month Treasury bill yields by 0.71 basis points on impact, and up to 4 basis points within 10 days, with limited spillovers to longer tenors," and that the effects are "increasing under Treasury market stress and with the scale of the stablecoin sector."26 These estimates are from the June 2026 revision, and because the identification strategy (an instrumental variable) is stated, they can be read, on the premise that the instrument's exclusion restriction holds, as an effect rather than a correlation. The authors describe the estimates as "statistically significant" and present the uncertainty through confidence intervals in figures in the body of the paper, so this book takes only the point estimates. The implication runs in the opposite direction from a run, and that is the authors' own word: "our estimates likely constitute a lower bound for outflow effects, as they are identified from a period of secular market growth that affords issuers discretion over the timing of purchases." If redemptions bunch up and reserve Treasuries have to be sold, yields could move through the same channel, and this is the place where the Fed note writes that "had the run unfolded differently, the pressure for [stablecoin] redemptions might have forced [the issuer] to liquidate backing assets (for example, U.S.Treasury securities), with potential knock-on effects on traditional financial markets."28 The size of the sector and its Treasury holdings as of the reference date are kept in the trend notes in Appendix A (A-18).

A lawyer's question

What does a stablecoin holder have? Gorton and Zhang ask, "In order for the stablecoins to be considered a deposit—let alone a demand deposit—one must determine whether the underlying contract between the holder of stablecoins and the stablecoin issuer is an equity contract or a debt contract," and write that the question has the same shape as the 1970s dispute over whether MMFs took "deposits."29 Is the holder a depositor (예금자) (and if so, is the holder within the scope of deposit insurance and bank regulation)? An unsecured creditor (무담보 채권자) (and if so, does the holder rank with general creditors (일반 채권자) if the issuer becomes insolvent)? Or the beneficiary (수익자) of a trust (신탁) over the reserve assets (and if so, are the reserve assets separated from the insolvency estate (도산재단))? In March 2023 the issuer publicly stated that it would "cover any shortfall using corporate resources, involving external capital if necessary" (Fed note §1, footnote 27). What rights does that statement give holders? If the law requires one-for-one backing, what must the legal structure of that "backing" be: segregated custody (분리 보관), priority (우선권), a trust? This book does not answer; it points to the survey by jurisdiction and the issue sections of Part 5. → Chapter 27 · Chapter 28

7. Summary

[Basic] A stablecoin is a token that carries a promise of redemption, and so it belongs not to the economics of outside money but to the economics of banking. Whether what backs the promise is fiat assets, crypto-assets held as overcollateral, an exchange into a second token, or a hedged derivatives position, the way 1 dollar breaks is the same. When redemptions bunch up, assets cannot be sold in time at full value, and the belief that the promise might break brings on redemptions. The collateral ratio is a number about solvency and the redeemable ratio a number about liquidity, and a run starts with the second. Diamond–Dybvig showed that a run is a second equilibrium that exists alongside the good one, that the choice between them can turn on signals unrelated to fundamentals, and what suspension of convertibility and deposit insurance each change. A stablecoin has no deposit insurance and has a secondary market, so closing the window does not stop a run. The run of March 2023 showed dynamics resembling this picture (the trigger was fundamental information, and the order of recovery only as far as the data tell), and the algorithmic type of May 2022 is a structure without liquidity transformation, so the correspondence differs; Chapter 26 reads that event. This chapter has not said which coin is safe. "Stability" is a property not of the price but of the balance sheet and the procedure. Chapter 25 asks about the opposite end: whether the word "bubble" can be attached by statistics to the price of an asset that promises nothing. The collapse of May 2022 is read as a structure of failure in Chapter 26.
