Part 3 · Economics

Chapter 25. Econometric tests for bubbles: what they measure and what they cannot

Key takeaway

The sentence "Bitcoin is a bubble" turns up often, in court and in papers, but before it can become a testable proposition two things have to be settled. What is the bubble a difference from (the fundamental value)? And what statistical shape does that difference take (explosive growth)? The standard tools econometrics has produced, the right-tailed unit root tests of PWY and PSY (SADF and GSADF), answer only the second question. They measure whether the price grew faster than a unit root for a while, and they put dates on the start and end of that interval. The first question is settled not by a test but by an assumption. That is why studies of the price of the same asset split, into a bubble that makes up 48.7% of the price under a stochastic bubble model (Cheah and Fry), rejection at the 1% level for Bitcoin alone under the PWY test (Hafner), and no explosive departure from the fundamental value (the marginal cost of mining) (Podhorsky). (The exchanges and periods also differ.) When volatility changes over time, textbook critical values cannot be trusted. Where variance rises they reject too often, and for some crypto-assets the error runs the other way (Hafner). And depending on how the fundamental value is set, the same price both is and is not a bubble (Podhorsky). This chapter uses no actual price data. It runs the tests on synthetic data with a planted explosive interval and sees, knowing the right answer, what the tests catch and what they miss. The conclusion of this chapter is the list of things to ask when a "bubble finding" is offered as evidence: the sample, the period, the fundamental-value assumption, the critical values, and the treatment of volatility.

Learning objectives

  1. Know the definition of a rational bubble (price minus fundamental value) and the two assumptions it demands of a test. Distinguish what the word "bubble" can and cannot mean in a legal judgment.
  2. [Intermediate] Read the ADF regression and the explosive coefficient (β>0, that is, ρ>1), and know what a right-tailed unit root test takes as its null hypothesis. Compute SADF and GSADF statistics on synthetic data and compare them with PSY's critical values.
  3. [Advanced] Read the double recursion of the GSADF statistic, the minimum-window rule, and date-stamping (BSADF), and confirm through size distortion under time-varying volatility why Monte Carlo critical values and wild bootstrap critical values differ.
  4. Read the bubble findings of 6 studies in the literature (1 retracted study listed separately) in a table, together with sample, period, fundamental-value assumption, and critical values, and point to where the conclusions part. Know how to handle a retracted paper in a line of citations.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. A "bubble finding" is a statistic saying that the price grew faster than a unit root for a while, and what the fundamental value is, is an assumption, not a test.

1. The question this chapter tries to answer

[Basic] Chapter 19 used models to see why the price of an asset that promises nothing can be other than 0, and those models said that the path of the price is not one but many: there are multiple equilibria. Some of those paths are called "bubbles." Blanchard and Watson made the definition clear in 1982: "Rationality of both behavior and of expectations often does not imply that the price of an asset be equal to its fundamental value. In other words, there can be rational deviations of the price from this value, rational bubbles." And they attached the second question right away, considering "whether the presence of bubbles in a particular market can be detected statistically. The task is much easier if there are data on both prices and returns. … In markets in which returns are difficult to observe, possibly because of a nonpecuniary component, such as gold, the task is more difficult. We consider the use of both 'runs tests' and 'tail tests' and conclude that they give circumstantial evidence at best."1 Bitcoin is an asset without returns (dividends), so it sits on Blanchard and Watson's "more difficult" side. This chapter looks at what econometrics, 40 years later, has made it possible to do on that difficult side, and at what still has to be assumed.

[Basic] For lawyers this question matters for one reason. A finding that "it was a bubble" can be submitted as evidence in cases of fraud, market manipulation, or breach of the duty to explain. Without knowing what that finding measured and what it assumed, a court receives rhetoric, not statistics, as evidence.

2. Two assumptions the definition of a bubble requires

[Basic] In 1985 Tirole defined a bubble as "the difference between the market price and the market fundamental" and wrote: "Since Samuelson [30] developed his consumption loan model it has been well known that there exist economies in which money has a positive value in spite of the fact that it is intrinsically useless (i.e., its market fundamental is zero). In other words there can exist a bubble on money …."2 The two assumptions of the test follow from this definition.

Assumption Content The problem for Bitcoin
Fundamental-value assumption A bubble is a difference, so there must be something to subtract (the fundamental value) It pays no dividends. Each study subtracts something different: estimated within the model and found indistinguishable from 0 (Cheah and Fry), the marginal cost of mining (Podhorsky), a power function of the number of active users (Wheatley et al.), or nothing at all, looking at the price itself (most of the PSY line of work)
Statistical-shape assumption Within a bubble interval the price grows faster than a unit root (explosively) If the fundamental value is itself explosive (like mining difficulty), explosiveness in the price is not evidence of a bubble

[Basic] Why the second assumption holds follows directly from the formula in Chapter 19. In Blanchard and Watson's equation (1) the bubble term must satisfy 𝔼(ct+1|Ωt)=(1+r)ct: its expected value must grow by a factor of (1+r) each period for holders to have a reason to keep it. A unit root process keeps its expected value where it is (𝔼(yt+1)=yt); a bubble's expected value grows. So a bubble test asks not "is the coefficient 1?" but "is the coefficient greater than 1?" It becomes a right-tailed unit root test. In PSY's words, "Right-sided unit root tests … are informative about mildly explosive or submartingale behavior in the data and are therefore useful as a form of market diagnostic or warning alert."3

3. [Intermediate] The ADF regression and the explosive coefficient

[Intermediate] The starting point is the ordinary unit root regression. PSY's equation (4) estimates, over a window running from the r1 fraction to the r2 fraction of the sample,

Δyt=α^r1,r2+β^r1,r2yt−1+∑i=1kψ^r1,r2iΔyt−i+ε^t

and takes the window's ADF statistic ADFr1r2 to be the t ratio of β.4 Reading the symbols: yt is the (log) price, Δyt=yt−yt−1, k is the number of lags for short-run dynamics, and rw=r2−r1 is the width of the window (as a fraction of the sample). The null hypothesis is β=0 (a unit root, with a weak drift allowed), and the alternative is β>0 (explosive). Written in levels, yt=α+ρyt−1+⋯ with ρ=1+β, and the t value is the same as for a test of ρ=1 against ρ>1. This is the opposite of the ordinary ADF test, which looks to the left (β<0, stationarity). A numerical example: if an interval with ρ=1.04 lasts 30 periods, the expected value grows 1.0430≈3.24 times. That is the size of "mild explosiveness."

[Intermediate] The PWY (2011) test fixes the start of the window at the beginning of the sample and extends the end, computing the ADF statistic each time and taking the maximum.

SADF(r0)=supr2∈[r0,1]ADF0r2

r0 is the width of the first window.5 The reason for expanding the window is simple. A single regression on the whole sample buries a short explosive interval in a long unit-root stretch, but a window that ends where the explosive interval ends catches it. One problem remains. Because the start of the window is fixed at the beginning of the sample, a second bubble, after the first has collapsed, is hard to catch because of the collapse that came before it. A sample that contains a collapse shows "pseudo stationary behavior." Solving that problem was the contribution of PSY 2015, and it is the subject of the next section.

[Intermediate] The three cells below are a demonstration of method: they run the tests on synthetic data with a planted explosive interval and see, knowing the right answer, what the tests catch and what they miss. No actual market price data are used.

# NB25-1: PWY/PSY tests on synthetic data — computes SADF and GSADF on a fake price series with a planted explosive interval (a demonstration of method; no actual market price data are used)
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(25)      # fixed seed — the same results are reproduced

def make_series(T=200, bubble=(100, 130), beta=1.04, sigma=1.0, collapse_to=None):
    """A driftless random walk in which only the interval [bubble[0], bubble[1]) grows as y_t = beta·y_{t-1} + e_t; when the interval ends, the series drops back to near its level before the interval."""
    y = np.empty(T); y[0] = 30.0
    e = rng.normal(0.0, sigma, T)
    for t in range(1, T):
        if bubble[0] <= t < bubble[1]:
            y[t] = beta * y[t - 1] + e[t]
        elif t == bubble[1]:
            y[t] = (collapse_to if collapse_to is not None else y[bubble[0] - 1]) + e[t]
        else:
            y[t] = y[t - 1] + e[t]
    return y

def adf_grid(y, min_win):
    """Computes at once the lag-0 ADF t statistic for every window [s, e] (Δy_t regressed on a constant and y_{t-1}; the t ratio of the y_{t-1} coefficient).
    Returns: a (T−1)×(T−1) array A, where A[s, e] is the t of the regression whose window uses Δy for observations s+1 … e+1. Windows that are too short are NaN."""
    x = y[:-1]; z = np.diff(y)                     # x_t = y_{t-1}, z_t = Δy_t, t = 1 … T−1
    n = len(z)
    def ps(a):                                    # prefix sums with a leading 0 — any range sum in one subtraction
        return np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(a)))
    Px, Pz, Pxx, Pxz, Pzz = ps(x), ps(z), ps(x * x), ps(x * z), ps(z * z)
    s = np.arange(n)[:, None]; e = np.arange(n)[None, :]
    cnt = (e - s + 1).astype(float)
    Sx = Px[e + 1] - Px[s]; Sz = Pz[e + 1] - Pz[s]
    Sxx = Pxx[e + 1] - Pxx[s]; Sxz = Pxz[e + 1] - Pxz[s]; Szz = Pzz[e + 1] - Pzz[s]
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        den = cnt * Sxx - Sx * Sx
        beta = (cnt * Sxz - Sx * Sz) / den
        alpha = (Sz - beta * Sx) / cnt
        rss = Szz - alpha * Sz - beta * Sxz
        s2 = rss / (cnt - 2)
        t = beta / np.sqrt(s2 * cnt / den)
    t[(cnt < min_win) | (e < s)] = np.nan
    return t

def sadf_gsadf(y, r0):
    T = len(y); w = int(np.floor(r0 * T))
    A = adf_grid(y, w)
    sadf = np.nanmax(A[0, :])                      # start fixed (0), end extended
    bsadf = np.nanmax(A, axis=0)                   # for each end r2, the maximum over all starts — for date-stamping
    gsadf = np.nanmax(bsadf)                       # the maximum over all (r1, r2)
    return sadf, gsadf, bsadf, A

T = 200
r0 = 0.01 + 1.8 / np.sqrt(T)                       # PSY's minimum-window rule → 0.137 (T = 200)
y = make_series(T)
sadf, gsadf, bsadf, A = sadf_gsadf(y, r0)
PSY_T200 = {"SADF 95%": 1.40, "SADF 99%": 1.90, "GSADF 95%": 2.08, "GSADF 99%": 2.70}   # PSY (2015) Table 1, finite sample, T=200, r0=0.137
print(f"Synthetic data: T = {T}, explosive interval t ∈ [100, 130), β = 1.04, then a collapse. Minimum window r0 = {r0:.3f} → {int(np.floor(r0*T))} observations")
print(f"SADF  = {sadf:.3f}   (PSY Table 1 critical values 95% {PSY_T200['SADF 95%']:.2f}, 99% {PSY_T200['SADF 99%']:.2f})")
print(f"GSADF = {gsadf:.3f}   (PSY Table 1 critical values 95% {PSY_T200['GSADF 95%']:.2f}, 99% {PSY_T200['GSADF 99%']:.2f})")
print(f"Single ADF on the full sample (start 0, end T) = {A[0, -1]:.3f}  ← the explosive interval is buried in the long unit-root stretch and does not show")
peak = int(np.nanargmax(bsadf)) + 1
print(f"Endpoint where BSADF is largest: t = {peak} (just before 130, the end of the planted interval, means the test caught it well)")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
Synthetic data: T = 200, explosive interval t ∈ [100, 130), β = 1.04, then a collapse. Minimum window r0 = 0.137 → 27 observations
SADF  = 11.918   (PSY Table 1 critical values 95% 1.40, 99% 1.90)
GSADF = 12.361   (PSY Table 1 critical values 95% 2.08, 99% 2.70)
Single ADF on the full sample (start 0, end T) = -2.466  ← the explosive interval is buried in the long unit-root stretch and does not show
Endpoint where BSADF is largest: t = 129 (just before 130, the end of the planted interval, means the test caught it well)

[Intermediate] The first cell shows three things. The ADF run once on the whole sample does not see the explosiveness. The SADF, which expands the window, and the GSADF, which sweeps every window, exceed PSY's finite-sample critical values (at T = 200 and r0=0.137, GSADF 95% 2.08 and 99% 2.70).6 And the endpoint where the BSADF is largest lies near the end of the planted interval. All of this was seen knowing the right answer. Real data come with no right answer, and that is why the next two sections are needed.

4. [Advanced] GSADF, the minimum window, date-stamping, and critical values

[Advanced] Double recursion and date-stamping

[Advanced] PSY's statistic moves both the start and the end of the window.

GSADF(r0)=supr2∈[r0,1]r1∈[0,r2−r0]ADFr1r2

Theorem 1 gives the limit distribution of this statistic under the null hypothesis (a random walk with asymptotically negligible drift) as a functional of Wiener processes, and that distribution depends on the minimum window r0.7 That is why the tables of critical values are given for each r0, and the smaller r0, the larger the critical value: "when r0 decreases from 0.190 to 0.055, the 95% asymptotic critical value of the GSADF statistic rises from 1.89 to 2.30." The more windows one sweeps, the more chances there are for a large value to turn up by accident. For the same reason the critical values of GSADF are larger than those of SADF ("when r0=0.10, the 95% asymptotic critical value of the GSADF statistic is 2.19 whereas that of the SADF statistic is 1.49").8

[Advanced] Date-stamping. Asking in real time "does this observation belong to a bubble interval?" is the regulator's question, and PSY answer it with the backward SADF. Fix the endpoint r2, move the start from 0 to r2−r0, and take the maximum of the ADF statistics: that is BSADFr2(r0), and PWY's recursive ADF (start fixed) is a special case of it.9 The origination date is the first observation at which BSADFr2 exceeds the critical value, and the termination date is the first observation, once LT more have passed, at which it falls below the critical value. A minimum-duration condition such as LT=log(T) is there "to exclude short lived blips in the fitted autoregressive coefficient," and it is adjusted to the frequency of the data.10 The second cell builds a sequence of critical values by Monte Carlo and stamps the dates.

# NB25-2: Monte Carlo critical values and date-stamping — generates many null (random walk) series to get the 95% and 99% quantiles of GSADF and the sequence of BSADF critical values, then stamps dates on the synthetic data (a demonstration of method)
def mc_critical_values(T, r0, reps=2000, seed=2025):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = int(np.floor(r0 * T))
    gs = np.empty(reps); bs = np.empty((reps, T - 1))
    for i in range(reps):
        yn = 30.0 + np.cumsum(g.normal(0.0, 1.0, T))           # null: driftless random walk
        A = adf_grid(yn, w)
        bs[i] = np.nanmax(A, axis=0); gs[i] = np.nanmax(bs[i])
    return gs, bs

gs_null, bs_null = mc_critical_values(T, r0)
cv95, cv99 = np.quantile(gs_null, [0.95, 0.99])
print(f"Null random walks, {len(gs_null)} replications → GSADF critical values 95% {cv95:.2f}, 99% {cv99:.2f}   (PSY Table 1: 2.08, 2.70 — this cell: 2,000 replications, lag 0, no drift; PSY: weak drift d=η=1)")
print(f"GSADF of the synthetic data {gsadf:.3f} → at 95%: {'reject (explosive)' if gsadf > cv95 else 'fail to reject'}, at 99%: {'reject' if gsadf > cv99 else 'fail to reject'}")

# date-stamping: for each endpoint t, use the 95% quantile of the null BSADF_t as the critical value (PSY use the SADF critical value based on ⌊T r2⌋ observations; here a sequence taken directly from the same Monte Carlo stands in for it)
bs_cv95 = np.nanquantile(bs_null, 0.95, axis=0)
LT = int(np.ceil(np.log(T)))                      # minimum duration log(T) ≈ 5.3 → 6 observations
flag = bsadf > bs_cv95
episodes, start = [], None
for t, f in enumerate(flag):
    if f and start is None: start = t
    if (not f or t == len(flag) - 1) and start is not None:
        end = t if not f else t + 1
        if end - start >= LT: episodes.append((start + 1, end + 1))   # +1: Δy index → time in the original series
        start = None
print(f"Explosive intervals stamped with the critical-value sequence (endpoint-wise BSADF 95%; minimum duration {LT} observations): {episodes}")
print(f"Planted interval: [100, 130). The start is usually caught a few observations late and the end just after the collapse — the test sees 'growing now', not 'has started to grow'.")
print("An interval caught outside the planted one is a false positive — allow 5% at every endpoint and somewhere among the 170-odd endpoints one crosses by chance (the multiplicity issue Oldani et al. describe).")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
Null random walks, 2000 replications → GSADF critical values 95% 2.11, 99% 2.65   (PSY Table 1: 2.08, 2.70 — this cell: 2,000 replications, lag 0, no drift; PSY: weak drift d=η=1)
GSADF of the synthetic data 12.361 → at 95%: reject (explosive), at 99%: reject
Explosive intervals stamped with the critical-value sequence (endpoint-wise BSADF 95%; minimum duration 6 observations): [(49, 63), (102, 130)]
Planted interval: [100, 130). The start is usually caught a few observations late and the end just after the collapse — the test sees 'growing now', not 'has started to grow'.
An interval caught outside the planted one is a false positive — allow 5% at every endpoint and somewhere among the 170-odd endpoints one crosses by chance (the multiplicity issue Oldani et al. describe).
[Advanced] When volatility changes: the wild bootstrap

[Advanced] Textbook critical values come from the assumption that the variance of the errors is constant. Crypto-asset prices do not behave that way. Hafner takes this up directly in his 2020 paper: "As shown by Harvey et al. (2016), the original test of PWY is biased in the presence of non-stationary volatility." Harvey et al. "suggest a wild bootstrap procedure to correct the size of the PWY test and show that it has good power properties," and Hafner extends the approach to stochastic volatility and applies it to 11 crypto-assets and the CRIX index. The result does not run in one direction. "Taking into account global heteroskedasticity has the effect of increasing the p-values that were found to be very close to zero … In other words, the evidence in favor of speculative bubbles is much less pronounced than when this effect is ignored." But "not all p-values increase, in particular the larger ones tend to decrease under the correction." For Bitcoin, with a PWY statistic of 5.0347, the textbook p-value of 0.0001 rises to a wild bootstrap p-value of 0.0032 (still a rejection at 1%), and "at the 1% level one would reject the null hypothesis in favor of a speculative bubble only for the Bitcoin," while at 5% the number grows to 9 of 12 series (11 crypto-assets + CRIX), or 8 of 11 counting the crypto-assets alone.11 In 2025 Oldani and coauthors wrote that PSY's critical values "are not robust to two potential inference issues: 1) time-varying unconditional heteroscedasticity in the ADF errors and 2) the multiplicity issue (the probability of a false positive increases with the number of hypotheses tested)," and built critical values with the composite wild bootstrap of Phillips and Shi (2020).12 The third cell shows this size distortion on synthetic data.

# NB25-3: size distortion under time-varying volatility, and the wild bootstrap — on null data with no bubble, where only the variance rises, how often do textbook critical values say "bubble"? (a demonstration of method)
def null_with_vol_break(T, g, s1=1.0, s2=3.0, brk=None):
    brk = T // 2 if brk is None else brk
    sig = np.where(np.arange(T) < brk, s1, s2)
    return 30.0 + np.cumsum(g.normal(0.0, 1.0, T) * sig)

g = np.random.default_rng(2526); reps = 400; w = int(np.floor(r0 * T))
rej_const = rej_break = 0
for i in range(reps):
    y0 = 30.0 + np.cumsum(g.normal(0.0, 1.0, T))                       # constant variance
    y1 = null_with_vol_break(T, g)                                      # variance 9x (standard deviation 3x) from the middle
    rej_const += np.nanmax(adf_grid(y0, w)) > cv95
    rej_break += np.nanmax(adf_grid(y1, w)) > cv95
print(f"{reps} null series of each kind, Monte Carlo 95% critical value {cv95:.2f} — nominal size 5%")
print(f"  constant variance:            rejection rate {rej_const / reps:.1%}")
print(f"  standard deviation 3x midway: rejection rate {rej_break / reps:.1%}   ← with no bubble at all, it says 'bubble' this often")

# wild bootstrap (the skeleton of the Hafner and Phillips–Shi approach): multiply the residuals of the observed data by ±1 or normal weights to rebuild null samples, and take the critical value from them — the change of variance over time is preserved as it is
def wild_bootstrap_cv(y, w, B=199, seed=7):
    gb = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    resid = np.diff(y) - np.mean(np.diff(y))                            # residuals under the null (unit root): Δy minus its mean
    stats = np.empty(B)
    for b in range(B):
        eb = resid * gb.normal(0.0, 1.0, len(resid))                    # wild: multiply each residual by an independent N(0,1)
        yb = y[0] + np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(eb)))
        stats[b] = np.nanmax(adf_grid(yb, w))
    return np.quantile(stats, 0.95)

# pick one null series that textbook critical values would call a "bubble" (trying seeds from 0 in order — reproducible)
for sd in range(200):
    y_break = null_with_vol_break(T, np.random.default_rng(sd))
    stat = np.nanmax(adf_grid(y_break, w))
    if stat > cv95: break
cv_wb = wild_bootstrap_cv(y_break, w)
print(f"\nOne null series with changing variance (seed {sd}): GSADF {stat:.2f}. Textbook critical value {cv95:.2f} → {'reject' if stat > cv95 else 'fail to reject'}; wild bootstrap 95% critical value {cv_wb:.2f} → {'reject' if stat > cv_wb else 'fail to reject'}")
print("The bootstrap critical value moves with the volatility structure of the data. The same statistic can be 'bubble' under one critical value and 'not a bubble' under another.")

# Output — bcbook (Python 3.13), exactly as run
400 null series of each kind, Monte Carlo 95% critical value 2.11 — nominal size 5%
  constant variance:            rejection rate 4.8%
  standard deviation 3x midway: rejection rate 34.0%   ← with no bubble at all, it says 'bubble' this often

One null series with changing variance (seed 0): GSADF 2.32. Textbook critical value 2.11 → reject; wild bootstrap 95% critical value 3.45 → fail to reject
The bootstrap critical value moves with the volatility structure of the data. The same statistic can be 'bubble' under one critical value and 'not a bubble' under another.

5. What to take as the fundamental value: three answers

[Basic] So far we have been testing the second assumption (the explosive shape). The first assumption (what to subtract) is a choice, not a test, and the literature has made three choices.

[Basic] Estimated, and indistinguishable from 0. The 2015 paper by Eng-Tuck Cheah and John Fry estimates the collapse-size parameter v of a stochastic bubble model and tests the null hypothesis "v=0". On data from January 1 to November 30, 2013, it found v=0.546 (standard error 0.090, t=6.06) and a growth rate of the long-run fundamental value of μ~=0.00166 (standard error 0.00195, p=0.394), and the authors wrote that "during the bubble price rises are so dramatic that the estimated long-term fundamental value is not statistically different from zero" and that "Equation (16) suggests that the bubble accounts for around 48.7% of observed prices." The third point of their conclusion is "the fundamental value of Bitcoin is zero."13 This conclusion is a proposition inside the model. Getting from the estimate that the growth rate of the fundamental value is indistinguishable from 0 to the conclusion that its level is 0 requires the model's equations (12) and (17), and those equations are assumptions.

[Basic] The marginal cost of mining. Andrea Podhorsky's 2024 paper derives the fundamental value from the world of Chapter 20. Because the protocol manages supply by adjusting difficulty, "the marginal cost of mining the target supply of bitcoins" is the fundamental value the model implies, and that fundamental value can itself be explosive. In the abstract's words, "the bitcoin's volatile and explosive price path is a consequence of the Bitcoin protocol's system of supply management." The empirical work has three steps. Both the price and the fundamental value have unit roots (ADF −2.51, p=.36; −1.90, p=.62); the two are cointegrated (Engle–Granger −2.74, p=.071, at the 10% level); and when the PSY tests are run on the price, SADF 3.7 and GSADF 3.9 exceed the 1% critical values (2.2 and 2.9), but when they are run on the residuals, the price minus the fundamental value, the values −.08 and 1.52 fall short of even the 10% critical values (1.3 and 2.2). "Since the raw price data indicates the presence of bubbles while the residuals ν̂t do not, … we can attribute the apparent bubbles in the price of the bitcoin to the fundamental value."14 Same price, different fundamental value, opposite conclusion.

[Basic] Network size. Spencer Wheatley and coauthors (Sornette among them) in 2019 took a "generalized Metcalfe's Law" (market capitalization as a power function of the number of active users) as the fundamental value, identified four intervals of large departure from it as bubbles, and then tried to predict the window for the time of the collapse with the LPPLS (log-periodic power law singularity) model. The estimated exponent is not 2 but about 1.69 ("a more sparsely connected network in which each user is on average linked to ≈N2/3 other users"), and the four bubbles are May–August 2012 (84 days), January–April 2013 (98 days), October–November 2013 (47 days), and June 2015 to December 2017 (924 days). (The market capitalization and growth-factor columns of their table are not carried over.)15 The authors themselves set out the model uncertainty at length: changing the fitting window produces "4 orders of magnitude difference between the predicted carrying capacities," and "precise inference based on a single model … is misleading, and long-term predictions effectively meaningless."16 This book does not carry over their market capitalization figures or their judgment of a "current overvaluation" (the notes to the reader in Chapter 3). What it keeps is the structure. If the fundamental value is set by the number of users, a bubble becomes "an interval in which the price is above what the number of users justifies," and that judgment hangs on a single exponent of a power function.

6. The literature's findings in one table: sample, period, assumptions, and critical values together

[Intermediate] Here the findings of the empirical studies read in this chapter are set out in one table. The findings are not carried over on their own. When the sample, period, fundamental-value assumption, and critical values differ, the same "rejection" is a different proposition. All the numbers are test statistics on past data, not prices, and this book has not carried over price levels, rates of return, or market capitalizations.

Study Data, sample, period Fundamental-value assumption Method and critical values Finding This book's note
Cheah and Fry (2015) CoinDesk index, daily, 2010-07-18 to 2014-07-17; test window 2013-01-01 to 11-30 0 (estimated within the model → indistinguishable from 0) Stochastic bubble model, H0:v=0 v=0.546 (SE 0.090); the bubble is about 48.7% of the price "Fundamental value 0" is a conclusion that hangs on the model's equations (12) and (17)
Cheung, Roca and Su (2015) Mt. Gox USD, daily, 2010-07-17 to 2014-02-18, N = 1,307 None (the log price itself) PSY GSADF, r0≈2% (20 observations), 99% critical value 99% critical value exceeded 33 times; three big bubbles: 2011-04-24 to 07-03 (66 days as reported in the paper; 71 days on the calendar counting both ends; cause of the difference not verified), 2013-01-27 to 04-15 (79 days), 2013-11-05 to 2014-02-18 (106 days) Prices from a single exchange; the third is cut off at the end of the sample (the closure of the exchange)

This gap among the text, the tables, and the abstract is a point for the reader to check directly

(2019) Bitstamp USD, hourly, 2012-01-01 to 2018-01-08; number of active users Generalized Metcalfe's law (exponent ≈ 1.69) Departure from the fundamental value + LPPLS Four bubbles (84, 98, 47, and 924 days; growth factors not carried over) The fundamental value hangs on a single power-law exponent; the authors state the model uncertainty

17 18 19

[Intermediate] What to take from the table is not the sum of the findings but the places where they part. For the same Bitcoin price, (a) if no fundamental value is subtracted, most studies find explosive intervals; (b) if the marginal cost of mining is subtracted, none are found; (c) if volatility is adjusted for, the evidence weakens, but Bitcoin remains; and (d) if the exchange, frequency, or period changes, the number and length of the intervals change. None of these four is an answer to "was it a bubble?" Each is an answer to "what did we decide to call a bubble?"

7. What the test says and what it does not

[Basic] What a right-tailed unit root test says: in some interval, the autoregressive coefficient of the (log) price was significantly greater than 1. The start and end of that interval can be estimated as dates. Multiple intervals can be caught (PSY). If volatility changes, the critical values must be rebuilt from the data (Hafner; Phillips and Shi).

[Basic] What it does not say: why it happened (a demand shock, a change in the fundamental value, or manipulation). Who did it (the test looks at a single price series). What comes after (PSY themselves describe the approach as "ex ante (or anticipative)," an "early warning alert system," but the content of that alert is "it is growing now," not "it is about to burst"). And what the fundamental value is: this is an assumption outside the test. The "circumstantial evidence at best" that Blanchard and Watson wrote in 1982 still holds, in that the structure of the question has not changed even as the tools have become more refined.

[Basic] One more thing should be recorded. The models of Chapter 19 said that bubbles can be rational. Tirole gave the conditions under which bubbles exist, and Blanchard and Watson wrote that "phenomena such as runaway asset prices and market crashes are consistent with rational bubbles." If so, a statistical finding that "it was a bubble" does not in itself imply anyone's irrationality or deception. To imply that, further premises are needed, and those premises are a matter for fact-finding, not for statistics.

A lawyer's question

An expert witness submits an opinion that "the price over the relevant period was explosive at the 1% level in a GSADF test and therefore was a bubble." After this chapter, the questions to ask are settled. What data (exchange, frequency, period)? What was taken as the fundamental value, or was none taken? Are the critical values from a textbook table or from a bootstrap built on the data? How was the change in volatility handled? What are the minimum window and the minimum-duration condition? And how is the finding, even if it is statistically correct, connected to which act of the defendant? Is the existence of an explosive interval evidence of market manipulation, evidence of fraudulent deception, or an observation that one of multiple equilibria was realized? Conversely, does a finding that "it was not a bubble" (cointegration with the marginal cost of mining, for instance) help the defendant? This book does not answer, and points to the issue section in Part 5. → Chapter 28

8. Summary

[Basic] A bubble is the difference between price and fundamental value, and testing for it rests on two assumptions: what is subtracted, and whether the difference takes an explosive shape. Right-tailed unit root tests (PWY's SADF, PSY's GSADF) deal only with the second. As the synthetic data showed, tests that move the window catch a planted explosive interval and mostly stamp its dates, but under time-varying volatility textbook critical values reject too often, and bootstrap critical values move with the data. The literature has given three answers to the first assumption (0, the marginal cost of mining, network size), and when the answer changes, the same price both is and is not a bubble. So when you receive a "bubble finding," ask about the sample, period, fundamental value, critical values, and treatment of volatility together. Part 3 ends here. It started from "where does value come from?" in Chapter 19, passed through the security budget, fees, token design, game theory, and stablecoins, and has arrived at "can a bubble be measured?", and the common answer was conditional. Models enumerate possibilities, tests measure shapes, and neither prophesies the one path that reality will take. Chapter 26 reads four cases in which those conditions actually broke down.
