Part 4 · Reading through cases

Chapter 26. Four cases: Mt.Gox, The DAO, Terra-Luna, FTX

Notice

From here on we read four cases. To say it in advance: this part does not follow "who made and who lost how much." It asks one thing: what broke? Was it the technology, the economic design, the governance, or was it fraud from the start? Names and figures are only those written in judgments and official investigation documents.

The full text of the notice is in the colophon (F.4 of Appendix F).

Key takeaway

This chapter places the four cases on the same diagnostic table. It has four columns: what broke (technology, economic design, governance, fraud); whether the incident happened on the chain or off it; what the code did and what people did; and what followed (insolvency proceedings, a hard fork, criminal proceedings). Facts are taken only from judgments and decisions (whether they are final is stated in the notes), official investigations, and insolvency documents, and each amount is given once, as written in those documents. The layer that broke is different in each of the four cases. Mt.Gox is a mismatch between the exchange's books and the chain (the manipulation of the books was found by the criminal judgments at first instance and on appeal, and no court document has decided the cause of the February 2014 loss); The DAO is a flaw in the contract code and the governance decision that followed; Terra is the reflexivity of the design and the issuer's statements; and FTX is the misuse of customer assets and the absence of internal controls. None of the four is a case in which the consensus rules and ledger integrity learned in Part 1 were broken by an outside attack. That sentence, though, can only be read once it is settled what "the blockchain itself" is, and this chapter says it only after defining that scope in three parts in Section 1. What the lawyer takes away is not the story of the cases but the diagnostic framework. Only once you sort out which layer broke can you see where each body of law comes in.

Learning objectives

  1. Put the four cases on the same diagnostic table (① the layer that broke, ② on or off the chain, ③ what the code did and what people did, ④ what followed) and read them side by side.
  2. Divide the phrase "the blockchain itself" into three layers (consensus rules and ledger integrity / properties of the protocol / the books, contracts, and issuers placed on top) and tell, for each case, which layer the story is about.
  3. For each case, distinguish what the primary documents (judgments, official investigations, insolvency documents) decided and what they did not decide. Exchange announcements and press reports are not primary documents.
  4. Note where the lawyer's questions arise in each case, and hand them over to the issue sections of Part 5.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. What broke is different in each of the four cases, and among them there is no case in which the consensus rules of Bitcoin or Ethereum were broken by an outside attack and the ledger was reversed. The places that gave way were the books off the chain, the contract code placed on the chain, the issuer's design and statements, and human hands.

1. How this chapter reads the cases: the diagnostic table and the scope of "the blockchain itself"

[Basic] Write the cases up one by one as stories and "who lost how much" becomes the axis. This book does not use that axis (the notes to the reader in Chapter 3). Instead it puts the four cases on the same table. There are four columns.

Column What it asks
① The layer that broke Was it technology (consensus rules, the ledger, cryptography), economic design (the structure of tokens, collateral, fees), governance (who changes the rules), or fraud (the gap between statements and reality)? It may be more than one
② On or off the chain Did the incident happen as a state transition on the ledger, or in books, bank accounts, or a company off the ledger?
③ Code and people Separate what the code did as written from what people did by hand. Here you can see that "it was executed as coded" is not a statement that erases responsibility
④ What followed Which of insolvency proceedings, a hard fork, criminal proceedings, and administrative investigation followed, and what did those documents decide?

[Basic] To fill in the second column, the scope of the phrase "the blockchain itself" has to be settled first. The phrase is used to point to three different things.

Layer Meaning Where this book covers it
(a) Consensus rules and ledger integrity The rules by which blocks are linked, the choice of the longest (heaviest) chain, signature verification, transaction validity rules. What the "cost of tampering" protects Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 9, Chapter 23
(b) Properties of the protocol Behavior the rules allow that the designers did not intend or that troubles the application layer. Transaction malleability (the property that changing a signature changes the transaction identifier), the power to decide ordering (MEV), and so on Chapter 5, Chapter 17
(c) What is placed on top An exchange's internal books, the code of a smart contract, the balance sheet and statements of a stablecoin issuer. The chain does not guarantee them Chapter 13, Chapter 14, Chapter 24

When this chapter writes "the blockchain itself did not break," it means (a). (b) may have been involved, depending on the case (Mt.Gox claimed so), and (c) is the stage for all four cases. Mixing the three layers to say "blockchains are safe" or "blockchains are dangerous" is something this chapter does not do, either way.

[Basic] The sources of fact are limited to three: judgments and decisions that are final or whose finality is stated, official investigation reports of regulators, and documents filed by courts, trustees, and debtors in insolvency proceedings. An exchange's press release is a source for the fact that "the party said so," not for the truth of what it says, and newspaper reports are not used. Two additions. For the technical description of The DAO's flaw, which the judgments and investigation documents do not give, this chapter uses Ethereum Foundation announcements and an EIP (what Chapter 22 handed over to this chapter). And the February 7, 2014, Mt.Gox announcement halting withdrawals is quoted from a secondary reproduction, because the original archive could not be opened, and this is stated where it is used.

2. Mt.Gox (2014): a mismatch between the books and the chain

What the documents record

[Basic] The company that ran the bitcoin exchange Mt.Gox (hereafter "Company M," as the judgment writes it) petitioned the Tokyo District Court (東京地方裁判所) for commencement of civil rehabilitation proceedings (民事再生, minji saisei) on February 28, 2014. The announcement the company issued that day gave its financial position as follows: total assets of JPY 3,841,866,163 and total current liabilities of JPY 6,501,119,371. It also wrote that behind the increase in current liabilities "ビットコインの消失，預り金の消失という原因が考えられ" (working gloss, not an official translation; the original controls: "the disappearance of bitcoins and the disappearance of deposited funds are thought to be the causes").1 The same announcement describes the course of events as follows. In early February 2014, "ビットコインのシステムのバグを悪用した不正アクセスにより" (gloss: "through unauthorized access exploiting a bug in the bitcoin system"), transactions in which a remittance was not completed normally increased; investigation revealed by about February 24 that almost all of roughly 750,000 BTC held by users and roughly 100,000 BTC held by the company itself had disappeared; on the same day a shortfall of at most about JPY 2.8 billion was found between the total of users' deposits and the balance of deposits at financial institutions; and at noon on February 25 all access to the site was suspended. On the cause, it wrote "第三者によるハッキングによる被害を含めて，複数の原因があると見込まれる" (gloss: "multiple causes are expected, including damage from hacking by third parties"). The words "transaction malleability" do not appear here.

[Basic] Three weeks later, on March 20, the company announced that it had rescanned an old-format wallet it had used before June 2011 and confirmed that about 200,000 BTC (199,999.99 BTC) remained in it, and it lowered its estimate of the loss from about 850,000 BTC to about 650,000 BTC. That announcement, too, says "ＢＴＣの消失の原因や消失したＢＴＣの数量は現在調査中" (gloss: "the cause of the disappearance of the BTC and the quantity of BTC that disappeared are currently under investigation").2 On April 16 the Tokyo District Court dismissed the petition for commencement of civil rehabilitation and issued a provisional administration order (保全管理命令, hozen kanri meirei), and on April 24 it made a decision commencing bankruptcy proceedings (破産手続, hasan tetsuzuki). The reason given in the decision is one line: "一件記録によれば，債務者が支払不能の状態にあることが認められる。" (gloss: "According to the entire record, it is found that the debtor is in a state of inability to pay.")3 In his report for the first creditors' meeting in July 2014, the bankruptcy trustee wrote that he had entrusted the investigation of the loss to outside accounting firms and that "the completion date is undetermined," and in his May 2016 report he wrote, "Due to the circumstances, such as the limited amount of information that exists, I believe it will be difficult to understand the full picture …." The March 2018 report records that, when the U.S. Department of Justice indicted the operator of another exchange in July 2017, the allegations included that "he obtained funds by hacking MtGox," and that the trustee had requested information.4 On a petition by some creditors in November 2017, civil rehabilitation proceedings were commenced on June 22, 2018, and the bankruptcy proceedings were stayed.5 Among the documents on the trustee's site, this book found none that settles and announces the cause of the loss.

What the exchange gave as the cause, and what the empirical study found

[Intermediate] Before the February 28 announcement, the company had announced on February 7 that it was halting all bitcoin withdrawals. That announcement said that "the increase in the flow of withdrawal requests has hindered our efforts on a technical level" and that "a temporarily [sic] pause on all withdrawal requests" was necessary; it gave no cause.6 The February 10 announcement was the first to name a cause. Under the heading "Addressing Transaction Malleability" it wrote: "A bug in the bitcoin software makes it possible for someone to use the Bitcoin network to alter transaction details to make it seem like a sending of bitcoins to a bitcoin wallet did not occur when in fact it did occur."7 This is the transaction malleability we saw in Chapter 5. Change the form of a signature and the transaction identifier (txid) changes, and exchange software that tracks the success or failure of transactions only by identifier can read a transaction that was actually sent as "failed" and send it again. In terms of the three layers above, this is the path by which a property of layer (b) deceived the books of layer (c).

[Intermediate] This claim can be tested by observing the network. Christian Decker and Roger Wattenhofer had been running a node on the Bitcoin network since January 2013 and recording the transactions relayed to it (the connected peers were about 20% of reachable nodes), and in that data they counted the traces of malleability attacks: pairs of transactions that spend the same inputs but differ only in the encoding of the signature. Their conclusion: "while MtGox claimed to have lost 850,000 bitcoins due to malleability attacks, we merely observed a total of 302,000 bitcoins ever being involved in malleability attacks. Of these, only 1,811 bitcoins were in attacks before MtGox stopped users from withdrawing bitcoins. Even more, 78.64% of these attacks were ineffective. As such, barely 386 bitcoins could have been stolen using malleability attacks from MtGox or from other businesses."8 Malleability attacks rose sharply after the February 10 announcement (after the announcement had made the method of attack known), and the amount before withdrawals were halted is about 1/470 of the claimed loss. The paper ends with "MtGox needs to explain the whereabouts of 849,600 bitcoins." What the empirical study says goes as far as "the amount explained by malleability attacks is very small"; it does not say where the rest went.

What the criminal judgments found: fictitious balances in the books

[Basic] The representative director was arrested and indicted in 2015, and on March 15, 2019, the Tokyo District Court sentenced the defendant for the offenses of 私電磁的記録不正作出 and 同供用 (shi-denjiteki kiroku fusei sakushutsu and dō kyōyō, "unauthorized creation of private electromagnetic records" and "use of such records") to 懲役2年6月·執行猶予4年 (imprisonment with work for 2 years and 6 months, suspended for 4 years), and acquitted the defendant on the counts of 業務上横領 (gyōmujō ōryō, "embezzlement in the course of business") and 会社法違反 (kaishahō ihan, "violation of the Companies Act"; aggravated breach of trust).9 On June 11, 2020, the Tokyo High Court (東京高等裁判所) dismissed the defendant's appeal; the acquittals were not before the appellate court, because the prosecution did not appeal them.10 This book has not verified whether a final appeal was filed or the date on which the judgment became final (as of 2026-10). What follows are the facts and determinations found in the texts of the two judgments. The "判示事項" (hanji jikō, "matters decided") summaries in case-law databases are editorial products and are not quoted.

[Basic] The first-instance judgment begins by describing the structure of the exchange. When a user sends money to a bank account designated by the company, or sends bitcoin to an address the company manages, the system confirms this automatically and increases the balance of the user's account. After that, even when trades are concluded between users, "本件取引システム上の口座残高に増減が生じるだけで，…ビットコインも同様に，本件取引システム上の口座残高に変動は生じるが，ブロックチェーン上に変動は生じない" (gloss: "only increases or decreases in the account balances on the Trading System arise, ... likewise with bitcoin, the account balances on the Trading System change, but no change arises on the blockchain"). In other words, trading inside the exchange is only the movement of numbers in the books, and the blockchain moves only when a user requests repayment or delivery and the company actually sends it.11 This is the relationship between the ledger seen in Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 and the layer (c) books placed on top of it. The judgment also reserves its position on the private-law nature of bitcoin: "ビットコインは「有体物」（民法８５条）ではなく，その帰属や利用者間での取引がどのような私法上の性質を有するかも一義的に明らかとはいえないが，本件の判断に影響のない限り，ビットコインの保有・所有や利用者間の売買などと表現し，日常的な意味合いで記載する。" (gloss: "Bitcoin is not a 「有体物」 (yūtaibutsu, "tangible thing") (Civil Code, Article 85), and it cannot be said to be unambiguously clear what private-law nature its attribution and the transactions between users have; but insofar as this does not affect the determination in this case, [this judgment] expresses these as the possession or ownership of bitcoin, sale and purchase between users, and so on, and writes in the everyday sense.")12 This is the sentence that the map of scholarly positions in 27.2, in Part 5, takes up.

[Intermediate] The skeleton of the facts found is three "balance-increasing acts."13 First, in August 2011, another exchange in Poland that the defendant's parent company (Ｄ社 in the first-instance judgment, Ｔ社 in the appellate judgment) had acquired lost 17,000 BTC through a system defect and took on "ブロックチェーン上に存在しない１万７０００ＢＴＣの返還債務" (gloss: "an obligation to give back 17,000 BTC that did not exist on the blockchain"); the defendant entered information increasing the U.S. dollar balance of his own account by USD 150,000, used those dollars to purchase about 18,000 BTC from users, and then deleted 17,500 BTC from the bitcoin balance of his account ("１５万米ドル増加行為," gloss: "the USD 150,000 increase act"). Second, in November 2011, when a French bank account the company used was temporarily frozen and about JPY 100 million could not be withdrawn, the defendant, on 8 occasions from November 2011 to April 2012, entered information increasing the bitcoin balance of his own account by 300,000 BTC without sending bitcoin to the company's addresses, and by February 2013 had sold a total of about 300,000 BTC to users and obtained about USD 1.3 million ("３０万ＢＴＣ増加行為," gloss: "the 300,000 BTC increase act"). Third, to recover from the resulting state in which "ブロックチェーン上には存在しないビットコイン３０万ＢＴＣが利用者間で取引されることとなった" (gloss: "300,000 BTC of bitcoin that did not exist on the blockchain came to be traded between users"), on 21 occasions from February to September 2013 he entered information increasing the dollar balance of his account by a total of USD 33.5 million, purchased about 300,000 BTC from users for about USD 29.77 million, and then deleted that bitcoin balance ("本件各行為," gloss: "the acts in this case"). What was charged was the third set of acts, and the court held that, because the third was a means of concealing the second, the two had to be viewed as a single whole.

[Intermediate] The issue was whether these entries created electromagnetic records "不正に" (fusei ni, "improperly"). The defense argued that, since the defendant was the only person with comprehensive authority to conduct the company's business, the defendant's acts were the company's will. The court separated the company's will from the defendant's inner intentions and read it from the terms of use and the nature of the system. The key sentence: "ビットコインの存在根拠及びその経済的価値の根拠は，取引されるビットコインが，ブロックチェーン上に存在することにかかっているのであって，ブロックチェーン上に存在しないビットコインは，仮に，本件取引システム上のビットコイン口座に残高が表示されたとしても，架空のビットコインといわざるを得ない。" (gloss: "The basis for the existence of bitcoin and the basis for its economic value depend on the traded bitcoin existing on the blockchain, and bitcoin that does not exist on the blockchain must be called fictitious bitcoin, even if a balance is displayed in a bitcoin account on the Trading System.") The terms of use stated that the seller "売却オファーの目的となる…ビットコインは，実際のビットコインに対応することを保証" (gloss: "guarantees that the ... bitcoins that are the object of a sale offer correspond to actual bitcoins"), and there was neither a provision nor an on-screen display permitting credit trading. So the company's will was that "Ｂ社管理のビットコインアドレスにおけるビットコインの受送付等による裏付けがある場合に限って，本件取引システム上の利用者の口座残高を増加させるべきである" (gloss: "users' account balances on the Trading System should be increased only where there is backing by the receipt or sending, etc., of bitcoin at bitcoin addresses managed by Company B"), and the defendant's authority was also limited to that scope.14 The appellate court said of this determination that it "概ね同旨をいうものとして是認できる" (gloss: "can be upheld as stating substantially the same"), and added that the evidentiary function of electromagnetic records rests on "それが作出されるべきシステムの設置運営主体の意思に基づき，正当に作出されることが当然の前提" (gloss: "the natural premise that they are created legitimately, based on the will of the entity that set up and operates the system in which they are to be created").15

[Intermediate] On money, by contrast, the conclusion was different. Money that users sent to the account designated by the company belonged to the company, and since at the time neither statute nor the terms of use required separate management, it could not be said that money corresponding to the dollar balances in the books had to be in the company's bank accounts.16 So the transfers from the company's accounts to accounts in the defendant's name and elsewhere were not embezzlement of users' money (the primary count); not embezzlement of the company's money (alternative count 1), because they were accounted for as short-term loans and there was a realistic possibility of repayment; and not aggravated breach of trust (alternative count 2). Set the two conclusions side by side and the structure of the case appears. On the bitcoin side, the requirement of backing, that it "must be on the chain," was found to be the company's will; on the money side, the requirement that it "must be in the bank" was not. What made the difference was the property of layer (a) in Section 1, that the "existence" of bitcoin is defined by the blockchain record, and the state of the law, that there was then no statute requiring separate management. Korea's current Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률) provides for the separate deposit or trust of users' deposits (Article 6) and for the separate custody of virtual assets together with the obligation to "동일한 종류와 수량의 가상자산을 실질적으로 보유" (gloss: "actually possess virtual assets of the same kind and quantity") (Article 7(2)); these are obligations placed in the two positions just described. Whether this case was the purpose of that legislation is not stated, because the legislative materials were not checked.17 What kind of right those provisions presuppose is asked in Chapter 28.

Diagnosis

[Basic] ① The layer that broke is the exchange's books and internal controls: layer (c). In the part on which the court found guilt, balances that were not on the chain appeared in the books, without any transfer on the chain, and were traded. Which layer the February 2014 loss belongs to is something no court document decided. The exchange cited a property of layer (b) (transaction malleability) and in its later announcement of February 28 also mentioned the possibility of hacking; the empirical study found the amount explained by malleability to be very small; and the trustee said it would be difficult to understand the full picture. ② Off the chain. ③ What the code did was to confirm users' remittances automatically and raise balances, and human hands entered where, as the appellate court wrote, "人が個々の取引やその履歴のデータ等を直接入力するようなことは想定されていなかった" (gloss: "it was not contemplated that a person would directly input individual transactions, their history data, and the like"). ④ What followed were insolvency proceedings (petition for civil rehabilitation → dismissal and provisional administration → bankruptcy → civil rehabilitation on a creditors' petition (2018)) and criminal determinations (guilty of the unauthorized creation of electromagnetic records, not guilty of embezzlement). Whether a final appeal was filed and whether the judgment is final are not verified.

3. The DAO (2016): a flaw in the contract code and the decision that followed

What the documents record

[Basic] The investigation report of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of July 25, 2017 (Release No. 81207) sets out the facts in the most orderly form. The DAO is one example of what is "a term used to describe a 'virtual' organization embodied in computer code and executed on a distributed ledger or blockchain," and it was created by the German company Slock.it and its co-founders. From April 30 to May 28, 2016, approximately 1.15 billion DAO Tokens were sold in exchange for approximately 12 million ETH, and the token holders were to vote on proposals and share in earnings.18 A proposal went to a vote only after a "Curator" had put it on a whitelist, and the White Paper wrote that the Curators had "considerable power."19 Then, page 9 of the report: "On June 17, 2016, an unknown individual or group (the 'Attacker') began rapidly diverting ETH from The DAO, causing approximately 3.6 million ETH—1/3 of the total ETH raised by The DAO offering—to move from The DAO's Ethereum Blockchain address to an Ethereum Blockchain address controlled by the Attacker (the 'Attack'). Although the diverted ETH was then held in an address controlled by the Attacker, the Attacker was prevented by The DAO's code from moving the ETH from that address for 27 days." After that, "Slock.it's co-founders and others endorsed a 'Hard Fork'," and "On July 20, 2016, after a majority of the Ethereum network adopted the necessary software updates, the new, forked Ethereum Blockchain became active." Footnote 32 records that a minority did not adopt the fork, on the ground that it would run counter to the concept that "a blockchain is immutable," and kept using the old chain, which is called "Ethereum Classic."20

[Basic] The technical description of the flaw was given not by the SEC report but by the Ethereum Foundation blog on the day of the attack (Chapter 22 noted that the SEC wrote only "a flaw in The DAO's code" and handed this description over to this chapter): "The attack is a recursive calling vulnerability, where an attacker called the 'split' function, and then calls the split function recursively inside of the split, thereby collecting ether many times over in a single transaction." And one sentence in the same post states the layer distinction of Section 1 as it is: "This is an issue that affects the DAO specifically; Ethereum itself is perfectly safe."21 Put into the EVM call model we saw in Chapter 13 (this is this book's reading; the primary document goes only as far as "calls the split function recursively"), the contract sent ether by an external call before updating the balance, and the receiving contract, inside that call, called the same function again and repeatedly drew out the balance that had not yet been updated. The code ran as written, without deviating by a single line. What diverged were the author's intention and the code.

[Basic] The foundation blog first wrote that a soft fork had been proposed (a rule making invalid any transaction that reduces the balance of The DAO and its child contracts, that is, accounts with the same code hash), and in the end it became a hard fork. The post of July 20, 2016, reads: "Block 1920000 contained the execution of an irregular state change which transferred ~12 million ETH from the 'Dark DAO' and 'Whitehat DAO' contracts into the WithdrawDAO recovery contract. The fork itself took place smoothly, with roughly 85% of miners mining on the fork". It also told users who wanted to follow the old chain to update their clients but run them with the --oppose-dao-fork flag.22 EIP-779, which documented this fork after the event, fixes its character in one sentence: "Unlike other hard forks, the DAO Fork did not change the protocol; all EVM opcodes, transaction format, block structure, and so on remained the same. Rather, the DAO Fork was an 'irregular state change' that transferred ether balances from a list of accounts ('child DAO' contracts) into a specified account (the 'WithdrawDAO' contract)."23

Diagnosis

[Basic] ① Two layers broke. One is a flaw in the contract code of the application layer (layer (c)), and the other is governance. The flaw itself was "an issue that affects the DAO specifically; Ethereum itself is perfectly safe." But the decision that followed, in which a majority of nodes updated their software and accepted an "irregular state change" moving the balances of particular accounts into another account, was a case of changing the state of the ledger without changing the rules of layer (a). The sentence of EIP-779 separates exactly these two. The consensus rules were not broken; participants rewrote the state within the rules (through the coordination of a client update). A minority did not follow, and the old chain survived. This is where Chapter 23 looked at "who decides which ledger is the real one" as a coordination game. ② The attack happened on the chain, as a state transition set by the contract code. ③ The code did what was written, and people made the decisions (i) to propose a soft fork and (ii) to adopt or reject a hard fork. ④ What followed were the hard fork and the coexistence of two chains, and, a year later, the SEC's investigation report. The SEC determined that "DAO Tokens are securities" while deciding not to pursue an enforcement action, and wrote: "The automation of certain functions through this technology, 'smart contracts,' or computer code, does not remove conduct from the purview of the U.S. federal securities laws."24 The framework of that determination (Howey) is taken up in Chapter 27, and whether tokens are securities in Chapter 28.

A lawyer's question

What was The DAO hard fork? Was it a remedy that recovered funds drained through the flaw? If so, a remedy on whose authority, by what procedure, and by what standard? Was it a forfeiture, in which a majority's software update took back what the attacker had acquired "according to the code"? If so, did the attacker have due process, and what did reversing a result the code permitted, on a platform that said "code is law," violate? Or was it a change of contract, in which a majority of the participants changed the rules among themselves? If so, was the dissenting minority's staying on the old chain a rescission of the contract, or a partition? EIP-779 writes that the DAO Fork "did not change the protocol" and was an "irregular state change." Does that distinction have legal meaning? This book does not answer, and points to the issue section of Part 5. → Chapter 28

4. Terra-Luna (2022): the reflexivity of the design and the issuer's statements

What the documents record

[Basic] The mechanism was set out in Section 2 of Chapter 24, from the 2022 report of the Bank for International Settlements. The algorithmic stablecoin UST sought to keep its peg by being convertible into "one dollar's worth of Luna," and the decisive condition of that arrangement was that "users would only be willing to exchange UST into Luna if Luna's market capitalisation exceeded that of UST."25 If that condition fails, redemptions mint more Luna, the increased supply lowers Luna's value, and that invites more redemptions: this feedback is the spiral that NB24-3 in Chapter 24 showed with a model. This chapter does not repeat that mechanism and looks only at what court documents wrote after May 2022.

[Basic] In SEC v. Terraform Labs Pte. Ltd. and Do Hyeong Kwon (No. 1:23-cv-01346-JSR) in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, the court granted summary judgment on December 28, 2023, on the SEC's claim that the defendants violated Section 5 of the Securities Act through unregistered offers and sales of securities, and on April 5, 2024, the jury returned its verdict on violations of the antifraud provisions. The verdict form reads as follows. On the claim under Section 17 of the Securities Act, Terraform "Liable," with the mental state "Recklessly"; Kwon "Liable," "Intentionally." On the claim for intentional or reckless violation of Rule 10b-5 under the Securities Exchange Act, both "Liable." On control person liability for Terraform's violation, Kwon "Liable."26 The final judgment of June 12, 2024, records that the defendants "consented to entry of this Final Judgment; waived findings of fact and conclusions of law; and waived any right to appeal," and set monetary remedies together with injunctions. For Terraform: disgorgement of USD 3,586,875,883, prejudgment interest of USD 466,952,423, and a civil penalty of USD 420,000,000 (the total of USD 4,473,828,306 is payable as provided for in the Chapter 11 plan confirmed in the bankruptcy case in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, and Terraform agreed to seek confirmation of a plan that treats that amount as a general unsecured claim of the SEC; p. 7). For Kwon: disgorgement of USD 110,000,000 (jointly and severally with Terraform), interest of USD 14,320,196, and a civil penalty of USD 80,000,000.27 The final judgment also barred the defendants from participating in the purchase or sale of "any crypto asset securities, including but not limited to UST, MIR, LUNA, wLUNA, and LUNA 2.0," and required Terraform to "burn or destroy" the private keys in its possession to the wallets for those tokens.

[Basic] The criminal case is United States v. Do Hyeong Kwon (No. 1:23-cr-00151-PAE) in the same court. This chapter writes from the judgment (Judgment in a Criminal Case, ECF No. 63) only. The defendant "pleaded guilty" to count 1s of the indictment (S1), "18 U.S.C. § 371 Conspiracy to Defraud," and to count 4s, "18 U.S.C. § 1343 and 2 Wire Fraud," and the date the offense ended is given as March 23, 2023, for both counts. The total sentence is 180 months (60 months on count 1s and 180 months on count 4s, to run concurrently; this follows the sentencing transcript, and the judgment's entry by count differs from it29). The court also directed credit for the time in custody since arrival in the United States on December 31, 2024, and for 17 months and 8 days of pre-extradition custody in Montenegro. No term of supervised release was imposed; the special assessment is USD 200, and forfeiture is governed by a separate order (Dkt. No. 47). The sentence was imposed on December 11, 2025, by Judge Paul A. Engelmayer.28 Page 2 of the judgment contains "the Court encourages any court in the Republic of Korea that may sentence the defendant to take this Court's sentence into account," and a statement of the court's support for an application for transfer to Korea after half the custodial term has been served.

Diagnosis

[Basic] ① The layers that broke are economic design and statements. Chapter 24 showed the reflexivity of the design with a model; what the court documents added is the determination that the statements of the issuer and its head fell under the antifraud provisions of the securities laws. The jury found Terraform "Recklessly" and Kwon "Intentionally," and the criminal court accepted guilty pleas to conspiracy to defraud and wire fraud. What was stated, and how, is not written in the primary documents within this chapter's scope (the verdict form and the judgments), and so it is not given here. ② On and off the chain overlap. The swap module ran on the chain as designed, and the statements were made off the chain. ③ The code did as designed; drawing the spiral when the condition failed was part of the design. What people did was choose the design and explain it. ④ What followed were civil proceedings (summary judgment, jury verdict, final judgment by consent), criminal proceedings (guilty plea, 180 months), and insolvency proceedings (United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware). "What does a holder of a stablecoin have?" is the question Chapter 24 posed, and it is taken up in Chapter 28 and in the stablecoin column of Chapter 27.

5. FTX (2022): misuse of customer assets and the absence of internal controls

What the documents record

[Basic] When the FTX Group filed for Chapter 11 in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware on November 11, 2022 (West Realm Shires Inc. on November 14), John J. Ray III, who became the new chief executive officer, filed the "Declaration of John J. Ray III in Support of Chapter 11 Petitions and First Day Pleadings" on November 17. He has handled large insolvencies including Enron, and in paragraph 5 he wrote: "Never in my career have I seen such a complete failure of corporate controls and such a complete absence of trustworthy financial information as occurred here. From compromised systems integrity and faulty regulatory oversight abroad, to the concentration of control in the hands of a very small group of inexperienced, unsophisticated and potentially compromised individuals, this situation is unprecedented."30 The declaration divides the group into four "Silos" (the FTX US group, Alameda, Ventures, and the FTX.com group) and states that "Each of the Silos was controlled by Mr. Bankman-Fried."31 It then lists the absence of controls item by item. Disbursements were approved on "an on-line 'chat' platform where a disparate group of supervisors approved disbursements by responding with personalized emojis,"32 and with respect to digital assets there were "the use of an unsecured group email account as the root user to access confidential private keys and critically sensitive data," "the absence of daily reconciliation of positions on the blockchain," "the use of software to conceal the misuse of customer funds," "the secret exemption of Alameda from certain aspects of FTX.com's auto-liquidation protocol," and "the absence of independent governance as between Alameda … and the Dotcom Silo."33 That at least USD 372 million was transferred without authorization on the petition date itself, and that FTT tokens worth approximately USD 300 million were afterward additionally minted by "an unauthorized source," are also facts the declaration states.34

[Basic] The criminal case is United States v. Samuel Bankman-Fried (No. 1:22-cr-00673-LAK) in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York. The judgment (Judgment in a Criminal Case, ECF No. 424) records that the defendant "was found guilty" on all of counts 1 through 7 of the (S6) indictment, and gives the offenses as wire fraud (counts 1 and 3, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1343 and 2), wire fraud conspiracy (counts 2 and 4, § 1349), securities fraud conspiracy (count 5, § 371), commodities fraud conspiracy (count 6, § 371), and money laundering conspiracy (count 7, § 1956(h)). The sentence was imposed on March 28, 2024, by Judge Lewis A. Kaplan.35 The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the judgment below on June 12, 2026. The appellate opinion summarizes the first-instance sentence as "25 years' imprisonment, to be followed by three years of supervised release" and "a forfeiture of approximately $11 billion," and states the government's theory of the case as follows: "The government's theory at trial was that Bankman-Fried secured investments in FTX by promising customers that their funds would be secure on the platform and used only for cryptocurrency transactions on FTX. Instead, Bankman-Fried freely transferred investor funds from FTX customer accounts to Alameda and elsewhere where he used those funds for purposes investors had not authorized, including for his own personal benefit." It then describes the evidence as "conservatively stated, robust," and writes that "while Bankman-Fried assured customers, investors, regulators and the public that FTX customer funds were safe, he transferred billions of dollars from FTX customer accounts to Alameda and elsewhere."36 This book has not verified whether a petition for a writ of certiorari has been filed (as of 2026-10).

Diagnosis

[Basic] ① The layers that broke are fraud and internal controls. Not the technology, not the economic design, not the governance of a chain. The items the declaration lists (access to private keys through a shared email account, the absence of daily reconciliation of positions on the chain, software to conceal the misuse of customer funds, the exemption of a particular account from auto-liquidation) all happened inside the company, in layer (c). ② Off the chain. The "balances" inside the exchange were book numbers of the same kind as at Mt.Gox, and the chain did not guarantee them, as at Mt.Gox. ③ If the code did anything, it did what people told it to: "the use of software to conceal the misuse of customer funds." What people did is everything. ④ Chapter 11, guilty verdicts on all 7 counts and a 25-year sentence, and affirmance on appeal followed. That the two exchange cases broke in the same place eight years apart shows that the layer distinction of Section 1 is not a question of technology but a question of who keeps the books, and how. That this is where Articles 6 and 7 of Korea's Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users place their obligations was noted in Section 2.

6. The four cases in one table

[Basic] The table below gathers the diagnoses of Sections 2–5. The parentheses in "The layer that broke" are the (a), (b), and (c) of Section 1.

Mt.Gox (2014) The DAO (2016) Terra-Luna (2022) FTX (2022)
① The layer that broke Exchange books and internal controls (c). The layer of the 2014-02 loss not decided by a court: the exchange cited (b) transaction malleability and in its later announcement of February 28 also mentioned the possibility of hacking; the empirical study found the amount explained by malleability very small Flaw in the contract code (c) + governance (a majority decision that changed the state without changing the rules) Reflexivity of the economic design (Chapter 24) + statements of the issuer and its head (securities-fraud verdict; guilty pleas to conspiracy to defraud and wire fraud) Fraud + absence of internal controls (c)
② On or off the chain Off (manipulation of the books). The layer of the 2014-02 loss not decided by a court On (state transition of contract code) → the fork, too, was a change of ledger state On (swap module) and off (statements) Off (company books, banks, private key management). The unauthorized transfers on the petition date were transfers on the chain, but the declaration says their circumstances are under investigation
③ Code and people Code: automatic confirmation of remittances → balance update. People: entered unbacked balances by hand ("人が…直接入力するようなことは想定されていなかった") Code: carried out the recursive calls as written. People: proposed a soft fork; adopted or rejected a hard fork Code: as designed (a spiral when the condition fails). People: choice of design, and statements Code: software to conceal the misuse (on people's instructions). People: everything
④ What followed Petition for civil rehabilitation (2014-02-28) → dismissal and provisional administration (04-16) → commencement of bankruptcy (04-24) → commencement of civil rehabilitation on creditors' petition (2018-06-22). Criminal: guilty at first instance (unauthorized creation of records), not guilty (embezzlement); appeal dismissed. Final appeal and finality not verified Hard fork (block 1,920,000, 2016-07-20) · two chains coexisting · SEC investigation report (2017; determination that the tokens are securities, no enforcement action) SEC civil: summary judgment (2023-12-28), jury verdict (2024-04-05), final judgment by consent (2024-06-12). Criminal: guilty plea, 180 months (2025-12-11). Insolvency (Bankr. D. Del.) Chapter 11 (2022-11-11; WRS 11-14). Criminal: guilty on 7 counts, 25 years (2024-03-28), affirmed on appeal (2026-06-12). Petition for certiorari not verified
Primary documents Judgments of the Tokyo District Court (東京地裁), March 15, 2019, and the Tokyo High Court (東京高裁), June 11, 2020; bankruptcy commencement decision; company announcements; trustee reports SEC Release 81207, EIP-779, 2 foundation announcements ECF 229 and 273 (civil), ECF 63 (criminal) Ray declaration D.I. 24, ECF 424, 2d Cir. opinion

7. The scope of "the blockchain itself did not break"

[Basic] Now the sentence held back in Section 1 can be written, with its scope set. None of these four is a case in which (a), the consensus rules and ledger integrity, was broken by an outside attack and the ledger of Bitcoin or Ethereum reversed. What the documents found at Mt.Gox and FTX was the books off the chain and matters inside a company; what the court decided at Terra was statements; and the attack on The DAO was a matter of an application-layer contract. In none of the four cases is there a primary document stating that the property Part 1 of this book explained as the "cost of tampering" was broken. Terra, though, happened on its own chain, not on Bitcoin or Ethereum, and the primary documents of this chapter do not deal with that chain's consensus layer.

[Basic] Two things must be added, though. First, for Mt.Gox it has to be put more narrowly. At the time the exchange cited transaction malleability, a property of layer (b), as the cause, but in its later announcement of February 28 it also mentioned the possibility of hacking; the empirical analysis found the amount explained by malleability attacks to be very small; the trustee said the full picture would be difficult to understand; and the criminal judgments at first instance and on appeal did not decide the cause of the loss. So using the sentence "the blockchain did not break" affirmatively about the Mt.Gox loss has no backing in any court determination. What this chapter can say goes as far as "there is no document saying that layer (a) broke." Second, The DAO hard fork was not a breaking of layer (a), but it was a case in which the state of the layer (a) ledger was changed by a majority decision. EIP-779's sentence that the DAO Fork "did not change the protocol" and the fact that "the state was rewritten" are not a contradiction but a pair, and that pair is exactly what the question box above asks about. What the cost of tampering protects is the ledger against "those who do not follow the rules," not against "a majority that has decided to change the rules." Here once more you can see what Chapter 7 meant when it wrote that immutability is a matter not of mathematics but of cost.

8. Summary

[Basic] Put the four cases on the same table and the narrative disappears, leaving the structure. The two exchanges broke in books off the chain, and the differences between them were whether the person who falsified the books was a single representative or an organization, and whether the law required separate management. For the token issuer, when the condition of the design failed, the code drew the spiral as designed, and what the court decided was not the design but the statements. The contract code was executed as written and betrayed its author's intention, and what reversed it was not code but the coordination of people. In none of the cases is there a primary document saying that the consensus rules of Part 1 were broken by an outside attack, and that sentence is true only within the scope set in Section 1. What the lawyer takes away is the columns of this table. Only after sorting out which layer broke can you see where property law, securities law, insolvency law, or criminal law comes in, and Chapter 27 and Chapter 28 survey those places. And that which law comes in depends on which name these four cases go under, "가상자산" (gasang jasan, "virtual asset"), "crypto-asset," "digital asset," "暗号資産" (angō shisan, crypto-asset), or "cryptoasset," is the subject of Chapter 30.

Pages 2–3 of the appellate judgment repeat the same facts as 「原判決が認定した前提事実等の骨子」 (the outline of the premise facts found by the judgment below) (that judgment writes 「Ｔ社」 and 「Ｍ社」 instead of 「Ｄ社」 and 「Ｂ社」, and 「Ａ口座」 instead of 「Ｃ口座」). The amounts and quantities in the text are those written in the judgment, and this chapter gives each of them once. ↑

Accordingly, it is found that Company B's will was that bitcoin corresponding to users' account balances on the Trading System should also exist on the blockchain under Company B's management, and that users' account balances on the Trading System should be increased only where there was backing by the receipt or sending, etc., of bitcoin at bitcoin addresses managed by Company B, and that the authority given to the defendant was also limited to this scope." The English original of the terms-of-use provision: "Seller warrants that the Bitcoins offered to sell or to transfer correspond to actual Bitcoins." ↑

Part 5 · Law

Chapter 27. The bridge between technology and law (1): why this book does not go deep, the map of scholarly positions, a survey by jurisdiction

Key takeaway

Part 5 is a map of questions, not a set of answers. It records which legal issue each of the twenty-three "A lawyer's question" boxes raised in Parts 1–4 reaches, and where the primary sources are for finding the judgments and statutes in the original. This chapter has three sections. 27.1 sets out the five reasons this book does not treat the law in depth. 27.2 lays out the scholarly positions on the private-law nature of the question "what is a virtual asset?" as a map of opposing views, and records in a correspondence table which technical facts from Parts 1–3 (exclusive control through the private key, fungibility, non-replicability, the probabilistic nature of finality, the absence of an issuer, the sharing of the record) each position relies on and which facts counter it. This is the contribution only this book can make, and it does not settle on any position. 27.3 compares five jurisdictions, Korea, the EU, the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom, in a table with a single frame (defined term, competent authority, issuance and circulation, stablecoins, private-law nature), and attaches a reference date to each axis. Statutory provisions are given only where they were checked against the text of the statute, and judgments only where the text of the judgment was checked, together with the court, the date of decision and the case number. Provisions not yet in force (the taxation of virtual assets under Korea's Income Tax Act (소득세법), the transfer of the definition into Japan's Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (金融商品取引法), the full commencement of the UK's 2026 Regulations, and the US GENIUS Act) are marked as not yet in force.

Learning objectives

  1. State the five reasons this book treats the law only at the level of a survey, and point to where in a legal judgment the technical and economic facts of Parts 1–4 enter.
  2. Lay out the positions on the private-law nature of virtual assets as a map of opposing views, and pair each position with the technical facts it relies on and the places where those facts counter it. Which position is right is left unsaid.
  3. Read the defined terms, competent authorities, regulation of issuance and circulation, treatment of stablecoins, and private-law nature of five jurisdictions in one table, and understand why each axis needs a reference date.
  4. Distinguish in writing between "in force," "promulgated but not yet in force," and "pending."

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. This Part is a map of questions, not a set of answers. The same technical fact serves as the ground for different conclusions in different jurisdictions and under different positions, and so knowing the technology is the first step toward finding where a legal judgment sits.

27.1 Why this book does not treat the law in depth

[Basic] This book was written on the assumption that legal scholars would read it, yet it does not treat the law in depth. There are five reasons.

  1. The law in this field changes quickly. A detailed doctrinal commentary would date sooner than any other Part of this book. The properties of hash functions (Chapter 4) and the structure of a bank run (Chapter 24) will be the same ten years from now, but the table in 27.3 below will change even while this book is being printed. Korea's provision on the taxation of virtual assets has had its commencement postponed three times since promulgation; Japan has promulgated an amendment moving the definition from one statute to another and is waiting for it to take effect; and the United Kingdom has set the full commencement of its new regulatory regime for 2027. So every statement about legal institutions carries a reference date, and values that date easily are kept in the trend notes of Appendix A.
  2. Each jurisdiction has its own system. Going deep would take a book per jurisdiction. Korea calls the same thing "가상자산" (gasang jasan, "virtual asset"), the EU "crypto-asset," the United States, depending on context, "security," "commodity," "property" or "digital asset," Japan "暗号資産" (angō shisan, "crypto-asset"), and the United Kingdom "cryptoasset," and the jurisdictions differ in which authority's competence and which statute's application each name calls forth (Chapter 30). Putting five jurisdictions in one table is only a starting point for comparison, not a commentary on any of them.
  3. The readers are lawyers. What this book can offer is not doctrinal commentary but a bridge that shows where in a legal judgment the technical and economic facts enter. To answer "what has a person who lost a private key lost?" (Chapter 5) you need to know where the "rightful holder" sits on a ledger that checks only signatures, and to answer "when was the payment completed?" (Chapter 9) you need to know that finality is a probability. Parts 1–3 supplied those facts, and plugging them into doctrine is the reader's task. The correspondence table in 27.2 is the device that shows where they plug in.
  4. The editor is a sitting judge. On cases pending in Korea, bills pending before the National Assembly (국회), and issues the Supreme Court of Korea (대법원) has not settled, this book states facts only and does not evaluate them. That is why Korean law is treated more thinly than foreign law. Of Korean judgments, only the three whose text was checked are cited, and the book does not say whether those judgments are right or which scholarly position is sound.
  5. It points to where to read further. Chapter 28 collects primary sources and treatises for each jurisdiction. Only bibliographic details confirmed in checking the sources are given, and those not confirmed are left blank.

[Basic] The survey of foreign law covers five jurisdictions: Korea, the EU, the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom. They were chosen because each took a different path: comprehensive codified regulation (EU MiCA), the coexistence of existing law with a special statute (the United States), a division of labor between a payment statute and a financial-instruments statute (Japan), the extension of common-law property categories together with the introduction of a new regulatory regime (the United Kingdom), and Korea, which legislated first on user protection and the regulation of unfair trading. There are six axes of comparison (defined term, competent authority, issuance and circulation, stablecoins, private-law nature, reference date). Each cell gives provision numbers, and the court, date of decision and case number, without commentary.

27.2 The map of scholarly positions on legal nature: positions matched against technical facts

[Basic] To the private-law question "what is bitcoin?", the scholarship and judgments of each jurisdiction have given different answers. It is a thing. It is not a thing, but it is the object of a right of control akin to a real right. It is not a claim. It is not a property right but a factual state. It is a third category of property. It is an electronic record capable of control. It is money, or it is not. It is a security, or it is not. It is a commodity. It is a pecuniary advantage. This section lays out those positions by the structure of their grounds, not by whether they are right or wrong. Which of the technical facts covered in Parts 1–3 does each position rely on, and which counter it? Recording that in a correspondence table is the work of this section, and it does not settle on any position.

[Basic] The starting point is a 2022 research report of the Judicial Policy Research Institute (사법정책연구원), Lee Hye-jeong (이혜정), 가상자산에 대한 민사집행 연구 [A study of civil execution against virtual assets]. To determine the object of civil execution, the report brings together the debates on legal nature in Korea, the United States, the Commonwealth, Germany and Japan (with an overview of regulation for the EU). It explains that "가상자산을 물건으로 보고 그에 대한 권리를 인정할지에 대해 견해가 통일되어 있지 않아, 가상자산을 취득한 자가 '가상자산을 소유하고 있다'고 단정 짓기 힘들고" (gloss: "views are not unified on whether to regard a virtual asset as a thing and recognize rights in it, so it is hard to state conclusively that a person who has acquired a virtual asset 'owns the virtual asset'"; working gloss, not an official translation; the original controls), and that it therefore uses the word "'소유' 대신 '보유'" (gloss: "'holding' (보유) instead of 'ownership' (소유)").1 This book uses "holding" for the same reason. The foreign primary sources are the 2023 final report of the Law Commission of England and Wales, the UK's Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025, the 2023 UNIDROIT Principles, Article 12 of the US Uniform Commercial Code (2022 amendments), a 2015 judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union, US decisions of 1946, 2018 and 2023 and the SEC's 2017 report, a 2019 judgment of the Tokyo District Court (東京地方裁判所) in Japan, and three judgments of the Supreme Court of Korea.

The correspondence table

[Basic] There are four columns: the position (whose, in which jurisdiction), its core claim, the technical facts that claim relies on (and the chapter of this book), and the place among those same technical facts that counters the claim. No row has an empty fourth column. Technical facts do not favor any position one-sidedly.

Position Core claim Technical facts relied on (chapter) Technical facts that counter it (chapter)
① Thing (movable) theory: the Korean affirmative view2 Only the person holding the private key can order a transfer (exclusive controllability), and an approved transfer cannot be double-spent short of hacking a majority (manageability), so it is a "관리할 수 있는 자연력" ("natural force that can be managed") under Article 98 of the Civil Act (민법) A signature controls the authority to spend (Ch. 5). A spent UTXO cannot be spent again (Ch. 11). The cost of tampering (Chs. 7, 8) A private key is information that can be copied (Ch. 5). A transfer is complete only once it is in a block, and that finality is a probability (Ch. 9). No energy can be extracted from bitcoin: the wording "자연력" ("natural force")
② Not a thing; a right of control akin to a real right: Korea3 The holder exercises sole and exclusive control over its property value and can assert it against anyone, so it is a right without a basis in statute, a "준물권적 구조를 가진 권리" ("right with a quasi-real-right structure") No one can move it without a signature (Ch. 5) The record is shared by all participants, so even with the private key it is hard to call this "sole control" (Chs. 6, 7, 12: anyone can download the ledger). The objection from the numerus clausus of real rights (Article 175 of Japan's Civil Code (民法)) raised against Japanese positions ②–④ sits in the same place
③ Claim theory rejected: Korea4 The performance of putting a transfer order into a block is carried out by the network's program, and each participant only contributes a little of its resources, so there is no "obligor." The network has neither assets available for liability nor a central body, so it cannot be treated as a legal person or an association Miners and validators are no one's agents (Ch. 8 question box). There is no issuer (Chs. 1, 19) There is room to regard coins deposited with an exchange as a claim against the exchange (a claim for the transfer of virtual assets, 가상자산이전청구권): the fact that the books and the chain are different layers (Ch. 26, Mt.Gox). It can be the object of a claim
④ Factual-state theory: Japanese positions ⑦ and ⑧5 There is no issuer, and the object of ownership is limited to tangible things, so holding carries no property right of any kind, whether real right, claim, membership right or intellectual property right; it is a factual state. (Another opinion supporting this position: as a result, real-right claims are excluded, which secures a money-like treatment based on the "coincidence of ownership and possession.") The ledger looks only at the validity of signatures; it does not know the "rightful holder" (Ch. 5). Absence of an issuer (Ch. 1) If it is a factual state, on what basis are coins transferred by mistake or stolen coins given back (Ch. 11; 28.1(a))? It is unclear whether a "normative agreement" of all participants exists as something distinct from the protocol (Ch. 23, coordination game)
⑤ Membership-right or partnership-right theory: Japanese position ⑤, Korean partnership-right view6 The holder is a member of an association, the network. Read the "프로그램 시스템" ("program system") as the content of a contract, the "블록체인의 내부적 거래" ("internal transactions of the blockchain") as a common undertaking and "취득" ("acquisition") as a contribution, and it is a partnership under Article 703 of the Civil Act The rules are maintained and changed by the coordination of participants (Ch. 23). A hard fork is a "vote" (Chs. 22, 26) There is no statute or declaration of intention for forming, joining or leaving the association. The sets of node operators, miners and holders do not coincide (Chs. 8, 10). The partnership-right view itself says that this partnership right is "이익분배에 대한 기대권이며, 실체적 권리가 아니라 조합원의 지위권" ("an expectancy of a distribution of profits, not a substantive right but a right of status as a partner")
⑥ Intellectual-property theory: Japanese position ⑥5 Possibly a work protected by copyright Code is a work (the contract code of Ch. 13) It is hard to regard mining as a process in which "사상이 창작적으로 표현" ("thoughts are creatively expressed"). A hash value is the output of a function (Ch. 4)
⑦ "Intangible interest": German scholarship in agreement7 Not a thing under the Civil Code, but an intangible interest falling under "object," the broader concept above it. Scholarship agrees that it is not a claim (p. 83) and that it lacks corporeality (p. 81) Absence of an issuer and of an obligor (Ch. 1). Data are not tangible things "Intangible interest" does not directly supply rules of execution or attribution: by what procedure is it attached (28.1(a))?
⑧ Third-category property theory: Law Commission of England and Wales, Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 202589 "some digital assets are neither things in possession nor things in action, but that nonetheless the law of England and Wales treats them as capable of being things to which personal property rights can relate." The legislation only confirms "that the fact that a thing is neither a thing in possession nor a thing in action does not prevent it from being a thing to which personal property rights can relate," and the common law draws the boundary Rivalrousness: one person's use excludes another's (Ch. 11, spending a UTXO). It exists independently, outside the system (Chs. 1, 7) A "balance" on an exchange's books may not be rivalrous (Ch. 26, Mt.Gox's fictitious balances). The report itself dropped "composed of data" from the criteria
⑨ Control-based: UNIDROIT Principles, US UCC Article 121011 "'Digital asset' means an electronic record which is capable of being subject to control," and a "controllable electronic record" is "a record stored in an electronic medium that can be subjected to control under Section 12-105." Control is made the connecting point for the definition and for the rules of transfer and security, while who holds the property right is itself left to "other law" (UNIDROIT Principle 3(3)(a)) Private key = authority to spend (Ch. 5). The exclusivity and transferability of control (Ch. 11) Control is not a right: a stolen key also gives control (Ch. 5 question box). How is control through multiple signatures (multisig) or through a custodian counted (Ch. 26, FTX's private-key management)?
⑩ Monetary character: negative and affirmative views (Korea), EU VAT, US tax law, Supreme Court of Korea12131415 Negative: it cannot serve as a measure of value, and its total issuance is fixed. Affirmative: the possibility of future acceptance. EU: "bitcoin" has "no purpose other than to be a means of payment," and exchange is exempt from VAT. US: for tax purposes it is "property" and "not … currency." Supreme Court of Korea: "형법을 적용하면서 법정화폐와 동일하게 보호해야 하는 것은 아니다" (gloss: "in applying the Criminal Act, it need not be protected in the same way as legal tender") A check of the functions of medium of exchange, measure of value and store of value (Ch. 19). A floor of demand from taxes is what sets legal tender apart (Ch. 19 model) What Chapter 19 showed is that "a positive price with an intrinsic value of 0" can be an equilibrium, not that it is money. "What changes when the law calls something money" differs by jurisdiction (Ch. 19 question box)
⑪ Security character: Korean view rejecting negotiable-instrument status, US Howey, SEC, Ripple, GENIUS Act1617181920 Korea: the prevailing view is that it is hard to treat it as a 유가증권 (negotiable instrument), because there is no issuer and a record on the chain is not an endorsement. US: an "investment contract" is "a contract, transaction or scheme whereby a person invests his money in a common enterprise and is led to expect profits solely from the efforts of the promoter or a third party"; DAO tokens are securities (2017); for the same token, sales to institutions are investment contracts and anonymous trading on exchanges is not (2023). Payment stablecoins were taken out of securities by statute (2025) A token standard is only a promise about function names and carries no rights (Ch. 14). The "efforts" of curators and issuers (Chs. 22, 26). In the secondary market the buyer does not know who the seller is (Ch. 15 AMM; Ch. 17) Look at substance rather than form, as in Howey ("Form was disregarded for substance and emphasis was placed upon economic reality"), and it is the promise outside, not the code, that determines security status (Ch. 14). That is why the same token is judged differently depending on the route of the transaction
⑫ Commodity character: US CFTC, McDonnell21 Virtual currencies are "'goods' exchanged in a market for a uniform quality and value" and fall within the Commodity Exchange Act's "commodity," and the jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is concurrent with that of other agencies Fungibility (Ch. 11 UTXO; Ch. 14 ERC-20). Underlying asset of futures and derivatives "Security" and "commodity" overlap on the same thing: naming divides jurisdiction (Ch. 30)
⑬ Pecuniary advantage, intangible property: Supreme Court of Korea222315 Bitcoin is "경제적인 가치를 디지털로 표상하여 전자적으로 이전, 저장과 거래가 가능하도록 한 가상자산의 일종으로 사기죄의 객체인 재산상 이익" (gloss: "a kind of virtual asset that represents economic value digitally so that it can be transferred, stored and traded electronically, and a pecuniary advantage that can be the object of fraud") (November 11, 2021); it can be confiscated as "재산적 가치가 있는 무형의 재산" (gloss: "intangible property having property value") (May 30, 2018); and a person who receives a transfer without legal cause may bear an obligation to make restitution of unjust enrichment but is not "타인의 사무를 처리하는 자" (gloss: "a person who administers another's business") (December 16, 2021) Electronic transfer, storage and trading (Chs. 11, 12). The property that "보관되었던 전자지갑의 주소만을 확인할 수 있을 뿐 그 주소를 사용하는 사람의 인적사항을 알 수 없고, 거래 내역이 분산 기록되어 있어 다른 계좌로 보낼 때 당사자 이외의 다른 사람이 참여해야 하는" (gloss: "only the address of the electronic wallet in which it was kept can be identified, and the personal particulars of the person using that address cannot be known, and the transaction history is recorded in a distributed manner, so that sending it to another account requires the participation of persons other than the parties") (technical facts stated by the judgment) A criminal-law finding of "pecuniary advantage" does not settle attribution in private law: the judgment itself states that "부당이득반환청구를 할 수 있는 주체가 피해자인지 아니면 거래소인지 명확하지 않다" (gloss: "it is not clear whether the party entitled to claim restitution of unjust enrichment is the victim or the exchange") (Ch. 26, books and chain)
⑭ Deposit, debt or equity: stablecoins (Gorton & Zhang)24 To decide whether a stablecoin is a demand deposit, one must first determine whether the contract between holder and issuer is an "equity contract or a debt contract": the same shape as the money market fund debate of the 1970s A token carrying a redemption promise is inside money (Ch. 24). Balance sheet and redemption procedure (Ch. 24) Because there is a secondary market, closing the window does not stop a run (Ch. 24): a point where it differs from a deposit. The legal effect of the issuer's "public declaration" (Ch. 24 question box)

How to read the table

[Basic] The third and fourth columns of the table often point to the same chapter. The fact from Chapter 5 that "a signature controls the authority to spend" is a ground for the thing theory (①), the control-right theory (②) and the control-based approach (⑨), and at the same time a ground for the objections that "a stolen key also gives control" and "a private key is information that can be copied." The fact from Chapter 9 that "finality is a probability" is where the manageability of a thing is shaken, and also where one asks "when was it completed?" (28.1(c)). So one cannot say that any position "fits the technology." Technical facts are not a referee that picks among the positions but a mirror that shows which facts each position presupposes and which facts it has to explain.

[Basic] Two further points. First, courts have avoided this question when they could. The 2019 judgment of the Tokyo District Court stated "ビットコインは「有体物」（民法８５条）ではなく，その帰属や利用者間での取引がどのような私法上の性質を有するかも一義的に明らかとはいえないが，本件の判断に影響のない限り，ビットコインの保有・所有や利用者間の売買などと表現し，日常的な意味合いで記載する" (gloss: "bitcoin is not a 'tangible thing' (Civil Code Article 85), and it cannot be said to be unambiguously clear what private-law nature its attribution and transactions between users have; but insofar as this does not affect the determination in this case, [the court] will describe it in everyday terms, as the holding and ownership of bitcoin, sales between users, and so on") and decided the case.25 The 2021 judgment of the Supreme Court of Korea likewise answered with "pecuniary advantage," a category of criminal law, and on attribution in private law it went no further than stating, on the ground that how the bitcoin in that case had been transferred was unclear, that "부당이득반환청구를 할 수 있는 주체가 피해자인지 아니면 거래소인지 명확하지 않다" (gloss: "it is not clear whether the party entitled to claim restitution of unjust enrichment is the victim or the exchange"). That is a judgment tied to the facts of the case, not an answer about attribution in general. Second, legislation answered by definition, not by nature. "경제적 가치를 지닌 것으로서 전자적으로 거래 또는 이전될 수 있는 전자적 증표(그에 관한 일체의 권리를 포함한다)" (gloss: "as something having economic value, an electronic token that can be traded or transferred electronically (including all rights relating to it)") in Article 2, subparagraph 1 of Korea's Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률; "the Virtual Asset User Protection Act"), and "a digital representation of a value or of a right" in Article 3(1)(5) of the EU's MiCA, are sentences that fix the object of regulation. They are not sentences that decide whether the holder has a real right or a claim.26 The UK's 2025 Act shows this most clearly: in two sections it confirms only that a thing is not prevented from being "the object of personal property rights," and leaves the boundary to the common law. Chapter 30 sets these definitional provisions side by side.

Question boxes linked to this section

[Basic] Of the boxes in Parts 1–3 and Part 6, six point to this section. For each, the table notes which rows of the correspondence table take it up.

Box Gist of the question Where this section takes it up
Chapter 5 What has a person who lost the private key lost: possession, ownership, or accessibility? On a ledger that looks only at the validity of signatures, where is the "rightful holder"? ①, ② and ⑨ rely on "private key = exclusive control," and ④ relies on "the ledger does not know the right holder." The UK report's "rivalrousness" (⑧), as a mark of what can be an object of property, and UNIDROIT's "control" (⑨), as the connecting point for the definition and the rules of transfer, are answers that bring in accessibility (neither of them decides attribution itself), and the Supreme Court of Korea (⑬) stated the property that "주소만 확인할 수 있을 뿐 그 주소를 사용하는 사람의 인적사항을 알 수 없" (gloss: "only the address can be identified, and the personal particulars of the person using that address cannot be known")
Chapter 19 Are legal tender and "money" the same thing? What changes when the law calls something "money"? ⑩. EU VAT answered "a means of payment," US tax law "property," and the Supreme Court of Korea "형법을 적용하면서 법정화폐와 동일하게 보호해야 하는 것은 아니" (gloss: "in applying the Criminal Act, it need not be protected in the same way as legal tender") (a judgment limited to the application of the Criminal Act). The taxation row of 27.3
Chapter 20 If a majority changes the issuance rules, are the holders' rights infringed? Is what the holder has a right to the "21 million cap," or only the ability to spend UTXOs? ④ (factual state), ⑤ (partnership right) and ⑨ (control) each imply a different answer. Under the factual-state theory there is no right to infringe; under the partnership-right theory the limits of majority rule are at issue; and on the control-based approach a change of rules changes the very object of control. The restriction on spending vulnerable coins in Chapter 29 asks the same structural question more sharply: 28.1(g)
Chapter 21 To whom does a burned fee belong: abandonment, an ownerless thing, consumption, a new category? No position directly explains "the extinction of value that belongs to no one." Under the thing theory it is the abandonment of ownership or the destruction of the thing; under the factual-state theory, the end of a state; on the control-based approach, the extinction of the object of control. This book chooses none of them
Chapter 23 After a hard fork, who decides which of the two chains is the "real" ledger? Did a holder before the fork have one or two? The rivalrousness criterion of ⑧ leaves room to treat the coins on the two chains as separate property, since they are not rivalrous with each other, and under the control criterion of ⑨ the same private key also gives control on both chains. Which chain's coin "the one bitcoin in the contract" refers to remains a question of contract interpretation: 28.1(g)
Chapter 30 When a definitional provision cannot keep up with the technology: analogy, or a legislative gap? The defined-term row of 27.3 and the concordance of provisions in Chapter 30. Since legislation answered by definition and not by nature, the debate on nature (this table) is called on again where a definition leaves a gap

27.3 A survey by jurisdiction

[Basic] The table below compares five jurisdictions on six axes. The cells contain provision numbers and the court, date of decision and case number of judgments, and no commentary. The reference date is 2026-10-25, and each axis distinguishes "in force," "promulgated, not yet in force," and "not verified." Notes by jurisdiction follow the table.

Axis Korea EU United States Japan United Kingdom
Defined term (provision) "가상자산": Virtual Asset User Protection Act §2(1) (enacted as Act No. 19563, now Act No. 21857; definition unchanged); Specified Financial Transaction Information Act §2(3) applies it mutatis mutandis "crypto-asset": MiCA Art. 3(1)(5); "asset-referenced token" (6), "e-money token" (7), "utility token" (9); unique and non-fungible assets excluded by Art. 2(3), financial instruments by Art. 2(4)(a) No single definition. "security" (Securities Act §2(a)(1), "investment contract": Howey), "commodity" (Commodity Exchange Act, cited by McDonnell as "Title 7 U.S.C. § 1(a)(9)"), "property" (IRS Notice 2014-21), "digital asset" and "payment stablecoin" (GENIUS Act §2(6), (22)), "controllable electronic record" (UCC §12-102) "暗号資産": Payment Services Act §2(14) (renamed from "仮想通貨" by 令和元年法律第28号 (Act No. 28 of 2019), in force 2020-05-01; paragraph 14 from 2023-06-01); "電子記録移転権利": Financial Instruments and Exchange Act §2(3); "電子決済手段": Payment Services Act §2(5) "cryptoasset": FSMA 2000 s. 417(1) (inserted by FSMA 2023 s. 69, in force 2023-08-29); "qualifying cryptoasset" and "qualifying stablecoin": RAO art. 88F, 88G (inserted by SI 2026/102)
Competent authority Financial Services Commission (Virtual Asset User Protection Act §14 investigation and measures, §13 supervision and inspection); head of the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit (Specified Financial Transaction Information Act §7 reporting) Member State competent authorities (Art. 93); issuers of significant ARTs and EMTs supervised by the EBA (Art. 117) Concurrent jurisdiction of the SEC and CFTC (McDonnell); for payment stablecoins, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and other "primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator" (GENIUS §2(25); for non-bank federally licensed issuers (§2(11)), the OCC under §2(25)(D)); FinCEN (MSB registration: SEC DAO report, footnote 20) Registration with the 内閣総理大臣 (Prime Minister) (Payment Services Act §63-2); Financial Services Agency (金融庁) FCA (SI 2026/102 reg. 1(3))
Issuance and circulation No provisions on issuance or disclosure (the Act's 22 articles cover protection of users' assets, prohibition of unfair trading, and supervision). Businesses file a report (Specified Financial Transaction Information Act §7); segregation of deposits (Virtual Asset User Protection Act §6); segregated custody and actual holding of virtual assets (§7) Obligation to draw up and publish a white paper (Title II, Art. 4); authorization of crypto-asset service providers (Art. 59); prohibition of market abuse (Title VI, Arts. 86–92) If a security, §5 registration or exemption (SEC DAO report); if a commodity, the CEA's anti-fraud provisions (McDonnell) Registration system for 暗号資産交換業 (angō shisan kōkangyō, "crypto-asset exchange business") (§63-2) The 2026 Regulations make the public offer of a "qualifying cryptoasset" and its admission to trading on an exchange designated activities, and its issuance, custody and the like regulated activities: full commencement 2027-10-25
Stablecoins No separate category (within Virtual Asset User Protection Act §2(1); "전자화폐" (electronic currency), "선불전자지급수단" (prepaid electronic means of payment) and electronic currency issued by the Bank of Korea are excluded: items (c) and (g)) ART (Title III, Art. 16 authorization), EMT (Title IV, Art. 48: credit institutions and electronic money institutions only): applies from 2024-06-30 GENIUS Act (enacted 2025-07-18): permitted issuers, not securities or commodities (§17): effective date under §20 no later than 2027-01-18, possibly earlier depending on the issuance of regulations (not verified) 電子決済手段 (Payment Services Act §2(5)) "qualifying stablecoin" (RAO art. 88G): 2027-10-25

Scholarly positions divided under the definition of a thing in Civil Act §98 (27.2). Compulsory tax collection: National Tax Collection Act §55(3), §66(2)(2); Local Tax Collection Act §61(3) MiCA is a regulatory instrument: within the provisions this book read, private-law nature is not decided (not verified). VAT: exchange is exempt (CJEU, October 22, 2015, C‑264/14) Property for tax purposes (2014-21); UCC Article 12 (2022 model law: state adoption not verified); security and commodity determinations made transaction by transaction Tokyo District Court (東京地裁), March 15, 2019: not a "有体物"; private-law nature reserved as "一義的に明らかとはいえない" Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025 s. 1 (in force 2025-12-02); Law Com No 412; a possible fiduciary duty of developers is a "serious issue to be tried" (Tulip Trading v van der Laan [2023] EWCA Civ 83, 2023-02-03)
