Korea

[Basic] The Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users was enacted on July 18, 2023 as Act No. 19563 and came into force on July 19, 2024. The current version is Act No. 21857, promulgated on August 4, 2026 and in force on October 2, 2026 (a consequential amendment following an amendment of the Criminal Procedure Act (형사소송법)). The definitions in Article 2 have not changed since enactment.27 In 22 articles, the Act provides for the protection of users' deposits (Article 6), the segregated custody and actual holding of virtual assets (Article 7), the prohibition of unfair trading (Article 10: use of material non-public information, market manipulation, fraudulent trading, and trading by a business in virtual assets it issued itself) and liability for damages (Article 10(6)), supervision and investigation by the Financial Services Commission (금융위원회) (Articles 13 and 14), and penalty surcharges and penal provisions (Articles 17 and 19). It has no provision governing issuance or disclosure. Entry for businesses is by a report to the head of the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit (금융정보분석원장) under Article 7 of the Act on Reporting and Using Specified Financial Transaction Information (특정 금융거래정보의 보고 및 이용 등에 관한 법률; "the Specified Financial Transaction Information Act"), and the definition of "virtual asset" in Article 2, subparagraph 3 of that Act points to Article 2, subparagraph 1 of the Virtual Asset User Protection Act.28 On taxation, Article 21(1), subparagraph 27 of the Income Tax Act made "가상자산을 양도하거나 대여함으로써 발생하는 소득" (gloss: "income arising from transferring or lending virtual assets") a category of other income. But since this provision was promulgated on December 29, 2020, its commencement has been postponed three times, from 2022 to 2023 to 2025 to January 1, 2027, and as of the reference date it is not yet in force. The "current" text on the Korean Law Information Center of the Ministry of Government Legislation (법제처 국가법령정보센터) displays this subparagraph as if it were in force, so quoting it as it stands would be wrong.29 In compulsory tax collection, Article 55(3) of the National Tax Collection Act (국세징수법) lets the head of a tax office who is attaching a virtual asset require the delinquent taxpayer, or the business holding the asset in custody, to transfer it: "해당 가상자산의 이전을 문서로 요구할 수 있" (gloss: "may request in writing the transfer of the virtual asset concerned"). Article 66(2), subparagraph 2 permits the direct sale of "가상자산사업자를 통해 거래되는 가상자산" (gloss: "virtual assets traded through a virtual asset service provider"), and Article 61(3) of the Local Tax Collection Act (지방세징수법) also provides for a similar request for transfer (though for local taxes it is a duty, "요구하여야 한다" (gloss: "shall request"), and the requirement of writing attaches only when the request is made to a third party).30 The Civil Execution Act (민사집행법) has no provision on virtual assets, and the Judicial Policy Research Institute's report proposed, as a legislative draft, procedures for attachment, transfer orders and sale orders, treating virtual assets as "그 밖의 재산권" (gloss: "other property rights").31 This book did not verify the legislative course after that (as of 2026-10, Appendix A).

EU

[Basic] The Regulation on markets in crypto-assets (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, MiCA) was adopted on May 31, 2023 and published in Official Journal L 150 (June 9, 2023). Under Article 149 it applies from December 30, 2024, while asset-referenced tokens (Title III) and e-money tokens (Title IV) apply from June 30, 2024.32 The definitions are in Article 3(1). A "crypto-asset" is "a digital representation of a value or of a right that is able to be transferred and stored electronically using distributed ledger technology or similar technology" (point 5), and beneath it come asset-referenced tokens (point 6), e-money tokens (point 7) and utility tokens (point 9). The dates of application have further exceptions in Article 149(4) (some provisions apply from entry into force). Crypto-assets that are "unique and not fungible" (Article 2(3)) and financial instruments and the like (Article 2(4)) are outside the scope.33 Circulation is built on drawing up and publishing a white paper (Article 4), authorization to issue asset-referenced tokens (Article 16, or a credit institution complying with Article 17), issuance of e-money tokens only by credit institutions and electronic money institutions (Article 48), and authorization of crypto-asset service providers (Article 59), and Title VI (Articles 86–92) prohibits insider dealing and market manipulation both on and off trading platforms.34 Supervision is carried out by the competent authorities designated by the Member States (Article 93), and issuers of asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens classified as "significant" are under the supervision of the European Banking Authority (EBA) (Article 117). Within the provisions this book read, the Regulation does not decide private-law nature. Since the whole Regulation was not read through, this is recorded as "not verified." On VAT, the Court of Justice of the European Union held on October 22, 2015 in Hedqvist that the exchange of bitcoin for traditional currencies is an exempt transaction under Article 135(1)(e) of the VAT Directive.13

United States

[Basic] The United States has no single definition. Depending on the shape of the transaction, the same token becomes a "security" under the securities laws, a "commodity" under the Commodity Exchange Act, and "property" under the tax laws. The test for a security is the definition of an investment contract laid down by the Supreme Court of the United States in Howey in 1946, and in its 2017 report of investigation on The DAO the SEC determined by that test that DAO tokens were securities (Chapter 26). On July 13, 2023, in a summary judgment decision in SEC v. Ripple Labs, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York stated that "XRP, as a digital token, is not in and of itself a 'contract, transaction[,] or scheme' …" and distinguished sales to institutional investors under written contracts, which were investment contracts, from sales to anonymous buyers on exchanges, which were not. The unit of judgment is the transaction, not the token.19 On commodity status, on March 6, 2018, in a preliminary-injunction decision in CFTC v. McDonnell, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York determined that virtual currency falls within the "commodity" of the Commodity Exchange Act (in the decision's notation, "Title 7 U.S.C. § 1(a)(9)") and that the CFTC's jurisdiction is concurrent with that of other agencies.21 In tax law, the Internal Revenue Service's 2014 notice (Notice 2014-21) stated that "virtual currency is treated as property," and its 2023 notice (Notice 2023-34) corrected only the background statement that virtual currency "does not have legal tender status in any jurisdiction," leaving the conclusions of the questions and answers as they were.14 On payment stablecoins, the GENIUS Act (Pub. L. 119-27), enacted on July 18, 2025, defines "payment stablecoin" (§2(22)) and states expressly that those issued by permitted issuers are neither securities nor commodities (§17). Its effective date is the earlier of 18 months after enactment and 120 days after the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators issue final regulations (§20). This book did not verify the state of rulemaking as of the reference date.20 On attribution in private law, the Uniform Law Commission and the American Law Institute approved Article 12 of the Uniform Commercial Code, "Controllable Electronic Records," in 2022. It is a model law, and whether each state has adopted it was not verified.11

Japan

[Basic] In Japan, the payments statute and the financial-instruments statute divide the work. The Payment Services Act (資金決済に関する法律, 平成21年法律第59号 (Act No. 59 of 2009)) replaced the defined term "仮想通貨" (kasō tsūka, "virtual currency") with "暗号資産" through 令和元年法律第28号 (Act No. 28 of 2019; promulgated 2019-06-07, in force 2020-05-01), and the current definition is in Article 2(14) (it moved from paragraph 5 to paragraph 14 with the version in force from 2023-06-01).35 Article 63-2 of the same Act establishes a registration system, providing that "暗号資産交換業は、内閣総理大臣の登録を受けた者でなければ、行ってはならない" (gloss: "no person other than one registered by the Prime Minister may carry on crypto-asset exchange business"), and Article 2(15) sets the scope of exchange business (buying and selling or exchanging; intermediation, brokerage or agency for these; management of users' money in connection with them; management of crypto-assets on behalf of others).36 Stablecoins that are assets denominated in legal tender are separately defined as "電子決済手段" (denshi kessai shudan, "electronic payment instruments") (Article 2(5)). Tokens with an investment character are governed by the financial-instruments statute as "電子記録移転権利" (denshi kiroku iten kenri, "electronically recorded transferable rights") in the parenthesis of Article 2(3) of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act. This pairs with the proviso to the crypto-asset definition, which excludes "金融商品取引法第二十九条の二第一項第八号に規定する権利を表示するもの" (gloss: "those that represent the rights specified in Article 29-2(1)(viii) of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act").37 令和8年法律第64号 (Act No. 64 of 2026), promulgated on July 23, 2026, is an amendment that moves the definition of crypto-asset from the Payment Services Act to Article 2(49) of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act. It has been promulgated and partly brought into force, but the part transferring the definition is not yet in force as of the reference date. The e-Gov statute search displays that version as scheduled to take effect on 2027-07-22, but the cabinet order that actually sets the commencement date could not be verified.38 On private-law nature, there is the Tokyo District Court judgment of March 15, 2019, which stated that bitcoin is not a "有体物" (yūtaibutsu, "tangible thing") and reserved its private-law nature as "一義的に明らかとはいえない" (gloss: "cannot be said to be unambiguously clear") (Chapter 26), and there are eight strands of scholarly opinion (27.2 table, ④–⑥).

United Kingdom

[Basic] The United Kingdom has legislated in both property law and regulatory law. On the regulatory side, the defined term "cryptoasset" was inserted into section 417(1) of FSMA 2000 by section 69 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023: "any cryptographically secured digital representation of value or contractual rights that— (a) can be transferred, stored or traded electronically, and (b) that uses technology supporting the recording or storage of data (which may include distributed ledger technology)," in force from August 29, 2023.39 On top of that, The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/102), made on February 4, 2026, made the "qualifying cryptoasset" (fungible, transferable, not solely a record of value or contractual rights; electronic money, fiat currency and tokens within a limited network excluded) and the "qualifying stablecoin" (one that aims at a stable value in relation to a particular fiat currency and for which fiat currency or other assets are held to maintain it) objects of regulated activities. The full commencement day of these Regulations is October 25, 2027. As of the reference date only the parts for preparatory purposes, such as the FCA's making of rules and guidance and the receipt and determination of applications for authorization, are in force (reg. 1(3)).40 On the property side, the Law Commission in its June 2023 final report (Law Com No 412) recommended legislation confirming the "third category," and the Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025 received Royal Assent on December 2, 2025 and came into force the same day. It has two sections. It states only that the fact that a thing is neither "a thing in possession" nor "a thing in action" does not by itself prevent it from being the object of personal property rights, and it does not decide what is property (27.2 ⑧).89 In case law there is Tulip Trading Ltd v van der Laan and others [2023] EWCA Civ 83 (decided February 3, 2023, Lewison, Popplewell and Birss LJJ) in the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) of England and Wales. In a case in which a company claiming to be the holder, which alleged it had lost its private keys to a hack, asserted fiduciary duties against the developers of the bitcoin network, the Court of Appeal said, "The conclusion is not that there is a fiduciary duty in law in the circumstances alleged by Tulip, only that the case advanced raises a serious issue to be tried," and overturned the first-instance judgment (High Court, Chancery Division, Falk J, [2022] EWHC 667 (Ch)), which had set aside permission to serve out of the jurisdiction. Birss LJ added: "If the decentralised governance of bitcoin really is a myth, then in my judgment there is much to be said for the submission that bitcoin developers, while acting as developers, owe fiduciary duties to the true owners of that property."41 This is the form in which Chapter 8's "whose agent is a miner?" and Chapter 23's "who decides the real ledger?" entered the courtroom, and 28.1(g) takes it up.

Question boxes linked to this section

[Basic] Three boxes point to this section. Chapter 14's "what did the person who bought an NFT buy?" is taken up by the defined-term row. The EU excluded "unique and not fungible" crypto-assets from the scope of MiCA (Art. 2(3)); the UK's 2026 Regulations made "fungible" a requirement of a "qualifying cryptoasset," which leaves out non-fungible tokens; and in Korea, Article 2, subparagraph 4 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률 시행령) (in force October 2, 2026), made under the delegation in item (h) of Article 2, subparagraph 1 of the Act, excludes "단일하게 존재하여 다른 전자적 증표로 대체할 수 없는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "an electronic token that exists singly and cannot be replaced by another electronic token"), but with a proviso that brings back in "특정 재화나 서비스의 지급수단으로 사용될 수 있는 전자적 증표 등 금융위원회가 정하여 고시하는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "electronic tokens determined and publicly notified by the Financial Services Commission, such as electronic tokens that can be used as a means of payment for particular goods or services") (the originals are in Chapter 30). The same box's "is the issuer's promise to share revenue in the code or outside it?" finds where its answer sits in the fact that the US determination of security status (Howey, SEC, Ripple) looks at the promise outside and at the shape of the transaction. Chapter 15's "does an AMM have an operator?" is taken up by the competent-authority and issuance-and-circulation rows. The regulatory provisions of four jurisdictions presuppose as their addressee "a person" (MiCA Art. 59), "者" (mono, "person") (Payment Services Act Article 63-2), "영업으로 하는 자" (gloss: "a person who does so as a business") (Virtual Asset User Protection Act Article 2, subparagraph 2) or "person" (GENIUS §2(7)) (the addressee provisions of the UK Regulations were not checked in this edition), and in a contract that runs a single constant-product formula that addressee is missing. That Article 2(7)(B)(v) of the GENIUS Act expressly excludes "participating in a liquidity pool or other similar mechanism for the provisioning of liquidity for peer-to-peer transactions" from "digital asset service provider" is a fact showing that the legislature recognized this gap; whether that was the right choice, this book does not say.42 Chapter 24's "is a stablecoin holder a depositor, a creditor or a beneficiary?" is taken up by the stablecoin row. The EU allowed only credit institutions and electronic money institutions to issue e-money tokens (Art. 48), the United States took payment stablecoins out of securities and commodities and set up a system of permitted issuers (GENIUS §17), Japan defined them separately as "電子決済手段," the United Kingdom made the issuance of a "qualifying stablecoin" a regulated activity, and Korea did not create a separate category. No jurisdiction decided the holder's private-law position (depositor, creditor, beneficiary) directly in those definitional provisions. That question is for Chapter 28.

What the table leaves out

[Basic] Two things should be stated. First, Singapore and Switzerland are not included in this edition (the original plan was "a line each if needed," and this book's source materials contained no primary sources for those two jurisdictions). Second, bills pending in each jurisdiction are not recorded. Under this book's principles they are matters on which facts alone may be stated, but this book's source materials did not contain the texts of the bills, so even the facts could not be verified. Japan's transfer to the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act is not "pending" but "promulgated, not yet in force," so it is in the table. The US GENIUS Act has also been enacted, so it is in the table, with only its effective date recorded as not settled.

Summary

[Basic] This chapter has done three things. It set out the five reasons for not treating the law in depth, paired fourteen positions on private-law nature with the technical facts of Parts 1–3, and compared five jurisdictions on six axes. Lay the two tables over each other and one thing comes into view. Legislation answered "what is regulated?" with definitions, courts avoided the question of nature, "what is it?", when they could, and scholarship used the same technical facts as grounds for different conclusions. Knowing the technical facts, then, is not a matter of choosing a position but of knowing what each position has to explain. What a person who lost a private key has lost (Chapter 5), when a payment is completed in a world where finality is a probability (Chapter 9), whether an asset with no issuer has an obligor (Chapter 19), what the minority can assert when the majority changes the rules (Chapters 22, 23, 26): these questions are taken up by the seven issue sections of Chapter 28. And what turns on five jurisdictions calling the same thing by five names is examined in Chapter 30, which sets the definitional provisions side by side.

  1. Lee Hye-jeong (이혜정), 가상자산에 대한 민사집행 연구 [A study of civil execution against virtual assets] (사법정책연구원 연구총서 2022-12 [JPRI research series 2022-12], published 2022-08-05), p. 103 (Ch. 2, Sec. 3, IV). Original: "한편, 가상자산을 물건으로 보고 그에 대한 권리를 인정할지에 대해 견해가 통일되어 있지 않아, 가상자산을 취득한 자가 '가상자산을 소유하고 있다'고 단정 짓기 힘들고, 이러한 고민은 가상자산 관련 다수의 논문과 판결에서 '소유' 대신 '보유'라는 단어를 사용하고 있는 것에서도 확인할 수 있다." (PDF p. 127). Page numbers in the footnotes below are printed page numbers.   2. Lee (2022), pp. 88–89 (Ch. 2, Sec. 3, III.1.A). Grounds of the affirmative view: "비트코인은 '비트코인 주소'에서 관리되고, 개인키를 가진 자에 의하여 기술적으로 통제받으므로 민법 제98조의 자연력에 해당한다는 견해" (footnote 417, Kim I-su (김이수)), "당해 가상자산지갑의 개인키를 가진 자만이 송금지시를 내릴 수 있고(배타적 지배가능성), 그러한 송금지시 내역이 분산원장에 빠짐없이 기록되며, 한 번 송금이 완료된…비트코인은 전 세계 비트코인 네트워크 참여자의 과반수를 동시에 해킹하지 않는 이상 현실적으로 이중지불 될 수 없으므로(관리가능성), 비트코인은 민법상 물건 중 동산이라는 견해" (footnote 418, Jeon Seung-jae (전승재) and Kwon Heon-young (권헌영)). Grounds of the negative view (p. 89): "개인키는 단순한 정보에 불과하고 복제가 가능할 뿐만 아니라, 정보에 대한 '점유'나 '보관'이라는 개념도 명확치 않아 엄격한 의미의 '배타성'이 있다고 보기 어렵다" (footnote 419, Ki No-seong (기노성)), "네트워크 참여자에 의한 승인이 없는 한 비트코인의 이전이 완결되지 않으므로 배타적 지배가능성이 다소 불완전하다" (footnote 420, Jeong Yeong-su (정영수)), "비트코인에서 에너지를 추출할 수 없으므로 전통적인 의미의 '자연력'으로 보기 어렵다" (footnote 421). Original of Article 98 of the Civil Act: "본법에서 물건이라 함은 유체물 및 전기 기타 관리할 수 있는 자연력을 말한다." (Korean Law Information Center (국가법령정보센터), accessed 2026-10-25). This book reproduces the scholarly positions as the report organizes them and did not check the individual articles in the original. Working gloss: footnote 417: "the view that bitcoin is managed at a 'bitcoin address' and is technically controlled by the person who has the private key, and so falls within the natural forces of Article 98 of the Civil Act"; footnote 419: "a private key is mere information and can be copied, and the concepts of 'possession' or 'custody' of information are also unclear, so it is hard to say that there is 'exclusivity' in the strict sense"; footnote 420: "unless approved by network participants, a transfer of bitcoin is not completed, so exclusive controllability is somewhat incomplete"; Article 98: "In this Act, 'things' means tangible things and electricity and other natural forces that can be managed." ↑

Original: "we conclude that some digital assets are neither things in possession nor things in action, but that nonetheless the law of England and Wales treats them as capable of being things to which personal property rights can relate."(¶2.45); "We recommend legislation confirming that the fact that a thing is neither a thing in possession nor a thing in action does not prevent it from being a thing to which personal property rights can relate. Introduction 0.6 states that "control" is not the same as 'control' in common law jurisdictions or 'possession' in civil law: "The concept of control used in these Principles, for instance, is not intended to be understood as 'control' as used in certain common law jurisdictions. Original: "the 'bitcoin' virtual currency with bidirectional flow, which will be exchanged for traditional currencies in the context of exchange transactions, cannot be characterised as 'tangible property' within the meaning of Article 14 of the VAT Directive, given that, as the Advocate General has observed in point 17 of her Opinion, that virtual currency has no purpose other than to be a means of payment."(¶24); "The 'bitcoin' virtual currency, being a contractual means of payment, cannot be regarded as a current account or a deposit account, a payment or a transfer."(¶42); "In the case in the main proceedings, it is common ground that the 'bitcoin' virtual currency has no other purpose than to be a means of payment and that it is accepted for that purpose by certain operators."(¶52); operative part 2: "Article 135(1)(e) of Directive 2006/112 must be interpreted as meaning that the supply of services such as those at issue in the main proceedings, which consist of the exchange of traditional currencies for units of the 'bitcoin' virtual currency and vice versa, …, are transactions exempt from VAT, within the meaning of that provision". Cellar XHTML (publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/bb73ad87-78a7-11e5-86db-01aa75ed71a1.0006.01/DOC_2, accessed 2026-10-25). The judgment interprets the VAT Directive and is not a ruling on private-law nature. ↑↑

Original: "가상자산은 국가에 의해 통제받지 않고 블록체인 등 암호화된 분산원장에 의하여 부여된 경제적인 가치가 디지털로 표상된 정보로서 재산상 이익에 해당한다(대법원 2021. 11. 11. 선고 2021도9855 판결 참조). 가상자산은 보관되었던 전자지갑의 주소만을 확인할 수 있을 뿐 그 주소를 사용하는 사람의 인적사항을 알 수 없고, 거래 내역이 분산 기록되어 있어 다른 계좌로 보낼 때 당사자 이외의 다른 사람이 참여해야 하는 등 일반적인 자산과는 구별되는 특징이 있다. 이와 같은 가상자산에 대해서는 현재까지 관련 법률에 따라 법정화폐에 준하는 규제가 이루어지지 않는 등 법정화폐와 동일하게 취급되고 있지 않고 그 거래에 위험이 수반되므로, 형법을 적용하면서 법정화폐와 동일하게 보호해야 하는 것은 아니다."; Reasons 3.A: "가상자산을 이체받은 자는 가상자산의 권리자 등에 대한 부당이득반환의무를 부담하게 될 수 있다. 그러나 이는 당사자 사이의 민사상 채무에 지나지 않고 … 피고인은 어떠한 경위로 이 사건 비트코인을 이체받은 것인지 불분명하여 부당이득반환청구를 할 수 있는 주체가 피해자인지 아니면 거래소인지 명확하지 않다." Full text of the judgment from the Korean Law Information Center (Open API, judgment serial number 219775, accessed 2026-10-25). The text of the judgment was read; its headnotes and summary were not cited. Working gloss: Reasons 3.C, first sentence: "A virtual asset is information, not controlled by the state, in which economic value conferred by an encrypted distributed ledger such as a blockchain is represented digitally, and it constitutes a pecuniary advantage (see Supreme Court Decision 2021Do9855 decided November 11, 2021)"; third sentence, up to "therefore": "such virtual assets have not so far been subjected under the relevant statutes to regulation equivalent to that of legal tender and are thus not treated the same as legal tender, and their trading involves risk"; Reasons 3.A: "a person who has received a transfer of virtual assets may come to bear an obligation to make restitution of unjust enrichment to the right holder of the virtual assets or others. Part 5 · Law

Chapter 28. The bridge between technology and law (2): an overview by issue, and where to read further

Key takeaway

This chapter takes up the sixteen "lawyer's question" boxes in Parts 1 to 4 that point to it under seven issues: (a) mistaken transfers and criminal liability, (b) the nature of tokens, NFTs, and staking, (c) smart contracts as contracts and the time of performance, (d) the right to deletion of personal information and immutability, (e) market regulation, (f) evidence, and (g) DAOs, hard forks, and governance. Each issue gets one or two pages. The chapter does three things. It takes up the question each box asked, as it was asked. It points to the chapter in Parts 1 to 3 that holds the technical facts the question rests on. And it records at what point in the question the primary sources whose originals were checked (for judgments, the court, the date of decision, and the case number; for provisions, the statute number and the effective date) touch it. It does not write the answers. The statement of the Supreme Court of Korea (대법원) that punishing "원인불명으로 재산상 이익인 가상자산을 이체받은 자" (gloss: "a person who received by transfer, for an unidentified cause, virtual assets that are a pecuniary advantage"; working gloss, not an official translation; the original controls) for breach of trust violates the principle of legality, the SEC's statement that automation through "smart contracts," or computer code, "does not remove conduct from the purview of the U.S. federal securities laws," and the description by the Court of Appeal of England and Wales (영국 항소법원) of developers' fiduciary duties as "a serious issue to be tried" are all examples that show such a point, not conclusions. Section 28.2 lists only the primary sources and introductory works whose bibliographic details were settled in checking the source materials, and the places where something is missing are left empty.

Learning objectives

  1. Have a map of where the sixteen question boxes land among the seven issues.
  2. For each issue, tell apart "the point where technical facts enter," "the point the primary sources have already answered," and "the point that is still empty."
  3. Be able to find judgments of Korean and foreign courts by the court, the date of decision, and the case number, and provisions by the statute number and the effective date.
  4. Use the distinction that a "statistical verdict" (Chapter 25), "executed as coded" (Chapters 13 and 16), and "the decision of a majority" (Chapters 22, 23, and 26) can each be evidence of some legal requirement but are not that requirement itself.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. In none of the seven issues does technology settle the answer. What technology settles is where the question arises, and knowing that place is all this chapter is about.

28.1 An overview by issue

(a) Mistaken transfers and criminal liability, and compulsory execution

[Basic] The box. Chapter 11 asked: to whom do coins sent by mistake belong? In the UTXO model, all that has happened is that "an output no one's key opens" has come into being; in the account model, "the balance figure of some address" has gone up. Where does the phrase "transfer of possession" fit? If the recipient has moved them to an address of their own, what is that act? If the recipient has lost the key and cannot move them, what becomes of the duty to return them?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. As Chapter 11 showed, Bitcoin has no "balance," only the sum of unspent outputs, while Ethereum does have balances. Either way, the ledger does not record the cause of a transfer. Whether it is the price in a sale or a mistake, the ledger does not know (Chapter 5: the ledger looks only at the validity of signatures). And there is no "undo." The sender cannot cancel the transaction (Chapter 9: finality); there is only a new transaction by which the recipient sends the coins back. What differs from a mistaken bank remittance is that there is no institution in the middle to carry out a refund. What is the same is that the recipient holds property that is "법률상 원인 없는" (beobryulsang wonin eomneun, "without legal cause").

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. The Supreme Court of Korea dealt with exactly this point in its judgment of December 16, 2021 (Supreme Court of Korea, 2020Do9789). The defendant had "알 수 없는 경위로 피해자의 … 거래소 가상지갑에 들어 있던 199.999비트코인 … 을 자신의 계정으로 이체받" (gloss: "received by transfer into his own account, by a course of events that cannot be known, 199.999 bitcoin … that had been in the victim's … virtual wallet at an exchange") and then moved most of it to another account of his own. The court below (원심), applying by analogy the case law on embezzlement (횡령) in a mistaken remittance (착오송금), found breach of trust (배임). The Supreme Court reversed and remanded: "가상자산 권리자의 착오나 가상자산 운영 시스템의 오류 등으로 법률상 원인관계 없이 다른 사람의 가상자산 전자지갑에 가상자산이 이체된 경우, 가상자산을 이체받은 자는 가상자산의 권리자 등에 대한 부당이득반환의무를 부담하게 될 수 있다. 그러나 이는 당사자 사이의 민사상 채무에 지나지 않고 이러한 사정만으로 가상자산을 이체받은 사람이 신임관계에 기초하여 가상자산을 보존하거나 관리하는 지위에 있다고 볼 수 없다." (gloss: "Where virtual assets have been transferred into another person's virtual-asset electronic wallet without a legal causal relationship, owing to a mistake by the holder of the rights in the virtual assets, an error in the virtual-asset operating system, or the like, the person who received the virtual assets may come to bear a duty to return unjust enrichment to the holder of the rights in the virtual assets or others. But this is no more than a civil obligation between the parties, and on this circumstance alone the person who received the virtual assets cannot be regarded as being in a position to preserve or manage the virtual assets on the basis of a relationship of trust.") And: "원인불명으로 재산상 이익인 가상자산을 이체받은 자가 가상자산을 사용·처분한 경우 이를 형사처벌하는 명문의 규정이 없는 현재의 상황에서 착오송금 시 횡령죄 성립을 긍정한 판례 … 를 유추하여 신의칙을 근거로 피고인을 배임죄로 처벌하는 것은 죄형법정주의에 반한다." (gloss: "In the present situation, in which there is no express provision imposing criminal punishment where a person who received by transfer, for an unidentified cause, virtual assets that are a pecuniary advantage uses or disposes of them, punishing the defendant for breach of trust on the basis of the principle of good faith (신의칙), by analogy to the case law … that affirmed the crime of embezzlement upon a mistaken remittance, violates the principle of legality (죄형법정주의).")1 The judgment touches the question in Chapter 11 in three ways. First, the judgment called virtual assets "재산상 이익" (jaesansang iik, "pecuniary advantage") and did not decide whether they are "재물" (jaemul, "property in the sense of a thing"). The embezzlement count (the primary charge, 주위적 공소사실) was reversed together with the breach-of-trust part only on the ground that it stood in "동일체의 관계" (gloss: "a relationship of identity") with it, and whether virtual assets are 재물 remains an issue on which scholarly views divide. Second, "부당이득반환청구를 할 수 있는 주체가 피해자인지 아니면 거래소인지 명확하지 않다" (gloss: "it is not clear whether the party that can claim the return of unjust enrichment is the victim or the exchange"). The two layers of the exchange's books and the chain that Chapter 26 looked at appear here again. Third, the judgment wrote that virtual assets are "법정화폐와 동일하게 취급되고 있지 않고 그 거래에 위험이 수반되므로, 형법을 적용하면서 법정화폐와 동일하게 보호해야 하는 것은 아니다" (gloss: "not treated in the same way as legal tender and their trading carries risk, so in applying the Criminal Act they need not be protected in the same way as legal tender"). What the duty to return that this judgment called a "민사상 채무" (gloss: "civil obligation") is a duty to return, the same quantity of coins or their value, lies outside the scope of what the judgment decided, and the discussion of legal nature in 27.2 has to fill that place.

[Basic] In Supreme Court of Korea, 2021Do9855, November 11, 2021, the same panel stated that "비트코인은 … 사기죄의 객체인 재산상 이익에 해당한다" (gloss: "Bitcoin … is a pecuniary advantage that can be the object of fraud"), and in Supreme Court of Korea, 2018Do3619, May 30, 2018, the Court, stating that under the Act on Regulation and Punishment of Criminal Proceeds Concealment (범죄수익은닉의 규제 및 처벌 등에 관한 법률) "재산적 가치가 인정되는 무형재산도 몰수할 수 있다" (gloss: "intangible property recognized as having property value may also be confiscated"), upheld the judgment below, which had identified, among the seized bitcoin, the quantity that constituted criminal proceeds and confiscated (몰수) it.2 Lay the three judgments over one another, and criminal law has treated bitcoin as property on the side of the one who obtains it (the object of fraud, the object of confiscation), while on the side of the one who received it without cause (is that person the subject of breach of trust?) it has denied punishment, citing the absence of a relationship of trust. Whether this asymmetry is right, this book does not say.

[Basic] Compulsory execution. The Civil Execution Act (민사집행법) has no provision on virtual assets. A report of the Judicial Policy Research Institute (사법정책연구원) treats virtual assets as "그 밖의 재산권" (geu bakkui jaesangwon, "other property rights") and, for reasons including that if they were treated as corporeal movables (유체동산) the requirements for an attachment (압류) to take effect could not be met, because "블록체인에 채무자의 가상자산이 압류되었다는 표시를 할 기술은 현재 그 구현이 불가능" (gloss: "the technology to place on a blockchain an indication that the debtor's virtual assets have been attached cannot at present be implemented"), proposed legislation under which, where the debtor manages the virtual assets personally, the virtual assets themselves are attached, and where an exchange manages them, the "가상자산이전청구권" (gloss: "claim for the transfer of virtual assets") is attached, and the assets are transferred to a court enforcement officer (집행관) and sold.3 For compulsory collection (강제징수) of taxes, legislation already exists. Article 55(3) of the National Tax Collection Act (국세징수법) provides that when the head of a tax office attaches virtual assets, the head "해당 가상자산의 이전을 문서로 요구할 수 있" (gloss: "may request in writing the transfer of the virtual assets concerned") of the delinquent taxpayer or of the business that keeps them in custody, and that the person so requested "이에 따라야 한다" (gloss: "shall comply with it") (inserted December 21, 2021); Article 66(2), subparagraph 2 allows "가상자산사업자를 통해 거래되는 가상자산" (gloss: "virtual assets traded through a virtual asset service provider") to be sold directly through the provider.4 The two provisions presuppose one technical fact: coins on a chain cannot be moved without the private key, so enforcement has no choice but to take the form of ordering the person who has the key to "move them" (Chapter 5). The last question in the Chapter 11 box, "if the recipient lost the key and cannot move them," is exactly the place this request does not reach, and no provision governs that case.

(b) The nature of tokens, NFTs, and staking, with taxation in brief

[Basic] The boxes. Chapter 10 asked: is a staking reward consideration for a service, fruits (과실) borne by the deposited coins, or original acquisition (원시취득) of new coins? Is a deposit that disappears through slashing a fine, a contractual penalty, or the enforcement of a security interest? Is a business that takes in other people's coins and stakes them on their behalf a trustee or a debtor? Chapter 14 asked: did the person who bought an NFT buy the token, the file, a right, or the fact of "pointing to"? If the issuer shuts down its server, what has perished (멸실)? If the issuer promised revenue sharing, is that promise in the code or outside it? Chapter 24 asked: is a holder a depositor, an unsecured creditor, or the beneficiary of a trust? What right does a public pledge to "cover any shortfall using corporate resources" give?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. The fact common to the three boxes is the one from Chapter 14: a token standard is only a promise about function names, and what a token carries is fixed by the issuer's promise outside the chain. The balance of an ERC-20 token, the (contract address, number) pair and tokenURI string of an ERC-721 token, the redemption promise of a stablecoin, and the issuance rules for staking rewards are all states on the chain, but the chain does not decide whether they are "rights." The fact from Chapter 10 is that staking rewards come from the protocol's issuance rules and that slashing is part of the same rules, and that the deposit is a design in which "punishment is part of security."

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. There are three strands.

First, whether something is a security turns on the promise outside the chain and on the shape of the transaction. In 2017 the SEC, finding that DAO Tokens were investment contracts, quoted the Supreme Court of the United States' precedent that "form should be disregarded for substance … and the emphasis should be on economic realities underlying a transaction, and not on the name appended thereto," and said that although token holders had voting rights, "DAO Token holders were substantially reliant on the managerial efforts of Slock.it, its co-founders, and the Curators."5 The 2023 summary judgment in Ripple distinguished the institutional sales of the same token, which were investment contracts, from anonymous trading on exchanges, which were not: "Programmatic Buyers could not have known if their payments of money went to Ripple, or any other seller of XRP."6 The answer of U.S. law to the last question in the Chapter 14 box is: "The promise is outside, and to whom and by what route that promise was conveyed decides whether there is a security." In 2025 the U.S. Congress, through the GENIUS Act, took payment stablecoins of permitted issuers out of securities and commodities (§17).7 Korea's Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률; below, the Virtual Asset User Protection Act) excludes from virtual assets the electronically registered stocks, etc. under the Act on Electronic Registration of Stocks, Bonds, etc. (주식·사채 등의 전자등록에 관한 법률) (Article 2, subparagraph 1(d)), and whether something is a security under the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act (자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률) is outside the scope of this book.

Second, on NFTs, the definitions of three jurisdictions part ways. EU MiCA does not apply to "crypto-assets that are unique and not fungible with other crypto-assets" (Art. 2(3)). The UK's Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026 make "fungible" a requirement of a "qualifying cryptoasset," taking non-fungible tokens out of the scope of regulated activities. In Korea, Article 2, subparagraph 4 of the Enforcement Decree (시행령), under the delegation in Article 2, subparagraph 1(h) of the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, excludes "단일하게 존재하여 다른 전자적 증표로 대체할 수 없는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "electronic tokens that exist singly and cannot be replaced by other electronic tokens"), with the proviso that "특정 재화나 서비스의 지급수단으로 사용될 수 있는 전자적 증표 등 금융위원회가 정하여 고시하는 전자적 증표는 제외" (gloss: "electronic tokens determined and publicly notified by the Financial Services Commission (금융위원회), such as electronic tokens that can be used as a means of payment for particular goods or services, are excluded").8 On the Chapter 14 box's "what did the person buy?", what the definitional provisions say goes as far as "does regulation come in," and no provision decides whether the object of the sale is a token, a file, or a right. Position ⑨ in 27.2 (the control-based view) implies an answer that takes "the ability to change the owner field of a (contract address, number) pair" as the unit of attribution, and under that answer the "object of control" remains even if the server shuts down and the image disappears. That is one possible reply to the box's question "what has perished?", not this book's reply.

Third, the position of stablecoin holders is what Chapter 24 asked in the words of Gorton and Zhang: "equity contract or a debt contract." The legislation of four jurisdictions (Korea has not set up a separate category; see 27.3) has fixed the qualifications of issuers and their reserve assets. The EU allows e-money tokens to be issued only by credit institutions and electronic money institutions (MiCA Art. 48). The U.S. GENIUS Act wrote into its definition that a permitted issuer is "obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value" (§2(22)(A)(ii)(I)). Japan defined the first type (item 1) of "電子決済手段" (denshi kessai shudan, "electronic payment instruments") as limited to "通貨建資産" (tsūka-date shisan, "currency-denominated assets"). And the UK made "fiat currency … or other assets are held for the purpose of maintaining a stable value" a requirement of a "qualifying stablecoin."9 None of these provisions decides, on the spot, whether a holder is a depositor, a creditor, or a beneficiary. Priority in the issuer's insolvency, the segregation of reserve assets, and the effect of a "public pledge" pass to each jurisdiction's insolvency law and trust law, and that point is where the Chapter 24 box pointed.

[Basic] Taxation, in brief. The Chapter 10 box's "what is a staking reward paid for?" is the question taxation is first required to answer, yet this book's source materials contain no primary source that records that answer. Two things can be written down. The U.S. Internal Revenue Service said in a 2014 notice that it treats virtual currency as "property" and applies the general principles of property transactions, and a 2023 notice left that conclusion as it was.10 Article 21(1), subparagraph 27 of Korea's Income Tax Act (소득세법) makes "가상자산을 양도하거나 대여함으로써 발생하는 소득" (gloss: "income arising from transferring or lending virtual assets") other income (기타소득), but as of 2026-10-25 it is not yet in force (effective January 1, 2027), and because its wording names only "양도·대여" (gloss: "transfer or lending"), where a staking reward falls cannot be read directly from the provision.11 This book does not go into that interpretation.

(c) Smart contracts as contracts and the time of performance

[Basic] The boxes. Chapter 13 asked: in a ten-line "contract," where are the offer (청약) and the acceptance (승낙)? Is deploying the code the offer and calling a function the acceptance, or are both factual acts (사실행위)? When the code behaves differently from what its author intended, is the "content of the contract" the code or the intention? If execution was reverted because the gas ran out but the fee remained paid, what was performed and what was not? If it becomes the "autonomous agent" the Yellow Paper spoke of, who is the one making the declaration of intention (의사표시)? Chapter 16 asked: the oracle put in a wrong value, and the code did not deviate by a single line. Is that performance (이행) or mistake (착오), whose mistake is it, and if no one ran the oracle, what did the person who pushed the value manipulate? Chapter 9 asked: when was the payment completed: when it was propagated, when it entered a block, or when z blocks were stacked on it? If the terms of service fix "6 confirmations," is that the standard? If the chain is reorganized and the transaction disappears, does the performance become something that never happened?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. The three boxes rest on three facts. First, Chapter 13: a smart contract is "a box that releases value only when conditions are met," a state transition takes place when a transaction enters a block, and when gas runs out the state is reverted but the fee remains. Second, Chapter 16: the chain cannot know outside facts by itself, and outside facts come in only by trusting someone. Third, Chapter 9: there is no moment of completion, only a probability of reversal that keeps getting smaller, and "6 confirmations" is a convention, not a rule. When the law uses concepts that have a time and an actor, such as "declaration of intention," "performance," and "completion," technology gives, for those three, the time as a probability and the actor as a blank.

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. On whether smart contracts are contracts, the SEC's 2017 report is the only primary source whose original this book has checked. The report says "The automation of certain functions through this technology, 'smart contracts,' or computer code, does not remove conduct from the purview of the U.S. federal securities laws," and in a footnote introduces "smart contract" with Nick Szabo's definition, "a computerized transaction protocol that executes terms of a contract."12 The point this sentence touches is that the fact that "the code executed" does not erase the actor. It does not say whether code is a contract. The DAO in Chapter 26 is the example: the code ran as written, and the SEC looked at the "efforts" of the people who deployed and promoted it. The Chapter 16 box's "what did the person who pushed the value manipulate?" may be reached by provisions of market regulation, and that is taken up in (e).

[Basic] The empty point. On the Chapter 9 box's "when is a payment completed?", this book could not cite a primary source. Chapter 9 described the finality of payment systems only through the concept of "a point of irrevocability fixed by rule," without identifying which rule of which system, and said that Part 5 would support it with primary sources on the law of settlement finality. But this book's source materials do not contain the originals of that law (statutes and directives on settlement finality), so this edition could not support it. It is left reserved and reported as such. What can be written is the structure. If the finality of a payment system is a point fixed by rule, the finality of a blockchain is a process in which a probability shrinks, so terms of service that fix "6 confirmations" lay the point of a rule over that process. Even if that overlay becomes the standard between the parties, the transaction itself can disappear if the chain is reorganized (Chapter 9, Section 4). That is the last question of the box, and which jurisdiction's primary sources sit at that point is a task for the next edition.

(d) The right to deletion of personal information and immutability

[Basic] The box. Chapter 7 asked: someone says that a transaction containing their personal information has been recorded on the chain and asks for it to be deleted. The chain is designed so that it cannot be altered, and altering it would require a great many participants to remake every block that follows. What does the right to deletion of personal information (개인정보 삭제권) demand on a ledger that cannot be erased? Against whom is deletion to be demanded, and what act, technically, is "deleting"? Does a design that keeps personal information off the chain from the start and puts only a hash on it solve the problem, or postpone it?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. What Chapter 7 showed is that immutability is not a mathematical impossibility but a cost of tampering. Change one character in one block and the hashes of every block after it no longer match, and removing the mismatch means re-mining everything after it (Chapters 7 and 8). So "deleting" is, technically, one of three things. (i) Remaking everything after that block. This needs the coordination of many, and this book's source materials contain no case in which past records were erased that way on a public mainnet. The DAO fork in Chapter 26 did not re-mine past blocks; it moved balances by putting an exceptional state change into the consensus rules at block 1,920,000 (EIP-779), so it is not of this type. (ii) Each node deleting the data from its own copy, in which case the data remain in other nodes' copies. (iii) Where the chain holds only a hash and the original is outside it, deleting the original outside. In (iii), the hash left on the chain is, as Chapter 4 showed, a fingerprint from which the original cannot be recovered, but if the original survives somewhere else, the hash comes back to life as proof that "that original existed then." That is why the box asked "solve, or postpone."

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. Article 36 of Korea's Personal Information Protection Act (개인정보 보호법) provides that a data subject "개인정보처리자에게 그 개인정보의 정정 또는 삭제를 요구할 수 있" (gloss: "may request the personal information controller to correct or delete the personal information") (paragraph (1); there is a proviso for personal information that other statutes specify as subject to collection), that the controller must take "지체 없이 그 개인정보를 조사하여 정보주체의 요구에 따라 정정·삭제 등 필요한 조치" (gloss: "without delay, after examining the personal information, necessary measures such as correction or deletion in accordance with the data subject's request") (paragraph (2); except where other statutes lay down a special procedure), and that "삭제할 때에는 복구 또는 재생되지 아니하도록 조치하여야 한다" (gloss: "when deleting, it shall take measures so that the information cannot be restored or regenerated") (paragraph (3)).13 Article 17 of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) provides, where one of the grounds listed in paragraph 1 applies (and none of the exceptions in paragraph 3 applies), for the data subject's right to obtain "the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay" and the controller's "obligation to erase personal data without undue delay," and provides that where the controller has made the information public and is obliged to erase it under paragraph 1, the controller, "taking account of available technology and the cost of implementation, shall take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform controllers which are processing the personal data."14 The two provisions touch the Chapter 7 box at three phrases. "개인정보처리자" (gaeinjeongbo cheorija, "personal information controller") and "controller": who is that on a public blockchain? (Chapter 8: a miner is nobody's agent.) "복구 또는 재생되지 아니하도록" (gloss: "so that it cannot be restored or regenerated"): is that possible in a structure where other nodes' copies and the hash remain? "available technology and the cost of implementation": is the cost of tampering exactly that "cost"? No court judgment from any jurisdiction is in this book's source materials, and this book does not judge.

(e) Market regulation: exchanges, market manipulation, MEV

[Basic] The boxes. Chapter 8 asked: whose agent is a miner? Does a miner who leaves a valid transaction out of a block have any duty? If a group of miners refuses every transaction from a particular address, what act is that, and toward whom? Chapter 15 asked: where in a constant-product AMM is the "operator" that exchange regulation presupposes, someone who registers, reviews listings, monitors for market manipulation (시세조종), and keeps customer assets segregated? Chapter 17 asked: the sandwich attacker did not change a single character of the victim's order. Is this market manipulation? Is there a "market price" (시세) that was manipulated, who is the "actor" who manipulated it, and where is the "market" that regulation presupposes? If the producer ran the sandwich itself, what did it do in its own block? Chapter 25 asked: is an expert opinion that the price "was explosive at the 1% level in a GSADF test" evidence of market manipulation, evidence of deception (기망), or an observation that one of multiple equilibria was realized?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. The four boxes rest on different facts. Chapter 8: a block producer is bound by no contract, and the majority of "one CPU, one vote" is not a body. Chapter 15: the price in an AMM is the ratio of the two quantities in the pool, and there is no quote, no operator, and no counterparty. Chapter 17: there is a power to decide the order, that power is not blocked by code, and after proposer–builder separation the order is sold at auction. Chapter 25: the verdict of an explosive unit-root test flips with the assumption about fundamental value, and "it was a bubble" is a statistical proposition, not a proposition about conduct.

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. For market regulation, the Korean and EU provisions and the U.S. judgment were checked in the original. Article 10 of Korea's Virtual Asset User Protection Act prohibits the use of material nonpublic information (paragraph (1)), matched trades and wash trades (paragraph (2)), "가상자산의 매매를 유인할 목적으로 가상자산의 매매가 성황을 이루고 있는 듯이 잘못 알게 하거나 그 시세를 변동 또는 고정시키는 매매 또는 그 위탁이나 수탁" (gloss: "trading, or the entrustment or acceptance of trading, that for the purpose of inducing the trading of virtual assets misleads others into believing that the trading of virtual assets is brisk, or that changes or fixes their market price") (paragraph (3)), and, among others, "부정한 수단, 계획 또는 기교를 사용하는 행위" (gloss: "the act of using a fraudulent means, scheme, or artifice") (paragraph (4)), as well as trading by a provider in virtual assets it issued itself (paragraph (5)), and it makes violators liable for damages (paragraph (6)). Paragraphs (2) to (4), which begin with "누구든지" (nugudeunji, "any person"), do not limit their addressees to providers.15 Title VI of EU MiCA applies, in respect of "crypto-assets that are admitted to trading or in respect of which a request for admission to trading has been made," to "any transaction, order or behaviour …, irrespective of whether such transaction, order or behaviour takes place on a trading platform," and prohibits insider dealing (Art. 89) and market manipulation (Art. 91).16 In the United States, the McDonnell decision recognized the CFTC's authority to apply the fraud prohibition of the Commodity Exchange Act to spot transactions in virtual currency.17 Entry for exchanges is by reporting in Korea (Article 7 of the Act on Reporting and Using Specified Financial Transaction Information (특정 금융거래정보의 보고 및 이용 등에 관한 법률)), authorization in the EU (MiCA Art. 59), registration in Japan (資金決済法 第63条の2, the Payment Services Act), and, in the UK, the regulated activities under SI 2026/102, scheduled to come into force in 2027 (27.3).

[Basic] Where the provisions reach the boxes and where they do not. The "시세를 변동 또는 고정시키는 매매" (gloss: "trading that changes or fixes the market price") of Korea's Article 10(3) and the "market manipulation" of MiCA Article 91 give a place in the wording into which the sandwich of Chapter 17 could go. They say "누구든지" and "any person," and nothing in the word "시세" (sise, "market price") limits it to a particular exchange. (How far that reaches is a matter of interpretation, and this book does not go into it.) But the two provisions stop at different places. MiCA presupposes crypto-assets that are "admitted to trading" or for which admission has been requested, and Korea's Article 10(3) requires "매매를 유인할 목적" (gloss: "the purpose of inducing trading"). The "operator" of the Chapter 15 box and the "agent" of the Chapter 8 box are filled by neither provision. The provisions only prohibit conduct. They do not say which of an AMM's deployer, its liquidity providers, and its governance majority is the "operator," or whether a block producer's refusal of transactions is an "act." That the GENIUS Act expressly excluded participation in liquidity pools from "digital asset service provider" (27.3) is one example of legislation knowingly leaving that gap empty. To the Chapter 25 box, an answer can be given from structure rather than from provisions. No provision has "an explosive interval" as a requirement. Korea's Article 10 makes "목적" (gloss: "purpose") and "매매" (gloss: "trading") its requirements, MiCA Article 91 "activities," and the Commodity Exchange Act "fraud." A statistical verdict can be evidence of such a requirement, but it is not the requirement itself, and as Chapter 25 showed, that verdict flips with the assumption about fundamental value and the choice of critical values. A verdict of "it was not a bubble" does not, for the same reason, directly help the defendant either.

(f) Evidence: hashes, time-stamps, and originals

[Basic] The boxes. Chapter 4 asked: only the hash value of a document was recorded on a public ledger, and years later it is submitted together with the original file. What does this hash value prove, and what does it not prove? "That bit string existed at that time," "that document was made at that time," and "the content of that document is true" are three different propositions. Which of the three do the evidence-law concepts of the original, the copy, and authenticity (진정성립) reach? Chapter 1 asked: if there are many ledgers, which copy is the original?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. As Chapter 4 showed, a hash is a fingerprint that cannot be reversed. The same input gives the same output, and if one character differs, the whole changes. So if the hash is on the chain and the original is submitted, recomputing the hash and matching it proves the proposition "this bit string existed before that block's time." But the meaning of the block's time has to be read precisely. As Chapter 7 set out from the original text of Haber and Stornetta, what a time-stamp chain guarantees is a boundary in two directions, "it cannot be stamped with a later time / it cannot be back-dated to an earlier time." The time in a Bitcoin header is "a rough time" that the miner writes, and the protocol only restricts it so that it does not stray far from the blocks before and after it (Chapter 8). And a hash says nothing about "making" or "truth." A false document also has a fingerprint. The decoding of the newspaper headline in the genesis block in Chapter 12 is a good example. That the block contains that phrase says only that the block was made after the phrase was published, and the block does not prove that the phrase was a real newspaper headline (which is why Chapter 12 wrote conditionally). For Chapter 1's "which copy is the original?", Chapters 6 and 7 give the place of the answer: since all the copies have the same root hash, none of them is "the original," and each of them is the same as the original.

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. Article 357 of Korea's Civil Procedure Act (민사소송법) provides "사문서는 그것이 진정한 것임을 증명하여야 한다" (gloss: "a private document shall be proved to be authentic"), Article 358 provides "사문서는 본인 또는 대리인의 서명이나 날인 또는 무인(拇印)이 있는 때에는 진정한 것으로 추정한다" (gloss: "a private document is presumed authentic when it bears the signature, seal, or thumbprint of the person or of an agent"), and Article 3 of the Digital Signature Act (전자서명법) provides that an electronic signature "전자적 형태라는 이유만으로 서명, 서명날인 또는 기명날인으로서의 효력이 부인되지 아니한다" (gloss: "shall not be denied effect as a signature, a signature and seal, or a name and seal solely because it is in electronic form").18 The point at which the three provisions touch the Chapter 4 box is that "authenticity" is a question about the author. A signature or seal raises a presumption about "who wrote it," and a hash proves "what existed." They are different propositions. The digital signature that Chapter 5 showed proves that the holder of the private key approved that bit string, and whose private key it is, is a fact outside the chain. A 2020 judgment of the Tokyo High Court (東京高等裁判所) wrote this about the evidentiary function of electromagnetic records (電磁的記録, denjiteki kiroku): "電磁的記録の証明機能は，それが作出されるべきシステムの設置運営主体の意思に基づき，正当に作出されることが当然の前提とされているもので" (gloss: "the evidentiary function of an electromagnetic record is premised as a matter of course on its being properly created in accordance with the will of the entity that set up and operates the system in which it is to be created"), and an electromagnetic record "それを使用することが予定されている一定のシステムやプログラムのもとで用いられて初めて本来の証明機能を果たし得る" (gloss: "can perform its proper evidentiary function only when it is used under the particular system or program in which its use is intended").19 It is an interpretation of a criminal provision, but it is a judgment that read what the figures in an exchange's books "prove" from what that system was supposed to do, and the answer to the Chapter 4 box's "what does a hash prove?" starts the same way, from what that chain was supposed to do (Chapter 7: a time boundary on existence).

(g) The legal status of DAOs, hard forks, and governance

[Basic] The boxes. There are four. Chapter 22: a majority of the governance tokens changed the rules. What can the minority assert? Is a DAO a partnership (조합) (do its members bear unlimited liability), a juridical person (법인) (under which law was it established), or nothing at all (to whom are the Curators' duties owed)? Chapter 23: after a hard fork both chains survived. Who decides which ledger is "real": a majority of the hash rate, a majority of the nodes, the exchanges, the developers, or no one? Did a person who had coins before the fork have one thing or two? A contract to "pay 1 bitcoin": 1 on which chain? What did the selfish miner violate? Chapter 26: was The DAO's hard fork a remedy, a forfeiture, or a change of contract by majority vote? Does the distinction that the DAO Fork "did not change the protocol" and was an "irregular state change" have legal meaning? And Chapter 29 in Part 6 asks: is blocking the spending of vulnerable coins by soft fork expropriation (수용), a measure for maintaining order, or the disposal of ownerless property (무주물), and whose agent is the party that decides?

[Basic] Where the technical facts enter. As Chapter 23 showed, rules are maintained by the coordination of participants, and deciding which chain "wins" is also coordination. As Chapter 22 showed, votes with governance tokens are counted by code and the results are executed automatically. As Chapter 26 showed, a hard fork can be "changing the state without changing the rules," and the minority can stay on the old chain. As Chapter 8 showed, the sets of miners, nodes, and holders do not coincide. When the law uses concepts such as "body" (단체), "member" (구성원), "representative" (대표), and "resolution" (결의), technology gives several sets that do not overlap and votes counted by code.

[Basic] Where the primary sources touch. In three places. First, the SEC's 2017 report calls The DAO "an unincorporated organization" and, citing the provision under which "person" in the definition of "issuer" in the securities laws includes "any unincorporated organization," said that The DAO was an issuer of securities.20 The report also reproduced in a footnote that The DAO white paper itself had written that "the legal status of [DAO Entities] remains the subject of active and vigorous debate and discussion."21 The answer of U.S. securities law to the Chapter 22 box's "or nothing at all?" is "something sufficient to be an issuer." Second, in its 2023 judgment in Tulip Trading, the Court of Appeal of England and Wales said that whether the developers of the Bitcoin network owe fiduciary duties (신인의무) to holders was "a serious issue to be tried," and wrote: "If the decentralised governance of bitcoin really is a myth, then … there is much to be said for the submission that bitcoin developers, while acting as developers, owe fiduciary duties to the true owners of that property."22 On the Chapter 23 box's "the developers?", the English court went as far as the point "that may be so, once the facts are established." It is not a conclusion on the merits. Third, EIP-779 documented The DAO fork in these words: "did not change the protocol … Rather, the DAO Fork was an 'irregular state change'," and the Foundation directed users who wanted to follow the old chain to the "--oppose-dao-fork" flag.23 On the Chapter 26 box's "does that distinction have legal meaning?", what the technical document gives is the distinction itself, and the meaning is for the law. In Korean law, Article 703(1) of the Civil Act (민법) provides "조합은 2인 이상이 상호출자하여 공동사업을 경영할 것을 약정함으로써 그 효력이 생긴다" (gloss: "a partnership takes effect when two or more persons agree to make mutual contributions and carry on a joint undertaking"), the partnership-right view (조합권설) in 27.2 ⑤ tried to read the network into that provision, and there is a counterargument that "단체의 성립·가입·탈퇴를 위한 법령이나 의사표시가 없다" (gloss: "there is no statute or declaration of intention for the formation of a body, or for joining or leaving it").24 There are no primary sources touching the Chapter 29 question in this book's source materials. Section 5 of Chapter 29 only introduces three strands of the discussion on the Bitcoin side (leave them as they are, burn them, limit their speed) and the policy options listed in one white paper, and this section records the fact that there is no statute or judgment touching that question.

[Basic] The empty points. On the Chapter 22 box's "is a DAO a juridical person, and under which law?", this book did not check through primary sources whether any jurisdiction has legislation granting legal personality to DAOs. On the Chapter 23 box's "the 1 bitcoin in a contract: 1 on which chain?", it did not look for judgments or provisions either. Both places are left as tasks for the next edition and reported as reserved.

28.2 Where to read further

[Basic] Below are the primary sources and introductory works whose bibliographic details were settled in checking the source materials and whose originals this book opened. They are where a reader who wants to do what Part 5 did not do, legal exposition, should go first. Bibliographic details that were not settled are not given, and jurisdictions for which something is missing are left empty.

Places left empty. Introductory works (textbooks and commentaries) for Japan, the UK, and the EU are not listed, because their bibliographic details could not be settled through OpenAlex or National Assembly Library records (one edited volume from the UK was identified only by title and editors through a book-review record, so its bibliographic details are incomplete). There are also no primary sources for the law of settlement finality (28.1(c)), the taxation of staking (28.1(b)), or legislation on the legal personality of DAOs (28.1(g)). These are places to fill in the next edition.

Summary

[Basic] Through the seven issues the same shape kept recurring. The questions the boxes asked arose from technical facts (the ledger does not know the cause, a token does not carry rights, there is no moment of completion, erasing has a cost, there is a power to decide the order, a hash proves only existence, votes are counted by code), and the primary sources touched one point in each question. The Supreme Court of Korea did not regard the recipient of a mistaken transfer as the subject of breach of trust, the SEC said that automatic execution by code does not erase the actor, the Court of Appeal of England and Wales left developers' fiduciary duties as an issue to be tried, and the legislation of five jurisdictions defined providers, and four of them stablecoin issuers. No source answered every question in a box, and the empty points (settlement finality, the taxation of staking, the legal personality of DAOs, the object of a contract after a fork) were recorded as empty. What a lawyer takes from this chapter is not answers but this table, which records which chapter of Parts 1 to 3 holds the premise facts of which issue. The next chapter looks, through the original text of definitional provisions, at one thing that runs through all of those issues: that five jurisdictions call the same thing by five names, and that those names divide jurisdiction, taxation, and the application of criminal law (Chapter 30).
