Part 6 · Open problems

Chapter 29. The quantum transition: signatures break, hashes stand, and the vulnerable coins

Key takeaway

What a quantum computer threatens is not "Bitcoin" but particular signature schemes. Shor's algorithm solves the discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve in polynomial time and extracts the private key from the public key; Grover's algorithm speeds up the preimage search of a hash function only by a square root. So the signatures of Chapter 5 break, while the hashes and proof of work of Chapters 4 and 8 stand. The size of the machine needed for an attack has come down from 2,330 logical qubits in 2017 to around 1,200 logical qubits in 2026. Estimates of physical qubits range, depending on the assumptions, from hundreds of thousands to the billions, and even within a single paper the target time alone moves them from 13 million to 1.9 billion. Estimates are functions of assumptions, not observations. What is at risk is coins whose public keys have already been revealed, and a secondary tally from the reference-date snapshot puts that range at about one third of issuance. The Bitcoin-side transition proposals (BIP-360 and BIP-361) are Drafts as of 2026-10, no post-quantum element has been activated, and an official Ethereum page has published a roadmap that gives 2029 as a planning target that may shift. What lawyers take away is not the technology but the last question: is blocking the spending of vulnerable coins by soft fork an expropriation, a measure for maintaining order, or the disposal of ownerless property, and whose agent is the majority that decides it? This chapter asks that question and does not answer it.

Learning objectives

  1. Explain how Shor's algorithm threatens signatures (ECDLP) and how Grover's algorithm threatens hashes, and the asymmetry between the two (signatures break, hashes stand).
  2. [Intermediate] Distinguish logical from physical qubits, and read from a table how resource estimates move by hundreds of times depending on the assumptions (error rate, code cycle, reaction time, connectivity, target time).
  3. Identify the three places where a public key is revealed on the chain (script type, reuse, the mempool), and read the amounts by type in the reference-date snapshot together with the caveat that they are a secondary tally.
  4. Know what the transition proposals (BIP-360 and BIP-361, NIST FIPS 203 to 205, Ethereum's four areas) change and what they do not change.
  5. Set out as a structure the three paths of the debate over "restricting the spending of vulnerable coins" (leave them, burn them, limit the speed), and hand the legal questions they lead to over to their place in Part 5.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. What a quantum computer breaks is not "Bitcoin" but a particular signature scheme, and the truly hard problem is not the technology but who decides on the transition, with what authority, and what is to be done with the coins left behind. The basis for misconception ⑤ in Appendix B ("When quantum computers arrive, Bitcoin is finished") is in this chapter.

1. Two algorithms, two targets: an asymmetry

[Basic] Part 1 used two cryptographic tools: the hash function of Chapter 4 and the public-key signature of Chapter 5. A quantum computer affects the two differently. A 2016 report of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) set out the difference in one table: symmetric-key cryptography (AES), "Larger key sizes needed"; hash functions (SHA-2, SHA-3), "Larger output needed"; and RSA, elliptic curve signatures (ECDSA), elliptic curve key exchange (ECDH) and finite field signatures (DSA), "No longer secure."1 Bitcoin's signature is ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve (Chapter 5), and since 2021 Bitcoin has also used Schnorr signatures over the same curve. Both belong to the third line. Bitcoin's proof of work runs SHA-256 twice (Chapter 8), and that belongs to the second line.

[Basic] Why the difference? The report names two algorithms. In 1994 Peter Shor of Bell Laboratories showed that a quantum computer can solve integer factorization and the discrete logarithm problem efficiently, thereby "rendering all public key cryptosystems based on such assumptions impotent."2 What Lov Grover's search algorithm offers, by contrast, is "a quadratic speedup on unstructured search problems," and the report says: "While such a speedup does not render cryptographic technologies obsolete, it can have the effect of requiring larger key sizes, even in the symmetric key case."3 In Chapter 5 the security of a signature rested on the fact that no fast way is known to find k from [k]G. That is true on a classical computer. On a quantum computer, Shor's algorithm finds exactly that k. In Chapter 4 the security of a hash rested on the fact that finding a preimage takes an expected 2256 attempts, and Grover's algorithm cuts that to around 2128 operations. That is still an astronomical number, and, as the table above has it, it is the kind of speedup that can be undone by a "[l]arger output."

[Basic] Among the literature this chapter opened, the earliest peer-reviewed paper to take on the quantum threat to Bitcoin directly put this asymmetry in numbers. It is a 2018 paper by Divesh Aggarwal and four co-authors. The conclusion of its abstract is two sentences: "We find that the proof-of-work used by Bitcoin is relatively resistant to substantial speedup by quantum computers in the next 10 years, mainly because specialized ASIC miners are extremely fast compared to the estimated clock speed of near-term quantum computers. On the other hand, the elliptic curve signature scheme used by Bitcoin is much more at risk, and could be completely broken by a quantum computer as early as 2027, by the most optimistic estimates."4 The year in the second sentence is a "most optimistic" extrapolation made in 2017, and this book takes no part in that extrapolation (Section 2). The structure of the first sentence has been confirmed again and again in the later literature. A 2026 white paper by the Google Quantum AI team and others says that Grover-based attacks on mining are "not something to worry about in the next several decades," and gives two reasons: the square-root speedup is almost entirely consumed by the cost of quantum error correction, and Grover's algorithm does not parallelize well, whereas mining is a world of hardware acceleration and massive parallelization.5

[Intermediate] In numbers it looks like this. Aggarwal et al. calculate that the number of logical qubits a Grover miner needs is fixed at 2,402 regardless of difficulty. Assuming the then-maximum gate speed of superconducting circuits, 66.7 MHz, a physical gate error rate of 5×10−4 and a difficulty of 1012, they put the effective hash rate of one quantum miner at 13.8 GH/s (with about 4.4 million physical qubits): "more than one thousand times slower than off the shelf ASIC devices which achieve hash rates of 14TH/s."6 The 2026 white paper reaches the same conclusion with a more extreme assumption. Even "Under the fantastical assumption that a CRQC could compute SHA-256 in a single 1 microsecond error correction cycle," it says, a quantum miner's hash rate is 0.25 TH/s, two orders of magnitude below the 110 TH/s of the common ASIC miner S19 Pro.7 As Chapter 8 showed, the security of proof of work rests not on absolute speed but on share, and nowhere in the literature this chapter opened is there an estimate that quantum miners would be fast enough to overturn the shares.

[Advanced] Why the asymmetry: a problem with structure and a problem without

[Advanced] The advanced box in Chapter 5 showed the problem of finding k given the points G and Q=[k]G on an elliptic curve (ECDLP). This problem has algebraic structure. The points form a group, and scalar multiplication is a periodic function on that group. Shor's algorithm reads out exactly that periodicity with the quantum Fourier transform. A 2017 paper by Martin Roetteler and colleagues at Microsoft sums it up like this: Shor "presented two polynomial-time quantum algorithms, one for integer factorization and another one for computing discrete logarithms in a finite field of prime order. Shor notes that the latter algorithm can be generalized to other fields. It also generalizes to the case of elliptic curves."8 Finding a preimage of a hash function, on the other hand, has no such structure. It is an "unstructured search" with no shortcut other than trying inputs one at a time. All that Grover's algorithm achieves there is to reduce N to N, and, by the 1997 result the NIST report cites, an exponential speedup for search problems is impossible (reference [3] of the report, Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani 1997). So under the same word "quantum," one problem falls to polynomial time and the other shrinks only by a square root. The three properties of Chapter 4 (preimage, second-preimage and collision resistance) can be restored by lengthening the output, but the signatures of Chapter 5 have to change the problem itself. That is the "post-quantum signature" of Section 4.

[Advanced] One more point. Aggarwal et al. show that a variant of hash-based proof of work that requires finding collisions (Momentum) allows even less quantum advantage than Grover's search does. Using the result that the quantum lower bound for finding collisions is |S|2/3 (Aaronson and Shi 2004), they argue that for an optimal classical time T the quantum time is at least T2/3: "unlike for the current proof of work in Bitcoin, with this proposal a quantum computer would not be able to achieve a quadratic advantage as soon as S is more than constant size."9 This book does not evaluate that proposal and records only the fact that "on the hash side, there is room to make designs that last longer."

2. Resource estimates: two kinds of qubit, five assumptions

[Basic] The proposition "quantum computers break signatures" is true. "When will such a quantum computer be built?" is a different question, and this book does not answer it (the notes to the reader in Chapter 3: the book makes no projections). Instead it shows how that question is counted. Two units have to be separated first. Logical qubits are the error-corrected, abstract qubits that an algorithm actually uses; physical qubits are the actual devices in the hardware. Making one logical qubit takes hundreds to thousands of physical qubits, and the multiple changes with the error rate of the devices, the error-correcting code and the target running time. So "1,200 logical" and "500,000 physical" describe the same machine in two units. The logical count moves with improvements in algorithms; the physical count moves with those and, in addition, with hardware assumptions.

[Intermediate] Estimates of the resources needed to solve ECDLP on a 256-bit prime-field elliptic curve with Shor's algorithm have come down as shown below. Only the four papers whose originals this book opened are listed.

Year Paper Target curve Logical qubits Non-Clifford gates (Toffoli) Physical qubits · time Assumptions
2017 Roetteler et al. NIST P-256 2,330 about 1.26×1011 (logical level only) general formula: 9n+2⌈log2n⌉+10 qubits, 448n3log2n+4090n3 gates
2018 Aggarwal et al. Bitcoin signatures (Roetteler as input) 2,334 (incl. 4 ancilla) 1.28×1011 1.7×106 · 6.49 days / 485,550 · 30 min surface code; error 5×10−4 · 66.6 MHz / error 10−5 · 10 GHz
2022 Webber et al. "the 256 bit elliptic curve encryption of keys in the Bitcoin network" (a prior circuit as input) 2,871 5.76×109 (T) 13 million · 1 day / 317 million · 1 hour / 1.9 billion · 10 min surface code; error 10−3 · code cycle 1 µs · reaction 10 µs
2026 Babbush et al. secp256k1 ≤1,200 / ≤1,450 ≤90 million / ≤70 million under 500,000 · 18–23 min (9–12 min from a primed state) surface code (yoke storage); error 10−3 · planar connectivity · reaction 10 µs

[Intermediate] The general formula in the first row is an upper bound that Roetteler et al. obtained by actually simulating the circuit: "elliptic curve discrete logarithms on an elliptic curve defined over an n-bit prime field can be computed on a quantum computer with at most 9n+2⌈log2(n)⌉+10 qubits using a quantum circuit of at most 448n3log2(n)+4090n3 Toffoli gates," and for P-256, "2330 logical qubits" and "about 1.26·1011 Toffoli gates."10 Aggarwal et al. took this circuit as input, applied it to Bitcoin signatures, and produced physical qubits and times under two hardware assumptions: "Using a surface code with a physical gate error rate of pg=5×10−4, … the time to solve the problem at 66.6 MHz clock speed is 6.49 days using 1.7×106 physical qubits. Looking forward to performance improvements, for 10GHz clock speed and error rate of 10−5, the signature is cracked in 30 minutes using 485550 qubits."11 Mark Webber and colleagues took a different prior circuit (2,871 logical qubits, 5.76×109 T gates) as input and showed how far the number of physical qubits moves when, within the same hardware assumptions, only the target time is changed: 13 million for a day, 317 million for an hour, 1.9 billion for 10 minutes.12 Ryan Babbush and colleagues did not publish their circuits; they published only the resource counts, made verifiable with a zero-knowledge proof. The counts are "≤1200 logical qubits and ≤90 million Toffoli gates or ≤1450 logical qubits and ≤70 million Toffoli gates," and on superconducting architectures the circuits run "in minutes using fewer than half a million physical qubits."13

[Intermediate] The code below plugs n=256 into the general formula of the first row and puts the logical resources of the four papers in one table. It does not compute physical qubits, because they are not a number that comes out of one formula but a function of five assumptions.

# NB29-1: ECDLP resources for Shor's algorithm — n=256 plugged into the general formula of Roetteler et al. (2017), and the logical resources of four papers compared (for study)
import math

def roetteler_bound(n):
    """Upper-bound formula in the abstract of Roetteler et al. (2017): logical qubits and Toffoli gates."""
    qubits = 9 * n + 2 * math.ceil(math.log2(n)) + 10
    toffoli = 448 * n**3 * math.log2(n) + 4090 * n**3
    return qubits, toffoli

for n in (192, 224, 256, 384, 521):
    q, t = roetteler_bound(n)
    print(f"n={n:>3}-bit: logical qubit bound {q:>5},  Toffoli bound {t:.3e}")

q256, t256 = roetteler_bound(256)
print()
print("n=256 — Toffoli bound from the formula", f"{t256:.4e}", "| value the paper reports from simulation: about 1.26e11 (the formula is an upper bound, so slightly larger)")
print("The 1.28e11 that Aggarwal et al. (2018) plugged in is the formula's bound as is →", f"{t256/1.28e11:.3f}", "x")

papers = [  # (year, paper, logical qubits, Toffoli or T gate count)
    (2017, "Roetteler et al. (P-256)",           2330, 1.26e11),
    (2018, "Aggarwal et al. (incl. 4 ancilla)",  2334, 1.28e11),
    (2022, "Webber et al. circuit (T gates)",    2871, 5.76e9),
    (2026, "Babbush et al. — low-qubit circuit", 1200, 9.0e7),
    (2026, "Babbush et al. — low-gate circuit",  1450, 7.0e7),
]
print()
print(f"{'Year':<6}{'Paper':<34}{'Logical qubits':>15}{'Gates':>12}{'Gates vs 2017':>20}")
for y, name, lq, gates in papers:
    ratio = "different unit (T)" if "T gates" in name else f"{1.26e11/gates:.0f}x"
    print(f"{y:<6}{name:<34}{lq:>15,}{gates:>12.2e}{ratio:>20}")
print()
print("Physical qubits are not computed here: they are a function of error rate, code cycle, reaction time, connectivity and target time (Section 2, advanced box).")

Year  Paper                              Logical qubits       Gates       Gates vs 2017
2017  Roetteler et al. (P-256)                    2,330    1.26e+11                  1x
2018  Aggarwal et al. (incl. 4 ancilla)           2,334    1.28e+11                  1x

Physical qubits are not computed here: they are a function of error rate, code cycle, reaction time, connectivity and target time (Section 2, advanced box).

[Basic] What to read from the table is the direction, not the figures. In nine years the logical qubits fell to almost half (2,330 → around 1,200), and the gate count fell more than a thousandfold. That is the result of movement in algorithms and error-correction theory, not in hardware, and that is why Babbush et al. say that "simple models, such as counting physical qubits, fail to adequately capture technological progress" and propose a threshold model instead: progress comes not continuously but in "discrete jumps corresponding to development of new internal capabilities and overcoming scaling challenges."14 Here, too, is a reason why this book does not name a date. The "as early as 2027" of the 2017 paper was an extrapolation of the hardware trends of the time, and the 2026 white paper records skepticism about exactly that way of extrapolating. The figures from an expert survey (published March 2026, 26 respondents) are put in Appendix A, not in the text, because opinions are not observations.

[Advanced] Five assumptions: estimates can be compared only under the same assumptions

[Advanced] Here the reasons physical-qubit estimates diverge by hundreds of times are taken one assumption at a time. (i) Physical error rate. Aggarwal et al.'s two scenarios differ 50-fold in error rate, 5×10−4 against 10−5, and also 150-fold in clock, 66.6 MHz against 10 GHz. Changing the error rate and the clock together moves the physical qubits from 1.7 million to 480,000 and the time from 6.49 days to 30 minutes, and most of the difference in time comes from the clock. (ii) Code cycle and reaction time. Webber et al.'s results assume a cycle of 1 µs and a reaction time of 10 µs. Slow platforms (ion traps and the like) have cycles of hundreds of µs, so running the same logical circuit takes far longer. That is why Babbush et al. separate "fast-clock" architectures (superconducting, photonic) from "slow-clock" architectures (neutral atoms, ion traps) and set out two scenarios: if the former arrives first, "on-spend" attacks, which can reach even transactions that are being spent, come with it; if the latter arrives first, "at-rest" attacks, which can reach only public keys exposed for a long time, come first.15 (iii) Connectivity. Babbush et al. assume degree-four connectivity on a planar grid. They note separately that other codes assuming more aggressive connectivity give numbers "closer to one hundred thousand," but that degree-seven connectivity "has yet to be demonstrated in actual superconducting qubit devices," and that the degree-ten Pinnacle architecture (for RSA-2048), with its more demanding device specifications, "would require nearly a month of runtime."16 (iv) Target running time. Within the single paper by Webber et al., a day, an hour and 10 minutes give 13 million, 317 million and 1.9 billion: a factor of 146. Why the target time matters for Bitcoin is shown in the next section, because the public key of a transaction being spent is exposed only in the short window before it enters a block. (v) The logical circuit itself. This is the drop from 2,330 to 1,200. So "Webber's 317 million ↔ Babbush's under 500,000" is a 600-fold difference, but the two differ in input circuit, in the way error-corrected qubits are stored and in target time. Estimates can be compared only under the same assumptions, and none of the figures is the true value.

3. What is exposed: three places where a public key appears

[Basic] The input that Shor's algorithm needs is the public key. If the public key cannot be seen, there is no private key to extract. In Chapter 5 we saw that a Bitcoin "address" is not the public key itself but its hash; that an address that has only received money through hash-type outputs (P2PKH, P2WPKH) has therefore not yet revealed its public key; and that the genesis output (P2PK) of Chapter 12 and the Taproot output (P2TR) carry the public key as it is. That distinction is the center of this chapter. A public key is revealed in three places.

  1. Outputs with the key in the script itself. P2PK (early mining rewards, including the genesis output), bare multisig (P2MS), and the P2TR of 2021. These are exposed from the moment of receipt.
  2. Reused hash-type addresses. Spending even once from a P2PKH or P2WPKH address publishes the public key in that input, and if money is received at the same address again, that balance is in effect locked with an exposed key. For P2SH and P2WSH, the script is published.
  3. The mempool. Whatever the type, the moment an output is spent its public key is broadcast to the network, and the minutes to hours until the transaction enters a block and gathers confirmations are the window of exposure.

[Basic] BIP-360 calls the first two a "long exposure attack" and the third a "short exposure attack," and sets out the vulnerability of each type in a table.17 Babbush et al. call the same distinction "at-rest" and "on-spend," and also count exposure off the chain: spending on another chain, sharing with third-party apps, and sharing extended public keys (xpubs).18

Output type Vulnerable to long exposure? (BIP-360 table) Why
P2PK Yes The public key sits in the locking script as it is
P2PKH No* Only a hash. Vulnerable if reused after spending
P2MS Yes The public keys sit in the locking script as they are
P2SH No* Only a script hash. Vulnerable if reused
P2WPKH No* Same as above (SegWit)
P2WSH No* Same as above (SegWit)
P2TR Yes The tweaked public key sits in the script as it is
P2MR (proposed) No* Only the Merkle root of the script tree (Section 4)

[Basic] Take note that the Taproot of 2021 is in the "Yes" column. As Chapter 5 said, Taproot puts a single public key directly in the output for key-path spending. Babbush et al. say that this, "from the standpoint of quantum security, constitutes a security regression."19 A design of 2021 brought back, for a different reason, the exposure that the P2PK of 2009 already had, and what BIP-360 in Section 4 sets out to do is precisely to remove that key path.

[Intermediate] How much, then, is exposed? This book bundles one secondary tally as of the reference date (2026-10-25). It is a tally by a third party that has made its SQL public (Project Eleven), covering the public Bitcoin dataset in BigQuery up to block 972,132 (produced 2026-10-19); this book did not rerun that SQL. The credibility of the source is 🟡, and a primary reproduction is a task for the next edition.20 The unit is BTC, and the denominator is the scheduled issuance up to that height, 20,100,415.625 BTC (an upper bound that includes the unspendable genesis output and unclaimed subsidies).

Category BTC Share of scheduled issuance
P2PK (key in the script) 1,715,077.0 8.53%
P2TR (key in the script) 217,063.2 1.08%
Bare P2MS (keys in the script) 416.6 0.002%
P2PKH reused (with a spending history) 1,185,672.2 5.90%
P2WPKH reused 2,098,570.4 10.44%
P2SH reused (script published) 1,199,814.7 5.97%
P2WSH reused 705,381.4 3.51%

[Intermediate] Cross-checks agree only in order of magnitude, because their dates and methods differ. A May 2025 report from mempool research divided the UTXO set at block 892,385 (2025-04-14) by script type alone and reports that P2PK is 0.03% of UTXOs by count but 8.70% (1,720,270 BTC) by value, while P2TR is 34.22% by count but 0.75% (147,912 BTC) by value.21 In the one category where the two tallies overlap (P2PK) they agree, at 1.71 million and 1.72 million, and that is the only ground for trusting these figures. Industry estimates gather in the same place; this book uses them only as secondary sources. A May 2025 report from Chaincode Labs, citing a 2023 query, says that P2PK "represents only ~0.025% of current UTXOs but locks a disproportionate ~8.68% of Bitcoin's value (~1,720,747 BTC)"; it gives the range including reuse as "Approximately 20-50% of all Bitcoin in circulation (4-10 million BTC)"; and it carries an earlier value from the same organization as this chapter's primary source (Project Eleven), about 6.26 million BTC. (The original says "as of mid January 2015 [sic]," which from the context appears to be a slip for 2025. It is not an independent cross-check.)22 An analysis by Deloitte (no date in the text; the date of the figures is unknown) gives "over 4 million BTC (about 25% of all Bitcoins)" for P2PK and reused P2PKH alone, and a February 2026 post by CoinShares gives, for P2PK alone, "approximately 1.6 million btc—about 8% of the total supply."23 The Motivation section of BIP-361 says that "As of March 1, 2026, over 34% of all bitcoin have revealed a public key on-chain …," but does not state how this was computed.24 Babbush et al., from their own tally, give "A little over 1.7 million bitcoin (nearly 9% of all bitcoin)" locked by P2PK and "∼6.9M total bitcoin across all protocols."25 The spread has three causes: whether reuse is counted, whether P2TR and P2SH are included, and when the snapshot was taken. For P2PK at about 1.7 million BTC, the four sources that tallied directly (the snapshot, mempool, Chaincode, Babbush et al.) converge in the 1.7 millions and the two industry sources give 1.6 to 2 million, so it is, together with the asymmetry of Section 1, the firmest number in this chapter.

# NB29-2: exposed amounts by type in the reference-date snapshot (a secondary tally) — reads the bundled file and recomputes subtotals and shares (for study)

from decimal import Decimal

FALLBACK = {  # the same values as data/exposed_output_types_2026-10-25.json (for environments without the file)

[Intermediate] Classifying the type takes a few bytes. The head of the locking script (scriptPubKey) determines which type it is, and so whether the key is revealed at the moment of receipt. The code below classifies the genesis output script of Chapter 12 (67 bytes, P2PK) from its real bytes, and shows the classification rules for the other types with fake bytes shaped to match. The fake bytes are not addresses and cannot send money anywhere (not for real use: this is a classifier for study).

# NB29-3: tells the output type, and "whether the public key is exposed at the moment of receipt," from the head of the locking script (for study — fake bytes, not for real use)
GENESIS_SPK = bytes.fromhex(  # scriptPubKey of the genesis coinbase output in Chapter 12 (67 bytes): PUSH65 <public key> OP_CHECKSIG
    "4104678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb649f6bc3f4cef38c4f35504e51ec112de5c384df7ba0b8d578a4c702b6bf11d5fac")

def classify(spk: bytes):
    """Standard locking-script type → (type, key exposed on receipt?, note). Same judgment as the 'long exposure' column of the BIP-360 table."""
    n = len(spk)
    if n in (67, 35) and spk[0] in (0x41, 0x21) and spk[-1] == 0xAC:
        return "P2PK", True, "public key (65 or 33 bytes) sits in the script as is"
    if n == 25 and spk[:3] == b"\x76\xa9\x14" and spk[-2:] == b"\x88\xac":
        return "P2PKH", False, "only the HASH160 of the public key (20 bytes) — key revealed when spent, vulnerable if reused"
    if n == 23 and spk[:2] == b"\xa9\x14" and spk[-1] == 0x87:
        return "P2SH", False, "only the HASH160 of the script — script revealed when spent"
    if n == 22 and spk[:2] == b"\x00\x14":
        return "P2WPKH", False, "SegWit v0, key hash of 20 bytes"
    if n == 34 and spk[:2] == b"\x00\x20":
        return "P2WSH", False, "SegWit v0, script hash of 32 bytes"
    if n == 34 and spk[:2] == b"\x51\x20":
        return "P2TR", True, "SegWit v1 (Taproot), tweaked x-only public key of 32 bytes sits there as is"
    if n == 34 and spk[:2] == b"\x52\x20":
        return "P2MR (proposed, BIP-360 Draft)", False, "proposed SegWit v2 — only the Merkle root of the script tree, 32 bytes, no key path"
    if n >= 3 and 0x51 <= spk[0] <= 0x60 and spk[-1] == 0xAE:
        return "P2MS (bare multisig)", True, "OP_m <keys> OP_n OP_CHECKMULTISIG — the public keys sit there as is"
    return "nonstandard/unclassified", None, "this classifier knows only the standard types"

samples = [
    ("genesis output (real bytes)", GENESIS_SPK),
    ("P2PKH shape (fake)",  b"\x76\xa9\x14" + bytes(20) + b"\x88\xac"),
    ("P2SH shape (fake)",   b"\xa9\x14" + bytes(20) + b"\x87"),
    ("P2WPKH shape (fake)", b"\x00\x14" + bytes(20)),
    ("P2WSH shape (fake)",  b"\x00\x20" + bytes(32)),
    ("P2TR shape (fake)",   b"\x51\x20" + bytes(32)),
    ("P2MR shape (fake)",   b"\x52\x20" + bytes(32)),
    ("P2MS 1-of-2 shape (fake)", b"\x51" + b"\x21" + bytes(33) + b"\x21" + bytes(33) + b"\x52\xae"),
]
print(f"{'Sample':<28}{'Bytes':>6}  {'Type':<32}{'Key exposed on receipt':<24}Note")
for name, spk in samples:
    kind, exposed, why = classify(spk)
    flag = {True: "yes", False: "no*", None: "?"}[exposed]
    print(f"{name:<28}{len(spk):>6}  {kind:<32}{flag:<24}{why}")
print()
print("* no = safe as long as it only receives. Spending reveals the key or script, so reusing the same address makes it vulnerable (the No* note in the BIP-360 table).")
print("Leading byte of the public key in the genesis output:", GENESIS_SPK[1:2].hex(), "(04 = uncompressed, 65 bytes) — written on the chain as is since 2009.")

[Basic] "Exposed" and "stolen" are not the same. Aggarwal et al. separated three situations: address reuse (an exposed key locks a balance: "completely insecure"), processed transactions (a transaction spent with blocks stacked after it; even if the private key is extracted, the double-spending attack of Chapter 9 would also have to be carried out, so it is "reasonably secure against quantum attacks"), and unprocessed transactions (seeing the public key in the mempool, extracting the private key before the transaction enters a block, and getting a different transaction in first: "We view item (3) as the most serious attack").26 For the third to work, the "target time" of Section 2 has to fit within the block interval, and Babbush et al., applying their own estimate (about 9 minutes) to Bitcoin's 10-minute average interval, put the probability of success at "slightly less than 41%" (under "idealized assumptions"), writing that the probability drops sharply on chains with shorter block intervals.27 That figure is the output of a model, not an observation. What this book takes from it is the shape: coins whose public keys are revealed open when the machine arrives, and coins whose keys are not revealed are at risk during the few minutes of spending. So the transition proposals go two ways: "outputs that do not reveal" and "signatures that are safe even when revealed."

4. Transition proposals: output types, signatures, sunset

4.1 BIP-360: Taproot with the key path removed

[Basic] BIP-360 proposes adding a new output type, "Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR)," by soft fork. As of 2026-10 its status is Draft (version 0.12.1), and it has not been activated.28 It does one thing: "P2MR outputs operate with nearly the same functionality as P2TR (Pay-to-Taproot) outputs, but with the key path spend removed." Where a Taproot output carried a tweaked public key, a P2MR output carries only the Merkle root of a script tree (Chapter 6). A public key may be inside a script, but that script stays hidden behind the tree until it is spent, and so exposure at the moment of receipt disappears.29 It uses SegWit version 2, and its addresses begin with bc1z. The proposers state clearly what this BIP does not do: "proposed P2MR outputs are only resistant to 'long exposure attacks' on elliptic curve cryptography"; protection against short exposure in the mempool "may require the introduction of post-quantum signatures in Bitcoin"; and "this proposal does not include the introduction of post-quantum signature schemes."30 The cost is small, too. A P2MR witness for a depth-1 tree is 135 bytes, larger than the 66 bytes of a Taproot key-path spend but 32 bytes smaller than the equivalent Taproot script-path spend.31 And in its conclusion it says that "This BIP does not take a position on any specific quantum computing timeline …."32

4.2 Post-quantum signatures: three standards and the problem of size

[Basic] The exit the asymmetry of Section 1 points to is "a signature that changes the problem." On August 13, 2024, NIST published three standards: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, lattice-based key encapsulation), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, lattice-based signatures) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, hash-based signatures).33 The last two are the signatures. FIPS 204 says that "ML-DSA is believed to be secure, even against adversaries in possession of a large-scale quantum computer," and FIPS 205 that SLH-DSA "is designed to provide resistance against attacks from a large-scale quantum computer." The problem in putting these into Bitcoin and Ethereum is not security but size. As Aggarwal et al. already wrote in 2017, "In the blockchain context the most important parameters of a signature scheme are the signature and public key lengths, as these must be stored in some capacity to fully verify transactions …."34 In a table:

Scheme Public key Signature Source
Schnorr (secp256k1, current Bitcoin) 32 bytes 64 bytes BIP-340 (Chapter 5); "signature (1 + 64 bytes)" in the witness calculation of BIP-360
ML-DSA-44 1,312 bytes 2,420 bytes FIPS 204 Table 2
ML-DSA-65 1,952 bytes 3,309 bytes FIPS 204 Table 2
ML-DSA-87 2,592 bytes 4,627 bytes FIPS 204 Table 2
SLH-DSA-128s (SHA2, SHAKE) 32 bytes 7,856 bytes FIPS 205 Table 2
SLH-DSA-128f 32 bytes 17,088 bytes FIPS 205 Table 2
SLH-DSA-256s 64 bytes 29,792 bytes FIPS 205 Table 2

[Basic] Lattice-based signatures are tens of times larger than the current signature, and hash-based signatures more than a hundred times larger. Chapter 18 showed that block space is a finite resource, and Chapter 21 that a price is put on it. If signatures grow 40-fold, the number of transactions that fit in a block falls by as much, and who bears that cost, and how, is a design question. Aggarwal et al. wrote that hash-based schemes have "the advantage of having provable security, at least assuming the chosen hash function behaves like a random oracle," but that because of Grover their quantum security level is half the classical level, and that at the same level of quantum security lattice-based schemes "have some advantage in signature plus public key length." The choice is still open, and BIP-360, too, says only that "Quantum-resistant signature algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA or SLH-DSA) … should be scrutinized before use."

4.3 BIP-361: the sunset of the old signatures

[Basic] If BIP-360 is a proposal to add a new output type, BIP-361 is a proposal to withdraw the old signatures. As of 2026-10 it is a Draft, its type is Informational, and it carries "Requires: TBD Post Quantum Signature BIP": it presupposes a post-quantum signature BIP that does not yet exist.35 There are two phases: "Phase A: Disallows sending of any funds to quantum-vulnerable addresses, hastening the adoption of PQ address types. Phase B: Restricts ECDSA/Schnorr spends by encumbering them with a quantum-safe rescue protocol, preventing theft of funds in quantum-vulnerable UTXOs. This is triggered by a well-publicized flag-day five years after activation." The table in the specification gives Phase A as "160,000 blocks (~3 years) after BIP-361 activation" and Phase B as "2 years after Phase A activation."36 A "rescue protocol" is a device that has the spender prove knowledge that a quantum attacker cannot have and that only the true owner has, such as the parent secret key of a BIP-32 wallet, and the proposers write that "If one or more rescue protocols can be designed to cover the majority of the Bitcoin supply, then restricting ECDSA/Schnorr verification will be at most mildly confiscatory …."37 They take the view that P2PK has no such asymmetry of knowledge, so that no rescue protocol can be built for it, and state that for those coins they support a separate proposal (Hourglass, Section 5).

[Basic] To put the character of this proposal in one line, it is a timetable that presupposes a signature BIP that does not yet exist. For that timetable to be adopted by "consensus," a majority of nodes and miners has to run the new rules, as Chapters 7 and 23 showed, and what that majority does in Phase B is to change after the fact the conditions for spending particular UTXOs. The question box in Chapter 20 asked whether the rights of holders are infringed if a majority changes the issuance rule. What changes here is not the issuance rule but spendability itself. Section 5 goes on to that question.

4.4 Ethereum: four areas and account abstraction

[Basic] Ethereum's exposure is structured differently from Bitcoin's. In the account model of Chapter 11, any account that has sent even one transaction has revealed its public key, and continuing to use an account is the basic pattern of use. On top of that, the validator signatures (BLS) used by the proof of stake of Chapter 10 and the KZG commitments used for the data availability of Chapter 18 both rely on elliptic curve pairings. The roadmap security page of the official Ethereum site (source commit 290d753c, 2026-07-12) lists four areas: validator consensus signatures (BLS), the commitments for data availability (KZG), account signatures (ECDSA), and the zero-knowledge proof systems of rollups.38 The sentence in bold on the same page is "No quantum computer can break Ethereum's cryptography today." The same page cites the March 2026 estimate of 1,200 logical qubits (Section 2) as "about 20 times fewer than earlier estimates" (the "20-fold" in Babbush et al. is on the side of physical qubits, under 500,000, while logical qubits fell by about 1.9 times, as the table in Section 2 shows). A subpage (quantum-resistance, commit 643a7a45, 2026-10-23) says that "Current quantum hardware is far from this scale, operating with a few thousand noisy physical qubits" (as of 2026-10, Appendix A).39

[Basic] The shape of the response is the reverse of Bitcoin's. Where the Bitcoin proposals are protocol changes that "add one output type and withdraw the old signatures," Ethereum intends to go for per-account choice in account signatures (a plan, as of 2026-10): "Rather than a single protocol-wide migration, Ethereum plans to use account abstraction (specifically EIP-8141, being considered for Hegotá in second half of 2026) to give users signature agility. Individual accounts could switch to a post-quantum signature scheme without waiting for the entire protocol to change."40 The higher-level roadmap page on the same site (2026-07-12 source) gives Hegotá a target of 2027, so the years on the two official pages differ. This book does not pick one but records both as they are (Appendix A-29). For validator signatures, the design on the official page is to switch to hash-based signatures (leanXMSS) and to solve, by aggregating them with zero-knowledge proofs, the problem that those signatures grow to "roughly 3,000 bytes" against the 96 bytes of BLS (a plan, as of 2026-10).41 The Foundation's post-quantum page (updated 2026-06-27) says that "We do not believe a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is imminent," while also saying that "Based on our team's current assessment, L1 protocol upgrades could be completed by 2029 …" (a planning target as of 2026-10, Appendix A).42 And on dormant assets, the problem of the next section, it says that "Unlike Bitcoin, where roughly 5% of the supply is associated with early address formats widely believed to be abandoned …, Ethereum's equivalent long-dormant exposure is closer to 0.1% (an EF estimate)"; that two scenarios exist, "do nothing, or freeze vulnerable coins"; and that the matter is "ultimately a community governance question."43

5. Vulnerable coins: three paths and one question

[Basic] However well the transition goes, coins that cannot move remain: coins whose keys were lost, coins whose owners have died, and, among the roughly 1.7 million BTC in P2PK of Section 3, those that have not moved once since 2009. Babbush et al. call this the problem of "dormant digital assets" and record two facts: that "a majority of the 1.7 millions [sic] bitcoin have not been transacted since 2009," and that "accounts believed to have been owned by Satoshi Nakamoto hold about 1 million bitcoin … behind these P2PK scripts." The latter is an attribution estimate, and this book takes no part in that attribution.44 These coins cannot be moved by a software update, because no one has the keys. So when the machine arrives, one of two things happens: someone takes them, or the rules are changed so that no one can take them.

[Basic] The discussion on the Bitcoin side has been sorted into three paths. Here is Babbush et al.'s summary as it stands: "Do Nothing: the protocol is kept unchanged allowing quantum attackers to acquire the dormant assets. Burn: the protocol is modified to render dormant assets unspendable after a certain date, effectively confiscating all assets locked by P2PK scripts. Hourglass [303]: the protocol is modified to limit the rate at which dormant assets may be spent."45 The authors of BIP-361 write the same three paths as "Allow anyone to steal vulnerable coins," "Allow throttled theft of coins" and "Allow no one to steal vulnerable coins," and classify the first two as proposals that create a "redistribution dilemma."46 Babbush et al. record that in an informal poll at a 2025 meeting the three paths received "roughly equal support," and write: "Consensus remains elusive."47 Burn and Hourglass are technically possible as soft forks, because forbidding or limiting the spending of particular UTXOs narrows the rules (Chapters 7 and 23). Doing nothing involves no change of rules. What is hard is not the technology.

[Basic] It is worth writing down what each of the three paths presupposes. "Do nothing" keeps Bitcoin's model of ownership, under which whoever knows the key is the owner, even after the machine arrives (Babbush et al. write that "a CRQC can quickly derive a private key from any public key, thus breaking the foundation of Bitcoin's model of ownership"48); "burn" suspends by majority vote the model under which whoever knows the key is the owner; and "Hourglass" regulates the speed in between. If the choice is to change the rules, the deciding body is a majority of nodes and miners, and whose agent that majority is, the box below asks. The Babbush et al. white paper goes further and lists options on the government side: "digital salvage" of abandoned property, the poor fit of the US Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act (RUUPA 2016) and its "holder" requirement, the doctrine of laches (sleeping on one's rights), national security responses, and dialogue with the community. It also argues that "Regulated Destruction of Dormant Assets is Not Viable Policy" (to erase blocks, the whole chain would have to be mined again, and forcing miners to censor transactions would send mining abroad or lead to a hard fork).49 This book only presents that argument. There are two reasons for not evaluating it: the statutes and judgments that deal with this problem are not among this book's source materials (28.1(g)), and the white paper itself is a document from institutions with an interest in the matter.

A lawyer's question

Suppose that one day a majority of nodes and miners introduces by soft fork the rule "old outputs whose public keys have been revealed can no longer be spent" (Phase B of 4.3, or "Burn"). At that moment the coins of the minority of holders who never lost their keys are locked as well. Is this an expropriation? If so, who is the expropriating party, and who pays compensation? Is it a measure for maintaining order, since it stops anyone from taking property that someone would take anyway once the machine arrives? Or is it the disposal of ownerless property, property whose key no one knows any longer? If so, what becomes of the minority who still know their keys? Does the character change if "Hourglass" only limits the speed? Conversely, if things are "left as they are" and whoever has a quantum computer takes first, is that acquisition first occupation, theft, or something that no provision of any jurisdiction has yet named? And is the majority that decides all this, the "participants who follow the rules" of Chapter 7, the agent of the coin holders, of the network, or of itself? What the box in Chapter 20 asked about the issuance rule, this chapter asks again about spendability. This book does not answer, and hands the question to Part 5. The answer to this question differs depending on which of the fourteen positions in 27.2 (factual-state theory, partnership-right theory, control-based, and others) one adopts, and 28.1(g) records that primary materials touching this question are not among this book's source materials. → Chapter 27 · Chapter 28

6. "As of 2026-10": what in this chapter will date

[Basic] Following the update rule in the notes to the reader in Chapter 3, this section collects the sentences in this chapter that describe the current state of affairs. All of them are entered in Appendix A, and when the edition changes, only that appendix is corrected.

  • BIP-360 is a Draft (version 0.12.1), BIP-361 is a Draft, and BIP-54 is Complete but has no deployment section and so is not described as activated: as of 2026-10 (Appendix A-27).
  • The post-quantum signature transition proposals this chapter examined (BIP-360 and 361, EIP-8141 and leanXMSS) have not been activated on the mainnet of either Bitcoin or Ethereum (they are at the proposal or planning stage): as of 2026-10 (Appendices A-27 and A-29). This does not mean that properties already in place, such as hash-based protection, are absent.
  • Hardware: the official Ethereum page says "a few thousand noisy physical qubits," and the estimate in the 2026 white paper is "fewer than half a million": as of 2026-10 (Appendix A-28). The figures from the survey of 26 experts (published March 2026) are likewise kept only in Appendix A.
  • Ethereum roadmap: EIP-8141 is "being considered" for the Hegotá upgrade, the target for the core post-quantum milestones is "approximately 2029," and "These are planning targets and may shift": as of 2026-10 (Appendix A-29).
  • Exposed amounts: the table in Section 3 is a secondary tally of block 972,132 of 2026-10-19, and there is no primary reproduction: as of 2026-10 (Appendix A-30).
  • The schedule for retiring ECDSA: the Ethereum page says, without naming the document, that NIST expects deprecation in 2030 and a ban in 2035, and BIP-360 gives 2030 as the CNSA 2.0 schedule and 2035 as that of NIST IR 8547. This book did not open the text of NIST IR 8547: a task (Appendix A-31).

7. Summary

[Basic] A quantum computer affects the two tools of Part 1 differently. Shor's algorithm brings the discrete logarithm problem underlying signatures down to polynomial time, and Grover's algorithm speeds up the preimage search of hashes only by a square root. So the threat lies not in "Bitcoin" but in signatures whose public keys are revealed, and proof of work stands up to the speed and parallelism of ASICs. The size of that machine has come down from 2,330 to around 1,200 logical qubits through advances in algorithms and error-correction theory, and estimates of physical qubits range from hundreds of thousands to the billions depending on five assumptions (error rate, code cycle, reaction time, connectivity, target time), so they can be compared only under the same assumptions. Revealed public keys are in three places (script type, reuse, the mempool), and the secondary tally on the reference date counts about one third of issuance as exposed (P2PK at about 1.7 million BTC is the firmest number, the one on which the sources that tallied directly converge). The transition proposals divide into outputs that do not reveal (BIP-360), signatures that are safe even when revealed (FIPS 204 and 205, with signatures tens to hundreds of times larger), the sunset of the old signatures (BIP-361) and per-account choice (Ethereum), and as of 2026-10 none of them has been activated. And coins that cannot move remain. Leave them, burn them, or limit their speed: all three paths are technically possible, and technology decides none of them. That fact is what lawyers take from this chapter. On the day the model under which whoever knows the key is the owner breaks, which law is to name the character of the decision that suspends that model and the status of the majority that decides, and how, is an empty place. The next chapter, Chapter 30, looks through the text of the provisions at that "naming" itself: five jurisdictions calling the same bit string by five names.

Part 6 · Open problems

Chapter 30. The naming problem: 가상자산, crypto-asset, digital asset, 暗号資産, cryptoasset

Key takeaway

The same string of bits is called "가상자산" (gasang jasan, "virtual asset") in Korea, "crypto-asset" in the EU, "security," "commodity," "property" or "digital asset" in the United States depending on the context, 「暗号資産」 (angō shisan, "crypto-asset") in Japan, and "cryptoasset" in the United Kingdom. This chapter sets the definitional provisions of five jurisdictions side by side in the original wording, and gives each provision its statute number, its date of entry into force and the reference date. It then looks at what the name decides under three heads: jurisdiction (which agency oversees it), taxation (as what it is taxed) and criminal law (of which offense it can be the object). Technology does not choose the name. What Part 1 showed was an 80-byte header, signatures and state transitions, and whether to call that a "currency," an "asset" or a "security" is in every case a choice made by law. That choice has changed even within a single jurisdiction. Japan changed 「仮想通貨」 (kasō tsūka, "virtual currency") to 「暗号資産」, the Supreme Court of Korea wrote "가상화폐" (gasang hwapye, "virtual currency") in 2018 and "가상자산" in 2021, and the US Internal Revenue Service deleted in 2023 the statement that virtual currency "does not have legal tender status in any jurisdiction." This chapter is the prose version of the concordance in Appendix C, and it was written so that its figures and provisions agree with the table in 27.3.

Learning objectives

  1. Read the definitional provisions of five jurisdictions in the original, and compare what each puts in and what each leaves out (the exclusion list).
  2. Sort out which agency's jurisdiction, which tax framework and which offense the five category words "currency/money," "asset," "security," "commodity" and "property" call in, in each jurisdiction.
  3. Confirm, from the original provisions and judgments, three cases in which the name changed within one jurisdiction (Japan 2020, the Supreme Court of Korea 2018→2021, the US IRS 2023).
  4. Find, in the wording of the provisions, the places where the definitions fail to keep up with technology: non-fungible tokens, automated markets, assets without an issuer.

What a reader of the [Basic] paragraphs alone takes away. Whether the same thing is called a "currency" or an "asset" changes its legal fate. Technology does not choose the name.

1. Why the name matters

[Basic] In Chapter 12 we took the 80 bytes of the genesis block apart by hand. They held a version, the previous hash, the Merkle root, a time, the bits and a nonce. The word "currency" was not there, and neither was the word "asset." The UTXO of Chapter 11 is an "unspent transaction output," and the account balance of Chapter 13 is a number in the state tree. Everything this book showed in Parts 1 to 3 is of that kind (bit strings, signatures, state transitions, issuance rules, equilibria), and it was law that put names on them. But each body of law put a different name on them, and the name decides which agency's jurisdiction, which tax law and which offense apply. The four cases of Chapter 26 showed this. The same token was found to be a "security" in the United States, and securities law came in (The DAO, Terra); it was found to be a "commodity," and the Commodity Exchange Act came in. In Korean criminal law it is a "재산상 이익" (jaesansang iik, "pecuniary advantage") and so can be the object of fraud, but whether it is a "재물" (jaemul, "property in the sense of a thing"), the object of embezzlement, is a question the Supreme Court of Korea did not decide. This chapter sets out the original text of those names side by side. What the concordance in Appendix C compressed into rows and columns is read here as sentences.

[Basic] There are three rules for reading the provisions. First, statutory text is reproduced as enacted. English-language provisions stand as they are. Korean and Japanese provisions are followed by a working gloss, marked as such, for reading only: a gloss is not an official translation, the original controls, and no statement in this book rests on a gloss (the book's principle: do not settle what a provision means from a translation). Second, each provision is given its statute number and date of entry into force, and the text states whether it is in force as of the reference date (2026-10-25). Third, the exclusion list of a definitional provision is read with the same weight as the main text. What a jurisdiction leaves out tells you where it places this thing.

2. The definitional provisions of five jurisdictions, in the original

2.1 Korea: "가상자산"

[Basic] Article 2, subparagraph 1 of the Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률; below, the Virtual Asset User Protection Act). This is the wording enacted by Act No. 19563 (promulgated July 18, 2023, in force July 19, 2024), and it is unchanged in the current Act No. 21857 (in force October 2, 2026). In force as of 2026-10-25.1

  1. "가상자산"이란 경제적 가치를 지닌 것으로서 전자적으로 거래 또는 이전될 수 있는 전자적 증표(그에 관한 일체의 권리를 포함한다)를 말한다. 다만, 다음 각 목의 어느 하나에 해당하는 것은 제외한다. 가. 화폐ㆍ재화ㆍ용역 등으로 교환될 수 없는 전자적 증표 또는 그 증표에 관한 정보로서 발행인이 사용처와 그 용도를 제한한 것 나. 「게임산업진흥에 관한 법률」 제32조제1항제7호에 따른 게임물의 이용을 통하여 획득한 유ㆍ무형의 결과물 다. 「전자금융거래법」 제2조제14호에 따른 선불전자지급수단 및 같은 조 제15호에 따른 전자화폐 라. 「주식ㆍ사채 등의 전자등록에 관한 법률」 제2조제4호에 따른 전자등록주식등 마. 「전자어음의 발행 및 유통에 관한 법률」 제2조제2호에 따른 전자어음 바. 「상법」 제862조에 따른 전자선하증권 사. 「한국은행법」에 따른 한국은행(이하 "한국은행"이라 한다)이 발행하는 전자적 형태의 화폐 및 그와 관련된 서비스 아. 거래의 형태와 특성을 고려하여 대통령령으로 정하는 것

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): 1. "Virtual asset" means, as something having economic value, an electronic token that can be traded or transferred electronically (including all rights relating to it); provided, however, that anything falling under any of the following items is excluded. (a) [가] an electronic token that cannot be exchanged for money, goods, services, etc., or information on such a token, being one whose places of use and purposes have been restricted by the issuer (b) [나] tangible or intangible results obtained through the use of game products under Article 32(1), subparagraph 7 of the Game Industry Promotion Act (c) [다] prepaid electronic means of payment under Article 2, subparagraph 14 of the Electronic Financial Transactions Act, and electronic currency under subparagraph 15 of the same Article (d) [라] electronically registered stocks, etc. under Article 2, subparagraph 4 of the Act on Electronic Registration of Stocks, Bonds, etc. (e) [마] electronic bills under Article 2, subparagraph 2 of the Issuance and Distribution of Electronic Bills Act (f) [바] electronic bills of lading under Article 862 of the Commercial Act (g) [사] money in electronic form issued by the Bank of Korea under the Bank of Korea Act (hereinafter "the Bank of Korea"), and services related to it (h) [아] anything prescribed by Presidential Decree in consideration of the form and characteristics of transactions

[Basic] Article 2 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률 시행령), to which item (h) delegates, has an exclusion list of five subparagraphs, and its subparagraph 4 reaches non-fungible tokens (Section 3 and footnote 15).

[Basic] The same wording first appeared in Article 2, subparagraph 3 of the Act on Reporting and Using Specified Financial Transaction Information (특정 금융거래정보의 보고 및 이용 등에 관한 법률; below, the Specified Financial Transaction Information Act). Act No. 17113 (promulgated March 24, 2020, in force March 25, 2021) put the text of the definition directly in that Act, and on July 19, 2024 the Addenda of the Virtual Asset User Protection Act turned it into the present cross-referencing wording.2

(As inserted by Act No. 17113; in force March 25, 2021 to July 18, 2024) 3. "가상자산"이란 경제적 가치를 지닌 것으로서 전자적으로 거래 또는 이전될 수 있는 전자적 증표(그에 관한 일체의 권리를 포함한다)를 말한다. 다만, 다음 각 목의 어느 하나에 해당하는 것은 제외한다. 가. ~ 바. (same as above) 사. 거래의 형태와 특성을 고려하여 대통령령으로 정하는 것
