"Virtual asset" means, as something having economic value, an electronic token that can be traded or transferred electronically (including all rights relating to it); provided, however, that anything falling under any of the following items is excluded. (a)–(f) [가 ~ 바] (same as above) (g) [사] anything prescribed by Presidential Decree in consideration of the form and characteristics of transactions

(Current) 3. "가상자산"이란 「가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률」 제2조제1호에 따른 가상자산을 말한다.

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): (Current) 3. "Virtual asset" means a virtual asset under Article 2, subparagraph 1 of the Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users.

[Basic] The tax provision is Article 21(1), subparagraph 27 of the Income Tax Act (소득세법). It was inserted by Act No. 17757 (promulgated December 29, 2020), its date of entry into force was postponed three times, and it enters into force on January 1, 2027; as of 2026-10-25 it is not yet in force.3

  1. 「가상자산 이용자 보호 등에 관한 법률」 제2조제1호에 따른 가상자산(이하 "가상자산"이라 한다)을 양도하거나 대여함으로써 발생하는 소득(이하 "가상자산소득"이라 한다)

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): 27. Income arising from transferring or lending virtual assets under Article 2, subparagraph 1 of the Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users (hereinafter "virtual assets") (hereinafter "virtual asset income")

2.2 EU: "crypto-asset"

[Basic] Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 (MiCA), Art. 3(1), points (5)–(9). Official Journal L 150 (June 9, 2023), p. 63. Under Article 149 it applies from 2024-12-30 (Titles III and IV from 2024-06-30). Applies as of 2026-10-25.4

(5) 'crypto-asset' means a digital representation of a value or of a right that is able to be transferred and stored electronically using distributed ledger technology or similar technology; (6) 'asset-referenced token' means a type of crypto-asset that is not an electronic money token and that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing another value or right or a combination thereof, including one or more official currencies; (7) 'electronic money token' or 'e-money token' means a type of crypto-asset that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing the value of one official currency; (8) 'official currency' means an official currency of a country that is issued by a central bank or other monetary authority; (9) 'utility token' means a type of crypto-asset that is only intended to provide access to a good or a service supplied by its issuer;

[Basic] The exclusion list is in Article 2.

  1. This Regulation does not apply to crypto-assets that are unique and not fungible with other crypto-assets.
  2. This Regulation does not apply to crypto-assets that qualify as one or more of the following: (a) financial instruments; (b) deposits, including structured deposits; (c) funds, except if they qualify as e-money tokens; (d) securitisation positions …; (e) non-life or life insurance products …; (f) pension products …; (g) officially recognised occupational pension schemes …; (h) individual pension products …; (i) a pan-European Personal Pension Product …; (j) social security schemes ….

2.3 United States: no single definition

[Basic] The United States has no single definitional provision covering this thing as a whole. Courts and agencies decide, according to the shape of the transaction, which category word of which statute the same thing falls under. Five category words have been confirmed in the original texts.

(a) "investment contract": securities. The Securities Act of 1933 includes "investment contract" in "security," and in 1946 the Supreme Court of the United States fixed its meaning as follows. Case law, good law as of 2026-10-25.5

an investment contract for purposes of the Securities Act means a contract, transaction or scheme whereby a person invests his money in a common enterprise and is led to expect profits solely from the efforts of the promoter or a third party, it being immaterial whether the shares in the enterprise are evidenced by formal certificates or by nominal interests in the physical assets employed in the enterprise.

(b) "commodity": commodities. In 2018 the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York quoted the definition in the Commodity Exchange Act and applied it as follows. District court decision, as of 2026-10-25; subsequent history in higher courts not verified.6

They fall well-within the common definition of "commodity" as well as the CEA's definition of "commodities" as "all other goods and articles . . . in which contracts for future delivery are presently or in the future dealt in." Title 7 U.S.C. § 1(a)(9).

(c) "property": property for tax purposes. IRS Notice 2014-21 (2014-16 I.R.B. 938). Administrative interpretation; only a background sentence modified by Notice 2023-34; in effect as of 2026-10-25.7

Virtual currency is a digital representation of value that functions as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and/or a store of value. In some environments, it operates like "real" currency -- i.e., the coin and paper money of the United States or of any other country that is designated as legal tender, circulates, and is customarily used and accepted as a medium of exchange in the country of issuance -- but it does not have legal tender status in any jurisdiction. (2014-21, Background, original text; 2023-34 revised the third sentence to read as below)

In certain contexts, virtual currency may serve one or more of the functions of "real" currency -- i.e., the coin and paper money of the United States or of any other country that is designated as legal tender, circulates, and is customarily used and accepted as a medium of exchange in the country of issuance -- but the use of virtual currency to perform "real" currency functions is limited. (2023-34 §3)

Q-1: How is virtual currency treated for federal tax purposes? A-1: For federal tax purposes, virtual currency is treated as property. General tax principles applicable to property transactions apply to transactions using virtual currency. (2014-21 §4)

(d) "digital asset" and "payment stablecoin": federal statute. GENIUS Act, Pub. L. 119-27, 139 Stat. 419 (July 18, 2025), §2(6) and (22). Enacted. Under §20 the effective date is 2027-01-18 at the latest and may be earlier depending on the publication of final regulations; whether those regulations had been published as of 2026-10-25 is not verified.8

(6) DIGITAL ASSET.—The term "digital asset" means any digital representation of value that is recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger. (22) PAYMENT STABLECOIN.—The term "payment stablecoin"— (A) means a digital asset— (i) that is, or is designed to be, used as a means of payment or settlement; and (ii) the issuer of which— (I) is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value, not including a digital asset denominated in a fixed amount of monetary value; and (II) represents that such issuer will maintain, or create the reasonable expectation that it will maintain, a stable value relative to the value of a fixed amount of monetary value; and (B) does not include a digital asset that— (i) is a national currency; (ii) is a deposit (as defined in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813)), including a deposit recorded using distributed ledger technology; or (iii) is a security, as defined in section 2 of the Securities Act of 1933 (15 U.S.C. 77b), section 3 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78c), or section 2 of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a–2), except that, for the avoidance of doubt, no bond, note, evidence of indebtedness, or investment contract that was issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer shall qualify as a security solely by virtue of its satisfying the conditions described in subparagraph (A), consistent with section 17 of this Act.

(e) "controllable electronic record": a private-law model act. Uniform Commercial Code Amendments (2022), §12-102(a)(1). Model law; adoption by individual states not verified.9

"Controllable electronic record" means a record stored in an electronic medium that can be subjected to control under Section 12-105. The term does not include a controllable account, a controllable payment intangible, a deposit account, an electronic copy of a record evidencing chattel paper, an electronic document of title, electronic money, investment property, or a transferable record.

2.4 Japan: 「暗号資産」

[Basic] Payment Services Act (資金決済に関する法律, 平成21年法律第59号, Act No. 59 of 2009; 資金決済法 for short), 第2条第14項 (Article 2(14)). The defined term, formerly 「仮想通貨」, was changed to 「暗号資産」 by 令和元年法律第28号 (Act No. 28 of 2019; promulgated 2019-06-07, in force 2020-05-01), and from the version in force on 2023-06-01 it moved from 第5項 to 第14項. In force as of 2026-10-25.10

この法律において「暗号資産」とは、次に掲げるものをいう。ただし、金融商品取引法第二十九条の二第一項第八号に規定する権利を表示するものを除く。 一　物品等を購入し、若しくは借り受け、又は役務の提供を受ける場合に、これらの代価の弁済のために不特定の者に対して使用することができ、かつ、不特定の者を相手方として購入及び売却を行うことができる財産的価値（電子機器その他の物に電子的方法により記録されているものに限り、本邦通貨及び外国通貨、通貨建資産並びに電子決済手段（通貨建資産に該当するものを除く。）を除く。次号において同じ。）であって、電子情報処理組織を用いて移転することができるもの 二　不特定の者を相手方として前号に掲げるものと相互に交換を行うことができる財産的価値であって、電子情報処理組織を用いて移転することができるもの

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): In this Act, "crypto-asset (angō shisan)" means the following; provided, however, that anything representing the rights provided for in Article 29-2, paragraph (1), item (viii) of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act is excluded. (i) [一] proprietary value (財産的価値) that can be used with unspecified persons (不特定の者) to pay the price when purchasing or borrowing goods, etc. or receiving the provision of services, and that can be bought and sold with unspecified persons as counterparties (limited to that which is recorded by electronic means on an electronic device or other object, and excluding Japanese currency and foreign currency, currency-denominated assets (通貨建資産) and electronic payment instruments (電子決済手段) (excluding those that fall under currency-denominated assets); the same applies in the following item), which can be transferred using an electronic data processing system (電子情報処理組織) (ii) [二] proprietary value that can be exchanged reciprocally for what is listed in the preceding item with unspecified persons as counterparties, which can be transferred using an electronic data processing system

[Basic] The first sentences before and after the change of name:

(Version of 2020-04-30, 第2条第5項) この法律において「仮想通貨」とは、次に掲げるものをいう。 (Version of 2020-05-01, 第2条第5項) この法律において「暗号資産」とは、次に掲げるものをいう。ただし、金融商品取引法（昭和二十三年法律第二十五号）第二条第三項に規定する電子記録移転権利を表示するものを除く。

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): (Version of 2020-04-30, 第2条第5項) In this Act, "virtual currency (kasō tsūka)" means the following. (Version of 2020-05-01, 第2条第5項) In this Act, "crypto-asset (angō shisan)" means the following; provided, however, that anything representing electronically recorded transferable rights (電子記録移転権利) provided for in Article 2, paragraph (3) of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (Act No. 25 of 1948) is excluded.

[Basic] The 「電子記録移転権利」 (denshi kiroku iten kenri, "electronically recorded transferable rights") that the proviso excludes are defined inside the parentheses of 第2条第3項 (Article 2(3)) of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (金融商品取引法; 金商法 for short).

…電子情報処理組織を用いて移転することができる財産的価値（電子機器その他の物に電子的方法により記録されるものに限る。）に表示される場合（流通性その他の事情を勘案して内閣府令で定める場合を除く。）に限る。以下「電子記録移転権利」という。）…

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): … limited to cases where represented on proprietary value that can be transferred using an electronic data processing system (limited to that which is recorded by electronic means on an electronic device or other object) (excluding cases specified by Cabinet Office Order (内閣府令) in consideration of transferability (流通性) and other circumstances); hereinafter referred to as "electronically recorded transferable rights".) …

[Basic] And 令和8年法律第64号 (Act No. 64 of 2026; promulgated 2026-07-23) is an amendment that moves this definition to 金商法 第2条第49項. It has been promulgated and is partly in force, but the part that transfers the definition is not yet in force as of 2026-10-25. The first sentence of the version not yet in force:

(金融商品取引法 第2条第49項, version not yet in force) この法律において「暗号資産」とは、次に掲げるものをいう。ただし、第二十九条の二第一項第八号に規定する権利を表示するものを除く。

Working gloss (not an official translation; the original controls): (金融商品取引法 第2条第49項, version not yet in force) In this Act, "crypto-asset (angō shisan)" means the following; provided, however, that anything representing the rights provided for in Article 29-2, paragraph (1), item (viii) is excluded.

2.5 United Kingdom: "cryptoasset"

[Basic] Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, s. 417(1). Inserted by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 (c. 29), s. 69(4)(a), in force 2023-08-29 (SI 2023/779, reg. 4(uu)). In force as of 2026-10-25.11

"cryptoasset" means any cryptographically secured digital representation of value or contractual rights that— (a) can be transferred, stored or traded electronically, and (b) that uses technology supporting the recording or storage of data (which may include distributed ledger technology).

[Basic] What falls within regulated activities is fixed by two articles that 2026 regulations inserted into the Regulated Activities Order: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/102, made 2026-02-04. Full commencement day 2027-10-25; as of 2026-10-25 only the parts for the FCA's rule-making are in force.12

88F.—(1) A qualifying cryptoasset. (2) A "qualifying cryptoasset" means a cryptoasset which is— (a) fungible, (b) transferable, (c) not solely a record of value or contractual rights, including rights in another cryptoasset, and (d) not excluded by paragraph (4). (3) For the purposes of paragraph (2)(b), the circumstances in which a cryptoasset is to be treated as "transferable" include where it confers transferable rights. (4) A cryptoasset does not fall within paragraph (1) if it is— (a) a specified investment cryptoasset, other than one specified by— (i) article 74A (electronic money); and (ii) article 88F (qualifying cryptoassets); (b) electronic money; (c) currency of the United Kingdom or any other country or territory, including a central bank digital currency; (d) a cryptoasset that— (i) cannot be transferred or sold in exchange for money or other cryptoassets, except by way of redemption with the issuer, and (ii) can only be used by the holder— (aa) to acquire goods or services from the issuer, or (bb) to acquire goods or services within a limited network of service providers which have direct commercial agreements with the issuer. 88G.—(1) A qualifying stablecoin. (2) A "qualifying stablecoin" means a qualifying cryptoasset where— (a) that cryptoasset seeks or purports to maintain a stable value in relation to a particular fiat currency ("the referenced fiat currency"), and (b) fiat currency (which may be referenced fiat currency referred to in sub-paragraph (a)) or other assets are held for the purpose of maintaining a stable value, in accordance with sub-paragraph (a). (3) Where a cryptoasset seeks or purports to maintain a stable value in relation to an asset other than a fiat currency, the cryptoasset is not to be regarded as falling within paragraph (2)(a) even if the asset is expressed in terms of a fiat currency. [(4) and (5) omitted]

[Basic] The provision on the property-law side is not a definition but a confirmation. Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025 (c. 29), s. 1. Royal Assent on 2025-12-02, in force the same day (England and Wales, Northern Ireland).13

A thing (including a thing that is digital or electronic in nature) is not prevented from being the object of personal property rights merely because it is neither— (a) a thing in possession, nor (b) a thing in action.

2.6 International: "virtual asset"

[Basic] As a point of reference outside the five jurisdictions, this chapter gives the definition of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), from the glossary of its updated guidance of October 28, 2021. A recommendation, with no legally binding force.14

A virtual asset is a digital representation of value that can be digitally traded, or transferred, and can be used for payment or investment purposes. Virtual assets do not include digital representations of fiat currencies, securities and other financial assets that are already covered elsewhere in the FATF Recommendations.

3. Reading the provisions on top of one another: what goes in and what is left out

[Basic] Laid on top of one another, the six definitions show one common skeleton: "a digital representation of a value (or a right)" + "electronic transferability." Korea has "경제적 가치를 지닌 것으로서 전자적으로 거래 또는 이전될 수 있는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "as something having economic value, an electronic token that can be traded or transferred electronically"); the EU, "a digital representation of a value or of a right that is able to be transferred and stored electronically"; the US GENIUS Act, "any digital representation of value that is recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger"; Japan, 「財産的価値…であって、電子情報処理組織を用いて移転することができるもの」 (gloss: "proprietary value (財産的価値) … which can be transferred using an electronic data processing system (電子情報処理組織)"); the United Kingdom, "digital representation of value or contractual rights that … can be transferred, stored or traded electronically"; and the FATF, "digital representation of value that can be digitally traded, or transferred." Of the technology shown in Part 1, the provisions picked up transferability alone. Hashes, signatures, consensus rules and finality appear in none of the definitions. Only the EU, the United Kingdom and the US GENIUS Act put in technical words, "distributed ledger technology" and "cryptographically secured"; Korea and Japan are technology-neutral.

[Basic] Where they diverge is the exclusion list.

Left out Korea EU United States (GENIUS) Japan United Kingdom (88F)
Legal tender, central bank digital currency item (g) (money in electronic form issued by the Bank of Korea) (8) "official currency" is a separate concept (no exclusion clause in the definition) (B)(i) national currency, in the payment stablecoin definition only; no exclusion in (6) digital asset 本邦通貨及び外国通貨, 通貨建資産 (4)(c) currency … including a central bank digital currency
Electronic money, prepaid instruments item (c) (4)(c) funds (but EMTs are included) — (deposits are left out separately by (B)(ii)) 電子決済手段 (defined separately in 第5項) (4)(b) electronic money
Securities, financial instruments item (d) (electronically registered stocks, etc.), items (e) and (f) (4)(a) financial instruments (B)(iii) security proviso: rights under 金商法 第29条の2第1項第8号 (電子記録移転権利) (4)(a) specified investment cryptoasset
Use-restricted tokens item (a) (the issuer restricted the places and purposes of use) — (utility tokens are included, (9)) — — (4)(d) redeemable only with the issuer, limited network
Game outputs item (b) — — — —
Non-fungible (NFT) item (h) → Enforcement Decree §2(4) (what the Financial Services Commission (금융위원회) designates by public notice, e.g. tokens that can be used as means of payment, is brought back in by a proviso) Art. 2(3) unique and not fungible — — (2)(a) fungible requirement
Delegation item (h) (Presidential Decree) — — — —

[Basic] Three things can be read from this table. First, "currency" is outside everywhere. Korea, Japan and the United Kingdom expressly leave legal tender and its digital forms out of the definition, the United States leaves "national currency" out of the definition of "payment stablecoin," and the EU keeps "official currency" as a separate concept. Japan changed the name itself from 「仮想通貨」 to 「暗号資産」. This is a legislative choice that pairs with the proposition Chapter 19 showed with a model, that "what sets legal tender apart is the floor of tax demand." Law has kept the name "currency" only for what it issues itself. Second, all of them draw a boundary with securities, but in different ways. Korea, the EU, the United Kingdom and the GENIUS Act say "if it is a security, it is outside this law," while Japan leaves it out by bringing a concept of financial-instruments law, 「電子記録移転権利」, into a proviso. US securities law itself goes the other way: if it is an "investment contract," it is inside this law, so the same token becomes a security or not depending on the shape of the transaction (SEC v. Ripple Labs, Inc., No. 1:20-cv-10832 (AT) (S.D.N.Y. July 13, 2023), ECF No. 874, pp. 15, 23, 34; footnote 19 of Chapter 27). Third, three jurisdictions left out non-fungible tokens, but at different levels. The EU left them out in the body of the Regulation (Art. 2(3)), and the United Kingdom in the definition for regulated activities (art. 88F(2)(a), "fungible"). In Korea, Article 2, subparagraph 4 of the Enforcement Decree, under the delegation in item (h) of Article 2, subparagraph 1 of the Act, leaves out "단일하게 존재하여 다른 전자적 증표로 대체할 수 없는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "an electronic token that exists singly and cannot be replaced by another electronic token"), but adds a proviso that brings back in "특정 재화나 서비스의 지급수단으로 사용될 수 있는 전자적 증표 등 금융위원회가 정하여 고시하는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "electronic tokens determined and publicly notified by the Financial Services Commission, such as an electronic token that can be used as a means of payment for specific goods or services").15 Whether the (contract address, number) pair of ERC-721 shown in Chapter 14 comes within the Financial Services Commission's notice as something "지급수단으로 사용될 수 있는" (gloss: "that can be used as a means of payment") depends on what the token points to and on the notice. It is one example of the place that the design for this chapter marked as "when the definitional provision cannot keep up with the technology."

4. What the name decides: jurisdiction, taxation, criminal law

Jurisdiction

[Basic] The name first decides who oversees it. In Korea, "가상자산" calls in supervision and investigation by the Financial Services Commission (Articles 13 and 14 of the Virtual Asset User Protection Act) and reporting to the head of the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit (금융정보분석원장) (Article 7 of the Specified Financial Transaction Information Act), while "전자등록주식등" ("electronically registered stocks, etc.") takes the thing outside that Act and over to the capital markets side. In the EU, "crypto-asset" calls in the competent authorities of the Member States (MiCA Art. 93) and, for significant asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens, the European Banking Authority (EBA) (Art. 117), while a "financial instrument" is outside MiCA. In Japan, 「暗号資産」 calls in registration with the Prime Minister (内閣総理大臣) (in practice the Financial Services Agency, 金融庁) under 資金決済法 第63条の2, and 「電子記録移転権利」 calls in 金商法. In the United Kingdom, "qualifying cryptoasset" calls in the FCA's regulated activities from 2027. In the United States the agencies choose the name: a "security" means the SEC, a "commodity" means the CFTC, and the 2018 decision called the two "concurrent."16 In Chapter 26, Terra is a case in which the SEC brought charges on the basis that it was a "security" and obtained a jury verdict, and The DAO is a case in which the SEC found a "security" and took no enforcement action. The "market without an operator" that the AMM of Chapter 15 and the MEV of Chapter 17 showed is a gap in jurisdiction, in that none of these names has an addressee there (28.1(e)), and the express exclusion of participation in liquidity pools from "digital asset service provider" in §2(7) of the GENIUS Act shows that the legislature knew about that gap.

Taxation

[Basic] Next, the name decides as what the thing is taxed. In 2014 the IRS decided to treat "virtual currency" as "property," so the general principles for property transactions (the difference between the acquisition price and the transfer price) apply, and because it is not "currency," the framework of foreign currency gain or loss does not come in (Q&A-2).17 Had the name been "currency," other provisions would have come in. EU value added tax read it the other way, toward "currency." In 2015 the Court of Justice of the European Union said that bitcoin has "no purpose other than to be a means of payment" and is not "tangible property," and it placed the exchange of bitcoin for traditional currencies under the exemption for transactions concerning "currency, bank notes and coins used as legal tender" (Art. 135(1)(e)). The judgment treated the exchange as a supply of services (operative part 1) and decided whether that supply was exempt.18 Korea made "가상자산소득" (gasang jasan sodeuk, "virtual asset income") one subparagraph of "기타소득" (gita sodeuk, "other income") (Income Tax Act, Article 21(1), subparagraph 27), and that provision is not yet in force. The same bit string is property in the United States, a means of payment for EU value added tax, and (once the provision is in force) a source of other income in Korea. Technology chose none of the three.

Criminal law

[Basic] Finally, the name decides of which offense the thing can be the object. The Supreme Court of Korea called bitcoin a "재산상 이익" (Supreme Court of Korea, 2021Do9855, November 11, 2021), so it can be the object of fraud, but the Court did not decide whether it is a "재물." The Court also held that punishing a person who received a transfer without legal cause for breach of trust, by analogy to the case law on mistaken remittances and on the basis of the principle of good faith, would, "명문의 규정이 없는 현재의 상황에서" (working gloss, not an official translation; the original controls: "in the present situation, in which there is no express provision"), violate the principle of legality in criminal law (Supreme Court of Korea, 2020Do9789, December 16, 2021).19 In confiscation, under the name "재산적 가치가 있는 무형의 재산" (gloss: "intangible property having proprietary value"), it became subject to confiscation under the Act on Regulation and Punishment of Criminal Proceeds Concealment (범죄수익은닉의 규제 및 처벌 등에 관한 법률) (Supreme Court of Korea, 2018Do3619, May 30, 2018). The same thing fills the places of fraud and confiscation under two names, "재산상 이익" and "무형재산" (muhyeong jaesan, "intangible property"). In the place of breach of trust, without any decision on whether it is a "재물," the conviction was reversed on the ground that the defendant was not "타인의 사무를 처리하는 자" (gloss: "a person who administers another's business"), and the embezzlement part was reversed and remanded along with it on the ground that the two were one and the same. The criminal judgments in Japan's Mt.Gox case show a different shape. The first-instance judgment (2019) came before the statute was renamed to 「暗号資産」 and so wrote 「仮想通貨」, while the appellate judgment (2020) came after the renaming and wrote 「暗号資産（仮想通貨）」.20 And the offenses the two judgments found proven were not offenses with bitcoin as their object but 私電磁的記録不正作出·同供用 (gloss: "unauthorized creation of private electromagnetic records, and use of such records"), whose object is the electronic records of the exchange's books. On the embezzlement of users' money the defendant was acquitted, on the ground that 「利用者が…送金した金銭は，Ｂ社に帰属する」 (gloss: "the money that users … remitted belongs to Company B") (Chapter 26). What the court fixed there was not the name of bitcoin but a criterion of existence, 「ブロックチェーン上に存在しないビットコインは…架空のビットコイン」 (gloss: "bitcoins that do not exist on the blockchain … fictitious bitcoins"), and that criterion came from the technical fact of Part 1: bitcoin exists only as a state recorded on a blockchain. The two US criminal judgments (Chapter 26) had "wire fraud," "securities fraud conspiracy" and "commodities fraud conspiracy" as counts, and "commodities fraud" and "securities fraud" standing side by side in one indictment is the criminal-law face of the fact that in the United States the same thing carries two names at once.21

5. Three cases in which the name changed within one jurisdiction

[Basic] Names differ between jurisdictions, and they have also changed within a single jurisdiction. Three cases have been confirmed in the original texts.

Jurisdiction Before After Document that made the change What changed
Japan 「仮想通貨」 (資金決済法 第2条第5項, version of 2020-04-30) 「暗号資産」 (version of 2020-05-01; now 第14項) 令和元年法律第28号 (promulgated 2019-06-07, in force 2020-05-01) The proviso excluding 電子記録移転権利 came in together with the defined term. The word "currency" (通貨) dropped out of the name
Korea (Supreme Court) "이른바 '가상화폐'의 일종" (Supreme Court of Korea, 2018Do3619, May 30, 2018) "가상자산의 일종" (2021Do9855, November 11, 2021); "가상자산은 … 재산상 이익" (2020Do9789, December 16, 2021) In between, Act No. 17113 amending the Specified Financial Transaction Information Act (in force March 25, 2021) brought "가상자산" in as a statutory term The judgments' word changed. The judgments do not say that the framework of decision (intangible property having proprietary value / pecuniary advantage) changed because of it
United States (IRS) "it does not have legal tender status in any jurisdiction" (Notice 2014-21, 2014) "the use of virtual currency to perform 'real' currency functions is limited" (Notice 2023-34, 2023) Notice 2023-34 §3 Only the background statement was revised; the conclusion "property" (Q&A-1 and 2) was left as it was

[Basic] None of the three happened because the technology changed. Bitcoin's protocol underwent no change between 2019, 2021 and 2023 that would call for a new name. What changed was where law decided to place it, and that decision was written into the name. This is what the one line the design set down for this chapter, "technology does not choose the name," means.

A lawyer's question

What does a lawyer do when a definitional provision cannot keep up with the technology? Does the (contract address, number) pair of ERC-721 fall within the "전자적 증표" ("electronic token") of Article 2, subparagraph 1 of Korea's Virtual Asset User Protection Act? The EU and the United Kingdom expressly left out what is "non-fungible," and in Korea Article 2, subparagraph 4 of the Enforcement Decree leaves it out but has a proviso that brings back in what the Financial Services Commission designates by notice (e.g., tokens "지급수단으로 사용될 수 있는," "that can be used as a means of payment"). How does that proviso apply to ERC-721? Under "발행인이 사용처와 그 용도를 제한한 것" (gloss: "one whose places of use and purposes have been restricted by the issuer") (item (a)), what happens to a token that has no "발행인" ("issuer")? Under "전자적으로 거래 또는 이전될 수 있는" (gloss: "that can be traded or transferred electronically"), is a balance on an exchange's books (the 300,000 BTC that were not on the chain, Chapter 26) an "이전될 수 있는 전자적 증표" (gloss: "an electronic token that can be transferred"), or a claim against the issuer (the exchange)? How is the Japanese provision's 「不特定の者を相手方として購入及び売却を行うことができる」 (gloss: "can be bought and sold with unspecified persons as counterparties") to be read for an AMM (Chapter 15), where there is no counterparty? Is this a gap to be filled by analogy, a void that legislation must fill, or a signal to accept the fact that the definitional provision does not determine the nature of the thing, and to go back to the discussion of its nature in 27.2? This book does not answer; it points to the map of scholarly positions in Part 5. → Chapter 27

6. Summary

[Basic] Set the definitional provisions of the five jurisdictions side by side and you see a common skeleton (a digital representation of value and electronic transferability) and exclusion lists that diverge. All of them keep currency outside, but at different levels; all of them draw a boundary with securities, but in different ways; and three of them leave out non-fungible tokens, but at different levels. The name decides jurisdiction (who oversees it), taxation (as what it is taxed) and criminal law (of which offense it is the object), and it has changed even within a single jurisdiction. None of those names is contained in the bit strings, signatures, state transitions and equilibria that this book showed in Parts 1 to 3. What a lawyer takes from this chapter is the habit of looking at two things together when reading a name. One is in which provision of which law the name is written and from when it has been in force; the other is what that provision left out. The concordance in Appendix C compresses this chapter into rows and columns, and the survey table in 27.3 records the agencies and procedures behind the names. Read the three on top of one another and you can see which questions are left empty in which jurisdiction.

Appendices

Appendix B. Common misconceptions: a verdict table

[Basic] Twelve statements often heard about blockchains are set out in four columns: verdict / why it looks that way / the actual structure / chapters. There are three verdicts: Holds (the statement is true as it stands), Holds in part (one piece of the statement is true and another is false, so it is wrong if used as it stands) and Does not hold (the statement is not true). The "actual structure" column carries over verbatim, or summarizes, sentences that the relevant chapter wrote after checking the originals, and the original sources are in that chapter's footnotes. This table adds no new material. A verdict of "Does not hold" does not mean that the opposite statement is true. It means that the statement cannot be used as it stands.

# Statement Verdict Why it looks that way The actual structure Chapters
① A blockchain cannot be tampered with Holds in part Change one character in a past block and every block after it falls out of line, so it feels as though "it cannot be altered." Introductory phrases such as "an immutable ledger" reinforce the feeling Tampering shows when compared with a hash and chain kept on record (hash chain), but the hash chain itself does not tell which of two histories is the original, and "shows" is not the same as "is prevented." A hash chain without proof of work can be re-threaded entirely at one hash per block (Chapter 7, NB07-1), and even with proof of work tampering is not impossible but a cost. Chapter 7: "The immutability of a blockchain is not a mathematical impossibility but an economic cost." That cost grows the further back the block lies, but it is finite, and once the share q exceeds 1/2, "is prevented" no longer holds (Chapter 9) 7·8·9
② Smart contracts are contracts Holds in part The word "contract" is the name of a data type in the code, and the explanation that "the code performs automatically" sounds like the performance of a contract On the technical side: the ten-line "contract" read in Chapter 13 "had no parties and no agreement"; it is a program that releases value when conditions are met. On the legal side: the primary source whose original this book checked (SEC Release No. 81207, 2017-07-25, p. 2) says only that "The automation of certain functions through this technology, 'smart contracts,' or computer code, does not remove conduct from the purview of the U.S. federal securities laws," and does not say whether code is a contract (28.1(c)). Code can be a means of performing a contract; whether it is a contract is decided outside the code. "Is the content of the contract the code or the intention?" is an open question in the box in Chapter 13 13·28.1(c)
③ Bitcoin is a Ponzi scheme Holds in part The pattern in which earlier entrants profit from the money of later entrants overlaps with trading on the secondary market, and the fact that the price rests on belief reads as a whiff of fraud What the economics of Chapter 19 showed is a listing of equilibria: "An outside money with no dividend has both a zero-price equilibrium and positive-price equilibria, and the positive-price equilibria are held up by the belief that 'others will accept it' and are not pinned down to one." In the language of that literature, the value of fiat money itself is a "bubble" (a defined term), not a term of abuse. The same literature (van Oordt 2024, in the advanced box of Chapter 19) writes that "Investors who participate in a bubble equilibrium for a cryptocurrency with non-negative money growth experience Ponzi-scheme equivalent payoffs in the aggregate": one piece of the statement is true inside the model. The other piece is different. The issuance rules shown in Chapter 22 are written in code, and the design "resembles a company's articles but has no enforcer"; there is no operator that promises returns, raises funds and controls payments. What the jury found in the Terra case of Chapter 26 was a violation of the antifraud provisions of the securities laws, and the statements came not from the protocol but from the issuer on top of it. Whether the price went through recurring speculative phases is a statistical question for Chapter 25 and a separate one 19·22·25·26
④ Bitcoin encrypts nothing Holds The name "cryptocurrency" gives the impression that the content of transactions is encrypted, so this statement is not a misconception but one that corrects a misconception Chapter 5: "Bitcoin's transactions and ledger are not encrypted." What is used is hashes (Chapter 4) and signatures (Chapter 5), not encryption. Every transaction is public (Chapters 1 and 11), and Chapter 12 read every byte of the genesis block as it stands. The scope, however, is "transactions and ledger" 4·5·12
⑤ When quantum computers arrive, Bitcoin is finished Holds in part It is true that Shor's algorithm breaks signatures, and that fact slides into "all of Bitcoin collapses" What breaks is the signatures (coins whose public keys are exposed); hashes and proof of work withstand Grover's square-root speedup (Chapter 29, Section 1). By a secondary tally on the reference date, exposed coins of all types together come to about 1/3 of the supply, the firmest figure among them being the roughly 1.7 million BTC in P2PK (close to 9% of the total), and coins that are not exposed can also become targets while a spending transaction is out and waiting for confirmation; that window runs from a few minutes to a few hours and is not fixed (Chapter 29, Section 3). Post-quantum signature standards (FIPS 204 and 205) were published in 2024, but Bitcoin's transition proposals (BIP-360 and 361) are Drafts as of 2026-10 and have not been activated on either of the two mainnets (Chapter 29, Section 4; Appendix A-27). The problem is not "finished" but the transition and the handling of the coins left behind, and that handling is a question not of technology but of governance and law (Chapter 29, Section 5) 29
⑥ Faster computers will break the blockchain Does not hold The hash rate has grown by nearly fourteen orders of magnitude since 2009 (Chapter 8, NB08-3), which reads as "someday it will all be broken" Chapter 8: "Mining is a lottery, not a puzzle, and even when machines get faster the winning interval is brought back to 10 minutes": difficulty is adjusted every 2,016 blocks. Chapter 8: the probability that the attacker finds the next block is the share q, and "Even if the total hash rate grows 10-fold, this probability stays the same as long as q is the same, and because difficulty adjustment brings the block interval back to 10 minutes, the shape of 'the race counted in blocks' also stays the same"; Chapter 9: the probability of a successful chase is a function of q and the number of confirmations z alone. The variable that breaks it is not absolute speed but share. The security of the hash function itself (preimage, collision) is a matter of the algorithm, not of speed (Chapter 4), and quantum speedup is taken up separately in ⑤ 4·8·9
⑦ "6 confirmations" means final Does not hold Exchanges and wallets wait for 6 confirmations and then show "completed," so it looks like a rule Chapter 9: "'6 confirmations' is a convention, not a rule." The probability of reversal falls exponentially in z but never becomes 0, and at q≥1/2 it does not fall. The white paper's formula is optimistic, and the exact formula requires more confirmations for the same level of safety (6 rather than 5 at q=0.1, and 32 rather than 24 at q=0.3). There is no moment of "done," only a probability that gets smaller; where this fails to line up with the legal concepts of "performance" and "completion" is taken up in 28.1(c) 9·28.1(c)
⑧ Blockchains are anonymous Does not hold An address is a string, not a person's name, so it reads as "no one knows who it is" Every transaction is public (Chapter 1: "transactions must be publicly announced"; Chapter 12 read every byte of the genesis block). Chapter 11: "In the UTXO model, privacy comes not from 'addresses being anonymous' but from 'the habit of switching addresses,' and that habit is broken by input merging and change patterns." It is not anonymous but pseudonymous, and §10 of the white paper itself writes "Some linking is still unavoidable with multi-input transactions …." The fact that there are output types in which the public key appears on the chain as it is (Chapter 29, Section 3) is evidence from the opposite side 1·11·12
⑨ Code is law Holds in part Smart contracts run as written and no one can stop them midway, so "the code is the rule" seems right Chapter 16: "'Code is law' holds inside the chain, and whether a condition is true comes in from outside it." Even if an oracle feeds in a wrong value, the code does not deviate by a single line. Chapter 26 (The DAO): "The contract code was executed as written and betrayed its author's intention, and what reversed it was not code but the coordination of people": a majority took back, by a software update, a result the code had allowed. And the primary source writes that "The automation of certain functions through this technology, 'smart contracts,' or computer code, does not remove conduct from the purview of the U.S. federal securities laws" (SEC Release No. 81207, 2017-07-25, p. 2; 28.1(c)). True as a rule of execution inside the chain, false as a norm that keeps the law outside the chain from applying 16·26·28.1(c)
⑩ Proof of stake is a structure in which the rich get richer Holds in part Validators are chosen in proportion to their stake and rewarded in proportion too, so "those who have more get more" Chapter 10: proportionality itself does not widen the ratio of the gap (NB10-1: if everyone grows at the same rate, the ratio stays the same). But the compounding of restaking rewards, economies of scale in running nodes, and the threshold of a 32 ETH minimum stake can work against small participants, and in proof of work, too, economies of scale in equipment and power work in the same direction. "Which system is more concentrated is a matter for measurement, and this book does not give those figures." Hence Holds in part 10
⑪ Stablecoins are stable Does not hold The name promises "stability," and the price stays near USD 1 for long stretches Chapter 24: "A stablecoin is a token that carries a promise of redemption, and so it belongs not to the economics of outside money but to the economics of banking." "'Stability' is a property not of the price but of the balance sheet and the procedure." The collateral ratio is a measure of solvency and the redeemable ratio a measure of liquidity, and a run starts from the second; there is no deposit insurance and there is a secondary market, so closing the window does not stop a run. The two episodes of May 2022 (algorithmic) and March 2023 (fiat-collateralized) differ in structure, and this book does not say which coin is safe. Since the name does not guarantee stability, the statement as it stands does not hold 24·26
⑫ If it is decentralized, no one is responsible Does not hold On a network with no company and no representative, "whom do we hold responsible?" seems to have no answer Having no responsible party is different from the responsible party being invisible (Chapter 23: a selfish miner can hide). Chapter 17: "the one who makes the block sets the order," and the rollups of Chapter 18 have someone who "decides the order" (the sequencer) and upgrade powers. Chapter 22: the record of governance tokens and The DAO is that majority voting, curators and splits were written in code but "there is no enforcer"; yet whoever holds the multisignature keys is "the de facto enforcer." Primary sources: the SEC (Release No. 81207, 2017-07-25) called The DAO "an unincorporated organization" and held it to be an issuer of securities, and the Court of Appeal of England and Wales (Tulip Trading Ltd v van der Laan [2023] EWCA Civ 83, 2023-02-03) held that whether Bitcoin developers owe fiduciary duties to holders is "a serious issue to be tried" (28.1(g)). It is not that no one is responsible; who, in which position, is still open 17·18·22·23·28.1(g)

[Basic] Of the twelve statements, one holds (④), five do not hold (⑥, ⑦, ⑧, ⑪, ⑫) and six hold in part (①, ②, ③, ⑤, ⑨, ⑩). There are many "in part" verdicts because these statements usually carry one true technical fact over to a false conclusion: tampering shows (true) → cannot be tampered with (false); signatures break (true) → Bitcoin is finished (false); code runs as written (true) → code is law (false). What a lawyer should take from this table is less the verdicts themselves than the habit of sorting out which piece is true. When a party argues in litigation that "a blockchain cannot be tampered with, so this record is authentic," reading the true piece (tampering shows) apart from the false piece (impossible) is the starting point of 28.1(f).

Sources

  • The "actual structure" in each row is carried over from the text, summaries and code output of the relevant chapter, and its original sources (the Nakamoto white paper, FIPS 180-4, Haber and Stornetta, Eyal and Sirer, Diamond and Dybvig, the SEC's 2017 report, Tulip Trading, BIP-360 and 361, Aggarwal et al., Babbush et al., and others) are in the footnotes of each chapter. This appendix adds no new material.
  • The verdict framework is a reader's version, cut down to four columns, of the hypothesis verdict table from the research round before writing (five columns: "verdict / key evidence / evidence hierarchy / counter-evidence / observations that would change the verdict"). The verdicts of that round were used only for reference, and all the evidence was checked again against the chapters of the text and their original sources.
  • There are no price, market capitalization or return data in any row.

E.1 The Merkle–Damgård construction: chaining compression functions

[Advanced] Chapter 4 showed that FIPS 180-4 describes SHA-256 in two stages, preprocessing (padding, splitting into blocks, initial values) and hash computation (updating the state value block by block, the stage this appendix calls the compression function; FIPS 180-4 itself does not use the term),1 and NB04-5 printed the intermediate values of that state as it passes from block to block. That design principle has a name: the Merkle–Damgård construction. The two people in the name each presented a paper at the same conference in 1989 (CRYPTO '89), Damgård's "A design principle for hash functions" and Merkle's "One-way hash functions and DES," and references [5] and [16] of Haber and Stornetta (1991) list the two.2 This book did not open the originals of those two papers, so the construction itself is described in the words of a textbook draft whose original this book did open. Narayanan et al. write: "Recall that we require that our hash functions work on inputs of arbitrary length. Luckily, as long as we can build a hash function that works on fixed‐length inputs, there's a generic method to convert it into a hash function that works on arbitrary‐length inputs. It's called the Merkle‐Damgard transform. SHA‐256 is one of a number of commonly used hash functions that make use of this method. In common terminology, the underlying fixed‐length collision‐resistant hash function is called the compression function. It has been proven that if the underlying compression function is collision resistant, then the overall hash function is collision resistant as well."3

[Advanced] In symbols the construction is as follows. There is a compression function f:{0,1}n×{0,1}b→{0,1}n: it takes an n-bit state and a b-bit block and outputs an n-bit state. For SHA-256, n=256 and b=512. Append padding bits and the length to the message M, cut it into b-bit blocks M(1),…,M(N), start from a fixed initial value H(0) and repeat

H(i)=f(H(i−1),M(i)),i=1,…,N

then take the last H(N) as the output. Reading the symbols: H(i) is the state value after the first i blocks have been taken in, and f is the 64-round compression function of NB04-5 in Chapter 4. A numerical example: when a two-block message was fed in in Chapter 4, the H(1) and H(2) that NB04-5 printed are exactly the two steps of this formula, and H(2) was equal to the value from hashlib.sha256.

[Advanced] Why collision resistance carries over can be shown by a short backtracking argument. Suppose two different messages M≠M′ produce the same output. If their lengths differ, the last blocks (the blocks holding the length) differ, so at the last step f(H(N−1),M(N))=f(H′(N′−1),M′(N′)) the inputs differ while the outputs are equal, which is at once a collision of the compression function. If their lengths are the same, they have the same number of blocks, and we go back from the last step to find the first step at which the inputs part. At any step where (H(i−1),M(i))≠(H′(i−1),M′(i)) but H(i)=H′(i), that is a collision of the compression function. Since the messages differ, such a step must exist. So "one collision of the whole function" mechanically gives "one collision of the compression function," and if the compression function is collision resistant, so is the whole. Putting the length into the padding (the reason the preprocessing of FIPS 180-4 appends the 64-bit message length) supports the first branch of this argument.

[Advanced] Narayanan et al. point out one more thing: "You may have noticed that the block chain construction is similar to the Merkle‐Damgard construction that we saw in the previous section. Indeed, they are quite similar, and the same security argument applies to both of them."4 The chain of Chapter 7, in which each block holds the hash of the previous block header, has the same shape, "the state value passes to the next step," and what Narayanan et al. say goes as far as this: thanks to that shape, the same security argument (a collision of the final hash reduces to a collision of some block) applies to both. Chapter 7's observation that changing a block in the middle puts everything after it out of line is a result of that argument, not the argument itself. As Chapter 7 showed, however, that shape alone makes "re-threading" free; what makes it expensive is the proof of work of Chapter 8.

확률적 최종성 probabilistic finality The property that there is no moment of "done," only a probability of reversal that gets smaller 9
도박꾼의 파산 gambler's ruin The probability model that §11 of the white paper uses for the attacker's chance of catching up 9
이기적 채굴 selfish mining A strategy of withholding blocks and then releasing them to increase one's share 23
지분증명 proof of stake Consensus that makes blocks through stake and voting 10

슬래싱 slashing The penalty of cutting the stake of a validator who breaks the rules 10
UTXO unspent transaction output A transaction output not yet spent: the unit of state in Bitcoin 11

스마트계약 smart contract A program on the chain that releases value when conditions are met 13

상수곱·슬리피지·비영구 손실 constant product / slippage / impermanent loss The AMM's formula, the worsening of the price with the size of the order, and the profit-and-loss structure of a liquidity provider 15
유동성 공급자 liquidity provider A participant who puts two tokens into a pool and receives fees 15
오라클 oracle A device that brings facts from outside the chain into it 16
최대 추출 가능 가치 MEV, maximum extractable value (formerly miner extractable value) Value extracted from the power to decide the order, inclusion and exclusion of transactions 17
선행매매·후행매매·샌드위치 front-running / back-running / sandwich Trading strategies that exploit order 17

보안 예산 security budget The flow cost that honest participants spend on security, funded by rewards 20

거버넌스 토큰·DAO governance token / decentralized autonomous organization A token that carries voting rights, and an organization written in code 22
스테이블코인 stablecoin A token with a redemption promise attached: fiat-collateralized, crypto-overcollateralized, algorithmic, synthetic 24

F.3 List of notebooks

[Basic] Colab notebooks that carry over the Python code of the text unchanged. The outputs are exactly the results of the editor's runs in Python 3.13 (conda environment bcbook), and the "Output" blocks in the text came from the same runs. There is no installation cell, and no external API is called. Cells that need the bundled data read the snapshots in data/, and if a file is missing they substitute constants with the same values. All the code is for study: do not use it with real assets, real private keys or real transactions.

Notice

This book is an academic self-study guide. It was written for studying the technology and economics of blockchains, and it does not recommend buying, selling or holding any particular crypto-asset, token or financial product. No sentence in this book should be read as an investment solicitation, investment advice or a price outlook.

The names of exchanges, projects and tokens in this book are used only to describe settled historical facts and are not recommendations or comparative evaluations. Every figure carries a reference date and a source and may have changed since. The code is meant to show principles and was not built to handle real assets. Do not use the code or the explanations in this book to manage real assets.

The editor is a sitting judge, but this book is the editor's personal study record and is unrelated to the views of the institution the editor belongs to. On ongoing cases and pending bills, it states only the facts and makes no evaluation. This book is not legal advice.
